concepts.title: Corner Camera
concepts.one_liner: A corner camera is an imaging system that uses intensity variations on the ground to reconstruct scenes hidden behind a vertical edge.
concepts.content: A corner camera is a real-world example of a general imager. As shown in (see figure: objects hidden behind a corner), a vertical edge partially blocks a scene from view, creating intensity variations on the ground. These variations are observable by viewing the ground from around the corner. Objects hidden behind the corner, such as the cylinders labeled A and B, cause very small intensity differences in the ambient illumination falling on the ground. The spatial mask is then multiplied by the observed reflected ground image as shown in (see figure: spatial mask multiplication).
concepts.motivation_md: The corner camera demonstrates how subtle environmental cues, like shadows and intensity variations on the ground, can be used to 'see' around obstacles and reconstruct hidden scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a vertical edge to create intensity variations on the ground from hidden objects.

key_passage.text: This is similar to the edge camera, but with slightly more complicated geometry. A vertical edge partially blocks a scene from view, creating intensity variations on the ground, observable by viewing those intensity variations from around the corner.

motivation.text: Objects, such as the cylinders labeled A and B, hidden behind a corner from a camera nonetheless cause very small intensity differences in the ambient illumination falling on the ground.

concepts.title: Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The spectrum is the decomposition of white light into its constituent colors.
concepts.content: Newton understood that white light could be decomposed into different colors and invented the term spectrum.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of the spectrum explains how white light is not a single entity but a mixture of various colors that can be separated and studied.
concepts.recap_md: - Refers to the decomposition of white light into different colors.

key_passage.text: Newton understood that white light could be decomposed into different colors and invented the term spectrum.

concepts.title: Diffraction
concepts.one_liner: Diffraction separates light into spectral components through the constructive interference of scattered light in different directions for different wavelengths.
concepts.content: Diffraction is a way to separate light into its spectral components. It occurs when constructive interference of scattered light happens in different directions for different wavelengths of light.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffraction provides a physical mechanism for separating light by wavelength, which is essential for spectroscopy and understanding the wave nature of light.
concepts.recap_md: - Separates light into spectral components via constructive interference.

key_passage.text: diffraction, where constructive interference of scattered light occurs in different directions for different wavelengths of light

motivation.text: A second way to separate light into its spectral components is through diffraction

concepts.title: Power Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The power spectrum is the light intensity measured at each wavelength.
concepts.content: The light intensity at each wavelength is called the power spectrum of the light. The color appearance of light is determined by this distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: The power spectrum quantifies how much energy light carries at different wavelengths, which is the physical basis for how we perceive color.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents light intensity as a function of wavelength.

key_passage.text: The light intensity at each wavelength is called the power spectrum of the light.

concepts.title: Reflectance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ describes how a surface scales incident light at each wavelength.
concepts.content: The reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of a surface describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how surfaces reflect different wavelengths allows us to model and predict the color of objects under various lighting conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - Denoted as $s(\lambda)$, it characterizes how a surface reflects light across the spectrum.

key_passage.text: incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and a reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of the surface

concepts.title: Transmittance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The transmittance spectrum of an attenuating filter defines the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling applied to incident light passing through it.
concepts.content: The transmittance spectrum of an attenuating filter describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of light. In this model, the incident power spectrum is multiplied at each wavelength by the transmittance spectrum of the filter. This scaling is similar to the diffuse reflection model, where a proportionality constant $k$ depends on the reflection geometry, characterizing most matte reflections.
concepts.motivation_md: The transmittance spectrum allows us to calculate how filters or semi-transparent materials modify the color and intensity of light passing through them.
concepts.recap_md: - Multiplies the incident power spectrum at each wavelength to determine transmitted light.

key_passage.text: The incident power spectrum is then multiplied at each wavelength by the transmittance spectrum of the attenuating filter.

motivation.text: Such wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is also a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter.

concepts.title: Fovea
concepts.one_liner: The fovea is a region of the eye where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.content: The fovea is a region of the eye characterized by a specific sampling pattern of photoreceptors. Near the fovea, there are no rods, and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.motivation_md: The fovea is the center of the eye's visual field and is responsible for sharp, detailed central vision due to its high density of cones.
concepts.recap_md: - Contains no rods and has a high density of close-packed cones.

key_passage.text: This sampling pattern was measured from near the fovea, where there are no rods, and the cones are close-packed.

concepts.title: Linearity and Transitivity of Color Matching
concepts.one_liner: The appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors due to the three classes of photoreceptors in the eye.
concepts.content: Human color matching performance can be inferred from the spectral sensitivity curves of eye receptors. Experimentation has shown that the appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors. This phenomenon is due to the presence of three classes of photoreceptors in our eyes. Furthermore, these color matches are transitive: if color A matches a specific combination of primaries and color B matches that same combination, then color A will match color B. As a result, the amount of each primary required to match a color serves as a set of coordinates for that color.
concepts.motivation_md: Linearity and transitivity in color matching provide the mathematical foundation for color spaces and the ability to reproduce colors using just three primary sources.
concepts.recap_md: - Any color can be represented as a linear combination of three primary colors.

key_passage.text: Through experimentation, it has been discovered that the appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors. It has also been found that these color matches are transitive—if color A matches a particular combination of primaries and color B matches the same combination of primaries, then color A will match color B.

motivation.text: This is due to the presence of three classes of photoreceptors in our eyes. Consequently, the amount of each primary required to match a color can serve as a set of coordinates indicating color.

concepts.title: Computer vision as a scientific quest
concepts.one_liner: Computer vision is an interdisciplinary scientific quest focused on understanding how natural intelligence and perception works.
concepts.content: Computer vision has become an exciting and fast-evolving area of research. It is important to understand the field within the scientific context of broader inquiry. Computer vision is not just an engineering discipline that tries to build systems that see; instead, it is another aspect of the interdisciplinary scientific quest focused on understanding how natural intelligence and perception works.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept frames computer vision not merely as a tool for building machines, but as a fundamental scientific endeavor to decode the principles of biological perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Computer vision is an interdisciplinary field beyond simple engineering.

key_passage.text: Computer vision is not just an engineering discipline that tries to build systems that see. Instead computer vision is another aspect of the interdisciplinary scientific quest that has focused on understanding how natural intelligence and perception works.

motivation.text: We believe it is important to understand the field of computer vision within the scientific context that has been laid out in the previous sections.

concepts.title: Learning-based vs model-based vision
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based approaches rely on flexible architectures and data to build models for perception rather than starting with fixed hypotheses.
concepts.content: While many previous perspectives on perception began with models about how perception might work, learning-based approaches take a different path. They rely on flexible architectures that incorporate as few hypotheses about perception as possible, and instead focus on data to learn to build the right model for perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional model-based approaches often fail when the underlying assumptions are wrong; learning-based methods allow the system to discover the structure of perception directly from data.
concepts.recap_md: - Model-based vision starts with hypotheses about how perception works.

key_passage.text: They rely on flexible architectures that incorporate as few hypothesis about perception as possible, and instead focus on data to learn to build the right model for perception.

motivation.text: While many previous perspectives on perception began with models about how perception might work, learning-based approaches take a different path.

concepts.title: Empiricism vs rationalism in vision
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision is rooted in empiricism, the philosophical tradition holding that knowledge is acquired through experience and data.
concepts.content: Learning-based vision has its roots in the philosophical tradition of empiricism, which holds that knowledge about the world should be acquired by experience, rather than solely through reason (an approach known as rationalism). The modern-day term for experience is "data," and learning is really all about data.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the philosophical roots of vision helps distinguish between systems built on human logic (rationalism) and those built on observed evidence (empiricism).
concepts.recap_md: - Empiricism emphasizes knowledge through experience or data.

key_passage.text: Learning-based vision has its roots in the philosophical tradition of empiricism, which holds that knowledge about the world should be acquired by experience, rather than solely through reason (an approach known as rationalism).

motivation.text: The modern day term for experience is "data," and learning is really all about data.

concepts.title: Programming vs learning algorithms
concepts.one_liner: Learning derives vision algorithms by fitting functions to data rather than writing explicit code or deriving rules from world models.
concepts.content: Learning derives vision algorithms by fitting functions to data. There are a few ways to "program" a vision algorithm (@fig-taxonomy-programming_vs_learning). One way is to write the algorithm directly in Python code, such as comparing pixel intensities and setting thresholds. Another approach is to derive the algorithm as the rational thing to do given an underlying model of the world; for example, detecting boundaries by looking for contrast edges produced by overlapping objects. The third approach—the learning approach—is to program algorithms via data: first collect examples of inputs and correct outputs, then fit a function that replicates these mappings.
concepts.motivation_md: Explicitly programming every visual rule is often impossible due to the complexity of the real world; learning from data provides a scalable alternative.
concepts.recap_md: - Algorithms can be written directly, derived from models, or learned from data.

key_passage.text: One way is to write the algorithm directly in Python code: first we will compare the intensity of this pixel and that pixel, then we will threshold about some such value, and so on. Another approach is to derive the algorithm as the rational thing to do given some underlying model of the world, for example, because overlapping objects generically produce contrast edges in the image, the optimal way to detect boundaries between objects is to look for such and such particular kind of contrast. The third approach --- the learning approach --- is to program algorithms via data: first collect a bunch of examples of inputs and the correct output, then fit a function that replicates these exemplar mappings from input to output.

motivation.text: Learning derives vision algorithms by fitting functions to data. One way to think about it is that our goal is to "program" a vision algorithm and there are a few ways to do so.

concepts.title: Perceptron learning algorithm
concepts.one_liner: The perceptron is a formal learning algorithm and early artificial neural net capable of recognizing simple visual patterns.
concepts.content: Learning algorithms have been a part of computer vision since the field's origins. In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt published one of the first formal learning algorithms, called the **perceptron** learning algorithm, and showed that it can, in principle, learn to recognize certain simple visual patterns. The perceptron was also one of the first artificial neural nets, a computational model of biological brains. The ability of perceptrons to learn to solve recognition problems created an explosion of interest in neural nets. Rosenblatt published the algorithm in the journal Psychological Review, illustrating the interdisciplinary nature of early AI.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron was the first attempt to model biological intelligence computationally to solve pattern recognition tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - The perceptron was one of the first formal learning algorithms and artificial neural nets.

key_passage.text: In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt published one of the first formal learning algorithms, called the perceptron learning algorithm, and showed that it can, in principle, learn to recognize certain simple visual patterns. The perceptron was also one of the first artificial neural nets, a computational model of biological brains.

motivation.text: The ability of perceptrons to learn to solve recognition problems created an explosion of interest in neural nets.

concepts.title: Cycles of interest in neural networks
concepts.one_liner: Interest in neural networks has fluctuated over time, notably declining after proofs showed the limitations of simple perceptrons.
concepts.content: Interest in neural nets has gone through a series of ebbs and flows (@fig-taxonomy-neural_net_enthusiam). These cycles have partially lined up with interest in learning algorithms generally, though there were phases where interest in neural nets was low while other learning algorithms remained popular. In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published *Perceptrons: an introduction to computational geometry*. Although it was an introduction, the book largely killed excitement by showing that perceptrons are incapable of learning basic logical operations, leading to the conclusion that they could not be the basis of intelligence.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the history of AI helps researchers recognize that current trends are part of longer cycles of optimism and skepticism.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural network popularity has historically moved in cycles of roughly 25 years.

key_passage.text: Interest in neural nets has since gone through a series of ebbs and flows. Note that these cycles have partially lined up with interest in learning algorithms more generally, but there have also been phases where interest in neural nets was low but interest in other learning algorithms was high.

question.text: What will happen next?

motivation.text: These cycles have partially lined up with interest in learning algorithms more generally, but there have also been phases where interest in neural nets was low but interest in other learning algorithms was high.

concepts.title: Deep learning
concepts.one_liner: Deep learning systems are modern neural networks built by stacking perceptrons to perform complex operations.
concepts.content: It wasn't until the 1980s that interest in learning algorithms, and neural nets in particular, began to surge again. The reason was because researchers showed that perceptrons could be stacked to create systems capable of complex operations, including logic. These systems were the precursors to the **deep learning** systems that are dominant today.
concepts.motivation_md: Deep learning overcomes the limitations of simple perceptrons by using multiple layers to represent complex hierarchical information.
concepts.recap_md: - Deep learning evolved from stacking perceptrons to handle complex logic.

key_passage.text: researchers showed that perceptrons could be stacked to create systems capable of complex operations, including logic. These systems were the precursors to the deep learning systems that are dominate today.

motivation.text: It wasn't until the 1980s that interest in learning algorithms, and neural nets in particular, began to surge again. The reason was because researchers showed that perceptrons could be stacked to create systems capable of complex operations, including logic.

concepts.title: Neocognitron
concepts.one_liner: The Neocognitron is a vision-specific architecture introduced by Kunihiko Fukushima as a precursor to modern convolutional neural networks.
concepts.content: In the 1980s, several architectures specific to vision were introduced, including Kunihiko Fukushima's Neocognitron, which was a precursor to modern convolutional neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: The Neocognitron was an early attempt to build a neural architecture specifically designed for the spatial challenges of visual data.
concepts.recap_md: - The Neocognitron was a foundational precursor to modern CNNs.

key_passage.text: Kunihiko Fukushima's, which was a precursor to modern convolutional neural networks

concepts.title: Law of closure
concepts.one_liner: When a line forms a closed figure, we do not simply see a line, we see a shape.
concepts.content: The Law of closure describes the fact that when a line forms a closed figure, we do not simply see a line, but rather a shape. This principle can even override proximity cues; for example, vertical lines that are physically closer to one another may still be grouped into separate shapes if the spatial arrangement suggests closed figures.
concepts.motivation_md: This law explains how the visual system prioritizes the perception of complete objects and shapes over fragmented or disconnected lines.
concepts.recap_md:
- Closed figures are perceived as unified shapes rather than individual lines.
 - The tendency toward closure can override other grouping cues like proximity.

key_passage.text: when a line forms a closed figure, we do not simply see a line, we see a shape.

motivation.text: We are very familiar with the fact that when a line forms a closed figure, we do not simply see a line, we see a shape.

concepts.title: Law of good continuation
concepts.one_liner: Lines that follow each other pointing in the same direction are likely to be grouped together.
concepts.content:
The Law of good continuation states that edges are likely to be smooth. Lines that follow each other pointing in the same direction are likely to be grouped together. For instance, an X-shape is perceived as two lines that cross each other instead of perceiving it as a V-shape on top of an inverted V.

Law of good continuation. The following shape:

[FIGURE:c51ef5b010d31b05 | ]

has two possible groupings:

[FIGURE:734850c366ad5501 | ]

The law of good continuation says that the one on the left is the one an observer perceives (although we just see an X and not two lines crossing each other...).
concepts.motivation_md: This principle helps the visual system resolve ambiguity in intersecting lines by assuming they continue along their established path.
concepts.recap_md:
- The visual system prefers smooth paths and continuous lines over abrupt changes in direction.
 - Intersecting lines are typically perceived as crossing rather than meeting and turning.

key_passage.text: Lines that follow each other pointing in the same direction are likely to be grouped together.

motivation.text: An X-shape is perceived as two lines that cross each other instead of perceiving it as a V-shape on top of an inverted V.

concepts.title: Laws of parallelism and symmetry
concepts.one_liner: Parallelism and symmetry act as grouping cues that induce clustering between visual elements.
concepts.content: The Laws of parallelism and symmetry are grouping cues with different strengths that induce clustering between visual elements.
concepts.motivation_md: These laws identify specific geometric relationships that the brain uses to organize complex visual scenes into related groups.
concepts.recap_md:
- Parallel elements tend to be grouped together.
 - Symmetrical arrangements are perceived as belonging to the same structure or object.

key_passage.text: There are many other grouping cues with different strengths that induce clustering between visual elements.

concepts.title: Common fate
concepts.one_liner: When two elements have a common motion, they tend to group together.
concepts.content: Common fate is a very important grouping cue based on motion. When two elements share a common motion—such as the same acceleration, direction, or rate of change—they tend to be perceived as a group.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion is a powerful indicator that separate elements belong to the same object, helping us track moving entities in a dynamic environment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Elements moving in the same direction at the same speed are grouped together.
 - Common motion (fate) is a primary cue for perceptual organization in dynamic scenes.

key_passage.text: Motion is a very important grouping cue. When two elements have a common motion (accelerations, direction, rate of change) they tend to group together.

concepts.title: Past experience in grouping
concepts.one_liner: Items grouped in the past are more likely to be perceived as a group in the future.
concepts.content: Past experience influences perceptual organization: items that have been grouped together in the past are more likely to be perceived as a group in the future.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle accounts for how learning and memory influence our current perception of the world.
concepts.recap_md:
- Prior exposure to specific groupings biases future visual interpretation.
 - Memory plays a role in how we organize visual stimuli.

key_passage.text: Items grouped in the past are more likely to be perceived as a group in the future.

concepts.title: Lightness perception
concepts.one_liner: Lightness is the visual system's attempt to extract reflectance based on the luminances in the scene.
concepts.content: Lightness is a perceptual quantity influenced by both the perceived reflectance and the perceived illumination of a surface. Adelson defines lightness as "the visual system's attempt to extract reflectance based on the luminances in the scene."
concepts.motivation_md: The visual system must distinguish between the inherent color of an object (reflectance) and the light falling on it (illumination) to perceive the world accurately.
concepts.recap_md:
- Lightness is a perceptual measure, not just a physical one.
 - It depends on the interaction between surface reflectance and environmental illumination.

key_passage.text: Lightness is a perceptual quantity that is influenced by both the perceived reflectance and the perceived illumination of a surface. Adelson defines lightness as "the visual system's attempt to extract reflectance based on the luminances in the scene."

motivation.text: Gestalists also studied the problem of lightness perception.

concepts.title: Koffka ring illusion
concepts.one_liner: The Koffka ring is an illusion illustrating how perceptual grouping and context influence lightness perception.
concepts.content: The Koffka ring is an illusion introduced by Kurt Koffka to illustrate the power of perceptual grouping in lightness perception. In this display, a ring of uniform gray is shown. Depending on the spatial configuration, the lightness of the ring's two sides can appear very different, even though they have the same gray level. For example, splitting the ring into two halves with white space makes the sides look different. This experiment demonstrates that lightness perception is not a local process but involves considering the context and principles of grouping.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion proves that our perception of an object's brightness is not just determined by the light hitting a single point on the retina, but by the surrounding context.
concepts.recap_md:
- Identical gray levels can appear different based on spatial configuration.
 - Lightness perception is a global process influenced by grouping and context.

key_passage.text: In each display, the two sides of the ring have the same gray level. Depending on the spatial configuration of the two sides, their lightnesses appear very different.

motivation.text: One can conclude from this experiment that lightness perception is not a local process and that it involves considering the context and the principles of grouping.

concepts.title: Amodal completion
concepts.one_liner: Amodal completion is the phenomenon of perceiving a whole object when only a part is visible.
concepts.content: Amodal completion is the visual phenomenon of perceiving a whole object even when it is partially occluded. For example, if a red square is placed on top of a blue square, we still see the blue shape as a complete square despite the occlusion. If a gap is introduced that breaks the illusion of occlusion, the perception of the whole object is lost. The term "amodal" refers to perception occurring without direct perceptual modality for the hidden parts. This is a process we use constantly to extend objects behind occlusions in everyday scenes.
concepts.motivation_md: Because most objects in the real world are partially hidden by other objects, amodal completion allows us to maintain a stable perception of whole entities.
concepts.recap_md:
- We perceive complete objects even when parts are hidden by occluders.
 - This process is essential for navigating and understanding 3D environments.

key_passage.text: This phenomenon of perceiving a whole object when only a part is visible is called amodal completion. The word amodal means that we have perception without using any direct perceptual modality.

motivation.text: Another striking proof of the importance of perceptual organization is the visual phenomenon of amodal completion. Amodal completion is something we do all the time when we explore a scene.

concepts.title: Backpropagation
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation is an efficient method for training neural networks, famously demonstrated by Yann LeCun et al. in 1989 for handwritten digit recognition.
concepts.content: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. showed how neural networks can be efficiently trained using backpropagation. Their system was successfully put into practical use by the US Postal Service for the task of recognizing handwritten digits.
concepts.motivation_md: Backpropagation was developed to provide a computationally efficient way to train multi-layer neural networks, moving them from theoretical models to practical tools for pattern recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation allows for the efficient training of neural network architectures.

key_passage.text: Yann LeCun et al. showed how these kinds of networks can be efficiently trained and their system was put into use for recognizing handwritten digits by the US Postal Service.

concepts.title: Parallel Distributed Processing (PDP)
concepts.one_liner: Parallel Distributed Processing (PDP) integrated neuroscience with computational models of distributed processing in artificial networks.
concepts.content:
One of the peaks of neural network research in the 1980s was the publication of *Parallel Distributed Processing* by David Rumelhart and Jay McClelland. This book mixed the neuroscience of the brain with computational models of distributed processing in artificial networks.

[FIGURE:a3cfb172cb1c2c7f | Rumelhart86 cover]
concepts.motivation_md: The PDP framework aimed to bridge the gap between biological brain function and artificial computational models, advocating for distributed rather than centralized processing.
concepts.recap_md: - PDP combines neuroscience insights with artificial network models.

key_passage.text: This book mixed the neuroscience of the brain with computational models of distributed processing in artificial networks.

motivation.text: One of the peaks of neural network research in the 1980s was the publication of by David Rumelhart and Jay McClelland.

concepts.title: Boosting
concepts.one_liner: Boosting is a simple learning algorithm used to create efficient and high-performing detectors, such as the Viola-Jones face detector.
concepts.content: In 2001, Paul Viola and Michael Jones published a method that used a simple learning algorithm called boosting to detect faces in photos. This method outperformed the complicated hand-engineered face detectors of the time in terms of computational efficiency and detection rate, and it eventually became a popular algorithm used in consumer cameras.
concepts.motivation_md: Boosting was used to overcome the limitations of hand-engineered features by automatically selecting and combining simple classifiers to achieve high accuracy and speed.
concepts.recap_md: - Boosting is a learning algorithm that can outperform complex hand-engineered systems.

key_passage.text: Paul Viola and Michael Jones published a method that used a simple learning algorithm called boosting to detect faces in photos.

motivation.text: This method outperformed the complicated hand-engineered face detectors of the time in terms of computational efficiency and detection rate, and even became a popular algorithm used in consumer cameras.

concepts.title: End-to-end learning and the ImageNet Moment
concepts.one_liner: End-to-end learning replaces manual pipelines with a single system that learns every processing stage from input pixels to output predictions.
concepts.content: End-to-end learning refers to a system where each processing stage, from the input pixels to the output predictions, is handled by learned modules rather than a manual pipeline. In 2012, a deep neural net called AlexNet dramatically outperformed all existing methods for image classification using this approach. This event, known as the "ImageNet Moment," was a watershed for learning-based vision. In the years following 2012, learning became the key ingredient in almost all computer vision research, and by the 2020s, deep learning is present in nearly every vision system pipeline.
concepts.motivation_md: End-to-end learning removes the need for human-designed feature engineering, allowing the system to optimize all stages of processing simultaneously for better performance.
concepts.recap_md: - End-to-end systems learn all stages from raw input to final prediction.

key_passage.text: Finally, in 2012, a deep neural net called AlexNet dramatically outperformed all existing methods for image classification, and did so with a system that used learning end-to-end (for each processing stage from the input pixels to the output predictions). This event has come to be called the "ImageNet Moment" since AlexNet's dramatic performance was first demonstrated at the 2012 ImageNet competition.

motivation.text: The ImageNet moment was a watershed for learning-based vision and for neural networks. In the few years after 2012, learning became the key ingredient in almost all research on computer vision.

concepts.title: Learning as a search for mapping
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision treats the development of vision algorithms as an automated search for the mapping between input and output.
concepts.content: Learning-based vision is similar to traditional approaches in that it studies the structure of input, the structure of output, and the mapping between the two. The primary difference is how that mapping is found. In this sense, learners act as a new kind of vision scientist, playing the same role as humans who previously determined how vision works through deep thought. While machine learners often arrive at similar algorithms as those designed by humans, they are more powerful and have far exceeded human-designed algorithms in raw performance.
concepts.motivation_md: By framing vision as a search for a mapping, researchers can use computational power to discover complex algorithms that are too difficult for humans to design manually.
concepts.recap_md: - Learning-based vision automates the discovery of the mapping between input and output.

key_passage.text: The big difference with learning-based vision is how you *find* the mapping. In this sense, learners are just like a new kind of vision scientist: they play the same role as the humans who, in previous eras, sat down and thought deeply to determine the way vision works.

motivation.text: The study of vision consists of the structure of the input, the structure of the output, and the mapping between the two. Learning-based vision does not fundamentally change any of these: the input and target output are the same as before, and the mapping is remarkably similar as in other approaches.

concepts.title: Future Directions in Vision Theories
concepts.one_liner: Future vision theories may address currently missing elements like visual common sense, multi-perceptual integration, and embodied perception.
concepts.content: From ancient Greek extramission theories to modern neural mechanisms and computer vision, our understanding of perception has evolved significantly. However, many elements are still missing from current theories. These include visual common sense (currently being addressed by large language models), the integration of vision with other perceptual systems, and a theory of embodied perception. There may be many other necessary steps for a complete theory of vision that remain currently unrecognized.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying gaps in current vision theories helps guide future research toward more holistic and human-like artificial perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Current vision theories lack visual common sense and embodied perception.

key_passage.text: For instance, we are missing visual common sense (now powered by large language models), integration with other perceptual systems, and, most importantly, a theory of embodied perception.

question.text: What theories will come next? What is missing now?

motivation.text: In a span of more than 2000 years, from the Greeks' extramission theories of vision to the understanding of the neural mechanisms and the engineering of computer vision systems, we have come a long way in our understanding of the nature of perception. Each step during the evolution of vision theories revealed important aspects of perception ignored by the previous theories.

concepts.title: Interdisciplinary Perspective on Computer Vision
concepts.one_liner: Studying computer vision from an interdisciplinary perspective provides a solid basis for creativity, technical depth, and understanding societal impact.
concepts.content: Computer vision is best understood by placing it within its historical context. An interdisciplinary perspective on the field benefits researchers by providing a solid basis for creativity and technical depth. Furthermore, this approach helps in understanding the societal impact of vision technologies.
concepts.motivation_md: An interdisciplinary approach prevents narrow technical focus and encourages well-rounded innovation by drawing on history, social science, and other fields.
concepts.recap_md: - Interdisciplinary study fosters creativity and technical depth in vision research.

key_passage.text: We believe that any researcher of computer vision would benefit by studying vision from an interdisciplinary perspective as it will provide a solid basis for creativity, technical depth, and an understanding of its societal impact.

motivation.text: We believe that any researcher of computer vision would benefit by studying vision from an interdisciplinary perspective as it will provide a solid basis for creativity, technical depth, and an understanding of its societal impact.

concepts.title: The 1966 Summer Vision Project
concepts.one_liner: The 1966 Summer Vision Project was an optimistic attempt at MIT to construct a significant part of a visual system in a single summer.
concepts.content: In 1966, Seymour Papert wrote a proposal for the "Summer Vision Project" at MIT. The goal was to use summer workers to construct a significant part of a visual system, dividing tasks among a group of students. This project reflected the intense optimism of the early days of computer vision, though the task of building such a system proved to be much harder than the researchers initially expected.
concepts.motivation_md: The project represents the early belief that vision was a relatively simple problem that could be solved quickly with basic task decomposition.
concepts.recap_md: - The 1966 Summer Vision Project aimed to build a vision system in a few months.

key_passage.text: In 1966, Seymour Papert wrote a proposal for building a vision system as a summer project. The abstract of the proposal starts by stating a simple goal: "The summer vision project is an attempt to use our summer workers effectively in the construction of a significant part of a visual system."

motivation.text: This project was a reflection of the optimism existing in the early days of computer vision. However, the task proved to be harder than anybody expected.

concepts.title: Extramission theory
concepts.one_liner: Extramission theory posits that vision occurs because the eye emits rays, like fingers sensing the world, composed of internal fire.
concepts.content:
Extramission theory, originating with Empedocles and followed by Plato and Euclid, provided one of the first theories of vision. Empedocles introduced the idea that all things are composed of four elements: fire, earth, air, and water. He claimed the eye contained these elements and that fire was responsible for creating rays that emanated from the eyes, functioning like fingers that sensed the world. This theory explained why some eyes, particularly those of cats, appeared to shine at night; it was assumed they contained so much fire that it became visible. While we now know this shine is reflected light, the theory was a logical attempt to explain vision without a modern understanding of light and reflection.

[FIGURE:5c6343e2e1c26338 | The extramission theory attributed the glow observed in cat eyes to the presence of fire inside them.]
concepts.motivation_md: This theory was an early attempt to explain the mechanism of sight and the phenomenon of eyes shining in the dark before the principles of light reflection were understood.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is caused by rays of fire emanating from the eye to sense the external world.

key_passage.text: Empedocles (approx. 494--434 BC) provided one the first theories of vision in his poem "On Nature", and introduced many other influential ideas such that all things are composed or four elements: fire, earth, air, and water. He said that the eye contained the four elements and that the fire was responsible of creating rays that emanated from the eyes, like fingers that sensed the world.

motivation.text: The extramission theory explained why sometimes eyes shined at night, in particular cat's eyes, which were assumed to contain so much fire that even humans could see it occasionally.

concepts.title: Plato's theory of vision
concepts.one_liner: Plato proposed that vision results from the coalescence of internal fire flowing from the eye with external light from the environment.
concepts.content: Plato's theory of vision combined elements of both intromission and extramission. He described the eyes as organs contrived to give light, where a pure, internal fire flows through the eye in a smooth, dense stream. When the light of day surrounds this stream of vision, the internal and external light coalesce to form a single body along the line of vision. This combined stream diffuses the motions of whatever it touches back to the soul, creating the perception of sight. At night, the stream of vision is cut off and extinguished because the external fire is absent. Plato notably considered vision less reliable than touch because it could only sense the side of an object facing the observer.
concepts.motivation_md: Plato sought to explain how the human soul interacts with the physical world through a medium (light) that shares a common nature with internal human elements.
concepts.recap_md: - Sight occurs when internal fire from the eye meets and merges with external daylight.

key_passage.text: And the pure fire which is within us and related thereto they made to flow through the eyes in a stream smooth and dense, compressing the whole eye, and especially the centre part, so that it kept out everything of a coarser nature, and allowed to pass only this pure element. When the light of day surrounds the stream of vision, then like falls upon like, and they coalesce, and one body is formed by natural affinity in the line of vision, wherever the light that falls from within meets with an external object.

motivation.text: Plato's theory of vision was very influential. Plato's theory contained both intromission and extramission elements.

concepts.title: Aristotle's critique of extramission
concepts.one_liner: Aristotle critiqued extramission by arguing that the eyes lack internal fire and that rays could not possibly reach distant stars.
concepts.content: Aristotle was critical of the extramission theory, pointing out that stars were too far away for rays from the eyes to reach them. He suggested that only certain objects, such as fire, are light sources, while other objects merely reflect rays that hit the eyes. Aristotle also rejected the belief that the eye contained internal fire, arguing instead that the element of perception must be water, as vision requires a transparent medium.
concepts.motivation_md: Aristotle used logical observation and the concept of transparency to challenge the physical plausibility of eyes emitting light over vast distances.
concepts.recap_md: - Objects are seen either because they are light sources or because they reflect light.

key_passage.text: Aristotle (384--322 BC), Plato's student, was critical of the extramission theory and pointed out that the stars were too far away for rays from the eyes to reach them (an argument also used by Euclid). Aristotle went further and suggested that only some objects are light sources (e.g., fire) and the other objects reflect the rays that hit the eyes.

motivation.text: Aristotle was critical of the extramission theory and pointed out that the stars were too far away for rays from the eyes to reach them. He also criticized the belief that the eye had fire inside.

concepts.title: Euclid's mathematical theory of vision
concepts.one_liner: Euclid established the first mathematical theory of vision by modeling light as rays traveling in straight lines forming a visual cone.
concepts.content:
Euclid provided the first mathematical theory of vision, describing how rays emitted by the eye travel in straight lines. These rays form a cone with its apex at the eye and its base at the boundaries of the observed scene.

[FIGURE:7036504f93c79364 | Modeling light as traveling along straight lines was a major discovery. This simple model of light sets the foundation upon which image formation, scene geometry, and computer vision rests.]
concepts.motivation_md: Euclid aimed to apply geometric principles to the phenomenon of sight, creating a foundation for understanding perspective and image formation.
concepts.recap_md: - Light is modeled as traveling along straight lines.

key_passage.text: Euclid (325 BC), a Greek mathematician, provided the first mathematical theory of vision, giving a mathematical description of how the emitted rays by the eye traveled on straight lines and formed a cone that reached the scene.

motivation.text: Modeling light as traveling along straight lines was a major discovery. This simple model of light sets the foundation upon which image formation, scene geometry, and computer vision rests.

concepts.title: Euclid's axioms of light
concepts.one_liner: Euclid's seven axioms of light define the geometric relationship between the eye, visual angles, and the perception of objects.
concepts.motivation_md: These axioms provide a formal framework to explain why objects appear at certain sizes and positions based on the geometry of the visual cone.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is contained within a cone with the eye at the apex.

key_passage.text: Let it be assumed that lines draw directly from the eye pass through a space of great extent; and that the form of the space included within our vision is a cone, with its apex in the eye and its base at the limits of our vision; and that those things upon which vision falls are seen, and that those things upon which vision does not fall are not seen.

concepts.title: Perspective
concepts.one_liner: Perspective is the technique of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface, rooted in Euclid's geometric discoveries.
concepts.content: Euclid's work set the basis of perspective. His discoveries regarding the straight-line travel of light and the visual cone influenced thinkers and artists in the centuries that followed.
concepts.motivation_md: Perspective allows for the accurate representation of spatial relationships and depth in art and technical drawings.
concepts.recap_md: - Euclid's geometric theories provided the foundation for the study of perspective.

key_passage.text: Euclid's work set the basis of perspective, and his discoveries influenced thinkers and artists in the following centuries.

concepts.title: Law of reflection
concepts.one_liner: The law of reflection states that light follows the shortest path between points, resulting in the angle of incidence equaling the angle of departure.
concepts.content: The law of reflection describes how light follows the shortest path between two points. This principle dictates that the angle of incidence is the same as the angle of departure.
concepts.motivation_md: This law explains how light behaves when it strikes a surface, which is essential for understanding mirrors and image formation.
concepts.recap_md: - The angle of incidence equals the angle of departure.

key_passage.text: light will follow the shortest path between two points, which means that the angle of incidence is the same as the angle of departure

concepts.title: Refraction
concepts.one_liner: Refraction is the phenomenon where light changes direction when passing from one medium to another, such as from air to water.
concepts.content: Refraction describes how light changes direction when changing medium, for example, when passing from air to water. This phenomenon was described by Ptolemy.
concepts.motivation_md: Refraction explains why objects appear distorted when viewed through different materials and is the basis for lens design.
concepts.recap_md: - Light changes direction when it moves between different media.

key_passage.text: how light changed direction (i.e., refraction) when changing medium (e.g., from air to water).

concepts.title: Ibn al-Haytham's scientific method in optics
concepts.one_liner: Hasan Ibn al-Haytham transformed optics into a scientific discipline by demonstrating that light rays bounce off objects and enter the eye to create vision.
concepts.content:
In the late tenth century, Hasan Ibn al-Haytham's work transformed initial Greek theories into a true scientific discipline. Ibn al-Haytham (965–1040 AD), known as Alhacen in the Latin world, published the Book of Optics between 1028 and 1038, a work considered by many to be the beginning of the scientific method. In this book, Ibn al-Haytham describes how light rays bounce off objects in all directions and that the rays only become visible when they reach the eye perpendicularly. He described the pinhole camera and invented the camera obscura.

(see figure: Alhacen's diagram of the eyes and the optic nerve (), drawn around the year 1027. It is one of the first drawings of the visual system. *Source*: MS Fatih 3212, vol. 1, fol. 81b, Süleimaniye Mosque...)

Ibn al-Haytham rejected the extramission theory, arguing that sight could be explained by light rays emitted by objects rather than rays emitted by the eye. His work built upon Ptolemy, Euclid, Galen, and Aristotle. While Ptolemy believed distance could be measured by a single eye feeling the length of a light ray, Ibn al-Haytham showed experimentally that both eyes were needed to perceive depth.
concepts.motivation_md: Ibn al-Haytham sought to replace speculative Greek theories of vision with an experimental framework, establishing the modern understanding that vision is the result of external light entering the eye.
concepts.recap_md: - He established the scientific method in optics by rejecting the theory that eyes emit rays.

key_passage.text: In his Book of Optics, Ibn al-Haytham describes how light rays bounce of objects in all directions and that the rays only become visible when they reach the eye perpendicularly. He described the pinhole camera and invented the camera obscura. Ibn al-Haytham rejected the extramission theory. He argued that sight could be explained by the light rays emitted by objects and that it was not necessary to assume that the eye emitted rays.

motivation.text: In the late tenth century Hasan Ibn al-Haytham's work transformed the initial Greek theories into a true scientific discipline, inspiring many of the works that followed, even through Johannes Kepler. This book is considered by many the beginning of the scientific method.

concepts.title: Camera obscura
concepts.one_liner: The camera obscura is an optical device invented by Ibn al-Haytham that projects an image of its surroundings onto a screen.
concepts.content: Ibn al-Haytham described the pinhole camera and invented the camera obscura.
concepts.motivation_md: The camera obscura was developed to demonstrate how light travels in straight lines and can project images through a small aperture, serving as a fundamental model for the eye.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a foundational optical invention by Ibn al-Haytham.

key_passage.text: He described the pinhole camera and invented the camera obscura.

concepts.title: Kepler's theory of retinal image formation
concepts.one_liner: Johannes Kepler provided the first complete description of how the crystalline lens focuses a reversed image onto the retina.
concepts.content: Kepler (1604 AD), building on Alhacen's work, provided the first complete description of how images are formed in the retina. Kepler understood lenses and how the eye projected a reverse picture into the retina. He understood the role of the crystalline lens as the focusing element of images in the eye, in contrast with previous theories that believed the crystalline lens was the sensitive element selecting only the perpendicular rays that reached the eye.
concepts.motivation_md: Kepler aimed to correct misconceptions about the crystalline lens, shifting its role from a sensor to a focusing element that forms a physical image on the retina.
concepts.recap_md: - He identified the retina as the surface where images are formed.

key_passage.text: Kepler understood lenses and how the eye projected a reverse picture into the retina. Kepler understood the role of the crystalline lens as the focusing element of images in the eye, in contrast with previous theories that believed that the crystalline lens was the sensitive element selecting only the perpendicular rays that reached the eye.

motivation.text: Kepler (1604 AD), building on Alhacen's work, provided the first complete description of how images are formed in the retina.

concepts.title: Lenses in the eye
concepts.one_liner: In the eye, the crystalline lens acts as a focusing element that projects a reversed image onto the retina.
concepts.content: Kepler understood lenses and how the eye projected a reverse picture into the retina. He understood the role of the crystalline lens as the focusing element of images in the eye, in contrast with previous theories that believed that the crystalline lens was the sensitive element selecting only the perpendicular rays that reached the eye.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the lens is crucial for explaining how the eye resolves light from the environment into a clear, focused image on the neural tissue of the retina.
concepts.recap_md: - The crystalline lens functions as a focusing element rather than a sensitive receptor.

key_passage.text: Kepler understood the role of the crystalline lens as the focusing element of images in the eye, in contrast with previous theories that believed that the crystalline lens was the sensitive element selecting only the perpendicular rays that reached the eye.

motivation.text: Kepler understood lenses and how the eye projected a reverse picture into the retina.

concepts.title: Trichromacy theory
concepts.one_liner: Trichromacy is the theory that the eye contains three classes of receptors, each sensitive to different wavelengths of light.
concepts.content:
The theory of trichromacy, codeveloped by Thomas Young, states that the eye has three classes of receptors, each sensitive to different wavelengths of light.

[FIGURE:4c0eccf5247e3f61 | ]
concepts.motivation_md: Trichromacy explains how the human visual system perceives a full spectrum of colors using only three types of color-sensitive cells.
concepts.recap_md: - The eye uses three distinct receptor types to process color information.

key_passage.text: the eye has three classes of receptors, each sensitive to different wavelengths of light

concepts.title: Ophthalmascope
concepts.one_liner: The ophthalmoscope is an instrument developed by Helmholtz to observe the human retina using collinear viewing and illumination.
concepts.content:
Helmholtz developed the ophthalmoscope, an instrument to observe the retina of the human eye. The key of the ophthalmoscope was to see the need for collinear viewing and illumination directions. The glass plates along the diagonal, labeled $a$ in the figure, allow for viewing the eye under study by the ophthalmologist while reflecting illumination from a light source into the eye. Helmholtz's drawings from the ophthalmoscope show blood vessels and branches of the retinal artery and vein over the optic nerve.

(see figure: Hermann von Helmholtz invented the ophthalmoscope at age 29. Images from @Helmholtz1925)
concepts.motivation_md: Before the ophthalmoscope, doctors could not see the interior of a living eye; Helmholtz solved this by aligning the light source with the observer's line of sight.
concepts.recap_md: - It enables direct observation of the retina and optic nerve.

key_passage.text: He also developed the ophthalmascope, shown in an instrument to observe the retina of the human eye. The key of the ophthalmascope was to see the need for colinear viewing and illumination directions.

motivation.text: The key of the ophthalmascope was to see the need for colinear viewing and illumination directions.

concepts.title: Perception as inference
concepts.one_liner: Perception is the process by which the mind finds the most likely representation of an object to explain sensory input.
concepts.content: Helmholtz was an important theorist in visual perception. He proposed that the general rule determining the ideas of vision is that objects are imagined as being present in the field of vision as would have to be there in order to produce the same impression on the nervous mechanism under ordinary conditions. Thus, the mind makes perceptions out of sensations, finding representations of the object most likely to explain the sensory input. This viewpoint relates to Bayesian methods for computer vision inference.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why vision is not just a passive recording of light, but an active mental construction that attempts to make sense of ambiguous sensory data.
concepts.recap_md: - The mind infers the most likely cause of sensory impressions.

key_passage.text: The mind makes perceptions out of sensations, finding representations of the object most likely to explain the sensory input.

motivation.text: This viewpoint relates to Bayesian methods for computer vision inference.

concepts.title: Bayesian methods in vision
concepts.one_liner: Bayesian methods in vision are computational frameworks that treat perception as a statistical inference problem.
concepts.content: This viewpoint relates to Bayesian methods for computer vision inference.
concepts.motivation_md: Bayesian methods provide a mathematical framework for the idea of 'perception as inference,' allowing computers to model the probability of different objects being present based on image data.
concepts.recap_md: - They relate visual perception to statistical inference techniques.

key_passage.text: This viewpoint relates to Bayesian methods for computer vision inference.

concepts.title: Supervised Learning
concepts.one_liner: Supervised learning is the process of observing example input-output behavior to infer a functional mapping that explains that behavior.
concepts.content:
Learning from examples is also called supervised learning. In this context, we are learning an algorithm, which is a computable mapping from inputs to outputs. A formal definition of an example is an {`input`, `output`} pair. For instance, a set of examples might consist of pairs such as:

$$\begin{aligned}
    &\{\texttt{input:} [2,3], \texttt{output:} 36\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} [7,1], \texttt{output:} 49\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} [5,2], \texttt{output:} 100\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} [2,2], \texttt{output:}16\}\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$

This kind of learning, where you observe example input-output behavior and infer a functional mapping that explains this behavior, is called supervised learning. Another name for this kind of learning is fitting a model to data.
concepts.motivation_md: Supervised learning allows us to automate decision-making by training algorithms on historical data where the correct answers are already known, enabling the model to predict outputs for new, unseen inputs.
concepts.recap_md: - Supervised learning involves inferring a functional mapping from provided input-output pairs.

key_passage.text: This kind of learning, where you observe example input-output behavior and infer a functional mapping that explains this behavior, is called **supervised learning**.

motivation.text: Learning from examples is also called **supervised learning**. Another name for this kind of learning is **fitting a model** to data.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Learning
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised learning involves finding useful representations or models of input data without being provided target outputs.
concepts.content: In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of input data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ but we are not told the target outputs $\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$. Instead, the learner has to come up with a model or representation of the input data that has useful properties, as measured by some objective function. The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: When labeled data is unavailable or expensive to obtain, unsupervised learning helps discover hidden patterns, structures, or efficient representations within raw data.
concepts.recap_md: - The learner is provided with input data but no corresponding target labels.

key_passage.text: In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of input data {x^(i)}_i=1^N but we are not told the target outputs {y^(i)}_i=1^N. Instead the learner has to come up with a model or representation of the input data that has useful properties, as measured by some objective function.

motivation.text: The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs.

concepts.title: Reinforcement Learning
concepts.one_liner: Reinforcement learning is a framework where a learner seeks to maximize a reward function that measures the quality of its outputs.
concepts.content: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a reward function that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output. To be precise, a reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores: $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The learner tries to come up with a function that maximizes rewards. This kind of learning is becoming an important part of computer vision, especially in the context of vision for robots.
concepts.motivation_md: Reinforcement learning is essential for agents that must learn to make a sequence of decisions in an environment to achieve a goal, guided only by occasional feedback or rewards.
concepts.recap_md: - A reward function $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ maps outputs to numerical scores.

key_passage.text: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a reward function that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output. To be precise, a reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores: r: Y → ℝ. The learner tries to come up with a function that maximizes rewards.

motivation.text: This kind of learning is becoming an important part of computer vision, especially in the context of vision for robots.

concepts.title: Key Ingredients of Learning
concepts.one_liner: A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients: an objective, a hypothesis space, and an optimizer.
concepts.content:
A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients:

1. Objective: What does it mean for the learner to succeed, or, at least, to perform well?
2. Hypothesis Space: What is the set of possible mappings from inputs to outputs that we will search over?
3. Optimizer: How, exactly, do we search the hypothesis space for a specific mapping that maximizes the objective?

These three ingredients, when applied to large amounts of data and run on sufficient hardware (referred to as compute), can do amazing things. A learner outputs an algorithm, $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, which maps inputs, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$, to outputs, $\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}$.

[FIGURE:606f041122e8e0fc | A learner outputs an algorithm f mapping inputs to outputs.]
concepts.motivation_md: Breaking down learning into these three components provides a structured framework for designing and analyzing any machine learning system.
concepts.recap_md: - The objective defines success, the hypothesis space defines possible models, and the optimizer defines the search method.

key_passage.text: A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients: What does it mean for the learner to succeed, or, at least, to perform well? What is the set of possible mappings from inputs to outputs that we will we search over? How, exactly, do we search the hypothesis space for a specific mapping that maximizes the objective?

motivation.text: These three ingredients, when applied to large amounts of data, and run on sufficient hardware (referred to as compute) can do amazing things.

concepts.title: Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: A loss function is an objective that scores model outputs or compares them to target answers, typically to be minimized.
concepts.content: The objective that the learner optimizes is typically a function that scores model outputs, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or compares model outputs to target answers, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. We will interchangeably call this $\mathcal{L}$ either the objective function, the loss function, or the loss. A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to minimize, whereas an objective function can be used to describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.
concepts.motivation_md: Loss functions provide a mathematical way to quantify the error of a model, giving the optimizer a clear signal on how to improve the learned function.
concepts.recap_md: - A loss function $\mathcal{L}$ measures the discrepancy between model outputs and targets.

key_passage.text: The objective that the learner optimizes is typically a function that scores model outputs, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or compares model outputs to target answers, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. We will interchangeably call this $\mathcal{L}$ either the objective function, the loss function, or the loss.

motivation.text: A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to minimize, whereas an objective function can be used to describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.

concepts.title: Learned Function
concepts.one_liner: The learned function is the specific mapping from inputs to outputs produced by a learning algorithm.
concepts.content: Commonly, $f$ is referred to as the learned function.
concepts.motivation_md: The learned function is the final product of the learning process, used to make predictions on new data.
concepts.recap_md: - The symbol $f$ is commonly used to denote the function produced by the learner.

key_passage.text: $f$ is referred to as the **learned function**.

concepts.title: Importance of Parameterization
concepts.one_liner: To fully define a learning algorithm, one must specify both the hypothesis space and how that space is parameterized.
concepts.content: The hypothesis space can be described by a set $\mathcal{F}$ of all the possible functions under consideration by the learner. For example, one hypothesis space might be "all mappings from $\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$" and another could be "all functions $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ that satisfy the conditions of being a distance metric." Commonly, however, we will not just specify the hypothesis space, but also how we parameterize the space. For example, we may say that our parameterized hypothesis space is $y = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$, where $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ are the parameters. Another choice could be $y = \theta_2\theta_1 x + \theta_0$, with parameters $\theta_0$, $\theta_1$, and $\theta_2$. These two choices parameterize exactly the same space, meaning any affine function can be represented by either and both can only represent affine functions. However, these two parameterizations are not equivalent because optimizers and objectives may treat different parameterizations differently. Because of this, to fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.
concepts.motivation_md: Different parameterizations of the same set of functions can significantly affect how easily an optimizer can find the best solution.
concepts.recap_md: - The hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all functions the learner considers.

key_passage.text: Commonly, however, we will not just specify the hypothesis space, but also how we parameterize the space. For example, we may say that our parameterized hypothesis space is y = θ₁ x + θ₀, where θ₀ and θ₁ are the parameters. These two choices parameterize exactly the same space, that is, any affine functions can be represented by either parameterization and both parameterizations can only represent affine functions. However, these two parameterizations are not equivalent, because optimizers and objectives may treat different parameterizations differently.

motivation.text: Because of this, to fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.

concepts.title: Overparameterization
concepts.one_liner: Overparameterized models use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data.
concepts.content: Overparameterized models, where you use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data, are especially important in modern computer vision; most neural networks are overparameterized.
concepts.motivation_md: In modern deep learning, using more parameters than data points often leads to better generalization and easier optimization, contrary to classical statistical intuition.
concepts.recap_md: - Overparameterization involves using more parameters than the minimum required to fit a dataset.

key_passage.text: Overparameterized models, where you use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data, are especially important in modern computer vision; most neural networks are overparameterized.

motivation.text: Overparameterized models, where you use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data, are especially important in modern computer vision

concepts.title: Width
concepts.one_liner: The number of neurons on a single hidden layer is called its width.
concepts.content: If you have a hidden layer with $N$ neurons, you can fit a scalar function with $\mathcal{O}(N)$ bumps. The number of neurons on a single hidden layer is called its width. If different layers have different numbers of neurons, then we may specify the width per layer. Here we will assume all layers have the same width and simply speak of the width of the network.
concepts.motivation_md: Width is a fundamental hyperparameter of neural networks that determines the capacity of a single layer to represent complex patterns or 'bumps' in a function.
concepts.recap_md:
- Width refers to the number of neurons in a specific hidden layer.
- Increasing width allows a network to fit more complicated functions with more features.

key_passage.text: The number of neurons on a single hidden layer is called its width.

motivation.text: Above we saw that if you have a hidden layer with N neurons, you can fit a scalar function with O(N) bumps.

concepts.title: Depth
concepts.one_liner: The depth of a network is defined as its number of layers.
concepts.content: As we increase the width of a network, we can fit ever more complicated functions. Another way to increase the capacity of the net is to increase the depth of a network, which is its number of layers. Its effect on capacity is a bit different than increasing width.
concepts.motivation_md: Depth allows neural networks to learn hierarchical representations, where deeper layers build upon the features extracted by earlier layers.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth is the total number of layers in a neural network.
- Increasing depth is an effective way to increase the functional capacity of a model.

key_passage.text: What if we instead increase the depth of a network, that is, its number of layers? It turns out that this can also be an effective way to increase the capacity of the net, but its effect is a bit different than increasing width.

question.text: What if we instead increase the depth of a network, that is, its number of layers?

motivation.text: It turns out that this can also be an effective way to increase the capacity of the net, but its effect is a bit different than increasing width.

concepts.title: Depth separations
concepts.one_liner: Depth separations describe cases where deep nets require far fewer parameters than wide nets to represent certain functions.
concepts.content: Interestingly, it is sometimes the case that deep nets require far fewer parameters to fit data than wide nets. Evidence for this statement comes mostly from empiricism, where researchers have found that deeper nets just work better in practice on many popular problems. However, there is also the beginning of a mathematical theory of when and why this can happen. The basic idea of this theory is to establish that there are certain classes of function that can be represented with a polynomial number of neurons in a depth $d$ network but require an exponential number of neurons in a depth $d^\prime$ network, for certain $d^\prime < d$. Arguments along these lines are called depth separations.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why deep architectures are often more efficient than shallow ones, providing a theoretical basis for the success of deep learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth separations occur when a deep network can represent a function using polynomially many neurons while a shallower one requires exponentially many.
- This theory helps explain why deep networks often outperform wide, shallow networks in practice.

key_passage.text: The basic idea of this theory is to establish that there are certain classes of function that can be represented with a polynomial number of neurons in a depth $d$ network but require an exponential number of neurons in a depth $d^\prime$ network, for certain $d^\prime < d$. Arguments along these lines are called depth separations.

motivation.text: it is sometimes the case that deep nets require far fewer parameters to fit data than wide nets. Evidence for this statement comes mostly from empiricism, where researchers have found that deeper nets just work better in practice on many popular problems.

concepts.title: Hebbian learning

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Hebbian learning is a bottom-up approach where neurons wire up based on feedforward activity patterns rather than backpropagated errors.
concepts.content: One intriguing alternative to backpropagation is called Hebbian learning. Backpropagation is a top-down learning algorithm, where errors incurred at the output (top) of the net are propagated backward to inform earlier layers how to update their weights and biases to minimize the loss, which is a form of learning based on feedback. Hebbian learning, in contrast, is a bottom-up approach, where neurons wire up just based on the feedforward pattern of activity in the net. The canonical learning rule in Hebbian methods is Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together." That is, we increase the weight of the connection between two neurons whenever the two neurons are active at the same time. Although this learning rule is not explicitly minimizing a loss function, it has been shown to lead to effective neural representations. For example, Hebb-like rules can learn infomax representations, which capture as much information as possible about the input signal, or lead to networks that act like memory banks. Hebbian learning is also of interest because it is considered to be more biologically plausible than backpropagation; Hebb's rule can be computed locally, whereas backpropagation requires global coordination.
concepts.motivation_md: Hebbian learning provides a biologically plausible alternative to backpropagation, focusing on local interactions rather than global error signals.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hebbian learning is a bottom-up, feedforward approach to updating neural weights.
- It relies on local rules where neurons that are active simultaneously strengthen their connections.
- It is considered more biologically plausible than backpropagation because it does not require global coordination.

key_passage.text: The canonical learning rule in Hebbian methods is Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together." That is, we increase the weight of the connection between two neurons whenever the two neurons are active at the same time.

motivation.text: Hebbian learning is also of interest because it is considered to be more biologically plausible than backpropagation. This is because Hebb's rule can be computed locally---each neuron strengthens and weakens its weights based just on the activity of adjacent neurons---whereas backpropagation requires global coordination throughout the neural network.

concepts.title: Hebb's rule

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Hebb's rule states that the weight of the connection between two neurons increases whenever they are active at the same time.
concepts.content: The canonical learning rule in Hebbian methods is Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together." That is, we increase the weight of the connection between two neurons whenever the two neurons are active at the same time.
concepts.motivation_md: Hebb's rule provides a simple, local mechanism for learning associations based on temporal correlation of neural activity.
concepts.recap_md:
- The rule is often summarized as "fire together, wire together."
- It increases connection weights based on simultaneous activity between adjacent neurons.

key_passage.text: we increase the weight of the connection between two neurons whenever the two neurons are active at the same time.

motivation.text: The canonical learning rule in Hebbian methods is Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together."

concepts.title: Infomax

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Infomax representations capture as much information as possible about the input signal within neural activations.
concepts.content: Hebb-like rules can learn infomax representations, which capture, in the neural activations, as much information as possible about the input signal.
concepts.motivation_md: The infomax principle aims to maximize the efficiency of information transmission within a neural network.
concepts.recap_md:
- Infomax stands for information maximization.
- It describes representations that preserve the maximum amount of input information in the network's activations.

key_passage.text: Hebb-like rules can learn infomax representations, which capture, in the neural activations, as much information as possible about the input signal

concepts.title: Tensor

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: A tensor is a multidimensional array and the primary data structure used in deep learning.
