concepts.content: The main data structure that we will encounter in deep learning is the tensor, which is just a multidimensional array. In general, everything in deep learning is represented as tensors—the input is one tensor, the activations are tensors, the weights are tensors, the outputs are tensors. If you have data that is not natively represented as a tensor, the first step is to convert it into a tensor format. Most often we use tensors of real numbers, where the elements are in $\mathbb{R}$. For example, a dataset $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ of images $\mathbf{x}$ and labels $\mathbf{y}$ can be viewed as two tensors: $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C_0 \times H \times W }$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}$. The first dimension represents the number of elements in the dataset, while the remaining dimensions represent the dimensionality of the data (e.g., color channels, height, and width for images).
concepts.motivation_md: Tensors provide a unified mathematical framework for representing and processing high-dimensional data and model parameters efficiently.
concepts.recap_md:
- A tensor is a multidimensional array of values, typically real numbers.
- All components of a deep learning system (inputs, weights, activations) are represented as tensors.

key_passage.text: The main data structure that we will encounter in deep learning is the tensor, which is just a multidimensional array.

motivation.text: In general, everything in deep learning is represented as tensors---the input is one tensor, the activations are tensors, the weights are tensors, the outputs are tensors. If you have data that is not natively represented as a tensor, the first step, before feeding it to a deep net, is to convert it into a tensor format.

concepts.title: Channels

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Channels refer to the number of neurons in a layer, analogous to the color channels of an input image.
concepts.content: The activations in the network are also tensors. For the MLP networks we have seen so far, the activation tensors have shape $N \times C_{\ell}$, where $C_{\ell}$ is the number of neurons on layer $\ell$, sometimes also called channels in analogy to the color channels of the input image. In later architectures like convolutional networks, activation layers may have additional dimensions, such as shape $N \times C_{\ell} \times H_{\ell} \times W_{\ell}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of channels allows us to organize neural activations into distinct features or components, similar to how images are organized into color components.
concepts.recap_md:
- Channels represent the number of neurons or feature maps in a specific layer.
- In MLPs, the channel dimension corresponds to the number of neurons $C_{\ell}$.

key_passage.text: the number of neurons on layer $\ell$, sometimes also called **channels** in analogy to the color channels of the input image.

motivation.text: In later chapters we will encounter other architectures where the activation layers have additional dimensions, for example, in convolutional networks we will see activation layers that are of shape $N \times C_{\ell} \times H_{\ell} \times W_{\ell}$.

concepts.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
concepts.one_liner: Cross-entropy loss is a continuous and differentiable function used to optimize classification models by maximizing the log likelihood of ground truth observations.
concepts.content:
Cross-entropy loss is commonly used because it is continuous and differentiable, making it easier to optimize than discrete alternatives. It is defined as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = H(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = - \sum_{k=1}^K y_k \log \hat{y}_k
\end{aligned}$$
In this context, $\hat{y}_k$ represents the probability the model assigns to class $k$. Under this interpretation, minimizing cross-entropy maximizes the log likelihood of the ground truth observation $\mathbf{y}$ under the model's prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard classification error is often NP-hard to optimize directly. Cross-entropy loss provides a smooth, differentiable surrogate that allows for efficient optimization via gradient-based methods while statistically maximizing the likelihood of the correct labels.
concepts.recap_md: - It is defined as the negative sum of ground truth labels multiplied by the log of predicted probabilities.

key_passage.text: $$\mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = H(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = - \sum_{k=1}^K y_k \log \hat{y}_k$$ The way to think about this is $\hat{y}_k$ should *represent the probability* we think the image is an image of class $k$. Under that interpretation, minimizing cross-entropy maximizes the log likelihood of the ground truth observation $\mathbf{y}$ under our model's prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.

concepts.title: Probability Mass Function (pmf)
concepts.one_liner: A probability mass function (pmf) is a $K$-dimensional vector with elements in the range $[0,1]$ that sum to 1.
concepts.content: For the interpretation of model outputs as probabilities to be valid, the prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ must represent a probability mass function (pmf). A pmf $\mathbf{p}$ over $K$ classes is defined as a $K$-dimensional vector with elements in the range $[0,1]$ that sums to 1. In other words, $\mathbf{p}$ is a point on the $(K-1)$-simplex, denoted as $\mathbf{p} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: To treat neural network outputs as probabilities, we need a mathematical structure that ensures the values are non-negative and represent a complete distribution over all possible outcomes.
concepts.recap_md: - A pmf must consist of values between 0 and 1 inclusive.

key_passage.text: A pmf $\mathbf{p}$, over $K$ classes, is defined as a $K$-dimensional vector with elements in the range $[0,1]$ that sums to 1.

motivation.text: For that interpretation to be valid, we require that $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ represent a (pmf).

concepts.title: Simplex
concepts.one_liner: The $(K-1)$-simplex is the set of all $K$-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1.
concepts.content: The $(K-1)$-simplex, denoted $\vartriangle^{K-1}$, is the set of all $K$-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1. In the context of classification, $K$-dimensional one-hot codes live on the vertices of $\vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The simplex provides a geometric representation of the space of all possible probability distributions over a finite set of categories.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the space of all valid probability mass functions for $K$ classes.

key_passage.text: The $(K-1)$-simplex, $\vartriangle^{K-1}$, is the set of all $K$-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1.

concepts.title: Softmax Function
concepts.one_liner: The softmax function squashes a vector of real numbers into a probability distribution that sums to 1.
concepts.content:
To ensure that the output of a learned function $f_{\theta}$ is a valid probability mass function (i.e., $f_{\theta} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$), we can apply the softmax function. This involves two steps: first applying a function $z_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^K$, then squashing and normalizing the output. 

Using softmax is a modeling choice; any function that squashes into a valid pmf (a nonnegative vector that sums to 1) could be used. The function is defined as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    &\mathbf{z} = z_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\\
    &\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \texttt{softmax}(\mathbf{z})\\
    &\quad \quad \hat{y}_j = \frac{e^{-z_j}}{\sum_{i=1}^K e^{-z_k}}.
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Raw model outputs (logits) can be any real numbers. The softmax function maps these values into a range $[0, 1]$ and ensures they sum to 1, allowing them to be interpreted as probabilities.
concepts.recap_md: - It transforms arbitrary real-valued vectors into points on the simplex.

key_passage.text: A popular way to squash is via the softmax function: $\hat{y}_j = \frac{e^{-z_j}}{\sum_{i=1}^K e^{-z_k}}$.

motivation.text: To ensure that the output of our learned function $f_{\theta}$ has this property, i.e., $f_{\theta} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$, we can compose two steps: (1) first apply a function $z_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^K$, (2) then squash the output into the range $[0,1]$ and normalize it to sum to 1.

concepts.title: Logits
concepts.one_liner: Logits are the unnormalized log probabilities of each class in a classification model.
concepts.content: The values in the vector $\mathbf{z}$ (the output of the model before the softmax function is applied) are called the logits. They can be interpreted as the unnormalized log probabilities of each class.
concepts.motivation_md: Logits provide a raw score for each class before normalization, which is often more numerically stable for certain calculations like loss functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Logits represent the input to the softmax function.

key_passage.text: The values in $\mathbf{z}$ are called the **logits** and can be interpreted as the unnormalized log probabilities of each class.

concepts.title: Softmax Regression
concepts.one_liner: Softmax regression is a family of learning methods that map input data to class labels using the softmax function and cross-entropy loss.
concepts.content:
Softmax regression is a family of learning methods for classification problems. It refers to the general form of mapping input data to class labels using a hypothesis space and an optimizer, typically involving the softmax function to produce class probabilities.

(see figure: Learning is a meta-algorithm, an algorithm that outputs algorithms; metalearning is just learning applied to learning, and therefore it is a meta-meta-algorithm.)

In this framework, the hypothesis space and optimizer are often left partially specified because softmax regression describes the whole family of methods sharing this structure. This modularity allows for developing the ingredients of the learning problem in isolation and then mixing and matching them.
concepts.motivation_md: Softmax regression generalizes binary logistic regression to multi-class problems, providing a standard framework for categorical prediction.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a general family of models for classification.

key_passage.text: Softmax regression is just one way to model a classification problem.

concepts.title: Metalearning (Learning to Learn)
concepts.one_liner: Metalearning, or learning to learn, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space consists of learning algorithms.
concepts.content:
Learning to learn, also called metalearning, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space is learning algorithms. While standard learners train on past instances to solve future instances, metalearning handles cases where the future problem is itself a learning problem, such as finding a least-squares line fit.

For example, given sets of input-output pairs that represent regression tasks:
$$\begin{aligned}
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[1,2]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = x\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[2,4]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = 2x\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[0.5,1]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = \frac{x}{2}\}\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$
A learner can fit these examples by learning to perform least-squares regression. Note that the metalearner might arrive at any solution that fits the examples well, not just the unique least-squares solution.

If learning is a meta-algorithm (an algorithm that outputs an algorithm), metalearning is a meta-meta-algorithm. It can be visualized by adding another outer loop on top of a learner.

(see figure: Learning is a meta-algorithm, an algorithm that outputs algorithms; metalearning is just learning applied to learning, and therefore it is a meta-meta-algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard learning algorithms are often hand-designed. Metalearning seeks to automate the discovery of learning algorithms, potentially finding more efficient ways to learn from small amounts of data.
concepts.recap_md: - It treats the process of learning itself as the task to be optimized.

key_passage.text: Learning to learn, also called metalearning, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space is learning algorithms.

motivation.text: The goal of metalearning is to handle the case where the future problem we will encounter is itself a learning problem, such as "find the least-squares line fit to these data points."

concepts.title: Evolution as a Learning Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Evolution is a learning algorithm according to the definition of learning as a meta-algorithm.
concepts.content: Evolution is a learning algorithm according to our present definition.
concepts.motivation_md: By viewing evolution as a process that improves a population's "performance" (fitness) based on "data" (environmental feedback), we can analyze biological processes using the tools of machine learning.
concepts.recap_md: - Evolution fits the formal definition of a learning algorithm.

key_passage.text: Evolution is a learning algorithm according to our present definition.

concepts.title: Unconscious inference
concepts.one_liner: Perception involves unconscious conclusions where the brain interprets sensory responses to infer the state of the world.
concepts.content: Psychic acts of ordinary perception can be viewed as unconscious conclusions, distinguishing them from common conscious conclusions. For example, while an astronomer computing star positions based on observations is making a conscious conclusion, seeing light when pressing on the eye is an unconscious conclusion about the world based on the eye's response. This concept of unconscious inference is a foundational topic in computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains that perception is not just a direct recording of the world but an active, inferential process. It provides a theoretical bridge between human psychology and the computational tasks of computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perception acts as a series of unconscious conclusions based on sensory data.
 - It differs from conscious reasoning, such as mathematical computation or formal observation.
 - This inferential framework is a core principle in the field of computer vision.

key_passage.text: Still, it may be permissible to speak of the psychic acts of ordinary perception as unconscious conclusions, thereby making a distinction of some sort between them and the common so-called conscious conclusions.

motivation.text: When you press on the eye and see light, that is an unconscious conclusion about what is in the world, given the responses of your eye. This unconscious inference is the topic of computer vision.

concepts.title: Active role of the viewer in perception
concepts.one_liner: Perception is an active process where viewers use their own movements to understand the stationary forms of objects.
concepts.content: Helmholtz emphasized the active role of the viewer in perception. He argued that if objects were simply passed before our eyes by a foreign force without our agency, we might never navigate the resulting optical phantasmagoria. By changing our position, we notice that we can obtain various images of an object, such as a table, at will. Through these movements, we discover that the stationary form of the object in space is the cause of the changing images in our eyes. This perspective foreshadows certain unsupervised learning methods used in modern computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: It explains how humans resolve visual ambiguity by interacting with the environment, suggesting that movement is key to learning the stable properties of objects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Viewers play an active role in perception through physical movement.
 - Movement allows the brain to link changing retinal images to stationary 3D forms.
 - This principle is a precursor to unsupervised learning in computer vision.

key_passage.text: Helmholtz emphasized the active role of the viewer in perception. But when we notice that we can get various images of a table in front of us simply by changing our position; and that we can sometimes have one view and sometimes another, just as we like at any time we find out by this means that it is the stationary form of the table in space which is the cause of the changing image in our eyes.

motivation.text: This foreshadows some unsupervised learning methods common in computer vision today.

concepts.title: Phi phenomenon
concepts.one_liner: The phi phenomenon is a visual illusion where two images presented in rapid succession create an impression of continuous motion.
concepts.content:
The phi phenomenon is a visual illusion that consists in presenting two images with a vertical bar at different locations in rapid succession, giving the impression that there is continuous motion between them.

concepts.motivation_md: It demonstrates that the brain perceives motion even when none exists in the physical stimuli, highlighting the gap between raw sensory input and perceived reality.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is a visual illusion of continuous motion created by static images.
 - It occurs when stimuli are presented at different locations in rapid succession.
 - It was a foundational observation for Gestalt psychology.

key_passage.text: the phi phenomenon, a visual illusion that consists in presenting two images with a vertical bar at different locations in rapid succession giving the impression that there is continuous motion between them

concepts.title: Gestalt theory: Wholes over parts
concepts.one_liner: Gestalt theory posits that perception is about experiencing wholes as single units rather than just a collection of constituent parts.
concepts.content: Gestalt theory postulates that perceived motion is a new phenomenon not present in individual stimuli, and that we perceive whole events as single units. Gestalt psychology emerged as a reaction to the trend that psychology must decompose stimuli into constituent elements to be a science. Instead, Gestalt theory argues that perception is about wholes more than it is about parts.
concepts.motivation_md: This theory addresses why we see coherent objects and scenes instead of a chaotic mess of individual pixels or features.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perception focuses on wholes rather than individual constituent parts.
 - Perceived phenomena (like motion) can exist in the whole even if absent in the parts.
 - It challenges the reductionist view of psychology.

key_passage.text: Gestalt theory argued that perception is about wholes more than it is about parts.

motivation.text: Gestalt psychology extended this interpretation to explain many other visual phenomena and emerged as a reaction of the existing trend that said that for psychology to be a science it had to decompose stimuli into its constituent elements.

concepts.title: Perceptual organization
concepts.one_liner: Perceptual organization is the study of how the visual system organizes individual features into coherent objects and wholes.
concepts.content: Perceptual organization studies how our visual system organizes individual visual features, such as colors and lines, into coherent objects and wholes. This field explores the rules used by the visual system to group elements on a display. Research in this area often involves observing how arrangements of dots and lines are grouped together into larger elements.
concepts.motivation_md: It seeks to explain the mechanisms by which the brain structures sensory input into meaningful entities.
concepts.recap_md:
- It describes the process of grouping individual features into coherent wholes.
 - It involves specific rules used by the visual system to organize elements.
 - It is often studied using simple arrangements of dots and lines.

key_passage.text: Perceptual organization studies how our visual system organizes individual visual features (i.e., colors, lines, ...) into coherent objects and wholes.

motivation.text: Wertheimer introduced the problem of perceptual organization. Wertheimer proposed a set of rules used by the visual system to organize elements on a simple display.

concepts.title: Gestalt grouping laws
concepts.one_liner: Grouping laws are visual cues that describe how elements are perceptually organized into units.
concepts.content: Gestalt psychologists called grouping laws the visual cues they uncovered. However, they are not strictly laws and not all grouping cues are equally strong.
concepts.motivation_md: These 'laws' provide a framework for predicting how humans will perceive and group visual information.
concepts.recap_md:
- Grouping laws are visual cues for perceptual organization.
 - They are not absolute laws and vary in strength.
 - They describe the conditions under which elements are seen as belonging together.

key_passage.text: Gestalt psychologists called grouping laws the visual cues they uncovered. However, they are not strictly laws and not all grouping cues are equally strong.

concepts.title: Law of proximity
concepts.one_liner: The law of proximity states that items located near each other are more likely to be perceived as a group.
concepts.content: The law of proximity states that items that are nearby are more likely to group together. While it is possible with effort to group items according to alternative arrangements, it is often hard to sustain those groupings perceptually. The law of proximity is also affected by the similarity of the items.
concepts.motivation_md: Proximity is one of the most basic ways the brain determines which features belong to the same object.
concepts.recap_md:
- Nearby items are more likely to be grouped together perceptually.
 - Proximity-based groupings are often stronger and easier to sustain than others.
 - This law interacts with the similarity of the items involved.

key_passage.text: Items that are nearby are more likely to group together.

motivation.text: The law of proximity is affected by the similarity of the items.

concepts.title: Law of similarity
concepts.one_liner: The law of similarity states that elements with similar features like color or size tend to be grouped together.
concepts.content: The law of similarity states that elements that have similar features, such as color, size, or orientation, group together, even when they are all equally distant.
concepts.motivation_md: Similarity allows the visual system to link related elements across a scene, even if they are not physically touching.
concepts.recap_md:
- Elements with similar features (color, size, orientation) are grouped together.
 - Similarity can override equal spacing in perceptual organization.
 - It is a fundamental Gestalt grouping cue.

key_passage.text: Elements that have similar features (color, size, orientation) also group together, even when they are all equally distant.

concepts.title: Gradient Descent
concepts.one_liner: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that minimizes a loss function by iteratively moving in the direction of steepest descent.
concepts.content:
Once you have specified a learning problem consisting of a loss function, hypothesis space, and parameterization, the next step is to find the parameters that minimize the loss. This is an optimization problem, and the most common optimization algorithm used is gradient descent. Gradient descent is analogous to a skier making their way down a snowy mountain, where the shape of the mountain represents the loss function.

There are many varieties of gradient descent, collectively referred to as gradient-based learning algorithms. All share the same basic idea: at some operating point, calculate the direction of steepest descent, then use this direction to find a new operating point with lower loss. The simplest version of gradient descent takes a step in the gradient direction of length proportional to the gradient magnitude.

(see figure: Gradient descent `GD`. Optimizing a cost function $J: \theta \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by descending the gradient $\nabla_{\theta} J$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Gradient descent provides a systematic way to find the optimal parameters for a machine learning model by following the local geometry of the loss function toward its minimum.
concepts.recap_md: - It is an iterative optimization algorithm used to minimize a loss function $J$.

key_passage.text: Gradient descent is like a skier making their way down a snowy mountain, where the shape of the mountain is the loss function. All share the same basic idea: at some operating point, calculate the direction of steepest descent, then use this direction to find a new operating point with lower loss.

motivation.text: Once you have specified a learning problem (loss function, hypothesis space, parameterization), the next step is to find the parameters that minimize the loss. This is an optimization problem, and the most common optimization algorithm we will use is gradient descent.

concepts.title: Operating Point
concepts.one_liner: An operating point refers to a particular setting of parameters where the loss is currently being evaluated.
concepts.content: We use the term operating point to refer to a particular point (setting of the parameters) where we are currently evaluating the loss.
concepts.motivation_md: This term provides a concise way to refer to the current state or location in the parameter space during an iterative optimization process.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the current parameter vector $\theta$ during optimization.

key_passage.text: We use the term operating point to refer to a particular point (setting of the parameters) where we are currently evaluating the loss.

concepts.title: Zeroth-Order Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Zeroth-order optimization is a method where the update function only observes the value of the cost function $J(\theta)$.
concepts.content: In the simplest setting, called zeroth-order optimization, the update function only gets to observe the value $J(\theta)$. The only way, then, to find $\theta$'s that minimize the loss is to sample different values for $\theta$ and move toward the values that are lower.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach is necessary when the gradient of the objective function is unknown, unavailable, or difficult to compute.
concepts.recap_md: - It relies solely on function values $J(\theta)$ rather than derivatives.

key_passage.text: In the simplest setting, called zeroth-order optimization, the update function only gets to observe the value J(θ). The only way, then, to find θ's that minimize the loss is to sample different values for θ and move toward the values that are lower.

motivation.text: The only way, then, to find θ's that minimize the loss is to sample different values for θ and move toward the values that are lower.

concepts.title: First-Order Optimization
concepts.one_liner: First-order optimization uses the gradient of the cost function to determine the direction of steepest descent for minimization.
concepts.content: For gradient-based optimization, also called first-order optimization, the update function takes as input the gradient of the cost with respect to the parameters at the current operating point, $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$. This reveals hugely useful information about the loss that directly tells us how to minimize it: just move in the direction of steepest descent, that is, the gradient direction.
concepts.motivation_md: Using the gradient allows the optimizer to know exactly which direction reduces the loss most efficiently, rather than relying on random sampling.
concepts.recap_md: - It utilizes the gradient $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$ to guide parameter updates.

key_passage.text: For gradient-based optimization, also called first-order optimization, the update function takes as input the gradient of the cost with respect to the parameters at the current operating point, $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$. This reveals hugely useful information about the loss that directly tells us how to minimize it: just move in the direction of steepest descent, that is, the gradient direction.

motivation.text: This reveals hugely useful information about the loss that directly tells us how to minimize it: just move in the direction of steepest descent, that is, the gradient direction.

concepts.title: Higher-Order Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Higher-order optimization methods use higher-order derivatives, such as the Hessian, to account for the local curvature of the loss landscape.
concepts.content: Higher-order optimization methods observe higher-order derivatives of the loss, such as the Hessian $H$, which tells you how the landscape is locally curving. The Hessian is costly to compute, but many methods use approximations to the Hessian, or other properties related to loss curvature, and these are growing in popularity.
concepts.motivation_md: By understanding the curvature of the loss landscape, these methods can take more informed steps that can lead to faster convergence than first-order methods.
concepts.recap_md: - These methods use the Hessian $H$ or its approximations to understand local curvature.

key_passage.text: Higher-order optimization methods observe higher-order derivatives of the loss, such as the Hessian $H$, which tells you how the landscape is locally curving.

motivation.text: The Hessian is costly to compute, but many methods use approximations to the Hessian, or other properties related to loss curvature, and these are growing in popularity

concepts.title: Learning Rate
concepts.one_liner: The learning rate $\eta$ is a hyperparameter that controls the size of the steps taken during gradient descent.
concepts.content: The gradient descent algorithm has two hyperparameters: the learning rate $\eta$, which controls the step size (calculated as the learning rate times the gradient magnitude), and the number of steps $K$. If the learning rate is sufficiently small and the initial parameter vector $\theta^0$ is random, then this algorithm will almost surely converge to a local minimum of $J$ as $K \rightarrow \infty$. However, to descend more quickly, it can be useful to set the learning rate to a higher value.
concepts.motivation_md: The learning rate balances the speed of convergence against the risk of overshooting the minimum or failing to converge.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a hyperparameter $\eta$ that scales the gradient to determine the update step size.

key_passage.text: the learning rate η, which controls the step size (learning rate times gradient magnitude)

motivation.text: However, to descend more quickly, it can be useful to set the learning rate to a higher value.

concepts.title: Learning Rate Schedule
concepts.one_liner: A learning rate schedule is a strategy that decays the learning rate over time to improve convergence.
concepts.content:
A generally useful strategy is to start with a high value for $\eta$ and then decay it until convergence according to a learning rate schedule. Schedules generally work by calling some function $\texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)$ to get the learning rate on each iteration $k$ of descent:
$$
\eta^{k} = \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)
$$
Generally, we want an update rule where $\eta^{k+1} < \eta^k$, so that we take smaller steps as we approach the minimizer. A few simple and popular approaches include:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-k} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-\lfloor k/M \rfloor} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{stepwise exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \frac{(K - k)}{K} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{linear decay}
\end{aligned}
$$

One downside of linear decay is that it depends on the total number of steps $K$, making it hard to compare optimization runs of different lengths. This is also true for more advanced schedules like cosine decay. The parameters $\beta$ and $M$ are additional hyperparameters of these methods.

(see figure: Gradient descent with learning rate decay algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: Starting with a high learning rate allows for rapid progress initially, while decaying it helps the model settle precisely into a minimum without overshooting in the final stages.
concepts.recap_md: - It adjusts the learning rate $\eta$ dynamically during training, typically decreasing it.

key_passage.text: A generally useful strategy is to start with a high value for η and then decay it until convergence according to a learning rate schedule. Researchers have come up with innumerable schedules, and they generally work by calling some function lr(η₀,k) to get the learning rate on each iteration of descent: ηᵏ = lr(η₀,k)

motivation.text: Generally, we want an update rule where ηᵏ⁺¹ < ηᵏ, so that we take smaller steps as we approach the minimizer.

concepts.title: Momentum
concepts.one_liner: Momentum is an optimization technique that uses a weighted combination of the previous update and the current gradient to accelerate convergence.
concepts.content:
Momentum is an optimization technique that makes the analogy to skiing more precise: it acts like the inertia of a skier, carrying them over small bumps and increasing speed along a straight path. In mathematical terms, momentum sets the parameter update to be a direction $\mathbf{v}^{k+1}$, given by a weighted combination of the previous update direction, $\mathbf{v}^{k}$, plus the current negative gradient:
$$
\mathbf{v}^{k+1} = \mu \mathbf{v}^{k} - \eta\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta^k)
$$
The weight $\mu$ is a hyperparameter sometimes simply called the momentum.

(see figure: Gradient descent with momentum algorithm.)

As seen in (Figure 1.1.6), some momentum can help the convergence rate (e.g., $\mu = 0.5$), but too much momentum (e.g., $\mu = 0.95$) can cause the trajectory to overshoot the optimum and fail to stop even when the optimum loss is achieved.

(see figure: (left) A simple loss function $J = \texttt{abs}(\theta)$. (right) Optimization trajectory for three different settings of momentum $\mu$. White line indicates value of the parameter at each iteration...)
concepts.motivation_md: Momentum helps the optimizer navigate through noisy gradients or flat regions of the loss landscape by maintaining a 'velocity' from previous steps.
concepts.recap_md: - It incorporates a fraction $\mu$ of the previous update direction into the current step.

key_passage.text: In math, momentum just means that we set the parameter update to be a direction $\mathbf{v}^{k+1}$, given by a weighted combination of the previous update direction, $\mathbf{v}^{k}$, plus the current negative gradient: $$\mathbf{v}^{k+1} = \mu \mathbf{v}^{k} - \eta\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta^k)$$

motivation.text: Momentum makes the analogy to skiing even more precise: momentum is like the inertia of the skier, carrying them over the little bumps and imperfections in the ski slope and increasing their speed as they descend along a straight path.

concepts.title: The Blocks World

position.section_title: A Simple World: The Blocks World

concepts.one_liner: The Blocks World is a simplified visual environment composed of simple 3D geometrical figures with flat surfaces resting on a horizontal ground plane.
concepts.content:
As the visual world is too complex, we can simplify it to build a simple visual system. The Blocks World is a world composed of simple 3D geometrical figures. For the purposes of this model, the world is composed of a simple yet varied set of objects. These simple objects are composed of flat surfaces that can be horizontal or vertical. These objects rest on a white horizontal ground plane. We can build these objects by cutting, folding, and gluing together pieces of colored paper. In this model, we do not assume that we know the exact geometry of these objects in advance.

[FIGURE:0cd8ad064f44ea7a]
concepts.motivation_md: The real visual world is too complex for early scene interpretation systems to process. By simplifying the environment into a "Blocks World" of basic geometric shapes, researchers can develop and test fundamental computer vision algorithms in a controlled setting.
concepts.recap_md: - A simplified environment used to build and test early visual systems.

key_passage.text: Larry G. Roberts introduced the Block world, a world composed of simple 3D geometrical figures.

motivation.text: As the visual world is too complex, we will start by simplifying it enough that we will be able to build a simple visual system right away.

concepts.title: Parallel (Orthographic) Projection
concepts.one_liner: Parallel projection is an image formation model where light rays travel parallel to each other and perpendicular to the camera plane.
concepts.content: One of the simplest forms of projection is parallel (or orthographic) projection. In this image formation model, the light rays travel parallel to each other and perpendicular to the camera plane. This type of projection produces images in which objects do not change size as they move closer or farther from the camera, and parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the 2D image. This is different from perspective projection, where the image is formed by the convergence of light rays into a single focal point. One way of generating images that can be described by parallel projection is to use the camera zoom. If we increase the distance between the camera and the object while zooming, we can keep the same approximate image size of the objects but with reduced perspective effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Parallel projection simplifies the relationship between 3D objects and 2D images by preserving parallel lines and object sizes, making it a useful mathematical approximation for distant objects or telephoto lenses.
concepts.recap_md: - Light rays are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the image plane.

key_passage.text: In this image formation model, the light rays travel parallel to each other and perpendicular to the camera plane. This type of projection produces images in which objects do not change size as they move closer or farther from the camera, and parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the 2D image.

motivation.text: One of the simplest forms of projection is parallel (or orthographic) projection. This is different from the perspective projection, to be discussed in , where the image is formed by the convergence of the light rays into a single point (focal point).

concepts.title: Perspective Projection
concepts.one_liner: Perspective projection is the standard image formation model where light rays converge into a single focal point, causing distant objects to appear smaller.
concepts.content: If we do not take special care, most pictures taken with a camera will be better described by perspective projection. In this model, the image is formed by the convergence of the light rays into a single point (focal point). This results in images where near edges appear larger than far edges, and parallel lines in 3D are generally not parallel in the 2D image.
concepts.motivation_md: Perspective projection accurately models how human eyes and standard cameras capture the world, where depth affects the perceived size of objects.
concepts.recap_md: - Light rays converge at a single focal point.

key_passage.text: most pictures taken with a camera will be better described by perspective projection

motivation.text: If we do not take special care, most pictures taken with a camera will be better described by perspective projection

concepts.title: The Hitchcock Zoom Effect
concepts.one_liner: The Hitchcock zoom effect involves changing the camera zoom to compensate for a moving camera, keeping a subject centered while the background shifts.
concepts.content: Changing the zoom to compensate for a moving camera can be used to create movie effects. This method was introduced by Alfred Hitchcock to create a sequence, centered on a subject, where the background moves away or closer to the subject.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows filmmakers to create a sense of unease or dramatic realization by distorting the background's perspective while keeping the main subject's size constant.
concepts.recap_md: - Simultaneously moves the camera and adjusts the zoom.

key_passage.text: Changing the zoom to compensate a moving camera can be used to create movie effects. This method was introduced by Alfred Hitchcock to create a sequence, centered in a subject, where the background moves away or closer to the subject.

concepts.title: Simple Projection Model Transformation
concepts.one_liner: This model characterizes how a point in world coordinates $(X,Y,Z)$ projects into the image plane $(x,y)$ using specific camera orientations.
concepts.content: The first step is to characterize how a point in world coordinates $(X,Y,Z)$ projects into the image plane. In this parameterization, the camera center is inside the 3D plane $X=0$, and the horizontal axis of the camera ($x$) is parallel to the ground plane ($Y=0$). The camera is tilted so that the line connecting the origin of the world coordinates system and the image center is perpendicular to the image plane. The angle $	heta$ is the angle between this line and the $Z$-axis. The image is parameterized by coordinates $(x,y)$. In this simple projection model, the origin of the world coordinates projects on the origin of the image coordinates; therefore, $(0,0,0)$ projects into $(0,0)$. Assuming square pixels and a constant factor $ eta=1$, the transformation is written as: $$\begin{aligned} x &=& X \\ y &=& \cos(\theta) Y - \sin(\theta) Z \end{aligned}$$ With this particular parametrization, the world coordinates $Y$ and $Z$ are mixed after projection. From the camera, a point moving parallel to the $Z$-axis will be indistinguishable from a point moving parallel to the $Y$-axis.
concepts.motivation_md: To interpret 2D images, we need a mathematical mapping that relates 3D world points to 2D pixel locations. This specific model simplifies the math by aligning the camera with the ground plane and world origin.
concepts.recap_md:
- Maps 3D world coordinates $(X,Y,Z)$ to 2D image coordinates $(x,y)$.
- Uses a tilt angle $\theta$ to define the relationship between the $Y$ and $Z$ axes in the projection.

key_passage.text: Taking into account all these assumptions, the transformation between world coordinates and image coordinates can be written as follows: x = X and y = cos(θ) Y - sin(θ) Z

motivation.text: The first step is to characterize how a point in world coordinates (X,Y,Z) projects into the image plane.

concepts.title: Image as Intensity Array

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

concepts.one_liner: An image can be represented as a function $\ell(x,y)$ that outputs the intensity value at a specific location.
concepts.content: The observed image is a function, $$\ell(x,y)$$ that takes as input location, $(x,y)$, and it outputs the intensity at that location. In this representation, the image is an array of intensity values (color values) indexed by location. This can be visualized as a surface where the vertical axis corresponds to image intensity.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing an image as a mathematical function or a numerical array allows computers to perform calculations and apply algorithms to visual data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Defines an image as a function $\ell(x,y)$ mapping location to intensity.
- Treats the image as a numerical array of values.

key_passage.text: The observed image is a function, ℓ(x,y) that takes as input location, (x,y), and it outputs the intensity at that location. In this representation, the image is an array of intensity values (color values) indexed by location.

concepts.title: Image Edge

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

concepts.one_liner: Edges denote image regions where there are strong changes of the image intensity with respect to location.
concepts.content: Edges denote image regions where there are strong changes of the image with respect to location. Those variations can be due to a multitude of scene factors, such as occlusion boundaries, changes in surface orientation, changes in surface albedo, or shadows.
concepts.motivation_md: Edges are critical features in computer vision because they often correspond to the boundaries of objects or significant physical changes in the scene.
concepts.recap_md:
- Corresponds to regions of sharp intensity variation.
- Caused by physical factors like depth, orientation, or lighting changes.

key_passage.text: Edges denote image regions where there are strong changes of the image with respect to location.

motivation.text: Those variations can be due to a multitude of scene factors (e.g., occlusion boundaries, changes in surface orientation, changes in surface albedo, shadows).

concepts.title: Classification of Image Boundaries

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

concepts.one_liner: Image edges can be classified by their cause, including object boundaries, surface orientation changes, and shadow edges.
concepts.content:
Image edges can be classified according to their most probable cause. The primary categories include:

- **Object boundaries**: Pixels that delineate the boundaries of any object, generally corresponding to changes in surface color, texture, and orientation.
- **Changes in surface orientation**: Locations where strong image variations occur because intensity is a function of the angle between the surface and incident light.
- **Shadow edges**: Transitions between dark and light; in the blocks world, these are often soft transitions.

Object boundaries are further divided into:
- **Contact edges**: A boundary between two objects in physical contact, where there is no depth discontinuity.
- **Occlusion boundaries**: Occur when an object is partially in front of another, generally producing depth discontinuities.
concepts.motivation_md: Classifying edges helps a vision system understand the 3D structure of a scene, distinguishing between a simple change in color and a physical boundary between two separate objects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Distinguishes between physical boundaries (occlusion, contact) and lighting effects (shadows).
- Identifies surface orientation changes based on intensity variations.

key_passage.text: One of the tasks that we will solve first is to classify image edges according to their most probable cause. We will use the following classification of image boundaries: Object boundaries, Changes in surface orientation, and Shadow edges.

motivation.text: We will use the following classification of image boundaries to classify image edges according to their most probable cause.

concepts.title: Underfitting
concepts.one_liner: Underfitting occurs when a learner fails to optimize the objective on the training data.
concepts.content: A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting. The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding underfitting helps diagnose why a model performs poorly. It distinguishes between a model that is too simple to capture the data's structure (underfitting) and one that captures noise instead of the signal (overfitting).
concepts.recap_md: - Underfitting is the failure to achieve a low error on the training dataset.

key_passage.text: either it failed to optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting. The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.

motivation.text: A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression extends linear regression by using polynomial functions as the hypothesis space.
concepts.content: Polynomial regression is just like linear regression except that the hypothesis space is polynomial functions rather than linear functions, that is, $$\begin{aligned} y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k \end{aligned}$$ where $K$, the degree of the polynomial, is a hyperparameter of the hypothesis space. We use the least-squares ($L_2$) loss function. Polynomial regression is highly related to linear regression; we can transform a polynomial regression problem into a linear regression problem by rewriting the polynomial as: $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)\\ \quad\quad\quad\quad \phi(x) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x \\ x^2 \\ \vdots \\ x^K \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ Now the form of $f_{\theta}$ is $f_{\theta}(x) = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)$, which is a linear function in the parameters $\theta$. Therefore, if we featurize $x$, representing each datapoint $x$ with a feature vector $\phi(x)$, then we have arrived at a linear regression problem in this feature space. The learning problem and closed form optimizer for $L_2$ polynomial regression use a data matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$: $$\mathbf{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x^{(1)} & x^{(1)^2} & ... & x^{(1)^K} \\ 1 & x^{(2)} & x^{(2)^2} & ... & x^{(2)^K} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x^{(N)} & x^{(N)^2} & ... & x^{(N)^K} \\ \end{bmatrix}$$ The matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is an array of the features (columns) for each datapoint (rows). It plays the same role as the data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ in standard linear regression.
concepts.motivation_md: Polynomial regression allows models to capture non-linear relationships between variables while still utilizing the efficient, well-understood optimization tools of linear regression through feature transformation.
concepts.recap_md: - Hypothesis space consists of polynomial functions of degree $K$.

key_passage.text: Polynomial regression is just like linear regression except that the hypothesis space is polynomial functions rather than linear functions, that is, $y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$ where $K$, the degree of the polynomial, is a hyperparameter of the hypothesis space.

motivation.text: It turns out polynomial regression is highly related to linear regression; in fact, we can transform a polynomial regression problem into a linear regression problem!

concepts.title: Data Generating Process
concepts.one_liner: The data generating process is the full mechanism, including the true relationship and noise, that produces observed data.
concepts.content: The observed data $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ is sampled from a ground truth relationship plus observation noise. We refer to the full process that generates the data as the **data generating process**: $$\begin{aligned} Y &= X^2 + 1 &\triangleleft \quad\text{true underlying relationship}\\ \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) &\triangleleft \quad\text{observation noise}\\ Y^\prime &= Y + \epsilon &\triangleleft \quad\text{noisy observations}\\ x,y &\sim p(X,Y^{\prime}) &\triangleleft \quad\text{data-generating process} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between the true underlying signal and the noise in the data generating process is fundamental to building models that generalize to new, unseen data.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines a true underlying relationship with stochastic observation noise.

key_passage.text: We refer to the full process that generates the data as the data generating process: Y = X^2 + 1 (true underlying relationship), ε ~ N(0,1) (observation noise), Y' = Y + ε (noisy observations), x,y ~ p(X,Y') (data-generating process)

concepts.title: Approximation Error
concepts.one_liner: Approximation error is the total cost incurred by a model on the training data set.
concepts.content: **Approximation error** is the gap between the model's fit and the training data points. Let $\{x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ be our training data set. Then the approximation error $J_{\texttt{approx}}$ is defined as the total cost incurred on this training data: $$\begin{aligned} J_{\texttt{approx}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$ Notice that approximation error is the cost function we minimize in empirical risk minimization.
concepts.motivation_md: Approximation error measures how well a model can 'memorize' or fit the specific data points it was trained on, serving as the primary objective during the training phase.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents the average loss calculated over the training dataset.

key_passage.text: Approximation error is the gap between the black line and the training data points. Then the approximation error $J_{\texttt{approx}}$ is defined as the total cost incurred on this training data.

motivation.text: Notice that approximation error is the cost function we minimize in empirical risk minimization.

concepts.title: Generalization Error
concepts.one_liner: Generalization error is the expected cost incurred when applying a model to new test points from the data generating process.
concepts.content: **Generalization error** is the gap between the model's fit and the ground truth relationship, that is, the expected cost we would incur if we sampled a new test point at random from the true data generating process. Generalization error is often approximated by measuring performance on a heldout validation set, $\{x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, which can simply be a subset of the data that we don't use for training or testing: $$\begin{aligned} J_{\texttt{gen}} &= \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [ \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]\\ &\approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of machine learning is to perform well on unseen data, making generalization error the most important metric for assessing a model's real-world utility.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the expected loss over the entire data distribution.

key_passage.text: Generalization error is the gap between the black line and the green line, that is, the expected cost we would incur if we sampled a new test point at random from the true data generating process.

motivation.text: Generalization error is often approximated by measuring performance on a heldout, which can simply be a subset of the data that we don't use for training or testing

concepts.title: Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity to avoid overfitting.
concepts.content: **Regularization** refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity so that we avoid learning too flexible a function that overfits. Typically, regularizers are terms we add to the objective that prefer simple functions in the hypothesis space, all else being equal. They therefore embody the principle of **Occam's razor**. The general form of a regularized objective is: $$\begin{aligned} J(\theta) = \overbrace{\frac{1}{N} \sum^N_{i=1} \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x)^{(i)}, y^{(i)})}^\text{data fit loss} + \underbrace{\lambda R(\theta)}_\text{regularizer} \end{aligned}$$ where $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter that controls the strength of the regularization.
concepts.motivation_md: Regularization helps find a 'Goldilocks' model that is expressive enough to fit the data but simple enough to generalize well to new observations.
concepts.recap_md: - Adds a penalty term $R(\theta)$ to the loss function to discourage complexity.

key_passage.text: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity so that we avoid learning too flexible a function that overfits. Typically, regularizers are terms we add to the objective that prefer simple functions in the hypothesis space, all else being equal.

motivation.text: We should prefer hypotheses (functions f) that are sufficiently expressive to fit the data, but not so flexible that they can overfit the data.

concepts.title: Occam's Razor
concepts.one_liner: Occam's razor is the principle that when multiple functions explain the data, preference should be given to the simplest.
concepts.content: Regularization embodies the principle of **Occam's razor**. When multiple functions can explain the data, give preference to the simplest. In practice, this means penalizing function complexity to avoid learning too flexible a function that overfits, preferring simple functions in the hypothesis space all else being equal.
concepts.motivation_md: This philosophical principle provides a heuristic for model selection: simpler models are less likely to capture random noise and more likely to capture the underlying phenomenon.
concepts.recap_md: - Suggests that the simplest explanation for a set of observations is usually the best.

key_passage.text: Regularizers are terms we add to the objective that prefer simple functions in the hypothesis space, all else being equal. They therefore embody the principle of Occam's razor.

motivation.text: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity so that we avoid learning too flexible a function that overfits.

concepts.title: Lp Regularizer
concepts.one_liner: An Lp regularizer penalizes the Lp norm of the model parameters to encourage simpler functions.
concepts.content: One of the most common regularizers is to penalize the $L_p$ norm of the parameters of our model, $\theta$: $$ R(\theta) = \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_{p}. $$ The $L_p$-norm of $\mathbf{x}$ is $(\sum_i |x_i|^{p})^{\frac{1}{p}}$. An especially common choice is $p=2$, in which case the regularizer is also known as **Tikonov regression** (or weight decay in neural networks). When $p=1$, the regularizer applied to regression is called the Lasso. For any $p$, the effect is to encourage most parameters to be zero, or near zero. When most parameters are zero, the function takes on a simpler, degenerate form. For example, in a quadratic hypothesis space $\theta_1 x + \theta_2 x^2$, a strong $L_p$ regularizer might force $\theta_2$ to zero if a linear fit is sufficient, embodying Occam's razor by preferring the simpler linear function.
concepts.motivation_md: Lp regularization provides a mathematical way to enforce simplicity by shrinking parameter values, effectively performing feature selection or reducing model sensitivity.
concepts.recap_md: - Penalizes the magnitude of parameters using the $L_p$ norm.

key_passage.text: One of the most common regularizers is to penalize the $L_p$ norm of the parameters of our model, $\theta$: $$R(\theta) = \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_{p}.$$ The $L_p$-norm of $\mathbf{x}$ is $(\sum_i |x_i|^{p})^{\frac{1}{p}}$.

motivation.text: For any $p$, the effect is to encourage most parameters to be zero, or near zero. When most parameters are zero, the function takes on a degenerate form, that is, a simpler form.

concepts.title: Color Metamerism
concepts.one_liner: Two different light spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes because they produce the same projection onto our color matching functions.
concepts.content: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes. There is a large space of metamers: any two vectors describing light power spectra that give the same projection onto a set of color matching functions will look the same to our eyes. There's a high-dimensional space of light spectra, and we're only viewing projections onto a 3D subspace in the colors we see.
concepts.motivation_md: Because human color vision is a 3D projection of high-dimensional light spectra, many different physical light distributions can result in the exact same perceived color. Understanding metamerism is essential for color reproduction, as it explains why we can simulate a wide range of colors using only three primary lights.
concepts.recap_md:
- Metamerism occurs when different light spectra result in the same perceived color.
 - It is a consequence of the eye projecting high-dimensional spectra onto a 3D subspace.
 - Spectra are metameric if they yield the same values when integrated with color matching functions.

key_passage.text: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes. There is a large space of metamers: any two vectors describing light power spectra that give the same projection onto a set of color matching functions will look the same to our eyes.

motivation.text: There's a high-dimensional space of light spectra, and we're only viewing projections onto a 3D subspace in the colors we see.

concepts.title: Color Reproduction System
concepts.one_liner: A color reproduction system is defined by spectral sensitivity curves that are linear combinations of the eye's own sensitivity functions.
concepts.content:
We can define a color reproduction system by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. We put these into the $3 \times N$ matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, where $N$ is the number of spectral samples over the visible illumination range. The three curves, $\mathbf{C}$, should be a linear combination of the eye's spectral sensitivity curves, or $$\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \, \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}},$$ where $\mathbf{R}$ is any full-rank $3 \times 3$ matrix. We can translate between any two different color spaces by applying a general $3 \times 3$ matrix transformation to change basis vectors. Note, the basis vectors do not need to be orthogonal, and most color system basis vectors are not.

(see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$, giving sensor activations $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. Combinations of those activations drive the...)
concepts.motivation_md: To accurately capture and display colors, artificial systems (like cameras and screens) must relate their sensor and display properties to the human eye's biological response. This mathematical framework allows for consistent color translation across different devices.
concepts.recap_md:
- A color reproduction system is characterized by a $3 \times N$ matrix $\mathbf{C}$ of spectral sensitivity curves.
 - These curves must be a linear combination of the eye's sensitivity curves $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$.
 - Transformations between color spaces are achieved via $3 \times 3$ matrix multiplications.

key_passage.text: We can define a color reproduction system, by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. We put these into the 3 × N matrix, C, where N is the number of spectral samples over the visible illumination range.

motivation.text: We can translate between any two different color spaces by applying a general 3 × 3 matrix transformation to change basis vectors.

concepts.title: Primary Lights
concepts.one_liner: Primary lights are a set of three lights whose weighted sum is used to match the eye's response to a given light spectrum.
concepts.content: A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input light. A camera with a screen display is an example of a color reproduction system, as the colors of objects in the world are measured, then reproduced on the screen display of the camera. We can match the eye's response to a given light spectrum through the appropriate control of a sum of three lights, which we'll call the primary lights. For the example of a display screen, the three color elements of each pixel are the primary lights.
concepts.motivation_md: Since human vision is trichromatic, we do not need to reproduce a full spectrum to create a specific color sensation; we only need to control three independent light sources to match the eye's response.
concepts.recap_md:
- Primary lights are the basic light sources used by a system to reproduce colors.
 - Most systems use three primary lights to match the trichromatic nature of human vision.
 - Examples include the red, green, and blue sub-pixels on a digital display.

key_passage.text: We can match the eye's response to a given light spectrum through the appropriate control of a sum of three lights, which we'll call the primary lights.

motivation.text: A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input light. A camera with a screen display is an example of a color reproduction system, as the colors of objects in the world are measured, then reproduced on the screen display of the camera.

concepts.title: Gamut
concepts.one_liner: The gamut is the range of colors that can be produced by a positive combination of a given set of primary lights.
concepts.content: Because primary lights are restricted to positive values, some input colors are outside the gamut—the range of colors that can be produced—of a the positive combination of a given set of primary lights.
concepts.motivation_md: Physical light sources cannot have negative intensity. This constraint limits the variety of colors a specific device can display, making it important to define the boundaries of what a system can actually reproduce.
concepts.recap_md:
- The gamut represents the total range of colors a specific system can reproduce.
 - It is limited by the fact that primary light intensities must be non-negative.
 - Some visible colors may fall outside the gamut of a particular set of primaries.

key_passage.text: the range of colors that can be produced---of a the positive combination of a given set of primary lights.

motivation.text: some input colors are outside the gamut

concepts.title: CIE Color Space
concepts.one_liner: The CIE XYZ color space is a standard defined by all-positive color matching functions that are linear combinations of the eye's sensitivities.
concepts.content:
A color space is defined by the matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, with three rows of color sensitivity functions. These three sensitivity functions, $\mathbf{C}$, must be some linear combination of the sensitivity functions of the eye, $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$. One color standard is the Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage (CIE) *XYZ* color space, $C_{\mbox{CIE}}$. The CIE color matching functions, the rows of $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{CIE}}$ were designed to be all-positive at every wavelength and are shown in (Figure 1.1.6).

(see figure: CIE color matching functions @cie1931)
concepts.motivation_md: The CIE XYZ color space was created to provide a mathematically convenient, universal standard for color measurement where all coordinates are positive, avoiding the negative values found in some other color-matching experiments.
concepts.recap_md:
- The CIE XYZ color space is a standard based on human spectral sensitivity.
 - Its color matching functions are designed to be non-negative for all wavelengths.
 - It serves as a foundation for defining other color spaces and chromaticity.

key_passage.text: A color space is defined by the matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, with three rows of color sensitivity functions. One color standard is the Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage (CIE) *XYZ* color space, $C_{\mbox{CIE}}$. The CIE color matching functions, the rows of $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{CIE}}$ were designed to be all-positive at every wavelength.

concepts.title: CIE Chromaticity Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: CIE chromaticity coordinates are normalized tristimulus values that represent color while removing overall intensity variations.
concepts.content: To find the CIE color coordinates, one projects the input spectrum onto the three color-matching functions, to find coordinates, called tristimulus values, labeled $X$, $Y$, and $Z$. Often, these values are normalized to remove overall intensity variations, and one calculates CIE chromaticity coordinates $x = \frac{X}{X+Y+Z}$ and $y = \frac{Y}{X+Y+Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: It is often useful to separate the 'quality' of a color (its hue and saturation) from its brightness. Normalizing XYZ values into chromaticity coordinates allows us to map colors on a 2D plane regardless of their intensity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tristimulus values $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are found by projecting a spectrum onto CIE functions.
 - Chromaticity coordinates $x$ and $y$ are calculated by normalizing these values by their sum.
 - This normalization removes intensity, focusing on the chromatic components of the light.

key_passage.text: Often, these values are normalized to remove overall intensity variations, and one calculates CIE chromaticity coordinates x = X/(X+Y+Z) and y = Y/(X+Y+Z).

concepts.title: Learning as a Meta-Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Learning is a meta-algorithm that extracts lessons from past experience to output an algorithm for solving future problems.
concepts.content:
The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past experience in order to solve future problems. Typically, this involves searching for an algorithm that solves past instances of the problem. This algorithm can then be applied to future instances of the problem. Past and future do not necessarily refer to the calendar date; instead they refer to what the learner has previously seen and what the learner will see next. Because learning is itself an algorithm, it can be understood as a meta-algorithm: an algorithm that outputs algorithms.

(see figure: Learning is an algorithm that outputs algorithms.)
concepts.motivation_md: Instead of manually hard-coding a solution for every specific problem, we use learning to automatically discover the best solution (an algorithm) based on available data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning is a meta-algorithm because its output is itself an algorithm.
 - It uses past experience (training data) to find a solution for future instances.
 - The 'past' and 'future' are defined by the learner's sequence of observations.

key_passage.text: Because learning is itself an algorithm, it can be understood as a meta-algorithm: an algorithm that outputs algorithms.

motivation.text: The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past experience in order to solve future problems. Typically, this involves searching for an algorithm that solves past instances of the problem.

concepts.title: Training and Testing Phases
concepts.one_liner: Learning consists of a training phase to find a high-performing algorithm and a testing phase to solve new problem instances.
concepts.content: Learning usually consists of two phases: the training phase, where we search for an algorithm that performs well on past instances of the problem (training data), and the testing phase, where we deploy our learned algorithm to solve new instances of the problem.
concepts.motivation_md: To ensure that a learned solution actually works and hasn't just memorized specific examples, we must separate the process of finding the solution from the process of evaluating its performance on unseen data.
concepts.recap_md:
- The training phase involves searching for an algorithm using past data.
 - The testing phase evaluates the learned algorithm on new, unseen instances.
 - This separation is fundamental to assessing the generalization of a learner.

key_passage.text: Learning usually consists of two phases: the training phase, where we search for an algorithm that performs well on past instances of the problem (training data), and the testing phase, where we deploy our learned algorithm to solve new instances of the problem.

concepts.title: Light Field Cameras
concepts.one_liner: Light field cameras use an array of tiny lenses to capture a scene from hundreds of different viewing angles, similar to how raindrops refract panoramas.
concepts.content: When it rains, every raindrop refracts a panorama of the scene around it. What you are seeing is not just one photo but hundreds of images of the scene, one in each raindrop, all from slightly different angles. Specially designed cameras called light field cameras have been made that do the same thing. These cameras use an array of tiny lenses rather than raindrops to capture what the scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles. From that density of information, they can achieve many interesting tricks, such as triangulating the depth of objects in the scene and synthetically refocusing the image after it has been taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard cameras collapse light into a single 2D projection, losing directional information. Light field cameras solve this by capturing the 'light field'—the direction and intensity of light rays—allowing for post-capture adjustments like refocusing and depth estimation.
concepts.recap_md: - Light field cameras use micro-lens arrays to capture a scene from multiple simultaneous angles.

key_passage.text: These cameras use an array of tiny lenses rather than raindrops, but the result is similar: they capture what the scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles, and from that density of information they can achieve many interesting tricks, such as triangulating the depth of objects in the scene and synthetically refocusing the image after it has been taken.

motivation.text: specially designed cameras have been made that do the same thing, and they are called light field cameras. These cameras use an array of tiny lenses rather than raindrops, but the result is similar: they capture what the scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles, and from that density of information they can achieve many interesting tricks, such as triangulating the depth of objects in the scene and synthetically refocusing the image after it has been taken.

concepts.title: Plato's Cave Metaphor for Vision
concepts.one_liner: An image is a crude projection of reality that collapses 3D geometry into a 2D grid, much like the shadows in Plato's Allegory of the Cave.
concepts.content: In the Allegory of the Cave, Plato imagined a group of prisoners chained up in a cave whose only experience of the outside world is through shadows cast on the cave's wall. When we look at images, we think we are directly seeing reality, but the situation is actually much more like Plato's cave. An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state. It collapses all the 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid of pixels. From any given viewing angle, most of the scene is occluded. Materials are only depicted in terms of how photons bounce off their surfaces; what's below the surface may be completely omitted. When you look at a picture, there is more you don't see than you do. One job of a vision system is to infer everything you can't see given everything you can.
concepts.motivation_md: This metaphor highlights the fundamental challenge of computer vision: reconstructing a complex, 3D world from incomplete, 2D projections that omit significant physical information.
concepts.recap_md: - Images are 2D projections that collapse 3D geometry and occlude much of the physical scene.

key_passage.text: In the *Allegory of the Cave*, Plato imagined a group of prisoners chained up in a cave whose only experience of the outside world is through shadows cast on the cave's wall. When we look at images, we think we are directly seeing reality, but actually the situation is much more like Plato's cave. An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state.

motivation.text: One job of a vision system is to infer everything you can't see given everything you can.

concepts.title: Visual Cues for Wetness

position.section_title: How Do You Know Something Is Wet?

concepts.one_liner: The human visual system can recognize material properties like wetness without physical contact by interpreting visual cues such as changes in darkness and reflectance.
concepts.content: Our visual system allows us to recognize not just objects, but also material. We can tell if something will feel hot or cold, soft or hard, smooth or rugged. We can also recognize if something is wet or not without touching it. For example, sand looks darker when it's wet. This raises interesting questions for vision: Does everything wet look darker than when it is dry? How can we tell which parts of a surface are dark because they are wet and which ones are dark because they are under a shadow?
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how materials change appearance under different physical states (like wetness) is crucial for computer vision systems to accurately interpret surface properties and lighting conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual systems identify material states like wetness through indirect cues like surface darkness.
