concepts.title: Algorithmic Fairness
concepts.one_liner: Algorithmic Fairness is the study of algorithm performance across different people and cultures to address and mitigate biases.
concepts.content: The field of Algorithmic Fairness studies the performance and fairness of algorithms across people, groups, and cultures. It seeks to address algorithmic biases and to develop strategies to ensure that computer vision algorithms don't reflect or create biases against different groups of people or cultures.
concepts.motivation_md: As computer vision systems are deployed in society, it is critical to ensure they do not produce discriminatory outcomes or perform poorly for specific demographic groups.
concepts.recap_md: - This field focuses on identifying and mitigating biases in algorithmic performance across diverse groups.

key_passage.text: The field of Algorithmic Fairness studies the performance and fairness of algorithms across people, groups, and cultures.

motivation.text: It seeks to address algorithmic biases, and to develop strategies to ensure that computer vision algorithms don't reflect or create biases against different groups of people or cultures.

concepts.title: Demographic Bias in Facial Analysis
concepts.one_liner: Facial analysis systems often exhibit significant performance variations and false positive rates across different demographic groups defined by sex, age, and race.
concepts.content: Facial detection asks whether there is a face in some image region, while facial analysis refers to measuring additional attributes of the face, including pose and identity. It is important to characterize the performance of facial analysis systems across demographic groups. A large Face Recognition Vendor Test by NIST examined the accuracy of face recognition algorithms for different demographic groups defined by sex, age, and race or country of birth. For one dataset, they found false positive rates were highest in West and East African and East Asian people, and lowest in Eastern European individuals. For many systems, this effect was large, with differences of up to a factor of 100 in recognition false positive rates between different countries of birth. However, more accurate systems showed less bias, and some supplied identification algorithms where false positive differentials were undetectable. It is critical to report both false negative and false positive rates for each demographic group to understand the biases of any facial analysis system in use.
concepts.motivation_md: Facial recognition is used in high-stakes scenarios like law enforcement and security; understanding demographic bias is essential to prevent systemic discrimination and improve system reliability.
concepts.recap_md: - Facial analysis accuracy can vary by a factor of 100 across different demographic groups.

key_passage.text: A large Face Recognition Vendor Test by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) examined the accuracy of face recognition algorithms for different demographic groups defined by sex, age, and race or country of birth. For one dataset, they found false positive rates were highest in West and East African and East Asian people, and lowest in Eastern European individuals.

motivation.text: It is important to characterize the performance of facial analysis systems across demographic groups, as certain studies have done. It is clearly important to understand the biases of any facial analysis system that is put into use, as these characteristics can vary greatly from system to system.

concepts.title: Dataset Biases
concepts.one_liner: Algorithmic bias often stems from training datasets that represent only a narrow slice of the world, frequently favoring Western or high-income households.
concepts.content:
One cause of algorithmic bias can be a bias in the contents of the training dataset. Any dataset represents only one slice of the possible images and labels that one could capture from the world. Furthermore, the samples taken may be influenced by the background of the researchers gathering the dataset. For example, object recognition systems often perform much better for images from first-world households than for those from lower-income or non-Western regions, possibly due to better representation of high-income imagery in training sets.

(see figure: Images of household items, and their recognized classes by five object recognition systems @DeVries2019. The systems tend to perform worse for non-Western countries and for lower-income households...) 

As shown in (see figure: ...), systems tend to perform worse for household items from non-Western countries and lower-income households.
concepts.motivation_md: Machine learning models are only as good as their data; if training sets lack diversity, the resulting models will fail to generalize to global populations and diverse socioeconomic contexts.
concepts.recap_md: - Datasets often reflect the socioeconomic and geographic biases of their creators.

key_passage.text: One cause of algorithmic bias can be a bias in the contents of the training dataset. Any dataset represents only one slice of the possible images and labels that one could capture from the world.

motivation.text: There are many subtleties in the creation and labeling of computer vision datasets. Furthermore, the samples taken may well be influenced by the background of the researchers gathering the dataset.

concepts.title: GAN-based Dataset Debiasing
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can mitigate dataset bias by synthetically producing balanced image sets with controlled variations in protected attributes.
concepts.content:
One way to mitigate a biased dataset is to synthetically produce the images needed to provide the necessary balance or coverage. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) can operate on a dataset to generate sets of images similar to those of the dataset, but differing from each other in controlled ways, such as changes in the apparent gender, age, or race of depicted people. 

One approach, Fairness GAN, includes a classifier trained to perform as poorly as possible on predicting a protected attribute, such as skin tone, while maintaining accuracy on a target label like attractiveness. Another approach uses GANs to generate pairs of realistic images that are balanced with respect to protected attributes to remove unwanted correlations. For example, if "wearing hat" is correlated with "wearing glasses" in the data, the GAN can augment the dataset with paired examples of people wearing hats both with and without glasses. A third approach injects constraints to require that model predictions follow the distributions observed within training data, assuming that data has the desired distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Collecting perfectly balanced real-world data is often impossible; GANs provide a way to 'fill in the gaps' synthetically, ensuring models learn target features without relying on biased correlations.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs can generate synthetic data to balance representation of protected attributes like race or age.

key_passage.text: Generative adversarial networks (GANs), described in , can operate on a dataset to generate sets of images similar to those of the dataset, but differing from each other in controlled ways, for example, with changes in the apparent gender, age, or race of depicted people. Such GANs have been used to develop debiased datasets and algorithms.

motivation.text: One way to mitigate a biased dataset is to synthetically produce the images needed to provide the necessary balance or coverage.

concepts.title: Counterfactual Analysis with Transects
concepts.one_liner: Counterfactual transects use GANs to modify a single face variable at a time, allowing researchers to isolate and assess specific algorithmic biases.
concepts.content:
It may be difficult to distinguish whether a given biased result is caused by algorithmic bias or by biases in the testing dataset. One way to disentangle those is through experimentation: modifying variables of a probe image and examining the algorithm's decision. GAN models, coupled with human labeling to learn directions in the latent space corresponding to changes in desired attributes, allow for such experimental intervention. These counterfactual studies can lead to different conclusions than observational studies, which are often influenced by biased correlations in the testing dataset. Researchers use transects—paths through the GAN's latent space where only one face variable is modified—to provide a clean assessment of bias related to that specific variable.

(see figure: A GAN creates sequences of faces, called **transects**, where only one attribute changes @Balakrishnan2020)
concepts.motivation_md: Observational testing cannot prove why a model is biased; counterfactual analysis allows for controlled experiments to pinpoint exactly which attributes trigger biased model behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Transects are paths in a GAN's latent space that vary exactly one attribute while keeping others constant.

key_passage.text: paths through the GAN's latent space where only one face variable is modified. The variation in an algorithm's classification results along the images of the transect provides a clean assessment of any bias related to the variable being modified.

motivation.text: It may be difficult to distinguish whether a given biased result is caused by algorithmic bias or by biases in the testing dataset. One way to disentangle those is through experimentation, that is, modifying variables of a probe image and examining the algorithm's decision.

concepts.title: Learning with a Perceptron

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A perceptron learns by adjusting weights and bias to minimize a classification loss that scores the number of misclassifications.
concepts.content:
A perceptron acts like a classifier that can learn from data. Given a dataset $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, we adjust the weights $\mathbf{w}$ and the bias $b$ to minimize a classification loss, $\mathcal{L}$, that scores the number of misclassifications:

$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{w}^*, b^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\mathbf{w}, b} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b, y^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$

This optimization process corresponds to shifting and rotating the decision boundary until a line is found that separates data labeled as $y = 0$ from data labeled as $y = 1$.

(see figure: Different possible decision surfaces of a perceptron.)

While the original perceptron paper proposed a specific "perceptron learning algorithm," modern approaches typically use general-purpose optimizers. For differentiable objectives, gradient descent is used, while zeroth-order methods are preferred for nondifferentiable objectives like the threshold function used in the standard perceptron objective.
concepts.motivation_md: To use a perceptron as a practical classifier, we need a systematic way to find the weights and bias that best separate different classes of data. Learning provides a mathematical framework to optimize these parameters based on training examples.
concepts.recap_md: - Learning involves minimizing a classification loss $\mathcal{L}$ by adjusting weights $\mathbf{w}$ and bias $b$.

key_passage.text: The idea is that given data, we will adjust the weights and the bias, in order to minimize a classification loss, that scores the number of misclassifications.

question.text: So a perceptron acts like a classifier, but how can we use it to learn?

motivation.text: The original perceptron paper proposed one particular algorithm, the "perceptron learning algorithm." This was an optimizer tailored to the specific structure of the perceptron.

concepts.title: Multilayer Perceptron
concepts.one_liner: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) is a network of neurons arranged in layers that can produce multiple outputs and solve non-linearly separable problems.
concepts.content:
Perceptrons can solve linearly separable binary classification problems, but they are limited. We can achieve multiple outputs by adding edges that fan out after the perceptron.

(see figure: Multiple outputs fan out from a neuron.)

This network maps an input layer of data $\mathbf{x}$ to a layer of outputs $\mathbf{y}$. The neurons in between inputs and outputs are called hidden units. For example, $h = g(z)$ where $z$ is a hidden unit and $g(\cdot)$ is an activation function. More commonly, many hidden units are stacked in a multilayer perceptron (MLP).

(see figure: Mutilayer perceptron.)

The equation for this MLP is:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} &= \mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}\\
    \mathbf{h} &= g(\mathbf{z}) &\triangleleft \quad \text{activation function}\\
    \mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{b}_2 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}
\end{aligned}$$

MLPs can be constructed with any number of layers following the pattern of linear layer and activation function. The activation function $g$ can be any pointwise nonlinearity $\tilde{g}$ that maps $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. This sequence is the prototypical motif in almost all neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: Single perceptrons are limited to linear classification and single outputs. MLPs overcome these limitations by stacking layers, allowing the network to learn complex, non-linear mappings and handle multiple output variables simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md: - An MLP consists of interleaved linear layers and pointwise activation functions.

key_passage.text: Because this network has multiple layers of neurons, and because each neuron in this net acts as a perceptron, we call it a multilayer perceptron (MLP). The equation for this MLP is: z = W₁x + b₁ (linear layer), h = g(z) (activation function), y = W₂h + b₂ (linear layer)

question.text: How many layers does this net have?

motivation.text: Perceptrons can solve linearly separable binary classification problems, but they are otherwise rather limited. For one, they only produce a single output. What if we want multiple outputs?

concepts.title: Activations and Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations are the values neurons take on as data is processed, while parameters are the weights and biases learned by the network.
concepts.content:
In deep nets, it is useful to distinguish between activations and parameters. The activations are the values that the neurons take on, denoted as a sequence $[\mathbf{x}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L]$, where $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the raw input data. These represent the neural representations of the data being processed.

[FIGURE:e4b298598d24ed71 | A multilayer network is a sequence of transformations $f_1, \ldots, f_L$ that produce a series of activations $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.]

Conversely, parameters are the weights and biases of the network, which are the variables being learned. Both activations and parameters are tensors. Each layer can be viewed as a function:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_{l+1} = f_{l+1}(\mathbf{x}_{l}, \theta_{l+1})
\end{aligned}$$
Each layer takes activations from the previous layer and parameters of the current layer to produce the next set of activations. This perspective allows for tricks like network prompting or visualization, where parameters are held fixed while activations are optimized.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between the data flowing through the network (activations) and the internal settings of the network (parameters) is essential for understanding how neural networks process information and how they are trained.
concepts.recap_md: - Activations are the neural representations of data as it passes through the network layers.

key_passage.text: The activations are the values that the neurons take on, $[\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{h}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{z}_{L-1}, \mathbf{h}_{L-1}, \mathbf{y}]$; slightly abusing notation, we use this term for both preactivation function neurons and postactivation function neurons. Conversely, parameters are the weights and biases of the network. These are the variables being learned.

motivation.text: From this perspective, anything we can do with parameters, we can do with activations instead, and vice versa, and that is the basis for a lot of applications and tricks.

concepts.title: Fast Activations and Slow Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations are fast functions of individual datapoints, whereas parameters are slow functions learned from entire datasets.
concepts.content: Activations and parameters differ in their relationship to data. Activations are "fast" functions of a datapoint, resulting from a few layers of processing that specific input. Parameters are also functions of data, but they are "slow" functions of datasets, arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset. Both are statistics of the data: parameters act as a metasummary specifying a functional transformation, while activations are a summary of the individual datapoint.
concepts.motivation_md: This distinction helps conceptualize the different timescales and scales of data involved in neural network operations: inference (fast, per-point) versus training (slow, per-dataset).
concepts.recap_md: - Activations change with every new input datapoint processed by the network.

key_passage.text: One way to think about it is that activations are *fast* functions of a data*point*: they are the result of a few layers of processing this datapoint. Parameters are *also* functions of the data (they are learned from data) but they are *slow* functions of data*sets*: the parameters are arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset.

motivation.text: So, both activations and parameters are statistics of the data, that is, information extracted about about the data that organizes or summarizes it. The parameters are a kind of metasummary since they specify a functional transformation that produces activations from data, and activations themselves are a summary of the data.

concepts.title: Deep Nets
concepts.one_liner: Deep nets are neural networks that stack the linear-nonlinear motif many times to perform complex nonlinear mappings.
concepts.content:
Deep nets are neural nets that stack the linear-nonlinear motif many times.

(see figure: Deep nets consist of linear layers interleaved with nonlinearities.)

Each layer is a function, making a deep net a composition of many functions:
$$\begin{aligned}
    f(\mathbf{x}) = f_{L}(f_{L-1}(\ldots f_2(f_1(\mathbf{x}))))
\end{aligned}$$
where $L$ is the number of layers. These functions are parameterized by weights $[\mathbf{W}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{W}_L]$ and biases $[\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_L]$, collectively referred to as $\theta$. Deep nets are powerful because they can perform nonlinear mappings; with sufficiently many neurons, they can fit almost any desired function arbitrarily closely.
concepts.motivation_md: By composing many simple functions, deep nets can represent highly complex, non-linear relationships that shallower architectures cannot easily capture.
concepts.recap_md: - A deep net is a composition of $L$ functions, each representing a layer.

key_passage.text: Deep nets are neural nets that stack the linear-nonlinear motif many times. Each layer is a function. Therefore, a deep net is a composition of many functions: f(x) = f_L(f_{L-1}(...f_2(f_1(x))))

motivation.text: Deep nets are powerful because they can perform nonlinear mappings. In fact, a deep net with sufficiently many neurons can fit almost any desired function arbitrarily closely.

concepts.title: Rectified linear unit (relu)
concepts.one_liner: The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is a pointwise nonlinearity that yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, facilitating gradient-based learning.
concepts.content: The Rectified linear unit (relu) is a pointwise nonlinearity. It acts as a graded version of a threshold function. Its primary advantage is that it yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, making it highly amenable to gradient-based learning methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional threshold functions have zero gradients almost everywhere, which prevents gradient descent from working. ReLU provides a non-linear activation that still allows gradients to flow during training.
concepts.recap_md: - ReLU is defined as a graded threshold function that is differentiable over half its domain.

key_passage.text: the Rectified linear unit (relu), which is like a graded version of a threshold function

motivation.text: it yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, thus being amenable to gradient-based learning

concepts.title: Universal approximation theorem
concepts.one_liner: The universal approximation theorem states that a neural network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary precision.
concepts.content: The universal approximation theorem states that deep nets can, in principle, perform any continuous input-output mapping. This holds true even for a network with just a single hidden layer, provided the number of neurons in that layer is sufficiently large to fit complicated functions. Technically, this theorem applies to continuous functions on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^N$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the theoretical justification for using neural networks as general-purpose function approximators, ensuring that they are capable of representing the complex patterns found in real-world data.
concepts.recap_md: - A single hidden layer is sufficient to approximate any continuous function given enough neurons.

key_passage.text: The universal approximation theorem states that this is true even for a network with just a single hidden layer.

motivation.text: Not only can deep nets perform nonlinear classification, they can in principle perform any continuous input-output mapping.

concepts.title: Intuition for Universal Approximation
concepts.one_liner: Universal approximation works because a relu-MLP can represent a sum of indicator functions, which can approximate any curve.
concepts.content:
To understand universal approximation, consider approximating a function $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with a relu-MLP. Any function can be approximated by a sum of indicator functions (bumps):
$$\begin{aligned}
    f(x) \approx \sum_i w_i \mathbb{1}(\alpha_i < x < \beta_i)
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Any function from $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ can be approximated arbitrarily well by a sum of elementary bumps.)

A relu-MLP can represent these bumps. While the weighted sum is handled by a linear layer, a single bump $\mathbb{1}(\alpha < x < \beta)$ can be approximated using four relu units:
$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{1}(\alpha < x < \beta) \approx \\
&\texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-(\alpha-\gamma)}{\gamma}\bigg) - \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-\alpha}{\gamma}\bigg) - \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-(\beta-\gamma)}{\gamma}\bigg) + \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-\beta}{\gamma}\bigg)
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: A bump can be represented as a weighted sum of shifted and scaled relu functions.)

As $\gamma \rightarrow 0$, the approximation becomes exact. A `linear`-`relu`-`linear` network can implement this construction. By summing many such bumps, a single hidden layer network can approximate any curve to arbitrary precision, though the number of neurons required may be unbounded.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing how simple ReLU functions can be combined to create 'bumps' helps demystify how neural networks transform simple linear inputs into complex, arbitrary function approximations.
concepts.recap_md: - Any continuous function can be decomposed into a sum of small 'bumps' or indicator functions.

key_passage.text: First observe that any function can be approximated arbitrarily well by a sum of indicator functions, that is, bumps placed at different positions. As the width, β−α, of the bumps goes to zero, the error in the fit goes to zero.

motivation.text: Here we show how a neural net can represent a function as a sum of basis functions. This idea is also foundational in signal processing, where signals are often represented as a sum of sine waves, boxes, or trapezoids.

concepts.title: Regularizers as Probabilistic Priors
concepts.one_liner: Regularizers can be interpreted as probabilistic priors that prefer certain solutions over others before looking at the data.
concepts.content: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others. Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$. Bayes' rule then states that the posterior $p(\theta \bigm | \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1})$ is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood. The log posterior is then the sum of the log likelihood and the log prior, plus a constant. Hence we arrive at the form of a regularized objective.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides a formal probabilistic foundation for regularization. By viewing regularizers as priors, we can use Bayesian inference to justify why we penalize certain model parameters and how to balance our pre-existing beliefs with observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - Regularizers act as a prior $p(\theta)$ that encodes preferences for specific types of solutions.

key_passage.text: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others. Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$. The log posterior is then the sum of the log likelihood and the log prior, plus a constant.

motivation.text: Bayes' rule then states that the posterior $p(\theta \bigm | \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1})$ is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood.

concepts.title: Bayesian Occam's Razor
concepts.one_liner: The Bayesian Occam's razor suggests that simpler hypotheses are more likely because complex hypothesis spaces must spread their prior probability mass more thinly.
concepts.content: The notion of the Bayesian Occam's razor derives priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis. This follows from the requirement that the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1. This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a mathematical justification for the principle of parsimony, explaining why we should prefer simpler models unless the data strongly suggests otherwise.
concepts.recap_md: - Complex hypothesis spaces assign less prior mass to individual hypotheses because the total probability must sum to 1.

key_passage.text: The notion of the Bayesian Occam's razor derives such priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis (the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1).

motivation.text: This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.

concepts.title: Model Capacity and Generalization
concepts.one_liner: Model capacity refers to the expressivity of a hypothesis space, for which the number of parameters is only a rough proxy.
concepts.content: The number of parameters in a model is a rough proxy for model capacity (i.e., the expressivity of the hypothesis space), but it is not the full story. A single parameter with infinite numerical precision can parameterize an arbitrarily complex function and overfit data. Conversely, a model with a million parameters that are heavily regularized (e.g., forced to be zero) may define a simple class of functions that does not overfit. Recent empirical findings show that complex hypothesis spaces like deep nets often do not overfit despite having many more parameters than datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that capacity is not just about parameter count helps explain why massive models like deep neural networks can generalize well when properly regularized.
concepts.recap_md: - Model capacity measures the expressivity of a hypothesis space.

key_passage.text: The number of parameters is just a rough proxy for model capacity (i.e., the expressivity of the hypothesis space).

motivation.text: A recent empirical finding is that some seemingly complex hypothesis spaces, such as deep nets (which we will see in later chapters), tend not to overfit, even though they have many more free parameters than the number of datapoints they are fit to.

concepts.title: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses as Search Tools

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Learning can be viewed as a search for truth using three primary tools: data, priors, and hypotheses.
concepts.content:
Learning is akin to searching for a "needle in a haystack," where the needle is the true function and the haystack is the hypothesis space. Three tools help pinpoint this truth:

1. **Data**: Observations of the world (e.g., photos) that prefer mappings fitting the observed evidence.
2. **Priors**: Regularizers that prefer some solutions over others a priori.
3. **Hypotheses**: The set of functions under consideration ($\mathcal{F}$), which places a hard constraint on what can be found.

(see figure: A cartoon of the tools for honing in on the truth.)

In this framework, the hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ (white circle) acts as a hard constraint, while the prior (yellow ellipse) and data (green ellipse) act as soft constraints. A learning algorithm searches over $\mathcal{F}$ to maximize the likelihood times the prior, finding a solution in the region where these constraints overlap. While approximation error is low in the data-fitting region, we bias our selection toward the prior's region to improve generalization.
concepts.motivation_md: This framework helps students visualize how different components of machine learning (architecture, regularization, and dataset) interact to isolate a single model from an infinite space of possibilities.
concepts.recap_md: - The hypothesis space provides a hard constraint on possible solutions.

key_passage.text: We have several tools at our disposal to help us pinpoint the location of the needle, and in this section we will focus on the following three: data, priors, and hypotheses. Together these three tools allow us to pinpoint one (or a few) good solutions in the space of all possibilities.

question.text: "Why are you looking there," a cop asks.

motivation.text: In vision, the data is observations of the world like photos and videos. Finding explanations consistent with the observed data is the centerpiece of learning-based vision. The hypothesis space constrains which solutions we can possibly find. If the true solution is not in our hypothesis space, then no amount of data or priors can help us find it.

concepts.title: The Trade-off Between Data and Modeling Tools

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: There is a fundamental trade-off where more data reduces the need for strong priors and structural constraints.
concepts.content: A central principle in learning is that the more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools. With enough data, the true solution can be pinpointed by data alone. However, when data is scarce, noisy, or incorrectly labeled, we rely on priors and hypothesis space constraints. These three tools—data, priors, and hypotheses—can constrain the search in similar ways, leading to the principle that what can be achieved with one tool can often be achieved with another. Note that the hypothesis space imposes hard constraints, while data and priors impose soft constraints that can be violated at the cost of a penalty. As Ilya Sutskever noted, many methods are essentially "extra training data in disguise."
concepts.motivation_md: This explains why domain expertise (priors/hypotheses) is critical in small-data regimes, whereas massive datasets allow for more flexible, less biased models.
concepts.recap_md: - Increasing data volume decreases the necessity for strong priors or structural constraints.

key_passage.text: The more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools. With enough data, the true solution will be pinpointed by data alone. However, when we don't have enough data, or when the data is noisy or incorrectly labeled, we can turn to our two other tools, which we will see next.

motivation.text: If you don't have much data, you can use strong priors and structural constraints instead. If you don't have much domain knowledge, you can collect lots of data instead.

concepts.title: Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: Neural networks are functions loosely modeled on the brain's network of interconnected neurons.
concepts.content:
Neural networks are functions loosely modeled on the brain. In the brain, billions of neurons connect to one another, where each neuron can be thought of as a node in a graph and the edges are the connections between them.

(see figure: A neural network can be drawn as a directed graph.)

These edges are directed, meaning electrical signals propagate in one direction. Outgoing edges are called axons and incoming edges are called dendrites. A neuron fires, sending a pulse down its axon, when the incoming pulses from the dendrites exceed a certain threshold.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks provide a flexible, biologically-inspired architecture for approximating complex functions by composing simple processing units.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural networks are directed graphs of nodes representing neurons and edges representing connections.

key_passage.text: Neural networks are functions loosely modeled on the brain. In the brain, we have billions of neurons that connect to one another. Each neuron can be thought of as a node in a graph, and the edges are the connections from one neuron to the next.

concepts.title: Perceptron

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A perceptron is a simple model of a single neuron that outputs a binary signal based on a weighted sum of its inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron serves as the fundamental building block of neural networks, demonstrating how linear combinations and non-linear thresholds can perform basic computation.
concepts.recap_md: - A perceptron computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, then applies a step-function activation.

key_passage.text: A perceptron is a neuron with n inputs {x_i}_{i=1}^n and one output y, that maps inputs to outputs according to the following equations: z = f(x) = sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b = w^T x + b; g(z) = 1, if z > 0; 0, otherwise; y = g(f(x)).

motivation.text: In words, we take a weighted sum of the inputs and, if that sum exceeds a threshold (here 0), the neuron fires (outputs a 1).

concepts.title: The Perceptron as a Classifier

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: Perceptrons can function as binary classifiers by splitting the input space into two regions.
concepts.content:
Perceptrons can learn to classify data by assigning class labels based on their output. For example, consider a perceptron with two inputs, $x_1$ and $x_2$, weights $w_1 = 2$, $w_2 = 1$, and bias $b=0$.

(see figure: Value of hidden unit ($z$) and output unit ($y$) in a perceptron, as a function of the input data.)

As shown in the figure, the output $y$ takes on values 0 or 1. This effectively creates a classifier that assigns a class label of 1 to the upper-right half of the plotted region and 0 to the other half.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept demonstrates the practical utility of the perceptron as a geometric decision-maker, showing how it can solve simple classification problems.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptrons act as linear classifiers that divide the input space into two classes.

key_passage.text: Notice that $y$ takes on values 0 or 1, so you can think of this as a classifier that assigns a class label of 1 to the upper-right half of the plotted region.

motivation.text: People got excited about perceptrons in the late 1950s because it was shown that they can learn to classify data.

concepts.title: Tree shadows and image formation
concepts.one_liner: The small openings between tree leaves act as pinhole cameras, projecting circular images of the sun onto the ground.
concepts.content: When walking under the shadow of a tree on a bright sunny day, light rays pass through the holes between leaves, creating spots on the floor. While one might expect these spots to have irregular shapes matching the openings, they appear circular and of similar size. This phenomenon occurs because the spacing between the leaves forms pinhole cameras. These tiny holes project copies of the sun onto the floor; when the openings are small enough, the shape of the projected light is dominated by the shape of the sun rather than the shape of the opening. This is clearly demonstrated during a solar eclipse, where the shadow of a tree contains many crescent-shaped copies of the sun.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains a common but often overlooked optical phenomenon, illustrating how simple apertures in nature can function as imaging systems (pinhole cameras) that project the shape of a light source.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaps between tree leaves act as natural pinhole cameras.
 - The circular spots seen in tree shadows are actually projected images of the sun.
 - During an eclipse, these spots change shape to match the sun's crescent profile.

key_passage.text: The tiny holes between the leaves of a tree create a multitude of pinholes. The pinholes created by the leaves project different copies of the sun on the floor. When the openings between leaves are small enough, the shape of the projected spot light is dominated by the shape of the sun.

question.text: What could be happening?

motivation.text: We would expect that the spots of light would have irregular shapes as the openings between leaves will have all kinds of irregular profiles. Instead, as shown in the passage, the spots appear to be circular and of similar size.

concepts.title: Pinhole camera
concepts.one_liner: A pinhole camera is an optical system where a small aperture projects an image of a light source onto a surface.
concepts.content: Pinhole cameras can be formed by the spacing between the leaves of a tree. The tiny holes between the leaves create a multitude of pinholes that project different copies of the sun on the floor. When the openings between leaves are small enough, the shape of the projected spot light is dominated by the shape of the sun rather than the shape of the aperture itself.
concepts.motivation_md: Pinhole cameras represent the simplest form of image formation, demonstrating how light traveling in straight lines through a small point can create a coherent image without lenses.
concepts.recap_md:
- Small apertures project the shape of the light source onto a surface.
 - The resulting image shape is dominated by the source (e.g., the sun) if the hole is small enough.
 - Natural examples include gaps between leaves in a tree canopy.

key_passage.text: The tiny holes between the leaves of a tree create a multitude of pinholes. The pinholes created by the leaves project different copies of the sun on the floor.

motivation.text: When the openings between leaves are small enough, the shape of the projected spot light is dominated by the shape of the sun. This is something we see often but rarely think about the origin of the spotlights that we see on the floor.

concepts.title: Perceiving horizontal and vertical surfaces
concepts.one_liner: The perception of a surface as horizontal or vertical is driven by the orientation of vanishing points and the resulting horizon line.
concepts.content: The perception of surface orientation, such as distinguishing between a floor and a wall, depends on the arrangement of vanishing points—the points where parallel lines appear to intersect. In a drawing of a horizontal surface, vanishing points are typically located above the drawing, compatible with a horizontal horizon line. Conversely, if a vanishing point is located below the figure, it can give the impression of looking at a vertical wall from a high camera angle. The horizon line of the plane, which connects the vanishing points, appears horizontal for ground surfaces and vertical for certain wall orientations, significantly altering how the viewer perceives the scene's geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how we perceive orientation helps explain how the human visual system and computer vision algorithms reconstruct 3D geometry from 2D images using perspective cues.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points are the locations where parallel lines appear to intersect in a 2D projection.
 - A horizontal horizon line connecting vanishing points suggests a horizontal surface like a floor.
 - The relative position of vanishing points determines whether a surface is perceived as vertical or horizontal.

key_passage.text: In the arrangement in the left, there are two vanishing points (the points in which parallel lines intersect) and both are above the drawing, compatible with the horizon line. However, on the drawing on the right, one of the vanishing points is below the figure and gives the impression that the camera is looking at a vertical wall (the camera seems to be higher than the visible part of the wall). The horizon line of the plane (the line that connects both vanishing points) is horizontal in the left drawing and vertical on the right one.

question.text: How do you know you are looking at a picture of the ground? How do you know the orientation of the camera?

motivation.text: The differences in the line orientations are subtle and yet it produces a very different perception.

concepts.title: Vanishing points
concepts.one_liner: Vanishing points are the points in a perspective drawing or image where parallel lines appear to intersect.
concepts.content: Vanishing points are the points in which parallel lines intersect in a projection. The arrangement of these points defines the horizon line of a plane (the line that connects both vanishing points). The position of these points relative to the image frame—whether they are above, below, or to the side—determines the perceived orientation of surfaces and the camera's viewpoint relative to those surfaces.
concepts.motivation_md: Vanishing points are fundamental to perspective projection, allowing 3D depth and orientation to be encoded into and recovered from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points are where parallel lines meet in perspective.
 - The line connecting two vanishing points on a plane forms that plane's horizon line.
 - Their location informs the viewer about the camera's orientation and height.

key_passage.text: the points in which parallel lines intersect

concepts.title: Understanding motion blur
concepts.one_liner: Motion blur occurs when a camera sensor collects light while moving, resulting in an average of translated image copies.
concepts.content: When taking a picture from a moving vehicle, images often appear blurry because the camera sensor collects light over a period of time while the car is in motion. The resulting picture is the average of several translated copies of the same image. Notably, the amount of blur is not uniform for all objects; things that are far away may remain sharp, while nearby objects appear very blurry. This blur is determined by the car's speed, the camera's exposure time, and the distance between the camera and the objects in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion blur is a critical concept in both photography and computer vision, as it provides cues about the relative depth of objects and the velocity of the observer.
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion blur is the temporal average of translated images during sensor exposure.
 - Nearby objects experience more motion blur than distant objects.
 - Blur intensity depends on speed, exposure time, and object distance.

key_passage.text: Blur is due to the fact that the camera sensor is collecting light during a period of time while the car is moving and the picture that results is the average of several translated copies of the same image.

motivation.text: When we are in a moving car and we take a picture from the passenger window, often images will appear blurring, especially when taken at night.

concepts.title: Accidents and the principle of continuity
concepts.one_liner: The principle of continuity suggests that smooth, continuous line segments likely belong to a single object rather than being a coincidental alignment.
concepts.content:
The principle of continuity, a concept from Gestalt psychology, posits that if you see smooth, continuous line segments, you assume they lie on a single object. This is based on the idea that it would be a significant coincidence for the contours of two separate objects to perfectly align. While the generic view principle suggests we should avoid interpreting scenes based on such "accidents," real photographs often contain coincidences due to the sheer complexity and number of elements they contain. For example, in Dorothea Lange's "Migrant Mother," one can find instances where a finger boundary aligns with a lip contour or creases on two different shirts align perfectly. Rule-based vision algorithms often fail when they do not account for these exceptions to the principle of continuity.

[FIGURE:2962e76f5808a7be]

Despite this, other groupings are also possible.

[FIGURE:d7efe27713f24942]
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the tension between perceptual rules (like Gestalt principles) and the reality of visual 'accidents' or coincidences, which is vital for building robust computer vision systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- The principle of continuity assumes continuous lines belong to the same object.
 - 'Accidents' occur when unrelated object contours coincidentally align from a specific viewpoint.
 - Vision algorithms must handle these coincidences to avoid errors in object segmentation.

key_passage.text: generically, if you see smooth, continuous line segments you assume that they lie on a single object because it's quite a coincidence for two objects to line up just so their contours perfectly align. The gestalt psychologists called this the principle of continuity.

question.text: Can you find more?

motivation.text: You have to be careful about this when developing vision algorithms. If you assume no accidents will happen, then you will be in for some trouble. This is one reason why older, rule-based methods failed, because they did not handle exceptions to the rules.

concepts.title: Principle of continuity
concepts.one_liner: The principle of continuity is a Gestalt rule stating that aligned contours are perceived as belonging to the same object.
concepts.content: The principle of continuity is a concept from Gestalt psychology which suggests that when contours or line segments perfectly align, the visual system assumes they lie on a single object. This is because it is considered a rare coincidence for two separate objects to align their boundaries so perfectly from a generic viewpoint.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle is a fundamental heuristic used by the brain to organize visual information and segment objects from their background.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is a Gestalt principle for visual grouping.
 - It assumes that continuous, smooth lines represent a single continuous object.
 - It helps resolve ambiguity in complex visual scenes.

key_passage.text: The gestalt psychologists called this the principle of continuity.

concepts.title: Cues for Support
concepts.one_liner: The relative location of an object and its shadow serves as a powerful visual cue for determining physical contact and support.
concepts.content: Determining whether one object supports another often relies on specific visual cues. The relative location between an object and its shadow on the ground is a powerful cue for contact; for instance, a drop shadow can indicate that a ball is hovering above a surface, while a slack string or the specific placement of a shadow can provide evidence that the ball is in contact with the surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying support relationships is essential for understanding the physical structure and stability of a 3D scene from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Shadows provide strong cues about the distance between an object and a surface.
 - Contact is perceived when the object and its shadow meet.
 - Other physical cues, like strings or points of contact, help confirm support relationships.

key_passage.text: When can we tell by looking that one object supports another? Consider the ball over a surface depicted in. The drop shadow provides a strong cue that the ball is above the surface in (a) and (c), while the slack string provides evidence for the ball being on the surface in figures (b) and (c).

question.text: In which of these figures does the ball appear to be in contact with the ground plane?

concepts.title: Paraxial Approximation
concepts.one_liner: The paraxial approximation assumes that deviations in angle from the optical axes are very small.
concepts.content:
Fig (a) The geometry of a thin lens. (b) Showing the labels of adding angles referenced in table @tbl-lensmaker, used to describe the conditions for the lens shape, $\theta_S$ to give the desired focusing. Geometry is distorted for visibility.

In imaging systems, the paraxial approximation is the assumption that the deviations in angle from the optical axes are very small. Under this approximation, along with the thin lens approximation, we can write simple expressions for the bending angles shown in @fig-lens-b as a function of $\theta_S$, the lens surface orientation at height $c$. These relations are summarized in the table below.

| **Angle** | **Description** | **Relation** | **Reason** |
|-----------|-----------------|--------------|------------|
| $\theta_1$ | Initial angle from optical axis | $\theta_1 = c/a$ | Small angle approx. |
| $\theta_2$ | Angle of refracted ray wrt front surface normal | $n \theta_2 = \theta_1 + \theta_S$ | Snell's law, small angle approx. |
| $\theta_3$ | Angle of refracted ray wrt back surface normal | $2 \theta_S  = \theta_2 + \theta_3$ | Symmetry of lens, thin lens approx. |
| $\theta_4 + \theta_S$ | Angle of ray exiting lens wrt back surface normal | $n \theta_3 = \theta_4+\theta_S$ | Snell's law, small angle approx. |
| $\theta_4$ | Final angle from optical axis | $\theta_4 = c/b$ | Small angle approx. |
concepts.motivation_md: This approximation simplifies the trigonometric functions in Snell's law (where $\sin \theta \approx \theta$), allowing for linear equations that make the analysis of complex optical systems mathematically tractable.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes light rays deviate only slightly from the optical axis.

key_passage.text: the deviations in angle from the optical axes are very small (i.e., the paraxial approximation)

motivation.text: Under those approximations, we can write simple expressions for the bending angles shown in a figure a function of θ_S, the lens surface orientation at height c.

concepts.title: Thin Lens Approximation
concepts.one_liner: The thin lens approximation models a lens as having negligible thickness compared with other distances along the optical axis.
concepts.content:
Fig (a) The geometry of a thin lens. (b) Showing the labels of adding angles referenced in table @tbl-lensmaker, used to describe the conditions for the lens shape, $\theta_S$ to give the desired focusing. Geometry is distorted for visibility.

The thin lens approximation models the lens as having negligible thickness compared with other distances along the optical axis. Under this approximation, and the paraxial approximation, we can write simple expressions for the bending angles shown in @fig-lens-b as a function of $\theta_S$, the lens surface orientation at height $c$. These relations are summarized in the table below.

| **Angle** | **Description** | **Relation** | **Reason** |
|-----------|-----------------|--------------|------------|
| $\theta_1$ | Initial angle from optical axis | $\theta_1 = c/a$ | Small angle approx. |

concepts.motivation_md: By ignoring the physical thickness of the lens, we can treat refraction as occurring at a single plane, which greatly simplifies the calculation of focal points and image positions.
