motivation.text: What if our data and activations are high-dimensional? The plots above only can visualize 1D and 2D data distributions. Deep representations are typically much higher-dimensional than this, and to visualize them, we need to apply tools from dimensionality reduction.

concepts.title: Disentangled Representation
concepts.one_liner: Disentangled representation occurs when a network reorganizes data so that different semantic classes become cleanly separated in representational space.
concepts.content: Layer by layer, deep nets transform data from its raw format to ever more abstracted and useful representations. This process can be viewed as a set of geometric transformations or as a kind of disentangling where initially messy data gets reorganized so that different data classes become cleanly separated. In a disentangled representation, each semantic class occupies a different part of the representational space. This is often observed in the final layers of a network, especially if the network has been trained to output a direct representation of semantics, such as through contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP).
concepts.motivation_md: Raw data is often 'tangled,' with different classes overlapping in complex ways. Disentangling these classes into distinct regions of space makes it easier for the model to perform classification or downstream tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Deep nets transform raw data into abstracted, disentangled representations.

key_passage.text: It can be helpful to think about this process as a set of geometric transformations of a data distribution, or as a kind of disentangling where initially messy data gets reorganized so that different data classes become cleanly separated.

motivation.text: Layer by layer, deep nets transform data from its raw format to ever more abstracted and useful representations. This is expected because the final layer in this visualization is near the output of the network, and this network has been trained to output a direct representation of semantics.

concepts.title: Computation Graph
concepts.one_liner: A computation graph is a visualization of a neural network as a sequence of modular blocks or layers chained together.
concepts.content:
A key idea of neural nets is to decompose computation into a series of layers. These layers are treated as modular blocks that can be chained together into a computation graph. For example, a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) can be represented as a sequence of layers in such a graph.

(see figure: In this chapter we will visualize neural nets as a sequence of layers, which we call a computation graph.)
concepts.motivation_md: Representing complex functions as computation graphs allows for modular design and provides a structured way to apply the chain rule for gradient calculations.
concepts.recap_md: - Decomposes complex computations into modular, chained blocks called layers.

key_passage.text: A key idea of neural nets is to decompose computation into a series of layers. In this chapter we will think of layers as modular blocks that can be chained together into a computation graph.

motivation.text: A key idea of neural nets is to decompose computation into a series of layers.

concepts.title: Forward Pass
concepts.one_liner: The forward pass is the operation where a layer takes inputs and transforms them into outputs.
concepts.content:
Each layer in a neural network takes in some inputs and transforms them into some outputs; this is called the $\texttt{forward}$ pass through the layer. If the layer has parameters $\theta$, these are considered an input to a parameter-free transformation:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}},\theta) \end{aligned}$$

Graphically, the forward operation of a layer is depicted as a block receiving inputs and producing an output.

(see figure: Forward operation of a neural net layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The forward pass is the fundamental process by which a model generates a prediction or output from a given input.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps input $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and parameters $\theta$ to an output $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$.

key_passage.text: Each layer takes in some inputs and transforms them into some outputs. We call this the forward pass through the layer. If the layer has parameters, we will consider the parameters to be an *input* to a parameter-free transformation

concepts.title: Reuse of Computation in Backpropagation

position.section_title: The Trick of Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation optimizes efficiency by calculating shared terms in the chain rule once and reusing them across multiple parameter gradients.
concepts.content:
The trick of backpropagation lies in the reuse of computation. Consider a computation graph that is a chain of functions $f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots f_2 \circ f_1$, each parameterized by $\theta_l$. To optimize these parameters with respect to a loss function $\mathcal{L}$ (outputting scalar $J$), we need the gradients $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_l}$.

(see figure: Basic sequential computation graph.)
(see figure: Computation graph as a tree.)

Using the chain rule, the gradients for $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \mathbf{x}_1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_1}{\partial \theta_1} \\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_2} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \theta_2} \end{aligned}$$

Most terms in these equations are shared. Rather than evaluating each gradient independently, backpropagation calculates the shared product once and reuses it for all preceding layers. This strategy is an application of dynamic programming.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating gradients independently for every parameter would be computationally prohibitive. Reusing intermediate results makes training deep networks feasible.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies shared terms in the chain rule to avoid redundant calculations.

key_passage.text: This is the whole trick of backpropagation: rather than computing each layer's gradients independently, observe that they share many of the same terms, so we might as well calculate each shared term once and reuse them.

motivation.text: Our goal is to update all the values highlighted in blue: θ₁, θ₂, and so forth. To do so we need to compute the gradients ∂J/∂θ₁, ∂J/∂θ₂, etc.

concepts.title: Backward Operation
concepts.one_liner: The backward operation iteratively computes gradients of the loss with respect to parameters and inputs by passing error signals backward through the network.
concepts.content:
The `backward` function is a general algorithm for reusing shared computation to update parameters. It relies on two key arrays of partial derivatives: $\mathbf{g}_l \triangleq \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l}$ (the gradient of the cost with respect to the layer output) and $\mathbf{L} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta]}$ (the local gradient of the layer).

(see figure: A generic layer in the computation graph. The braces represent the part of the computation graph we need to consider in order to evaluate $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$, $\mathbf{L}$, and $\mathbf{g}in$.)

The gradient needed to update $\theta$ is calculated as:
$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\theta}$$

While $\mathbf{L}$ is computed locally using the derivative of the layer's function $f'$, $\mathbf{g}$ is computed iteratively using a recurrence relation:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$$

This recurrence sends error signals backward from the last layer to the first. The full `backward` operation for a generic layer takes three inputs ($\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$) and produces two outputs ($\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}$).
concepts.motivation_md: To minimize loss, we must know how changing each parameter affects the final error. The backward operation provides a systematic, efficient way to calculate these sensitivities for every layer.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a recurrence relation to propagate gradients $\mathbf{g}$ backward through the graph.

key_passage.text: This recurrence is essence of backprop: it sends error signals (gradients) backward through the network, starting at the last layer and iteratively applying to compute g for each previous layer.

question.text: The remaining question is clear: how do we get g_l and L^θ_l for each layer l?

motivation.text: Computing g is a bit trickier; it requires evaluating the chain rule, and depends on all the layers between x_out and J. However, this can be computed iteratively: once we know g_l, computing g_{l-1} is just one more matrix multiply!

concepts.title: Output Layer
concepts.one_liner: The output layer maps a neural representation to a desired output representation, such as class labels or image pixel values.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks generate internal high-dimensional representations that are not directly usable for tasks like classification or image generation. The output layer bridges this gap by transforming these internal features into a format that matches the target data space and can be evaluated by a loss function.
concepts.recap_md: - Softmax layers convert inputs into probability distributions for classification tasks.

key_passage.text: The last piece we need is an output layer that maps a neural representation---a high-dimensional array of floating point numbers---to a desired output representation.

motivation.text: The output layer is the input to the loss function, thus completing our specification of the deep learning problem.

concepts.title: Temperature Parameter
concepts.one_liner: The temperature parameter $\tau$ is used in the softmax function to scale the confidence or 'peakiness' of predictions.
concepts.content: In the softmax definition, the temperature parameter $\textcolor[rgb]{0.2, 0.6, 1.0}{\tau}$ is used to scale how peaky, or confident, the predictions are.
concepts.motivation_md: Adjusting the temperature allows a model to control the entropy of its output distribution, making it either more uniform or more concentrated on the highest-scoring class without changing the underlying model weights.
concepts.recap_md: - The parameter $\tau$ scales the input values within a softmax function.

key_passage.text: In the softmax definition, we have added a **temperature** parameter τ, which is used to scale how peaky, or confident, the predictions are.

concepts.title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

concepts.one_liner: Neural networks are effective because they are high-capacity, differentiable, parallelizable, and build useful abstractions that reflect real-world structures.
concepts.content:
Neural networks are a powerful architecture for five primary reasons:

1. High Capacity: Large networks are universal approximators, ensuring that a close approximation to the true solution likely exists within the hypothesis space.
2. Differentiability: Parameters can be optimized efficiently via gradient descent to search for solutions within the hypothesis space.
3. Inductive Biases: Architectures impose constraints and regularizers that bias the search toward solutions capturing true structures of the visual world, aiding generalization.
4. Efficiency: Most computations, such as matrix multiplies and pointwise operations, can be parallelized on modern hardware like GPUs and applied to image batches.
5. Abstraction: Layer by layer, neural nets build increasingly abstracted internal representations of input data that are useful beyond the net's overall input-output behavior.

Deep nets are especially effective in computer vision because they can be constructed to specifically reflect visual structure. Furthermore, architectures like convolutional networks and transformers are currently our best models for explaining computation in animal brains.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding why deep learning works provides insight into why it has become the dominant paradigm in computer vision and AI, highlighting the synergy between mathematical flexibility, optimization, and hardware efficiency.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural nets are universal approximators that can be trained via gradient descent.

key_passage.text: They are high capacity (big enough nets are universal approximators). They are differentiable (the parameters can be optimized via gradient descent). They have good inductive biases (neural architectures reflect real structure in the world). They run efficiently on parallel hardware. They build abstractions.

question.text: why are deep nets such a good architecture?

motivation.text: almost all modern computer vision algorithms involve deep nets in one way or another. So you may be wondering: why are deep nets such a good architecture?

concepts.title: Neural Networks as Distribution Transformers
concepts.one_liner: Deep networks can be viewed as stacks of functions that perform geometric transformations on data distributions.
concepts.content: Deep nets are stacks of simple functions which compose to achieve interesting mappings from inputs to outputs. A useful way of thinking about deep nets is to view each layer as a geometric transformation of a data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing neural networks as distribution transformers helps visualize how complex data is reshaped and simplified as it passes through the layers of a model.
concepts.recap_md: - Each layer acts as a geometric transformation of the data distribution.

key_passage.text: The idea is to think of each layer as a geometric transformation of a data distribution.

motivation.text: So far we have seen that deep nets are stacks of simple functions, which compose to achieve interesting mappings from inputs to outputs. This section will introduce a slightly different way of thinking about deep nets.

concepts.title: A Different Way of Plotting Functions

position.section_title: A Different Way of Plotting Functions

concepts.one_liner: Functions can be visualized as mappings that rearrange input space by plotting the output axis horizontally.
concepts.content:
Each layer in a deep net is a mapping from one representation of the data to another: $f: \mathbf{x}_{\text{in}} \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{\text{out}}$. If $\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}}$ are both one-dimensional (1D), we can consider a different way of plotting the mapping where we rotate the $y$-axis to be horizontal rather than vertical.

(see figure: The traditional way of plotting the function $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$.)

This depiction makes it obvious that functions are mappings that rearrange the input space.

(see figure: An alternative way of plotting a function. Functions are mappings that rearrange the input space. The identity function $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}}=\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$, shown here, means "no...)

The identity mapping $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$ shows datapoints mapped to unchanged positions.

(see figure: Mapping plots for several simple functions that could be neural layers.)
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional function plots focus on the relationship between variables, but rotating the axes emphasizes how a function physically moves or 'warps' the space where data resides.
concepts.recap_md: - Rotating the output axis to be horizontal helps visualize how functions rearrange input space.

key_passage.text: Now, we will instead consider a different way of plotting the mapping, where we simply rotate the y-axis to be horizontal rather than vertical.

motivation.text: Functions are mappings that rearrange the input space. The depiction makes it obvious that the plot 𝐱_out = 𝐱_in is the identity mapping: datapoints get mapped to unchanged positions.

concepts.title: Deep networks as distribution transformers

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Deep networks reshape data distributions layer by layer to match a target configuration, such as one-hot encoded labels.
concepts.content:
An incoming data distribution can be reshaped layer by layer into a desired configuration. For example, a binary softmax classifier moves class 0 points to $(1,0)$ and class 1 points to $(0,1)$ on the output layer, corresponding to their one-hot codes. A deep net stacks these operations.

(see figure: Mapping plot for a `linear`-`relu` stack.)

We can think of a deep net as transforming an input data distribution $p_{\text {data }}$ into an output data distribution $p_{\text {out}}$. Each layer of activations is a different representation or embedding of the data, denoted as $p_{\ell}$ for layer $\ell$. Layer by layer, the net transforms $p_{\text {data }}$ into $p_{\texttt{1}}$, then $p_{\texttt{2}}$, and so on. Most loss functions penalize the divergence between the resulting output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective explains the 'work' a neural network does: it iteratively warps the geometry of the data until the different classes or values are easily separable or identifiable by the final layer.
concepts.recap_md: - Deep nets transform an input distribution $p_{\text{data}}$ into an output distribution $p_{\text{out}}$ through successive layers.

key_passage.text: We can think of a deep net as transforming an input data distribution, $p_{\text{data}}$, into an output data distribution, $p_{\text{out}}$. Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data, and we can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. Then, layer by layer, a deep net transforms $p_{\text{data}}$ into $p_{\texttt{1}}$ into $p_{\texttt{2}}$, and so on until finally transforming the data to the distribution $p_{\text{out}}$.

motivation.text: Most loss functions can also be interpreted from this angle: they penalize the divergence, in one form or another, between the output distribution $p_{\text{out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.

concepts.title: Embedding

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: An embedding is a representation of data at a specific layer of activations within a neural network.
concepts.content: Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or **embedding** of the data. We can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. A deep net transforms the input data distribution $p_{\text {data }}$ layer by layer through these embeddings until it reaches the final output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Embeddings allow the network to translate raw input into a more useful, structured space where the relevant features for the task are highlighted.
concepts.recap_md: - An embedding refers to the internal representation of data at a specific layer.

key_passage.text: Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data, and we can consider the distribution of activations on some layer ℓ to be pℓ.

motivation.text: We can think of a deep net as transforming an input data distribution, p_data, into an output data distribution, p_out. Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data, and we can consider the distribution of activations on some layer ℓ to be pℓ.

concepts.title: Sparsity in ReLU networks

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: ReLU layers induce sparsity by mapping large portions of the high-dimensional embedding space onto the axes.
concepts.content:
Visualizing 2D-to-2D mappings provides insight into how neural net layers transform data. 

(see figure: 2D mapping diagrams for several neural layers. The `linear` layer mapping will shift, stretch, and rotate depending on its weights and biases.)

A ReLU layer maps many points to the axes of the positive quadrant. In high-dimensional embeddings, this effect is exaggerated. For a width-$N$ layer, the strictly positive region occupies only $\frac{1}{2^N}$ proportion of the embedding space; consequently, almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes. This leads to sparse high-dimensional neural representations where most of the representational volume is unoccupied by datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding sparsity helps explain how ReLU networks compress information and why high-dimensional representations often reside on low-dimensional manifolds.
concepts.recap_md: - ReLU layers map any point not in the positive quadrant to an axis, creating data density along these boundaries.

key_passage.text: In particular, for a width-N layer, the region that is strictly positive occupies only 1/2^N proportion of the embedding space, so almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes after a relu layer. The geometry of high-dimensional neural representations may become very sparse because of this, where most of the volume of representational space is not occupied by any datapoints.

motivation.text: One interesting thing to notice here is that the relu layer maps many points to the axes of the positive quadrant. In general, with relu-nets, a lot of data density will build up along these axes, because any point not in the positive quadrant snaps to an axis.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Algorithm

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The backpropagation algorithm computes gradients by performing a forward pass to evaluate activations and a backward pass to iteratively calculate gradients layer by layer.
concepts.content:
The full backpropagation algorithm consists of two main stages. First, a forward pass is computed through the entire network, starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating layer by layer to produce the sequence of activations $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.

(see figure: Forward pass.)

Next, a backward pass is performed. This involves iteratively evaluating the gradients $\mathbf{g}$ to obtain the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer. The gradient update for parameters $\theta_l$ can be computed once the local Jacobian $\mathbf{L}_l$ and the incoming gradient $\mathbf{g}_l$ are available.



The algorithm ensures that operations are ordered so that the necessary arrays are ready when updating each layer.
concepts.motivation_md: To train a neural network using gradient descent, we need the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter. Backpropagation provides an efficient way to compute these gradients by reusing intermediate results from a forward pass and propagating errors backward through the chain rule.
concepts.recap_md: - Perform a forward pass to store activations for every layer.

key_passage.text: The way to do it is to first compute a forward pass through the entire network, which means starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating layer by layer to produce the sequence $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$. Next, we compute a backward pass, iteratively evaluating the $\mathbf{g}$'s and obtaining the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer.

motivation.text: So, we just need to order our operations so that when we get to updating layer $l$ we have these two arrays ready.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Over Data Batches
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation in batch mode computes the gradient for a whole dataset by averaging the gradients calculated for each individual datapoint.
concepts.motivation_md: In practice, neural networks are trained on large datasets. Computing gradients for the entire dataset at once is computationally efficient and provides a more stable estimate of the true gradient than using a single point.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient of the average loss is the average of the gradients of individual losses.

key_passage.text: The gradient of a sum of terms is the sum of the gradients of each term. Therefore, to compute a gradient update for an algorithm like stochastic gradient descent, we apply backpropagation in batch mode, that is, we run it over each datapoint in our batch (which can be done in parallel) and then average the results.

motivation.text: As you may recall from previous sections, the total cost function we wish to minimize will typically be the average of the losses over all the datapoints in a training set. However, once we know how to compute the gradient for a single datapoint, we can easily compute the gradient for the whole dataset.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Linear Layer
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for a linear layer involves matrix multiplications where the gradient with respect to inputs uses the weight matrix and the parameter gradient is an outer product.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers are the building blocks of MLPs. Deriving efficient matrix-based backward passes allows us to use optimized linear algebra libraries for training, avoiding the computational cost of explicit Jacobian matrices.
concepts.recap_md: - The input gradient is the output gradient multiplied by the weight matrix: $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}$.

key_passage.text:
The definition of a linear layer, in forward direction, is as follows: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}
\end{aligned}$$ Next we need the gradients of this function, with respect to its inputs and parameters.

motivation.text: `Forward` and `backward` for a linear layer are also very easy to write in code, using any library that provides matrix multiplication (`matmul`) as a primitive. Notice that all these operations are simple expressions, mainly involving matrix multiplies.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Pointwise Nonlinearity
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for pointwise nonlinearities involves an element-wise multiplication of the incoming gradient with the derivative of the activation function.
concepts.content:
Pointwise nonlinearities have simple backward functions. For a scalar nonlinearity $h$ with derivative $h^{\prime}$, the layer function is $f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$. The local Jacobian $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$ is a diagonal matrix $\mathbf{H}^\prime$ containing the derivatives of the activations. The backward operation is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{H}^\prime
\end{aligned}$$

This can be simplified to an element-wise product:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}[i] = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[i]h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[i]) \quad \forall i 
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: Nonlinearities are essential for neural networks to learn complex patterns. Because they are applied element-wise, their gradients are sparse (diagonal), allowing for very efficient computation without full matrix multiplication.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass for a pointwise layer is an element-wise multiplication by the derivative of the activation function.

key_passage.text: Define a pointwise layer using h as f(x_in) = [h(x_in[0]), ..., h(x_in[N-1])]^T. Then we have g_in = g_out H', which can be simplified as g_in[i] = g_out[i]h'(x_in[i]) for all i.

motivation.text: Pointwise nonlinearities have very simple backward functions.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for Loss Layers
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass for a loss layer, such as $L_2$ loss, computes the initial gradient signal as the error between predictions and ground truth.
concepts.content:
The loss layer is the final layer in an MLP. For an $L_2$ loss function $\left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2$, where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the prediction and $\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth, the gradient with respect to the input $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &= \frac{\partial \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}$$

Since the output of the loss layer is the cost $J$ itself, $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$. Thus, the backward signal $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ is simply $2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$, which is a row vector of per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of an $L_2$ loss layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The loss layer provides the starting point for the backward pass. It quantifies the error, which is then propagated back through the network to inform how parameters should be adjusted.
concepts.recap_md: - For $L_2$ loss, the initial backward gradient is the vector of differences $2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$.

key_passage.text: So, the backward signal sent by the $L_2$ loss layer is a row vector of per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.

motivation.text: The last layer we need to define for a complete MLP is the loss layer. This layer has no parameters so we only need to derive the backward equation for this layer.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through an MLP
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through an MLP involves a forward pass to compute activations and a backward pass where linear layers use transposed weights and nonlinearities act as gates.
concepts.content:
In a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), the forward pass computes activations layer by layer.

(see figure: Forward pass through an MLP.)

For the backward pass, if we treat gradients as column vectors, the operation for a linear layer becomes $\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{W}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. This shows that the backward pass for a linear layer is the same operation as the forward pass, but using the transposed weight matrix.

(see figure: Backward pass through an MLP.)

In contrast, a `relu` layer in the backward pass acts as a gating matrix, masking out gradients where the forward activation was negative. Notably, all backward operations in the chain are matrix multiplications. Parameter gradients are computed at each step as an outer product between the layer's input activations $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and the incoming gradients $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the full MLP backpropagation reveals that the entire training process is composed of standard linear algebra operations, making it highly efficient to implement on modern hardware.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass through a linear layer is equivalent to a forward pass using transposed weights.

key_passage.text: This reveals an interesting connection between `forward` and `backward` for linear layers: `backward` for a linear layer is the same operation as `forward`, just with the weights transposed!

motivation.text: Let's see what happens when we put all these operations together in an MLP.

concepts.title: Backpropagation as a Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: The full backpropagation algorithm can be viewed as a single large neural network where the forward pass parameterizes the backward pass.
concepts.content:
The backward pass through a neural network can be implemented as another neural network, specifically a linear network where parameters are determined by the weights and activations of the original forward network. Consequently, the entire backpropagation process—forward pass followed by backward pass—is itself one large computation graph or neural network.

(see figure: The computation graph for backpropagation through a three-layer MLP. It's just another neural net! Solid lines are involved in computing data/activation gradients and dotted lines are involved in...)

This structure is an example of a **hypernetwork**, where one network (the forward pass) outputs values that parameterize another (the backward pass). An interesting property is that the backward network consists entirely of linear layers. This is because the chain rule involves products of Jacobian matrices, which represent locally linear approximations of the loss surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing backpropagation as a neural network helps unify the concepts of inference and training into a single framework of computation graphs, which is the basis for modern deep learning libraries.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation is a hypernetwork where the forward pass provides parameters for the backward pass.

key_passage.text: the backward pass through an neural network can itself be implemented as another neural network, which is in fact a linear network with parameters determined by the weight matrices of the original network as well as by the activations in the original network. Therefore, the full backward pass is a neural network! Since the forward pass is also a neural network (the original network), the full backpropagation algorithm---a forward pass followed by a backward pass---can be viewed as just one big neural network.

motivation.text: The parameter gradients can be computed from this network via one additional matrix multiply (matmul) for each layer of the backward network.

concepts.title: Hypernetwork
concepts.one_liner: A hypernetwork is a setup where one neural network outputs values that serve as the parameters for another neural network.
concepts.content: A hypernetwork is a general term for a setup where one neural network outputs values that parameterize another neural network. In the context of backpropagation, the forward network can be seen as a hypernetwork that parameterizes the backward network, as activations from layers like `relu` are transformed to become the parameters of the linear layers in the backward pass.
concepts.motivation_md: Hypernetworks allow for dynamic parameter generation, enabling a network to adapt its behavior or its own learning process based on input data.
concepts.recap_md: - A hypernetwork is a neural network that generates parameters for another network.

key_passage.text: There is a general term for this setup, where one neural net outputs values that parameterize another neural net; this is called a hypernetwork.

motivation.text: One is that activations from the `relu` layers get transformed to become parameters of a `linear` layer of the backward network.

concepts.title: Batch

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: A batch is a collection of images or data points processed in parallel through a neural network.
concepts.content: Normally, we don't process one image at a time through a neural net. Instead we run a batch of images all at once, and they are processed in parallel. A batch sampled from the training data can be denoted as $\{\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\texttt{batch}}}$. The batch represented as a tensor has shape $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C_0 \times H \times W}$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times K}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Processing data points individually is computationally inefficient. Batching allows for parallelization, taking advantage of modern hardware like GPUs to speed up training and inference.
concepts.recap_md: - A batch consists of multiple training examples processed simultaneously in parallel.

key_passage.text: Instead we run a *batch* of images all at once, and they are processed in parallel.

motivation.text: Normally, we don't process one image at a time through a neural net.

concepts.title: Linear Layers
concepts.one_liner: Linear layers are the primary components of deep networks, containing the weights and biases parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers provide the fundamental transformation of data in a neural network, allowing the model to learn weighted relationships between input features.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear layers apply a weight matrix and a bias vector to the input.

key_passage.text: Linear layers are the workhorses of deep nets. Almost all parameters of the network are contained in these layers; we call these parameters the weights and biases.

motivation.text: Linear layers are the workhorses of deep nets. Almost all parameters of the network are contained in these layers; we call these parameters the weights and biases.

concepts.title: Activation Layers
concepts.one_liner: Activation layers add nonlinearity to neural networks, typically through pointwise functions applied to each dimension of the input.
concepts.motivation_md: Without activation layers, a multi-layer neural network would be mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer, making it unable to learn complex, non-linear patterns in data.
concepts.recap_md: - Activation layers introduce non-linearity by applying pointwise functions to inputs.

key_passage.text: Activation layers add nonlinearity. Activation layers are typically pointwise functions, applying a scalar to scalar mapping on each dimension of the input vector.

motivation.text: If a net only contained linear layers then it could only compute linear functions. This is because the composition of N linear functions is a linear function.

concepts.title: Normalization Layers
concepts.one_liner: Normalization layers are nonlinearities that perturb each neuron based on the collective behavior of a set of neurons.
concepts.content: Normalization layers add another kind of nonlinearity. Instead of being a pointwise nonlinearity, like in activation layers, they are nonlinearities that perturb each neuron based on the collective behavior of a set of neurons.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalization layers help stabilize the training of deep networks by adjusting activations based on the statistics of other neurons, rather than just applying a fixed pointwise function.
concepts.recap_md: - Normalization layers use the collective behavior of neurons to apply non-linear transformations.

key_passage.text: Normalization layers add another kind of nonlinearity. Instead of being a pointwise nonlinearity, like in activation layers, they are nonlinearities that perturb each neuron based on the collective behavior of a set of neurons.

concepts.title: Batchnorm
concepts.one_liner: Batchnorm standardizes each neural activation with respect to its mean and variance over a batch of datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Batchnorm was introduced to stabilize and accelerate the training of deep neural networks by ensuring that activations maintain a consistent distribution across batches.
concepts.recap_md: - Batchnorm standardizes activations using the mean and variance of the current batch.

key_passage.text: Batchnorm standardizes each neural activation with respect to its mean and variance over a batch of datapoints.

motivation.text: where γ and β are learned parameters of this layer that maintain expressivity so that the layer can output values with non-zero mean and non-unit variance.

concepts.title: L2 normalization
concepts.one_liner: L2 normalization projects inputs onto the unit hypersphere to bound activations to unit vectors.
concepts.motivation_md: L2 normalization is used to constrain the magnitude of activation vectors, which can help in stabilizing training and ensuring that the direction of the vector is the primary information preserved.
concepts.recap_md: - L2 normalization scales the input vector so that its Euclidean norm is equal to one.

key_passage.text: L2 normalization projects the inputs onto the unit hypersphere, which is useful for bounding the activations to unit vectors

motivation.text: L2 normalization projects the inputs onto the unit hypersphere, which is useful for bounding the activations to unit vectors

concepts.title: Layernorm
concepts.one_liner: Layernorm standardizes the vector of input activations for each individual datapoint.
concepts.motivation_md: Layernorm provides a way to normalize activations that does not depend on other examples in the batch, making it suitable for tasks where batch sizes are small or data points should be processed independently.
concepts.recap_md: - Layernorm standardizes activations based on the mean and variance of a single datapoint's features.

key_passage.text: Layernorm is similar except that it standardizes the vector of input activations: [...] Notice that layernorm, like $L_2$-normalization, maps the activation vector to the surface of a hypersphere, but it also centers the activations to have zero mean, and then scales and shifts the activations via $\gamma$ and $\beta$.

concepts.title: Batchnorm vs Layernorm
concepts.one_liner: While both standardize activations, batchnorm uses statistics across the batch, whereas layernorm uses statistics across the features of a single datapoint.
concepts.content:
Notice that layernorm also looks quite similar to batchnorm. Both standardize activations but do so with respect to different statistics. Layernorm computes a mean and variance over elements of a datapoint $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$, and will do so separately for each such datapoint in a batch. Batchnorm computes the mean and variance per channel over datapoints in a batch. If we have a batch stored in the tensor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C}$, then what layernorm does looks just like a "transpose" of what batchnorm does. Batchnorm standardizes each element of the tensor by the mean and variance of its column. Layernorm standardizes each element by the mean and variance of its row:

(see figure: Batchnorm vs layernorm. Gray indicates the region over which mean and variance are computed. See also Figure 2 of \cite{wu2018group} for more such visualizations.)

One issue with batchnorm is that it requires processing a batch of datapoints all at once, and introduces a dependency between each datapoint in the batch. This violates the principle that datapoints should be processed independently and identically (iid), and this can lead to bugs if your method relies on the iid assumption. Layernorm does not have this problem and does indeed process each datapoint in an iid fashion.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the difference between batchnorm and layernorm is crucial for choosing the right normalization technique, especially when the iid assumption is important or batch sizes are constrained.
concepts.recap_md: - Batchnorm normalizes across the batch (columns), while layernorm normalizes across the features (rows).

key_passage.text: Batchnorm computes the mean and variance per channel over datapoints in a batch. If we have a batch stored in the tensor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C}$, then what layernorm does looks just like a "transpose" of what batchnorm does. Batchnorm standardizes each element of the tensor by the mean and variance of its column. Layernorm standardizes each element by the mean and variance of its row.

motivation.text: One issue with batchnorm is that it requires processing a batch of datapoints all at once, and introduces a dependency between each datapoint in the batch. This violates the principle that datapoints should be processed independently and identically (iid), and this can lead to bugs if your method relies on the iid assumption. Layernorm does not have this problem and does indeed process each datapoint in an iid fashion.

concepts.title: Anti-causal Filters
concepts.one_liner: An anti-causal filter is a filter where the output depends only on future values, such that $h [n,m,t ]=0$ for all $t>0$.
concepts.content: Anti-causal filters are defined as the opposite of causal filters; in these systems, the output depends only on the future. Formally, a filter is anti-causal if $h [n,m,t ]=0$ for all $t>0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Anti-causal filters are used in theoretical signal processing and non-real-time applications where future data points are available, allowing for processing that considers subsequent inputs.
concepts.recap_md: - An anti-causal filter's output depends exclusively on future inputs.

key_passage.text: This is the opposite, when the output only depends on the future: $h \left[n,m,t \right]=0$ for all $t>0$.

concepts.title: Heaviside Step Function
concepts.one_liner: The Heaviside step function $u[t]$ is an infinite length function that is 0 for $t < 0$ and 1 otherwise.
concepts.content:
The Heaviside step function, $u [t]$, is an infinite length function defined as:
$$
u [t] = \begin{cases}
    0     & \quad \text{if }  t <0 \\
    1     & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}$$

[FIGURE:3bdfa12be361a5d6 | ]
concepts.motivation_md: The Heaviside step function is a fundamental tool in signal processing used to represent signals that switch on at a specific time and stay on indefinitely.
concepts.recap_md: - $u[t] = 0$ for $t < 0$ and $u[t] = 1$ for $t \ge 0$.

key_passage.text: u [t] = {0 if t <0, 1 otherwise}

concepts.title: Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) Filters
concepts.one_liner: Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters are filters described by difference equations where the impulse response has infinite support.
concepts.content: Most filters described by difference equations have an impulse response with infinite support. They are called IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters. IIR filters can be further classified as stable and unstable. Stable filters are those that, given a bounded input $| \ell _{in} [n,m,t ] |<A$, produce a bounded output $| \ell _{out} [n,m,t ] | <B$. For stability to occur, the impulse response must be bounded. In unstable filters, the amplitude of the impulse response diverges to infinity. For example, a filter may be stable if and only if $| \alpha | < 1$.
concepts.motivation_md: IIR filters are used to model systems where the current output depends on all previous inputs, allowing for efficient recursive implementations of complex frequency responses.
concepts.recap_md: - IIR filters have an impulse response that never returns to zero indefinitely.

key_passage.text: Most filters described by difference equations have an impulse response with infinite support. They are called IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters.

motivation.text: IIR filters can be further classified as stable and unstable. Stable filters are the ones that given a bounded input, $| \ell _{in} \left[n,m,t \right] |<A$, produce a bounded output, $| \ell _{out} \left[n,m,t \right] | <B$.

concepts.title: Nulling Filter
concepts.one_liner: A nulling filter is a filter designed to cancel objects moving at a specific velocity by computing derivatives along space-time orientations.
concepts.content: A nulling filter $h$ is designed to cancel any objects moving at a specific velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. By using different filters, each one computing derivatives along different space-time orientations, output sequences can be created where specific objects disappear, as shown in @fig-tunedfilter.
concepts.motivation_md: Nulling filters are essential in computer vision and motion analysis to isolate or remove specific moving components from a video sequence based on their velocity.
concepts.recap_md: - A nulling filter removes objects moving at a specific velocity from a sequence.

key_passage.text: This filter is called a nulling filter.

motivation.text: By using different filters, each one computing derivatives along different space-time orientations, we can create output sequences where specific objects disappear.

concepts.title: Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one to enable computer processing.
concepts.content: In nature, most signals we measure, such as sound and light, are defined over continuous domains like time and space. In order to process these signals with computers, the continuous domain must be transformed into a discrete one. Sampling is the specific process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one.
concepts.motivation_md: Since digital computers cannot process continuous data directly, sampling is required to convert real-world signals into a format that can be stored and manipulated digitally.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling converts continuous signals (like sound or light) into discrete data.

key_passage.text: Sampling is the process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one.

motivation.text: In order to process them with computers, we need to transform the continuous domain into a discrete one.

concepts.title: Sampling Period
concepts.one_liner: The sampling period $T_s$ is the time interval between successive samples in the conversion of a continuous signal to a discrete one.
concepts.content: Consider a one-dimensional (1D) continuous time signal $\ell (t)$ and its sampled version $\ell [n] = \ell(n T_s)$, where $T_s$ is the sampling period. In this sampling process, some information is inevitably lost. To recover the continuous signal $\ell (t)$ from its sampled version $\ell [n]$ through interpolation, one must ensure information loss is minimized. Decreasing $T_s$ results in a more accurate approximation of the continuous signal $\ell (t)$, but increases the memory needed to store $\ell [n]$ and the computational cost of processing. Therefore, choosing the appropriate $T_s$ is necessary to find optimal sampling parameters and allow for signal reconstruction.
concepts.motivation_md: The sampling period determines the balance between signal fidelity and resource consumption (memory and CPU), making its selection critical for efficient digital signal processing.
concepts.recap_md: - The sampling period $T_s$ defines the interval at which a continuous signal is measured.

key_passage.text: $\ell [n] = \ell(n T_s)$, where $T_s$ is the **sampling period**

motivation.text: One way of ensuring that information is not lost is to decrease $T_s$, which will result in a more accurate approximation of the continuous signal $\ell (t)$ at the expense of the amount of memory needed to store $\ell [n]$. Therefore, it is important to choose the appropriate $T_s$.

concepts.title: Aliasing
concepts.one_liner: Aliasing is the confusion of frequencies that occurs when a signal is sampled improperly.
concepts.content: When parameters for sampling are chosen such that different frequencies become indistinguishable, a specific qualitative behavior occurs. This confusion of frequencies is called aliasing.
concepts.motivation_md: Aliasing represents a fundamental limit in sampling; understanding it is crucial to avoid distortions where high-frequency signals masquerade as lower-frequency ones.
concepts.recap_md: - Aliasing is the phenomenon where different signal frequencies become indistinguishable due to sampling.

key_passage.text: This confusion of frequencies is called aliasing.

motivation.text: It is important to mention that there is nothing special about how the parameters have been chosen for this example.

concepts.title: Band-limited signal
concepts.one_liner: A band-limited signal is a signal with no spectral content above a specific maximum frequency $w_{max}$.
concepts.content:
A band-limited signal $\ell (t)$ is a signal that contains no spectral content above a certain frequency $w_{max}$. An example of such a signal is one characterized by the following Fourier transform:

concepts.motivation_md: The concept of band-limiting is central to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, as it defines the conditions under which a continuous signal can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples.
concepts.recap_md: - A signal is band-limited if its Fourier transform is zero for all frequencies above $w_{max}$.

concepts.title: Center-Surround Organization
concepts.one_liner: Retinal ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization that performs contrast enhancement.
concepts.content: Steven Kuffler demonstrated that retinal ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization. By recording the response of ganglion cells to small spots of light, he identified two primary types. On-center cells are activated when light falls within a small central region of the receptive field and are deactivated when light hits a surrounding ring. Off-center cells exhibit the opposite behavior. This organization suggests that the retina performs a contrast-enhancing operation, a discovery that has motivated extensive research in computational neuroscience and neuromorphic engineering. For his discoveries on how the eye processes visual information, Haldan Keffer Hartline received the Nobel Prize in 1967.
concepts.motivation_md: This organization allows the visual system to detect edges and changes in light intensity rather than just absolute light levels, effectively performing contrast enhancement at the very first stage of visual processing.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Retinal ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields organized into a center and a surrounding ring.",
  "- On-center cells activate when light hits the center, while off-center cells activate when light hits the surround.",
  "- This structure enables the retina to perform contrast enhancement and edge detection."
]

key_passage.text: He did this by shining a small spot of light on different parts of the retina and recording the response of a ganglion cell as he changed the location of the spot of light. First Hartline, and then Kuffler, showed that there were two types of ganglion cells; a first group of cells, called on-center, would get activated when the spot of light was inside a small region in the middle of the receptive field and would get deactivated (firing bellow their average rate) when the spot light was projected inside a ring around the center. A second group had the opposite behavior, called off-center.

motivation.text: These results are fascinating because they reveal that the retina seems to be performing some sort of contrast enhancing operation and their work motivated a large number of studies in computational neuroscience and neuromorphic engineering that tried to reproduce the operations made in the retina.

concepts.title: On-Center and Off-Center Ganglion Cells
concepts.one_liner: On-center cells activate when light hits the receptive field's center, while off-center cells activate when light hits the surrounding ring.
concepts.content: Retinal ganglion cells are categorized into two functional groups based on their response to light. On-center cells are activated when a spot of light is inside a small region in the middle of the receptive field and are deactivated, firing below their average rate, when the light is projected inside a ring around that center. A second group, called off-center cells, exhibits the opposite behavior, responding to light in the surround rather than the center.
concepts.motivation_md: These two cell types provide a dual representation of visual information, allowing the brain to efficiently process both increases and decreases in local illumination.

]

A second group had the opposite behavior, called off-center.

concepts.title: Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
concepts.one_liner: The lateral geniculate nucleus is a six-layered structure that relays visual signals from the retina to the cortex while receiving significant feedback.
concepts.content: The axons of ganglion cells from both eyes project to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a structure composed of six layers of neurons that outputs to the visual cortex. Although it receives inputs from both eyes, the signals are not mixed, and the neurons remain monocular. LGN neurons possess concentric center-surround receptive fields. While its role is not fully understood, it may be involved in temporal decorrelation, attention modulation, and saccadic suppression. Interestingly, only 5 percent of the input connections come from the retina, while 95 percent are feedback connections from the primary visual cortex and other areas.
concepts.motivation_md: The LGN acts as a sophisticated relay station that filters and modulates visual information from the retina before it reaches the cortex, likely integrating top-down signals for attention and focus.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The LGN is a six-layered relay center in the thalamus for the visual pathway.",
  "- It maintains separate channels for each eye and utilizes center-surround receptive fields.",
  "- Most of its input comes from cortical feedback rather than the retina itself."
]

key_passage.text: The LGN is composed of six layers of neurons and its output goes to the visual cortex and other visual areas. This structure receives inputs from both eyes but the signals are not mixed and the neurons in this area remain monocular.

motivation.text: The role of the LGN is not completely understood but it may be involved in temporal decorrelation, attention modulation and saccadic suppression.

concepts.title: Oriented Simple Cell
concepts.one_liner: Oriented simple cells in the visual cortex increase their firing rate when stimulated by a bar of light at a specific orientation.
concepts.content: Oriented simple cells are found in the visual cortex and respond to specific geometric stimuli. Unlike the concentric cells of the retina, an oriented simple cell shows an increased firing rate when stimulated with an oriented bar in the positive region of its receptive field, provided the bar matches the cell's preferred orientation.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple cells represent a higher level of visual processing where the brain begins to assemble basic points of light into meaningful geometric features like lines and edges.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Simple cells are selective for the orientation and position of a stimulus.",
  "- They respond most strongly to bars of light aligned with their preferred orientation.",
  "- These cells are a fundamental building block for edge detection in the primary visual cortex."
]

key_passage.text: An oriented cell shows increased firing rate when stimulated with an oriented bar in the positive region of the RF with the preferred orientation.

concepts.title: Organization of the Primary Visual Cortex (V1)
concepts.one_liner: The primary visual cortex is organized into functional columns and hypercolumns that process orientation, ocular dominance, and color.
concepts.content: The first visual area in the cortex, V1, is a sheet of neurons arranged in several layers. Hubel and Wiesel discovered that V1 neurons are organized into columns. Within a vertical column, all cells are selective to the same orientation. Moving horizontally, the preferred orientation changes smoothly (orientation columns), while moving perpendicularly reveals alternating eye preferences (ocular dominance columns). A hypercolumn, measuring approximately 1 $\times$ 3 mm, covers all orientations and both eyes for a small portion of the visual field. Additionally, color-sensitive neurons are organized in blobs surrounded by orientation-sensitive neurons.
concepts.motivation_md: This highly regular architecture ensures that every point in the visual field is systematically analyzed for all possible orientations and inputs from both eyes.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- V1 is organized into vertical columns where neurons share the same orientation preference.",
  "- Ocular dominance columns alternate between inputs from the left and right eyes.",
  "- Hypercolumns are functional units that process all orientations and both eyes for a small area of the visual field."
]

key_passage.text: Hubel and Wiesel found that neurons in V1 are organized along columns. When probing with an electrode, as the electrode went from the surface to the bottom of V1, all the cells found were selective to the same orientation. When moving the electrode along one horizontal direction, they found that the preferred orientation changed smoothly (orientation columns), and when moving the electrode along the perpendicular horizontal direction, the cells changed the eye preference, alternating between the two eyes with some binocular cells between them (ocular dominance columns).

motivation.text: A section of around 1 × 3 mm (called a hypercolumn) covers all orientations and both eyes for a small portion of the visual field.

concepts.title: Cortical Columns
concepts.one_liner: Cortical columns are vertical arrangements of neurons in V1 that share functional properties like orientation selectivity or eye preference.
concepts.content: Neurons in V1 are organized along columns. When probing with an electrode from the surface to the bottom of V1, all cells found are selective to the same orientation. When moving the electrode along one horizontal direction, the preferred orientation changes smoothly (orientation columns). Moving along the perpendicular horizontal direction reveals ocular dominance columns, where cells change eye preference, alternating between the two eyes with some binocular cells between them.
concepts.motivation_md: Organizing neurons with similar properties into columns minimizes the length of connections required for local processing, making the brain's visual analysis more efficient.

concepts.title: Hypercolumn
concepts.one_liner: A hypercolumn is a functional module of the visual cortex that processes all orientations and eye inputs for a small visual field area.
concepts.content: A hypercolumn is a section of the primary visual cortex measuring around 1 $\times$ 3 mm. It covers all orientations and both eyes for a small portion of the visual field, acting as a complete functional unit for visual processing in that specific area.
concepts.motivation_md: Hypercolumns serve as the fundamental building blocks of the visual cortex, ensuring that the brain has a complete set of feature detectors for every part of the image we see.

concepts.title: Ventral and Dorsal Streams
concepts.one_liner: Visual information flows through ventral and dorsal streams specialized for object recognition and motion processing, respectively.
concepts.content: Cells in the visual cortex project their outputs to a diverse set of other visual areas following two main streams: the ventral stream and the dorsal stream. These pathways project into specialized areas performing motion processing (area MT), face processing (fusiform face area [FFA]), and object recognition (IT).
concepts.motivation_md: The brain divides visual tasks into 'what' (ventral) and 'where/how' (dorsal) pathways to process complex scenes and coordinate actions simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The ventral stream is primarily involved in object and face recognition.",
  "- The dorsal stream is specialized for motion processing and spatial awareness.",
  "- These pathways project to specialized areas like the FFA for faces and MT for motion."
]

key_passage.text: Cells in the visual cortex project their outputs to a diverse set of other visual areas following two main streams (the ventral stream and the dorsal stream) and project into specialized areas performing motion processing (area MT), face processing (fusiform face area [FFA]), and object recognition (IT).

concepts.title: 1D Convolution
concepts.one_liner: The 1D convolution computes output values as a linear weighted sum of an input signal and a kernel, where weights depend on their relative positions.
concepts.content:
The convolution, denoted $\circ$, between a signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$ and the convolutional kernel $h\left[n \right]$ is defined as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =  \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[n-k \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$

The convolution computes the output values as a linear weighted sum. The weight between the input sample $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$ and the output sample $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right]$ is a function $h\left[n, k \right]$ that depends only on their relative position $n-k$. Therefore, $h\left[n, k \right]=h\left[n-k \right]$. If the signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$ has a finite length, $N$, then the sum is only done in the interval $k \in \left[0,N-1\right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution is a fundamental operation in signal processing and neural networks that allows for translation-invariant filtering. By using weights that only depend on the relative distance between input and output samples, it enables the same local pattern-matching operation to be applied consistently across an entire signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution is defined as $\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[n-k] \ell_{\texttt{in}}[k]$.

key_passage.text: The convolution, denoted $\circ$, between a signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$ and the convolutional kernel $h\left[n \right]$ is defined as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[n-k \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$

The weight between the input sample $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$ and the output sample $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right]$ is a function $h\left[n, k \right]$ that depends only on their relative position $n-k$.

concepts.title: Convolution Versus Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Convolution and correlation are related operators that use the same kernel, but convolution mirrors the kernel around the origin.
concepts.content:
The convolution is related to the correlation operator. In the correlation, the weights are defined as $h\left[n, k \right]=h\left[k-n \right]$. The convolution and the correlation use the same kernel but mirrored around the origin. The correlation is also translation invariant.

Most of the literature in neural networks calls convolution to the correlation operator. As the kernels are learned, the distinction is not important most of the time.
concepts.motivation_md: While mathematically distinct due to the mirroring of the kernel, convolution and correlation perform similar tasks of measuring similarity or filtering. In deep learning, the distinction is often ignored because the network can simply learn a mirrored version of the kernel if needed.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution and correlation use the same kernel, but the kernel is mirrored in convolution.

key_passage.text: The convolution and the correlation use the same kernel but mirrored around the origin.

concepts.title: Commutative Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: One important property of the convolution is that it is commutative, meaning the order of the signal and kernel can be swapped.
concepts.content:
One important property of the convolution is that it is commutative: $h\left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right] \circ h\left[n\right]$. This property is easy to prove by changing the variables, $k = n - k'$, so that:

$$h \left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[n-k \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right] = \sum_{k'=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[k' \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-k' \right]  = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] \circ h \left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Commutativity simplifies mathematical analysis and implementation, as it allows us to treat the filter and the signal symmetrically.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution is commutative: $h[n] \circ \ell[n] = \ell[n] \circ h[n]$.

key_passage.text: One important property of the convolution is that it is commutative: $h\left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right] \circ h\left[n\right]$.

motivation.text: One important property of the convolution is that it is commutative: $h\left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right] \circ h\left[n\right]$.

concepts.title: Convolution Procedure
concepts.one_liner: The convolution procedure involves mirroring the kernel, shifting it to a target location, and calculating a weighted sum of the surrounding input values.
concepts.content: The convolution operation can be described in words as: first take the kernel $h\left[k\right]$ and mirror it $h\left[-k \right]$, then shift the mirrored kernel so that the origin is at location $n$, then multiply the input values around location $n$ by the mirrored kernel and sum the result. Store the result in the output vector $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right]$. For instance, if the convolutional kernel has three non-zero values: $h\left[-1 \right] =1$, $h\left[0 \right] = 2$ and $h\left[1 \right] = 3$, then the output value at location $n$ is $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = 3 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-1\right]+2 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] + 1 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+1\right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the step-by-step mechanical procedure of convolution (flip, shift, multiply, sum) is essential for implementing the algorithm and for building an intuition of how kernels interact with signals.
concepts.recap_md: - To convolve, mirror the kernel, shift it to the target index, multiply with the input, and sum.

key_passage.text: The convolution operation can be described in words as: first take the kernel $h\left[k\right]$ and mirror it $h\left[-k \right]$, then shift the mirrored kernel so that the origin is at location $n$, then multiply the input values around location $n$ by the mirrored kernel and sum the result. Store the result in the output vector $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right]$.

concepts.title: Convolution in Matrix Form
concepts.one_liner: For finite length signals, convolution can be explicitly represented as a matrix-vector multiplication.
concepts.content:
For finite length signals, it helps to make explicit the structure of the convolution writing it in matrix form. For instance, if the convolutional kernel has only three non-zero values, then:
$$\begin{bmatrix}
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 0 \right] \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 1 \right] \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 2 \right] \\
\vdots \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ N-1 \right]
\end{bmatrix}
 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  h\left[0\right] ~&~ h\left[-1\right] ~&~ 0 ~&~ ... ~&~ 0 \\
  h\left[1\right] ~&~ h\left[0\right] ~&~ h\left[-1\right] ~&~... ~&~ 0 \\
  0 ~&~ h\left[1\right] ~&~ h\left[0\right] ~&~... ~&~ 0 \\
  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots \\
  0 ~&~ 0 ~&~ 0 ~&~... ~&~ h\left[0\right] 
 \end{bmatrix}
~
 \begin{bmatrix}
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[0\right] \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[1\right] \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[2\right] \\
  \vdots \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[N-1\right]
 \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Representing convolution as a matrix operation allows us to leverage linear algebra tools and optimized matrix multiplication libraries for computation.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution of finite signals can be expressed as a matrix-vector product.

key_passage.text: For finite length signals, it helps to make explicit the structure of the convolution writing it in matrix form.

concepts.title: 2D Convolution
concepts.one_liner: In two dimensions, convolution involves flipping a kernel vertically and horizontally and sliding it over an image to record inner products.
concepts.content:
In two dimensions, the processing is analogous: the input filter is flipped vertically and horizontally, then slid over the image to record the inner product with the image everywhere. Mathematically, this is:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = h \left[n,m\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] =  \sum_{k,l}h \left[n-k,m-l \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k,l \right]$$

The next figure shows the result of a 2D convolution between a $3 \times 3$ kernel with a $9 \times 9$ image. The particular kernel used in the figure averages in the vertical direction and takes differences horizontally. The output image reflects that processing, with horizontal differences accentuated and vertical changes diminished. To compute one of the pixels in the output image, we start with an input image patch of $3 \times 3$ pixels, we flip the convolutional kernel upside-down and left-right, and then we multiply all the pixels in the image patch with the corresponding flipped kernel values and we sum the results.

concepts.title: Properties of the Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolution is a linear operation characterized by properties such as commutativity, associativity, distributivity, and shift-invariance.
concepts.content:
The convolution is a linear operation that is important to be familiar with. Its properties include:

-   **Commutative**. The convolution is commutative, $h\left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right] \circ h\left[n\right]$, which means that the order of convolutions is irrelevant. This is not true for the correlation.

-   **Associative**. Convolutions can be applied in any order: $\ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_2 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right] = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]) = (\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right]) \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]$. In practice, for finite length signals, the associative property might be affected by boundary conditions.

-   **Distributive** with respect to the sum: $\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] + \ell_3\left[n\right] ) = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right] +  \ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right]$

-   **Shift**. If the input signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$ is translated by a constant $n_0$, the output is translated by the same constant: $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] =  h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right]$. Translating the kernel is equivalent.

-   **Support**. The convolution of a discrete signal of length $N$ with another of length $M$ results in a signal with length $L \leq M+N-1$.

-   **Identity**. The convolution has an identity function, the impulse $\delta \left[n\right]$, which is 1 for $n=0$ and zero elsewhere. The convolution of the impulse with any signal returns the same signal: $\delta \left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right]$.
