concepts.title: The eye of the artist
concepts.one_liner: Learning to paint teaches one to see the world not just as objects, but as a series of light, shadows, and strokes that create the illusion of reality.
concepts.content: Learning to paint is a great way of learning to see. Starting from a white canvas and a finite set of acrylic paints, the goal is to paint an object that looks real, with shadows, 3D shape, and reflections. Artists learn to see the world not by what it represents, but by why it looks the way it does. The following sequence @fig-agata_painting, painted by Agata Lapedriza, shows different steps in the painting process of a strawberry. Layer after layer, the artist replicates the light that will fool your eye into seeing a strawberry instead of acrylic paint. It is interesting to see that the realism does not increase monotonically as the painting progresses; for instance, from step 3 to 4, the right side of the strawberry has lost realism, but those new strokes will become the shading that makes the strawberry pop out from the canvas. ![The following sequence shows different steps in the process of painting a strawberry. Source: Original images by Agata Lapedriza.](figures/visionscience/strawberries.png){#fig-agata_painting}
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the artistic process provides insight into how visual cues like shading and highlights are constructed to create the perception of three-dimensional form.
concepts.recap_md: - Painting requires understanding the underlying reasons for an object's appearance.

key_passage.text: Artists learn to see the world not by what it represents, but as why it looks the way it does.

motivation.text: Learning to paint is a great way of learning to see. You start from a white piece of canvas and a finite set of acrylic paints, and your goal is to paint an object that should look real, with shadows, 3D shape, and reflections.

concepts.title: Linear interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Linear interpolation consists of interpolating linearly between two consecutive values using a triangular kernel.
concepts.content:
In 1D, popular interpolation kernels include nearest interpolation and linear interpolation. Nearest interpolation consists of assigning to each time instant the value of the nearest sample in time. Linear interpolation consists of interpolating linearly between two consecutive values.

Both methods can be modeled as a linear convolution with a kernel $h(t)$:

(see figure: (top) Nearest interpolation. (bottom) Linear interpolation. Both interpolation methods can be modeled by a convolution with the kernel shown in the middle (a box and a triangle).)

The nearest neighbor interpolation is the result of the convolution of $\ell_\delta (t)$ with a box of width $T_s$. In linear interpolation, the interpolation kernel $h(t)$ is a triangle of width $2T_s$.
concepts.motivation_md: Interpolation is necessary to reconstruct a continuous signal from discrete samples. Linear interpolation provides a simple way to estimate values between samples by assuming a straight-line relationship, which is more accurate than nearest-neighbor assignment.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear interpolation estimates values by connecting consecutive samples with straight lines.

key_passage.text: Linear interpolation consists of interpolating linearly between two consecutive values.

concepts.title: Lanczos-1 interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Lanczos-1 interpolation uses the central lobe of the sinc function as a kernel to provide smooth local interpolation.
concepts.content: Lanczos-1 interpolation consists of using as a kernel only the central lobe of the sinc function. This provides an interpolation that is smooth while using only a local neighborhood. Other interpolation methods, such as cubic interpolation, can also be written as convolutions. Note that the convolution of two box filters of width $T_s/2$ results in a triangle of length $T_s$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard linear interpolation can be too blocky or sharp. Lanczos-1 uses a windowed sinc function to provide a smoother reconstruction of the signal while keeping the computation efficient by only looking at a local neighborhood of samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the central lobe of the sinc function as the interpolation kernel.

key_passage.text: Lanczos-1 interpolation consists of using as kernel only the central lobe of the sinc function. This provides an interpolation that is smooth using only a local neighborhood.

motivation.text: This provides an interpolation that is smooth using only a local neighborhood.

concepts.title: Rectangular sampling
concepts.one_liner: Rectangular sampling is a 2D sampling pattern where a continuous image is sampled on a regular grid.
concepts.content:
When sampling 2D signals to form discrete images, a continuous image $\ell (x,y)$ can be sampled using a rectangular grid as $\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (nT_x, mT_y)$. This is a specific case of a more general sampling pattern defined as:

$$\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (an+bm, cn+dm)$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are constants. If $a=T, b=0, c=0, d=T$, the result is regular rectangular sampling. Other patterns, such as hexagonal or irregular sampling, are also possible.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Rectangular sampling is the standard method for digital imaging because it aligns perfectly with the matrix-based representation of images in computer memory and displays.
concepts.recap_md: - Samples a continuous 2D signal on a regular grid defined by fixed intervals $T_x$ and $T_y$.

key_passage.text: If we have a continuous image ℓ (x,y) we can sample it using a rectangular grid as ℓs [n,m] = ℓ (nTx, mTy). We can do a very similar analysis to the one we just did for the 1D case. But in 2D, we can have more interesting sampling patterns.

motivation.text: Let's now analyze what happens when sampling 2D signals to form discrete images. In 2D, things get more interesting.

concepts.title: Hexagonal sampling
concepts.one_liner: Hexagonal sampling is a 2D sampling pattern that can be defined by specific linear combinations of sample indices.
concepts.content:
In 2D signal sampling, we can define a discrete image using the general form:

$$\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (an+bm, cn+dm)$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are constants. If we set $a=T_1, b=-T_2 / 2, c=0, d=T_2$, we obtain hexagonal sampling. This is one of several possible patterns for arranging samples in a 2D space.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Hexagonal sampling is more efficient than rectangular sampling, providing better radial symmetry and requiring fewer samples to represent the same amount of high-frequency information.
concepts.recap_md: - A 2D sampling pattern where samples are arranged in a hexagonal lattice.

key_passage.text: if we set $a=T_1,b=-T_2 / 2,c=0,d=T_2$, then we obtain a **hexagonal sampling**.

motivation.text: In 2D, we can have more interesting sampling patterns.

concepts.title: Irregular sampling
concepts.one_liner: Irregular sampling involves placing signal samples at random locations rather than on a fixed grid.
concepts.content:
Beyond regular patterns like rectangular or hexagonal grids, 2D signals can be sampled by placing the samples at random locations, known as irregular sampling. This contrasts with grid-based sampling where sample positions are determined by linear combinations of indices $n$ and $m$.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Irregular sampling can help reduce aliasing artifacts that appear as structured patterns (like Moire patterns) by turning them into less distracting random noise.
concepts.recap_md: - Samples are placed at random or non-grid locations in the 2D plane.

key_passage.text: We can also place the samples at random locations (irregular sampling).

concepts.title: Fourier transform of 2D sampled signals
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a 2D sampled signal is a sum of shifted replicas of the continuous signal's spectrum.
concepts.content:
To study aliasing in 2D, we model sampling by multiplying a continuous image $\ell(x,y)$ by a 2D delta train:

$$\ell_{\delta} (x,y) = \ell (x,y) \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta (x- an-bm, y - cn-dm)$$

Using vector notation where $\mathbf{x} = (x,y)^T$, $\mathbf{n} = (n,m)^T$, and $\mathbf{A}$ is the sampling matrix, the delta train is $\delta_{\mathbf{A}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \delta ( \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{n} )$. The continuous Fourier transform of this sampled signal is:

$$\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (\mathbf{w}) =  \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{|\mathbf{A}|} \sum_{\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \mathscr{L} ( \mathbf{w} - 2 \pi \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{k} )$$

For a $2\times2$ matrix, the inverse is $\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \frac{1}{|\mathbf{A}|} \left[ \begin{array}{cc} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{array} \right]$. In the case of rectangular sampling, this simplifies to:

$$\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w_x, w_y ) =  \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{T^2} \sum_{k_1=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum_{k_2=-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L} (w_x - \frac{2\pi}{T}k_1, w_y - \frac{2\pi}{T}k_2 )$$
concepts.motivation_md: Analyzing the Fourier transform of sampled signals allows us to understand how the sampling pattern affects the spectral content and to determine the conditions necessary to avoid aliasing in 2D.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling in the spatial domain results in periodic replication of the spectrum in the frequency domain.

key_passage.text: Therefore, the Fourier transform of the sampled signal ℓ_δ (x,y) is: 𝓛_δ (𝐰) = (2π)²/|𝐀| ∑_{𝐤 ∈ ℤ²} 𝓛 (𝐰 - 2π 𝐀^{-1} 𝐤)

question.text: What is the optimal 2D sample arrangement given a fixed number of samples?

motivation.text: As we did with the 1D case, we can answer this question by studying the relationship between the Fourier transform of the continuous signal and the sampled one, which will reveal how aliasing happens and what sampling pattern minimizes it.

concepts.title: Optimal 2D sampling arrangement
concepts.one_liner: Regular hexagonal sampling is the optimal 2D strategy, maximizing resolution for a fixed number of samples.
concepts.content:
The optimal sampling arrangement is the one that allows the best reconstruction of a continuous signal from a fixed number of samples by maximizing the region of valid frequencies without aliasing.

(see figure: Sketch of the Fourier transforms of the rectangular and hexagonal samplings. The red boundary denotes the spectral content that gets periodically repeated.)

Regular hexagonal sampling is the optimal strategy. While computer vision typically uses rectangular grids, hexagonal sampling achieves approximately a 10 percent increase in resolution for the same number of samples. This pattern is found in nature; for example, the distribution of photoreceptors in the primate fovea closely resembles a hexagonal array.

(see figure: Distributions of cones in the fovea of a Monkey \cite{Curcio1990)]

Hexagonal grids also allow for more efficient convolutional filters and better radial symmetry.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding the optimal sampling pattern is crucial for maximizing information capture and minimizing aliasing when resources (like the number of pixels or sensors) are limited.
concepts.recap_md: - Hexagonal sampling is more efficient than rectangular sampling, offering higher resolution for the same sample count.

key_passage.text: The optimal sampling strategy is the regular hexagonal sampling. This is not the sampling used in computer vision as all images are always represented on a rectangular grid, but a hexagonal sampling achieves an increase of around 10 percent in resolution for the same amount of samples.

motivation.text: The optimal sampling will be the one that makes that region as large as possible for a fixed number of samples. In fact, the distribution of photoreceptors at the center of the retina closely resembles a hexagonal array over small patches.

concepts.title: Sampling finite size images
concepts.one_liner: Sampling results for infinite signals can be applied to finite images by extending them with zero padding.
concepts.content: While standard sampling analysis assumes signals of infinite length, real-world images have a finite size. The theoretical results derived for infinite signals can be applied to finite images by extending the image to infinity using zero padding.
concepts.motivation_md: Mathematical models of sampling often assume infinite domains for simplicity, but practical applications require a way to bridge this theory with finite, real-world data.
concepts.recap_md: - Finite images are treated as infinite signals via zero padding to apply standard sampling theory.

key_passage.text: The same results can be applied by extending the image to infinity with zero padding.

motivation.text: The analysis we have presented in this chapter assumes signals of infinite length. However, images will have a finite size.

concepts.title: Amplitude and Periodic Patterns

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The amplitude is effective for capturing images with strong periodic patterns and provides a degree of location invariance.
concepts.content: The amplitude is great for capturing images that contain strong periodic patterns. In such cases, the amplitude can be better than the phase. This observation has been the basis for many image descriptors. The amplitude is somewhat invariant to location, although it is not invariant to the relative location between different elements in the scene. However, the phase is a complex signal that does not seem to make explicit any information about the image.
concepts.motivation_md: Amplitude is used in image processing because it effectively captures periodic structures and offers some degree of location invariance, making it a robust feature for certain image descriptors.
concepts.recap_md: - The amplitude is particularly effective for representing images with strong periodic patterns.

key_passage.text: The amplitude is great for capturing images that contain strong periodic patterns. In such cases, the amplitude can be better than the phase.

motivation.text: This observation has been the basis for many image descriptors. The amplitude is somewhat invariant to location (although it is not invariant to the relative location between different elements in the scene).

concepts.title: Convolution kernel
concepts.one_liner: The convolution kernel, or impulse response, represents a linear filter as a spatial operation.
concepts.content: Linear filters can be written as convolutions: [FIGURE:21b02035587ce06b | Convolutional linear filter.] where $h \left[n,m \right]$ is the impulse response of the system, or convolution kernel. We can also write this as a product in the Fourier domain.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining the convolution kernel allows us to represent linear systems mathematically, enabling the transformation of spatial filtering operations into simpler algebraic products in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The convolution kernel $h[n, m]$ is the impulse response of a linear system.

key_passage.text: where h[n,m] is the impulse response of the system, or convolution kernel.

motivation.text: From the previous section we know that we can write linear filters as convolutions.

concepts.title: Transfer function
concepts.one_liner: The transfer function is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel, representing how a filter reweights spectral components.
concepts.content: A convolution can be written as a product in the Fourier domain: [FIGURE:eb36ec0cfa3e5a10 | Transfer function of a linear filter.] The function $H \left[u, v \right]$ is called the **transfer function** of the filter. The transfer function of a filter is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel. The transfer function allows us to interpret filters by how they modify the spectral content of the input signal. As the Fourier transform of the output is just a product between the Fourier transform of the input and the transfer function, a linear filter simply reweights the spectral content of the signal. It does not create new content; it can only enhance or decrease the spectral components already present in the input.
concepts.motivation_md: The transfer function simplifies the analysis of filters by showing exactly how they enhance or decrease specific frequency components of a signal.
concepts.recap_md: - The transfer function $H[u, v]$ is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel.

key_passage.text: The transfer function of a filter is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel.

motivation.text: The transfer function will allow us interpret filters by how they modify the spectral content of the input signal. As the Fourier transform of the output is just a product between the Fourier transform of the input and the transfer function, a linear filter simply reweights the spectral content of the signal.

concepts.title: Spectral content in convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolution between two signals reweights existing spectral components but does not create new ones.
concepts.content: A convolution between two signals does not create new spectral content. To create new spectral components not present in the input we need to apply nonlinearities.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that convolution is a linear operation helps clarify why linear filters are limited to frequency suppression or enhancement, necessitating non-linear methods for generating new frequencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution is a linear operation that cannot generate new spectral components.

key_passage.text: A convolution between two signals does not create new spectral content.

motivation.text: To create new spectral components not present in the input we need to apply nonlinearities.

concepts.title: Amplitude gain
concepts.one_liner: Amplitude gain is the magnitude of the transfer function, representing the factor by which spectral components are scaled.
concepts.content: If we use the polar form: $$H \left[u,v \right] = \left|H \left[u, v \right] \right| \exp \left( {j \, \angle H \left[u, v \right]} \right) $$ The magnitude $\left| H \left[u, v \right] \right|$ is the **amplitude gain**. The magnitude at the origin, $\left| H \left[0, 0 \right] \right|$, is the **DC gain** of the filter (the average value of the output signal is equal to the average value of the input times the DC gain).
concepts.motivation_md: Amplitude gain quantifies how much a filter amplifies or attenuates specific frequencies, which is essential for designing filters like low-pass or high-pass systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Amplitude gain is defined as the magnitude $|H[u, v]|$ of the transfer function.

key_passage.text: The magnitude |H[u, v]| is the amplitude gain, and the phase ∠H[u, v] is the phase shift.

concepts.title: Phase shift
concepts.one_liner: Phase shift is the angle of the transfer function in polar form, representing the displacement of spectral components.
concepts.content: If we use the polar form: $$H \left[u,v \right] = \left|H \left[u, v \right] \right| \exp \left( {j \, \angle H \left[u, v \right]} \right) $$ The phase $\angle H \left[u, v \right]$ is the **phase shift**. The magnitude at the origin, $\left| H \left[0, 0 \right] \right|$, is the **DC gain** of the filter (the average value of the output signal is equal to the average value of the input times the DC gain).
concepts.motivation_md: Phase shift is critical in signal processing because it determines how different frequency components are delayed or shifted, which can significantly impact the structure and appearance of an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Phase shift is the angle of the filter's transfer function in polar form.

key_passage.text: the phase $\angle H \left[u, v \right]$ is the **phase shift**.

concepts.title: DC gain (transfer function)
concepts.one_liner: DC gain is the magnitude of the transfer function at the origin, determining the output signal's average value.
concepts.content: If we use the polar form: $$H \left[u,v \right] = \left|H \left[u, v \right] \right| \exp \left( {j \, \angle H \left[u, v \right]} \right) $$ The magnitude at the origin, $\left| H \left[0, 0 \right] \right|$, is the **DC gain** of the filter. The average value of the output signal is equal to the average value of the input times the DC gain.
concepts.motivation_md: DC gain is important because it controls the overall brightness or baseline level of a signal after filtering, ensuring the average intensity is preserved or scaled appropriately.
concepts.recap_md: - DC gain is the magnitude of the transfer function evaluated at the zero frequency, $|H[0, 0]|$.

key_passage.text: The magnitude at the origin, $\left| H \left[0, 0 \right] \right|$, is the **DC gain** of the filter (the average value of the output signal is equal to the average value of the input times the DC gain).

motivation.text: the average value of the output signal is equal to the average value of the input times the DC gain

concepts.title: Filter classification by frequency
concepts.one_liner: Filters are often classified by the frequency ranges they allow to pass, such as low-pass, band-pass, or high-pass.
concepts.content: The Fourier domain shows that, in many cases, what a filter does is to block or let pass certain frequencies. Filters are many times classified according to the frequencies that they let pass through the filter (low, medium, or high frequencies) as shown in (see figure: Sketch of the frequency responses of low-pass, band-pass, and high-pass filters.). When filtering images, low-pass filters will output a blurry picture encoding the **coarse** elements of the image. A band-pass filter will highlight middle size elements, while the output of a high-pass filter will show the **fine** details of the image. The three images in    show the output image processed by three filters corresponding to the frequency responses of low-pass, band-pass, and high-pass filters. There are many other properties of a filter that can be used to classify linear systems (e.g., causality, stability, phase-changes). Some filters have their main effect over the phase of the signal and they are better understood in the spatial domain. In general, filters affect both the magnitude and the phase of the input signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Classifying filters by frequency allows engineers to select the right tool for specific tasks, such as smoothing noise (low-pass) or detecting edges (high-pass).
concepts.recap_md: - Filters are categorized as low-pass, band-pass, or high-pass based on the frequency ranges they transmit.

key_passage.text: Filters are many times classified according to the frequencies that they let pass through the filter (low, medium, or high frequencies)

motivation.text: The Fourier domain shows that, in many cases, what a filter does is to block or let pass certain frequencies.

concepts.title: Aliasing in 2D images
concepts.one_liner: Sampling a 2D image at an insufficient frequency causes high-frequency details to appear as low-frequency artifacts, such as stripes changing orientation.
concepts.content:
Sampling with the wrong frequency has interesting effects in 2D. For example, a picture downsampled at different resolutions (412×512, 103×128, 52×64, and 26×32) and then reconstructed to the original resolution shows the effects of aliasing. The stripes on a zebra's body may change orientation as we downsample them, and at the lowest resolutions, the animal may become difficult to recognize. 

When we multiply the image with a delta train (one every four samples along each dimension), the image Fourier transform changes. The magnitude of the DFT of the sampled image changes substantially from one resolution to the next due to aliasing. (see figure: Subsampling with aliasing. (a) The zebra sampled with aliasing starts looking like a cow. (b) Fourier transform of the continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$ multiplied by delta trains: $\ell_{\delta}(x,y)$. (c) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding sampled signals, $\ell\left[n,m\right)$. (d) Fourier transform of the reconstructed signal with aliasing. (e) Sampled image after processing it with an anti-aliasing filter. (f) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding anti-aliased sampled images, $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. Note that now the central part of the Fourier transform is not changing.]
concepts.motivation_md: Aliasing in 2D images occurs when the sampling rate is too low to capture high-frequency spatial details, leading to visual distortions like Moire patterns or incorrect textures. Understanding this helps in designing better image sensors and reconstruction algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Aliasing in 2D causes high-spatial frequencies to be misinterpreted as lower frequencies.", "- Visual artifacts include changes in the orientation of patterns or loss of object recognition.", "- The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of a sampled image changes significantly across resolutions when aliasing is present."]

key_passage.text: The images in (a) show the effects of aliasing. The stripes on the zebra's body change orientation as we downsample them. And for the lowest resolution image, it is even hard to recognize the animal as being a zebra.

motivation.text: Sampling with the wrong frequency has interesting effects in 2D.

concepts.title: Anti-aliasing filter
concepts.one_liner: An anti-aliasing filter is a low-pass filter applied before sampling to make a signal band-limited and prevent high-frequency interference.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Subsampling with aliasing. (a) The zebra sampled with aliasing starts looking like a cow. (b) Fourier transform of the continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$ multiplied by delta trains: $\ell_{\delta}(x,y)$. (c) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding sampled signals, $\ell\left[n,m\right)$. (d) Fourier transform of the reconstructed signal with aliasing. (e) Sampled image after processing it with an anti-aliasing filter. (f) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding anti-aliased sampled images, $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. Note that now the central part of the Fourier transform is not changing.]

In order to reduce aliasing artifacts, we need to filter the continuous signal with a low-pass filter to make it band-limited. This allows us to sample the signal while avoiding high-spatial frequencies that interfere with the low-frequency content of the image. While the anti-aliasing filter does not prevent the loss of information contained in high spatial frequencies, it prevents that information from corrupting lower frequencies. Each resolution requires a different filter. The anti-aliasing filter can be a box filter with support equal to the appropriate region in the Fourier domain.
concepts.motivation_md: To prevent high-frequency noise and details from 'folding' into lower frequencies during sampling, which creates permanent distortions that cannot be removed later.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Filters the continuous signal with a low-pass filter before sampling occurs.", "- Ensures the signal is band-limited to avoid high-frequency interference with low-frequency content.", "- Prevents aliasing artifacts but does not recover the lost high-frequency information."]

key_passage.text: In order to reduce aliasing artifacts, we need to filter the continuous signal with a low-pass filter to make it band-limited. Then we will be able to sample it, avoiding high-spatial frequencies that interfere with the low-frequency content of the image.

motivation.text: In order to reduce aliasing artifacts, we need to filter the continuous signal with a low-pass filter to make it band-limited. Then we will be able to sample it, avoiding high-spatial frequencies that interfere with the low-frequency content of the image.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal sampling extends sampling theory to $N$ dimensions, accounting for both spatial grids and temporal intervals.
concepts.content: Spatiotemporal sampling can be studied using general sampling equations in $N$ dimensions. Temporal aliasing is responsible for the typical illusion in which we see wheels or fans changing their sense of rotation in movies. To avoid those artifacts, it is important to apply an anti-aliasing filter to the signal before sampling.
concepts.motivation_md: Capturing moving images requires sampling in both space and time. Understanding this allows engineers to prevent temporal artifacts like the 'wagon-wheel effect'.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Applies N-dimensional sampling theory to both spatial and temporal domains.", "- Temporal aliasing causes visual illusions like wheels appearing to rotate backwards.", "- Anti-aliasing filters are necessary to prevent spatiotemporal artifacts."]

key_passage.text: Spatiotemporal sampling can be studied with the tools we have already seen. In particular, can explain sampling in the N-dimensional case.

motivation.text: Temporal aliasing is responsible for the typical illusion in which we see wheels or fans changing the sense of rotation in movies. To avoid those artifacts, it is important to apply an anti-aliasing filter as before.

concepts.title: Global Shutter Mode
concepts.one_liner: Global shutter mode is a regular sampling method where all pixels in a 2D grid are exposed simultaneously at regular time intervals.
concepts.content: The most common type of spatiotemporal sampling is regular sampling. In this mode, all the pixels are sampled in a regular spatial 2D grid and at regular time instants in which all the pixels are exposed simultaneously. This is also called global shutter mode.
concepts.motivation_md: Global shuttering ensures that the entire frame represents a single point in time, preventing geometric distortion in images of fast-moving objects.
concepts.recap_md: ["- All pixels are exposed at the exact same instant.", "- Uses a regular spatial 2D grid and regular time intervals.", "- Avoids the spatial distortions common in rolling shutter systems."]

key_passage.text: all the pixels are sampled in a regular spatial 2D grid and at regular time instants in which all the pixels are exposed simultaneously. This is also called global shutter mode.

concepts.title: Rolling Shutter Mode
concepts.one_liner: Rolling shutter mode samples image rows at different time instants, allowing for faster sampling rates but potentially causing spatial distortions.
concepts.content: In many cameras, such as DSLRs and mobile phones, the most commonly used sampling is the rolling shutter mode. In this mode, every row in the image is sampled simultaneously, but different rows are sampled at different instants. This sampling mode allows for a faster sampling rate with current hardware implementations, but it can create spatial distortions in the image if the camera moves or when taking pictures of moving objects.
concepts.motivation_md: Rolling shutters are easier and cheaper to implement in CMOS sensors, allowing for high-resolution capture even if it introduces 'jello' effects or skewing during motion.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Rows of pixels are sampled sequentially rather than all at once.", "- Enables faster sampling rates in consumer hardware.", "- Can cause spatial distortions (skewing) when the camera or subject moves."]

key_passage.text: In many cameras (DSLRs, mobile phones, etc.), the most commonly used sampling is the rolling shutter mode. Here, every row in the image is sampled simultaneously. But different rows are sampled at different instants.

motivation.text: This sampling mode allows for a faster sampling rate with current hardware implementations, but it can create spatial distortions in the image if the camera moves or when taking pictures of moving objects.

concepts.title: Moire Patterns
concepts.one_liner: Moire patterns are interference patterns that appear when superposing semitransparent patterns on top of each other.
concepts.content:
Moire patterns, also related to aliasing, are interference patterns that appear when superposing semitransparent patterns on top of each other.

[FIGURE:c1949ca908869fea | ]
concepts.motivation_md: Moire patterns are a physical manifestation of aliasing that occurs when two repetitive structures overlap, creating a new, lower-frequency pattern.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Result from the superposition of semitransparent patterns.", "- Closely related to the phenomenon of aliasing.", "- Appear as distinct interference patterns not present in the original individual layers."]

key_passage.text: Moire patterns, also related to aliasing, are interference patterns that appear when superposing semitransparent patterns on top of each other.

concepts.title: Aliasing and Superresolution
concepts.one_liner: While often an artifact, aliasing can be used by superresolution algorithms to recover high-frequency details that would otherwise be lost.
concepts.content: Aliasing is a common artifact that appears whenever an image is captured by sampling a continuous light field, and it also affects images during upsampling or downsampling. However, aliasing is not always bad; it may be possible to use aliasing to recover high-frequency content that would be otherwise lost. Superresolution algorithms can learn to extract fine image details from the aliasing pattern. Additionally, when an image is encoded by multiple channels, aliasing in one channel does not mean information is lost, as multiple channels may contain complementary information allowing the recovery of high-resolution details.
concepts.motivation_md: To shift the perspective of aliasing from a purely destructive artifact to a potential source of hidden information that can be exploited to enhance image quality.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Aliasing occurs during sampling of continuous light fields or during rescaling.", "- Superresolution algorithms can exploit aliasing patterns to reconstruct fine details.", "- Multiple channels can provide complementary information to overcome aliasing in a single channel."]

key_passage.text: However, aliasing is not always bad and it might be possible to use aliasing to recover high-frequency content that would be otherwise lost. Superresolution algorithms can learn to extract, from the aliasing pattern, fine image details.

motivation.text: Therefore, understanding how aliasing introduces artifacts and the best way to avoid it is an important skill.

concepts.title: Strided Convolution
concepts.one_liner: A strided convolution is a convolution operation followed by decimation, commonly used in neural networks.
concepts.content: A convolution followed by decimation is also called strided convolution in the neural networks literature.
concepts.motivation_md: Strided convolutions allow neural networks to downsample feature maps while simultaneously performing feature extraction, increasing the receptive field and reducing computational load.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Combines convolution and decimation into a single step.", "- Known as 'strided convolution' specifically within neural network contexts."]

key_passage.text: A convolution followed by decimation is also called strided convolution in the neural networks literature.

concepts.title: Complex Exponential Wave
concepts.one_liner: A complex exponential wave is a signal defined by $e_{u}[n] = \exp(2 \pi j \frac{u n}{N})$ that relates to sine and cosine waves via Euler's formula.
concepts.content: Another important signal is the complex exponential wave: $$e_{u}\left[n\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j   \frac{u\, n}{N}   \right)$$ Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: $$ \exp \left(j a\right) = \cos (a) + j \sin (a)$$ As the values are complex, the plot shows the real component on the $x$-axis and the imaginary component on the $y$-axis. As $n$ goes from 0 to $N-1$, the function rotates along the complex circle of unit magnitude. (see figure: Complex exponential wave with (a) $N=40$, $k=1$, $A=1$; and (b) $N=40$, $k=3$, $A=1$. The red and green curves show the real and imaginary waves. The black line is the complex exponential. The dots...)
concepts.motivation_md: Complex exponentials provide a unified mathematical framework for representing oscillations, simplifying the analysis of periodic signals by combining real and imaginary components into a single rotating vector.
concepts.recap_md: - The discrete complex exponential is defined as $e_{u}[n] = \exp(2 \pi j \frac{u n}{N})$.- It links trigonometric functions through Euler's formula, $\exp(j a) = \cos(a) + j \sin(a)$.- The signal traces a unit circle in the complex plane as the index $n$ increases.

key_passage.text: Another important signal is the complex exponential wave: e_{u}[n] = exp(2π j u n / N). Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: exp(j a) = cos(a) + j sin(a). As n goes from 0 to N-1 the function rotates along the complex circle of unit magnitude.

concepts.title: Euler's Formula
concepts.one_liner: Euler's formula relates complex exponentials to trigonometric functions by stating that $\exp(j a) = \cos(a) + j \sin(a)$.
concepts.content: Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: $$ \exp \left(j a\right) = \cos (a) + j \sin (a)$$
concepts.motivation_md: This formula is fundamental for signal processing because it allows sinusoidal oscillations to be expressed as complex exponentials, which are much easier to manipulate algebraically.
concepts.recap_md: - Euler's formula establishes the identity $\exp(j a) = \cos(a) + j \sin(a)$.- It connects exponential growth and decay with circular motion and oscillation.

key_passage.text: Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: exp(ja) = cos(a) + j sin(a)

concepts.title: Orthogonality of Complex Exponentials
concepts.one_liner: Complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images, allowing any finite signal to be decomposed into a linear combination of these waves.
concepts.content: A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For images of size $N \times M$, $$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$ Therefore, any finite length discrete image can be decomposed as a linear combination of complex exponentials.
concepts.motivation_md: Orthogonality ensures that each frequency component in a signal can be analyzed independently, which is the mathematical foundation for the Fourier Transform.
concepts.recap_md: - Complex exponentials serve as an orthogonal basis for finite discrete signals.- The inner product of two distinct basis elements is zero, while the inner product with itself is $MN$.- This property allows for the unique decomposition of any discrete image into frequency components.

key_passage.text: A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For images of size $N \times M$, $$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$

motivation.text: Therefore, any finite length discrete image can be decomposed as a linear combination of complex exponentials.

concepts.title: Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms a finite-sized image into a complex frequency-domain representation using a sum of complex exponentials.
concepts.content: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms an image $\ell\left[n,m \right]$, of finite size $N \times M$, into the complex image Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ as: $$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = \mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n,m \right] \right\} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)}$$ We will call $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ the Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: The DFT allows us to analyze the frequency content of digital signals and images, enabling tasks like filtering, compression, and feature extraction that are difficult in the spatial domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The DFT maps a spatial signal $\ell[n,m]$ to its frequency representation $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$.- It is computed by summing the product of the image and complex exponential basis functions.

key_passage.text: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms an image ℓ[n,m], of finite size N × M, into the complex image Fourier transform ℒ[u,v]

concepts.title: Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform reconstructs a spatial signal or image from its complex frequency-domain representation.
concepts.content: By applying $\frac{1}{MN} \sum_{u=0}^{M-1} \sum_{v=0}^{N-1}$ to both sides of the Fourier transform equation and exploiting the orthogonality between distinct Fourier basis elements, we find the inverse Fourier transform relation: $$\ell\left[n,m \right] = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\} = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \exp{ \left(+2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }$$
concepts.motivation_md: The inverse transform is essential for returning to the spatial domain after performing operations like noise reduction or sharpening in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The IDFT reconstructs the original signal $\ell[n,m]$ from its Fourier coefficients $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$.- It uses a positive exponent in the complex exponential and includes a normalization factor of $1/NM$.

key_passage.text: we find the inverse Fourier transform relation $$\ell\left[n,m \right] = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\} = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \exp{ \left(+2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }$$

concepts.title: Periodicity of the DFT
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform and its inverse are inherently periodic functions with periods corresponding to the dimensions of the input signal.
concepts.content: As $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is obtained as a sum of complex exponentials with a common period of $N,M$ samples, the function $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is also periodic: $\mathscr{L}\left[u+aN,v+bM \right] = \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$. Also, the result of the inverse DFT is a periodic image. Indeed, you can verify from the inverse Fourier transform equation that $\ell\left[n+aN,m+bM \right] = \ell\left[n,m \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding periodicity is crucial for correctly interpreting DFT results and avoiding artifacts like aliasing or edge effects when processing finite-length signals.
concepts.recap_md: - Both the DFT and the IDFT produce results that are periodic in both dimensions.- The periods are defined by the dimensions $N$ and $M$ of the discrete signal.

key_passage.text: As $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is obtained as a sum of complex exponential with a common period of $N,M$ samples, the function $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is also periodic: $\mathscr{L}\left[u+aN,v+bM \right] = \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$.

concepts.title: Uniqueness of Fourier Decomposition
concepts.one_liner: The decomposition of a signal into a sum of complex exponentials is unique, meaning only one specific linear combination exists for any given signal.
concepts.content: One very important property is that the decomposition of a signal into a sum of complex exponentials is unique: there is a unique linear combination of the exponentials that will result in a given signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Uniqueness ensures that the frequency representation of a signal is well-defined, allowing for consistent analysis and perfect reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Any signal has exactly one representation as a sum of complex exponential basis functions.- This uniqueness guarantees that the Fourier coefficients for a signal are distinct and unambiguous.

key_passage.text: the decomposition of a signal into a sum of complex exponentials is unique: there is a unique linear combination of the exponentials that will result in a given signal.

motivation.text: One very important property is that the decomposition of a signal into a sum of complex exponentials is unique: there is a unique linear combination of the exponentials that will result in a given signal.

concepts.title: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
concepts.one_liner: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is an efficient algorithm that reduces the computational complexity of the DFT from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.content: The DFT became very popular thanks to the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. The most common FFT algorithm is the Cooley–Tukey algorithm, which reduces the computation cost from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Before the FFT, calculating the DFT for large signals was computationally prohibitive; the FFT's efficiency made real-time digital signal processing and modern image analysis possible.
concepts.recap_md: - The FFT is a highly efficient algorithm for computing the Discrete Fourier Transform.- It reduces computational complexity from quadratic $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.- The Cooley–Tukey algorithm is the most widely used implementation of the FFT.

key_passage.text: The most common FFT algorithm is the Cooley–Tukey algorithm that reduces the computation cost from O(N²) to O(N log N).

motivation.text: The DFT became very popular thanks to the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm.

concepts.title: Ringing Artifacts
concepts.one_liner: Ringing artifacts are undesired oscillations or halos introduced into an image by certain low-pass anti-aliasing filters.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Output of three different low-pass anti-aliasing filters. (left) Ideal low-pass filter. (center) Hamming window. (right) Binomial filter.)

The ideal low-pass filter introduces ringing artifacts in the output image. Despite removing frequencies that produce aliasing after downsampling, it does so at a high cost by introducing undesired image structures, which is exactly what anti-aliasing filters aim to prevent. The Hamming windowed sinc reduces the oscillation, but a halo is still present around edges because one oscillation remains on the filter impulse response. Applying an anti-aliasing binomial filter avoids these undesired structures. For most applications, using a binomial filter ($b_2$ or $b_4$) is sufficient because it reduces aliasing without introducing ringing artifacts.
concepts.motivation_md: While low-pass filters are necessary to prevent aliasing, some filters (like the ideal low-pass filter) create visual distortions known as ringing or halos. Understanding these artifacts helps in selecting filters, such as binomial filters, that balance alias reduction with visual fidelity.
concepts.recap_md: - Ringing artifacts are undesired oscillations or halos that appear near sharp edges in an image.

key_passage.text: Note how the ideal low-pass filter introduces ringing artifacts in the output image. Despite that it removes frequencies that will produce aliasing after downsampling, it does that at a high cost because it introduces undesired image structures, which is exactly what we want to prevent with the anti-aliasing filter.

motivation.text: Despite that it removes frequencies that will produce aliasing after downsampling, it does that at a high cost because it introduces undesired image structures, which is exactly what we want to prevent with the anti-aliasing filter.

concepts.title: Downsampling
concepts.one_liner: Downsampling is the process of applying an anti-aliasing filter to a signal followed by decimation.
concepts.content:
Downsampling is defined as the sequence of applying an anti-aliasing filtering followed by decimation:

$$\begin{aligned}
    z[n,m] &= \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] \circ h_k \left[ n,m \right]  & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}\\
    \ell_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] &= z[kn,km]  & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{decimation}
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Downsampling by 2 uses a binomial filter as the anti-aliasing filter followed by decimation by 2.)

In anti-aliased downsampled images, fine details are removed while the smooth details of the image are preserved. Even at very low resolutions, such as $32 \times 32$, some orientations of patterns and shading due to three-dimensional shapes can remain visible when proper anti-aliasing is used.

(see figure: Successive downsampling by a factor of 2 with anti-aliasing. Compare these results with the ones from @fig-subsampled_textures.)
concepts.motivation_md: Downsampling reduces the resolution of an image. Simply removing pixels (decimation) causes aliasing; therefore, a low-pass filter must be applied first to preserve the integrity of the remaining signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Downsampling consists of a convolution with an anti-aliasing filter followed by decimation.

key_passage.text: We will call downsampling the sequence of applying an anti-aliasing filtering followed by decimation

motivation.text: In the anti-aliased downsampled images shown in fig-subsampled_antialiasing_textures, fine details are gone while preserving the smooth details of the image.

concepts.title: Matrix representation of downsampling
concepts.one_liner: Downsampling can be represented as a matrix operator because convolution and decimation are linear operations.
concepts.content:
As convolution and downsampling are linear operators, it is sometimes useful to write the process as a matrix. For a 1D signal of length $N=8$ samples downsampled by a factor $k=2$, using repeat padding for boundary handling and a binomial kernel as an anti-aliasing filter, the downsampling operator can be written as:

$$\mathbf{D}_2 = \frac{1}{4} \left[ 
\begin{array}{cccccccc}
3 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1  
\end{array}
\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Representing downsampling as a matrix allows the operation to be integrated into linear algebra frameworks, making it easier to analyze, invert, or combine with other linear transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - The downsampling operator $\mathbf{D}_k$ combines filtering and decimation into a single linear transformation matrix.

key_passage.text: As the convolution and downsampling are linear operators, sometimes it will be useful to write it as a matrix.

motivation.text: As the convolution and downsampling are linear operators, sometimes it will be useful to write it as a matrix.

concepts.title: Multi-stage downsampling
concepts.one_liner: Downsampling by a factor of $k=2^n$ is typically achieved through a sequence of $n$ stages of binomial filtering and downsampling by 2.
concepts.content: Downsampling by a factor $k=2^n$ is usually performed by a sequence of $n$ stages, where each stage consists of binomial filtering followed by downsampling by 2. For non-integer downsampling factors, an interpolation step is required instead of simple decimation.
concepts.motivation_md: Large downsampling factors are more computationally efficient and numerically stable when broken down into smaller, repeated steps of downsampling by 2.
concepts.recap_md: - Large power-of-two downsampling is implemented as a sequence of smaller 'downsample-by-2' operations.

key_passage.text: Downsampling by a factor $k=2^n$ is usually done by a sequence of $n$ stages of binomial filtering followed by downsampling by 2.

motivation.text: Non-integer downsampling factors require an interpolation step instead of decimation.

concepts.title: Upsampling vs Super-resolution
concepts.one_liner: Upsampling increases image resolution by interpolating existing information, whereas super-resolution attempts to recover or predict missing high-resolution details.
concepts.content: Upsampling involves increasing the resolution of an image from a low-resolution source. This is a challenging task because it requires recovering information not present in the low-resolution image. While super-resolution refers to the problem of creating new details, standard upsampling focuses on the simpler problem of creating an image with $k$ times more pixels that contains the same amount of information as the original. This procedure does not require predicting missing high-resolution details. Upsampling requires interpolating sample values to obtain a new image $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$ with more samples than the input $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$. To interpolate a new sample $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$ at continuous coordinates $a$ and $b$, various interpolation functions can be used.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between upsampling and super-resolution clarifies whether the goal is simply to resize an image (interpolation) or to enhance its semantic detail (super-resolution).
concepts.recap_md: - Upsampling creates a higher-resolution grid using the same information content as the original image.

key_passage.text: Upsampling requires increasing the resolution of an image from a low resolution image. This is a very challenging task that requires recovering information that is not available on the low resolution image. The problem of making up new details will be called super-resolution.

motivation.text: Upsampling requires increasing the resolution of an image from a low resolution image. This is a very challenging task that requires recovering information that is not available on the low resolution image.

concepts.title: Nearest Neighbor Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Nearest neighbor interpolation assigns the value of the closest input sample to each output coordinate, resulting in a piecewise-constant image.
concepts.content:
In nearest neighbor interpolation, the value assigned to an output coordinate $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$ is the closest value from the input $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b) = \ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n, m ]$$
where $n-0.5<a<n+0.5$ and $m-0.5<b<m+0.5$. In this context, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$ is treated as a continuous image. This method results in an image that is piecewise-constant.

(see figure: Nearest neighbor interpolation in 1D and 2D.)
concepts.motivation_md: This is the simplest and fastest interpolation method, useful when computational resources are limited or when preserving the exact original pixel values is more important than smoothness.
concepts.recap_md: - Nearest neighbor interpolation selects the single closest pixel value for each new sample point.

key_passage.text: In nearest neighbor interpolation we assign to ℓ_out(a,b) the closest value of the input ℓ_in: ℓ_out(a,b) = ℓ_in[n,m] where n-0.5<a<n+0.5 and m-0.5<b<m+0.5.

concepts.title: Linear and Bilinear Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Bilinear interpolation calculates output values by performing linear interpolation across two dimensions using the four nearest input samples.
concepts.content:
For 1D signals, the value $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a)$ is the result of linear interpolation between the two closest input values $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n+1]$, where $n<a<n+1$. Interpolation is also a key operation when performing image warping.

For 2D signals, the output value $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$ is interpolated using four input samples: $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n,m ]$, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n+1,m ]$, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n,m+1 ]$, and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n+1,m+1 ]$, where $n<a<n+1$ and $m<b<m+1$. Bilinear interpolation consists of first applying linear interpolation to obtain intermediate values $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,m)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,m+1)$, and then applying linear interpolation again between those two values to obtain the final result $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$.

(see figure: 1D linear interpolation and 2D bilinear interpolation.)
concepts.motivation_md: Bilinear interpolation provides a smoother result than nearest neighbor interpolation by accounting for the distance to all four surrounding pixels, reducing blocky artifacts during upsampling or warping.
concepts.recap_md: - Bilinear interpolation uses a weighted average of the four nearest pixels based on their distance to the target coordinate.

key_passage.text: Bilinear interpolation consists of first applying linear interpolation to obtain ℓout(a,m) and ℓout(a,m+1) and then again applying linear interpolation between those two values to obtain ℓout(a,b).

motivation.text: Interpolation is also a key operation when performing image warping.

concepts.title: Upsampling as expansion and interpolation
concepts.one_liner: For integer factors, upsampling can be efficiently implemented as a sequence of expansion followed by a convolutional interpolation.
concepts.content: Linear and bilinear interpolations are linear operations. When the upsampling factor $k$ is an integer, the resampling operator can be efficiently implemented as a sequence of two operations: expansion and interpolation. Because the interpolation operation is linear and spatially stationary, it can be efficiently implemented as a convolution.
concepts.motivation_md: Treating upsampling as expansion followed by convolution allows the use of optimized signal processing libraries and hardware designed for fast convolution.
concepts.recap_md: - Integer upsampling is equivalent to inserting zeros (expansion) and then applying a low-pass filter (interpolation).

key_passage.text: In the case when the upsampling factor k is an integer value, the resampling operator can be efficiently implemented as a sequence of two operations: expansion and interpolation. The interpolation operation, as it is linear and spatially stationary, can be efficiently implemented as a convolution.

motivation.text: The linear (and bilinear) interpolations are linear operations.

concepts.title: DC gain of a spatial filter
concepts.one_liner: The DC gain of a spatial filter is the gain it has for a constant value input, representing the lowest possible input frequency.
concepts.content:
One important property of a low-pass filter is the DC gain, which is the gain it has for a constant value input (the lowest possible input frequency). If the input signal is a constant $\ell[n,m] = a$, where $a$ is a real number, the result of convolving the image with a box filter $h_{N,M}$ is also a constant:

$$
\ell_{\text{out}} \left[n,m\right] = \sum_{k,l} a \text{box}_{N,M} \left[k,l \right] = a \sum_{k,l} \text{box}_{N,M} \left[k,l \right]  = a (2N+1)(2M+1)
$$

The DC value of a signal is its mean value. In general, the DC gain of an arbitrary filter $h [n,m]$ is the sum of its kernel values:

$$
\text{DC~gain} = \sum_{n,m} h [n,m]
$$

In the frequency domain, the DC gain refers to the gain at a frequency of 0, represented by $H[0,0]$, where $H$ is the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the filter's kernel $h$. This can be verified by setting spatial frequencies to zero in the DFT definition. For example, the DC gain of a 1D box filter with $N=1$ is 3, which can be seen as $|\text{Box}_1[0]|$ in @fig-boxfilter. The DC gain of a filter changes the mean value of the input signal.

(see figure: 1D Box Filter.)

(see figure: Fourier transform of Box Filter.)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding DC gain is essential for predicting how a filter will affect the overall brightness or average intensity of an image. It ensures that the filtered output maintains a predictable relationship with the original signal's mean value.
concepts.recap_md: - The DC gain is the sum of all values in a filter's spatial kernel.

key_passage.text: In general, the DC gain of an arbitrary filter h [n,m] is the sum of its kernel values: DC gain = ∑_{n,m} h [n,m]

motivation.text: The DC gain of a filter will change the mean value of the input signal.

concepts.title: Limitations of the box filter
concepts.one_liner: The box filter is limited by non-monotonic frequency attenuation and the fact that repeated convolutions do not produce another box filter.
concepts.content:
The box filter is simple to implement and understand, but it has several limitations:

- **The box filter is not a perfect blurring filter.** A blur filter should ideally attenuate higher spatial frequencies more strongly. However, the box filter's attenuation is not monotonic with spatial frequency. For example, an oscillating signal $[..., 1, -1, 1, -1, ...]$ filtered with $\text{box}_{1}$ results in the same oscillating signal, while a lower frequency wave might result in zero. This can cause artifacts, as shown in @fig-boxfilter. While even-sized filters could address some issues, they are not centered around the origin and cause half-pixel translations, making odd filter sizes preferable.

[FIGURE:b08aebefbd75544f]

Convolved with the kernel $[1,1,1]$ results in:

[FIGURE:87007ce110b1a43f]

- **Convolving two boxes does not result in another box.** Instead, it produces a triangular filter. For instance, $\text{box}_{1,0} \circ \text{box}_{1,0} = [1, 1, 1] \circ [1, 1, 1] = [1,2,3,2,1]$. The output is a triangular filter with length $2 \times (L-1)$, where $L$ is the length of the box filter. Consequently, blurring an image twice with box filters is not equivalent to blurring once with a larger box filter.
concepts.motivation_md: While computationally efficient, the box filter's mathematical shortcomings—like frequency leakage and lack of closure under convolution—motivate the use of more sophisticated kernels like the Gaussian filter for high-quality image processing.
concepts.recap_md: - Box filters do not attenuate high frequencies monotonically, which can lead to unwanted artifacts.

key_passage.text: If you convolve two boxes, you do not get another box. Instead, you get a triangle.

motivation.text: The box filter is simple to implement and to understand, but it has a number of limitations. This is not a desirable behavior for a blurring filter, and it can cause artifacts to appear.

concepts.title: Triangular filter
concepts.one_liner: A triangular filter is the result of convolving two box filters, resulting in a kernel with a linear ramp-up and ramp-down profile.
concepts.content:
If you convolve two box filters, you do not get another box; instead, you get a triangle. For instance, in the simple case where $N=1, M=0$:

$$
\text{box}_{1,0} \circ \text{box}_{1,0} = \left[1, 1, 1\right] \circ \left[1, 1, 1\right] = \left[1,2,3,2,1\right]
$$

The output is a triangular filter with length $2 \times (L-1)$, where $L$ is the length of the box filter. When convolving two box filters of different lengths, the result will be a truncated triangle. This means that blurring an image twice with box filters is not equivalent to blurring only once with a larger box filter.
concepts.motivation_md: Triangular filters provide a slightly smoother blurring effect than standard box filters and arise naturally when multiple box-filter passes are applied to a signal.
concepts.recap_md: - A triangular filter is created by convolving two box filters together.

key_passage.text: The output is a triangular filter with length 2 × (L-1), with L=3 the length of the box filter.

motivation.text: Although that is not a problem at first sight, it means that if you blur an image twice with box filters, what you get is not the equivalent to blurring only once with a larger box filter.

concepts.title: Gaussian filter
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian filter is a fundamental low-pass filter that models natural blurring and possesses unique mathematical properties for image processing.
concepts.content:
The Gaussian filter is one of the most important blurring (low-pass) filters in computer vision. It is a good model for many naturally occurring filters and possesses several unique properties. The Gaussian distribution is defined in continuous variables as:

$$g(x; \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp{ \left( -\frac{x^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$

In two dimensions, it is defined as:

$$g(x,y; \sigma) = \frac{1}{2 \pi \sigma^2} \exp{ \left(- rac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$

The parameter $\sigma$ (standard deviation) adjusts the spatial extent of the Gaussian, and the normalization constant ensures the function integrates to 1. The Gaussian kernel is positive and symmetric, making it a zero-phase filter. By adjusting $\sigma$, one can control the level of image detail in the blurred result.

(see figure: Gaussian filter with $\sigma=2$.)

(see figure: Gaussian filter with $\sigma=4$.)

(see figure: Gaussian filter with $\sigma=8$.)
concepts.motivation_md: The Gaussian filter is preferred in computer vision because it effectively suppresses high-frequency noise while maintaining a smooth, natural appearance without the artifacts common to box filters.
concepts.recap_md: - The Gaussian filter is a symmetric, positive low-pass filter defined by its standard deviation $\sigma$.

key_passage.text: The Gaussian filter is important because it is a good model for many naturally occurring filters. The Gaussian kernel is positive and symmetric (a zero-phase filter).

motivation.text: One of the important blurring (low-pass) filters in computer vision is the Gaussian filter. The Gaussian filter is important because it is a good model for many naturally occurring filters. It also has several properties, as we will discuss here, that make it unique.

concepts.title: Discretization of the Gaussian filter
concepts.one_liner: Discretization of the Gaussian filter involves sampling the continuous function and truncating it to a finite support, typically within three standard deviations.
concepts.content:
To use a Gaussian filter in practice, we must consider discrete locations and approximate the function with finite support. Typically, samples are only considered within three standard deviations $x \in (-3\sigma, 3\sigma)$, where the amplitude is approximately 1% of its central value. Many properties of the continuous Gaussian are only approximated in this discrete form.

For a given $\sigma$, the discretized Gaussian kernel is:

$$g \left[ n,m; \sigma \right] = \exp{ \left( -\frac{n^2 + m^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$

[FIGURE:750fb1caf06dd3e4]

In this discrete definition, the normalization constant is often removed so the value at the origin is 1. However, in practice, the discrete kernel should be normalized by the sum of its values to ensure the DC gain is 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Since digital images are discrete grids, continuous mathematical filters must be discretized and truncated into finite kernels to be computationally applicable.
concepts.recap_md: - Discrete Gaussian kernels are usually truncated at $3\sigma$ and normalized by the sum of their values.

key_passage.text: For a given standard deviation parameter, σ, the discretized Gaussian kernel is g[n, m; σ]: g[n,m; σ] = exp(-(n²+m²)/(2σ²))

motivation.text: In order to use this filter in practice, we need to consider discrete locations and also approximate the function by a finite support function.

concepts.title: Separability of the Gaussian filter
concepts.one_liner: A 2D Gaussian filter is separable, meaning it can be computed as a sequence of two 1D Gaussian convolutions to improve efficiency.
concepts.content:
The $n$-dimensional Gaussian filter has the computational advantage of being separable; it can be applied as a concatenation of $n$ 1D Gaussian filters. For a 2D Gaussian, letting $g^x$ and $g^y$ be the 1D kernels in the horizontal and vertical directions:

$$
g \left[n,m \right] \circ \ell \left[n,m\right] 
= \sum_{k} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(n-k)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }
\left( \sum_{l} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(m-l)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) } \ell \left[k,l \right] \right)
= g^x \circ (g^y \circ \ell \left[n,m \right])
$$

This saves significant computation time. A direct 2D convolution with an $N \times N$ kernel scales in proportion to $N^2$ multiplications per pixel. Using a cascade of two 1D kernels scales in proportion to $2N$.
concepts.motivation_md: Separability drastically reduces the computational cost of blurring, making real-time processing of high-resolution images feasible.
concepts.recap_md: - Separability allows a 2D Gaussian convolution to be performed as two 1D passes, reducing complexity from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$.

key_passage.text: The n-dimensional Gaussian filter has the additional computational advantage that it can be applied as a concatenation of n 1D Gaussian filters.

motivation.text: This can save quite a bit in computation time when applying the convolution. If the 2D convolution kernel is N × N samples, then a direct convolution of that 2D kernel scales in proportion to N², since it requires one multiplication per image position per kernel sample. Using the cascade of two 1D kernels, resulting in an equivalent 2D filter of the same size, scales in proportion to 2N.

concepts.title: Properties of the Continuous Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The continuous Gaussian filter is characterized by its circular symmetry, separability, and the fact that its Fourier transform is also a Gaussian.
concepts.content:
The Gaussian filter possesses several key mathematical properties:

- **Symmetry and Separability:** It is the only completely circularly symmetric operator that is also separable.
- **Fourier Transform:** The continuous Fourier transform (FT) of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian. In 2D, it is $G (w_x, w_y; ho) = \exp{ \left(- \frac{(w_x^2+w_y^2) \sigma^2} {2} \right) }$. This function is radially symmetric and monotonically decreasing in magnitude.
- **Scaling:** The width of the Gaussian's Fourier transform decreases as the spatial $\sigma$ increases.
- **Convolution:** The convolution of two $n$-dimensional Gaussians with variances $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ results in another Gaussian with variance $\sigma_3^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2$.
- **Heat Equation:** The Gaussian is the solution to the heat equation.
- **Central Limit Theorem:** Repeated convolutions of any function concentrated at the origin result in a Gaussian.
- **Impulse Limit:** As $\sigma \rightarrow 0$, the Gaussian becomes an impulse.
concepts.motivation_md: These unique properties, such as the Fourier transform being another Gaussian, ensure that Gaussian blurring is well-behaved in both the spatial and frequency domains, avoiding the artifacts found in other filters.
concepts.recap_md: - The convolution of two Gaussians is always another Gaussian with a variance equal to the sum of the original variances.

key_passage.text: The continuous Fourier transform (FT) of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian. The convolution of two n-dimensional Gaussians is an n-dimensional Gaussian.

motivation.text: The convolution of two n-dimensional Gaussians is an n-dimensional Gaussian. This is a remarkable property of Gaussian filters and is the basis of the Gaussian pyramid that we will see later.

concepts.title: Gaussian Symmetry and Separability Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The $n$-dimensional Gaussian is the unique operator that is both completely circularly symmetric and separable.
concepts.content: The $n$-dimensional Gaussian is the only completely circularly symmetric operator that is separable.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem identifies the Gaussian as a unique tool in image processing, allowing for isotropic (direction-independent) filtering while maintaining the high efficiency of separable 1D operations.
concepts.recap_md: - The Gaussian is the only filter that is both separable and circularly symmetric.

key_passage.text: The $n$-dimensional Gaussian is the only completely circularly symmetric operator that is separable.

concepts.title: Oversampled Transform
concepts.one_liner: A transform is oversampled when the number of output coefficients $M$ is greater than the number of input samples $N$.
concepts.content: A transform is defined as **oversampled** when $M > N$, where $M$ represents the number of coefficients and $N$ represents the number of input samples. In contrast, the transform is considered critically sampled when $M=N$.
concepts.motivation_md: Oversampling is used to create redundant representations that can be more robust to noise or provide more flexibility in signal analysis than critically sampled transforms.
concepts.recap_md: - A transform is oversampled if $M > N$.

key_passage.text: The transform is oversampled when $M > N$, and undersampled when $M < N$.

concepts.title: Undersampled Transform
concepts.one_liner: A transform is undersampled when the number of output coefficients $M$ is less than the number of input samples $N$.
concepts.content: A transform is defined as **undersampled** when $M < N$, where $M$ is the number of coefficients and $N$ is the number of input samples. This is distinguished from the oversampled case ($M > N$) and the critically sampled case ($M=N$).
concepts.motivation_md: Undersampling is often used in compression or dimensionality reduction, where a signal is represented by fewer coefficients than its original sample count.
concepts.recap_md: - A transform is undersampled if $M < N$.

key_passage.text: The transform is oversampled when M > N, and undersampled when M < N.

concepts.title: Overcomplete Representation
concepts.one_liner: An overcomplete representation is one that is both oversampled and complete, allowing for inversion via the pseudoinverse.
concepts.content: An overcomplete representation occurs when a transform is both oversampled and complete. In such cases, the inverse transform $\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T})^{-1}$ can be obtained using the pseudoinverse: $$\mathbf{Q}=(\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T})^{-1}\mathbf{P}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Overcomplete representations provide redundancy, which can be useful for denoising or capturing features that are not easily represented in a basis.
concepts.recap_md: - Overcomplete means the transform is both oversampled and complete.

key_passage.text: If it is overcomplete (oversampled and complete), then the inverse can be obtained using the pseudoinverse $\mathbf{Q}=(\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T})^{-1}\mathbf{P}$.

concepts.title: Self-inverting Transform
concepts.one_liner: A self-inverting transform is a special case where the transform matrix satisfies $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}} = \mathbf{I}$.
concepts.content: An important special case is when the transform is **self-inverting**, meaning $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}} = \mathbf{I}$. The values of $\mathbf{P}$ can be real or complex. For complex transforms, the transpose $\mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T}$ should be replaced by the complex conjugate transpose $\mathbf{P}^{*\mathsf{T}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Self-inverting transforms simplify the reconstruction process because the same operator (or its adjoint) can be used for both analysis and synthesis.
concepts.recap_md: - A transform is self-inverting if $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}} = \mathbf{I}$.

key_passage.text: An important special case is when the transform is self-inverting, then P P^T = I.

motivation.text: For complex transforms, we should replace the P^T by P^*T (i.e., complex conjugate transpose).

concepts.title: Gaussian Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian pyramid is a sequence of images where each level is a blurred and subsampled version of the previous one.
concepts.content:
The Gaussian pyramid is a recursive algorithm for creating a multiresolution version of an image. A Gaussian filter is used to blur the image, as multiple successive applications of a Gaussian filter are equivalent to applying a single, wider Gaussian filter. 

The algorithm involves two steps: convolving the image with a low-pass filter (such as the fourth binomial filter $\mathbf{b}_4 = [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16$, normalized to sum to 1 and applied separably in each dimension), and then subsampling the result by a factor of 2. Each level is obtained by filtering the previous level with a stride of 2. Applied recursively, this generates a sequence of images $\mathbf{g}_0, \mathbf{g}_1, . . ., \mathbf{g}_N$, where subsequent images are smaller, lower-resolution versions of the earlier ones. The first level, $\mathbf{g}_0$, is the input image $\boldsymbol\ell$.
