concepts.title: The Full Transformer Architecture

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities, often augmented with normalization layers and residual connections.
concepts.content:
A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities. These two steps are analogous to linear layers interleaved with neuronwise nonlinearities in an MLP.

(see figure: The basic transformer architecture versus an MLP.)

Beyond this basic template, there are many variations that can be added, resulting in different particular architectures within the transformer family. Some common additions are normalization layers and residual connections. In (see figure: The ViT transformer architecture~\cite{dosovitskiy2020vit}. This set of layers forms a computational block, shaded in gray, that can be repeated $L$ times for a depth $L$ ViT. To clarify where the...) we see the ViT architecture, showing where these additional pieces enter the picture.

This architecture uses layer normalization before each attention layer and before each token-wise MLP layer. The normalization is performed within each token, where the token code vector is treated akin to a layer; each dimension is standardized by the mean and variance over all dimensions of that vector. This operation is referred to as `token norm`. Residual connections are added around each group of layers.

The output of a transformer is a set of tokens $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. To produce a different format, such as a single vector of logits for image classification or an image for image-to-image tasks, a task-specific output layer is typically defined. For example, to produce logit predictions, one could sum all the token code vectors in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$ and then project the resulting $d$-dimensional vector into a $K$-dimensional vector using a single linear layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Transformers solve the problem of processing sequences or sets of data by interleaving global information sharing (attention) with independent local processing (tokenwise MLPs). This modular structure allows the model to scale effectively while maintaining the flexibility to handle various input and output formats through task-specific heads.
concepts.recap_md: - A transformer alternates between self-attention layers for global context and tokenwise MLPs for local processing.

key_passage.text: A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities.

motivation.text: The output of a transformer, as we have so far defined it, is a set of tokens. Often we want an output of a different format, such as a single vector of logits for image classification, or in the format of an image for image-to-image tasks.

concepts.title: Permutation Equivariance

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Transformers are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence because their constituent layers—attention and tokenwise MLPs—are themselves permutation equivariant.
concepts.content:
An important property of transformers is that they are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence. This follows from the fact that both tokenwise layers, $F_{\theta}$, and attention layers, $\texttt{attn}$, are permutation equivariant:

$$\begin{aligned}
    F_{\theta}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))\\
    \texttt{attn}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{attn}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

where $\texttt{permute}$ is a permutation of the order of tokens in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ (i.e., permutes the rows of the matrix). This means that if you scramble the patches in the input image then apply attention, the output will be unchanged up to a permutation of the original output. Since the full transformer architecture is a composition of these two types of layers (plus residual connections and token normalization, which are also permutation equivariant), and because composing two permutation equivariant functions results in a permutation equivariant operation, we have:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{transformer}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{transformer}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

This property is visualized in (see figure: Transformers are permutation equivariant. For notational simplicity, we omit layer indices on the token variables here.).
concepts.motivation_md: Permutation equivariance ensures that the model treats the input as a set of entities rather than a fixed grid, allowing it to process information based on content and relationships rather than just absolute spatial position.
concepts.recap_md: - Transformers are permutation equivariant, meaning scrambling input tokens results in an identically scrambled output.

key_passage.text: An important property of transformers is that they are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence. This follows from the fact that both tokenwise layers, $F_{\theta}$, and attention layers, $\texttt{attn}$, are **permutation equivariant**.

motivation.text: This means that if you scramble (i.e. permute) the patches in the input image then apply attention, the output will be unchanged up to a permutation of the original output. Since the full transformer architecture is just composition of these two types of layers (plus, potentially, residual connections and token normalization, which are also permutation equivariant), and because composing two permutation equivariant functions results in a permutation equivariant operation, we have permutation equivariance at the full transformer level.

concepts.title: Equivariance and Invariance in Layers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Layers can be categorized by their symmetries, with attention being both translation and permutation equivariant, while convolutions are translation equivariant but not necessarily permutation equivariant.
concepts.content:
It is often useful to understand layers in terms of their invariances and equivariances. Convolutational layers are translation equivariant but not necessarily permutation equivariant, whereas attention layers are both translation equivariant and permutation equivariant. Since translation is a special kind of permutation, any permutation equivariant layer is also translation equivariant. Other layers can be catalogued similarly: global average pooling layers are permutation invariant, ReLU layers are permutation equivariant, and per-token MLP layers are also permutation equivariant (with respect to sets of tokens rather than sets of neurons).

A generally good strategy is to select layers that reflect the symmetries in your data or task. In object detection, translation equivariance makes sense because a bird is a bird no matter where it appears in an image. Permutation equivariance might also make sense for the same reason, but only to an extent: if you break up an image into small patches and scramble them, this could disrupt spatial layout that is important for recognition. Transformers address this by using positional codes to reinsert information about spatial layout.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the symmetries of different layers helps in designing architectures that naturally respect the properties of the data, such as the spatial consistency required for image recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Attention layers are both translation and permutation equivariant.

key_passage.text: It is often useful to understand layers in terms of their invariances and equivariances. Convolutational layers are translation equivariant but not necessarily permutation equivariant whereas attention layers are both translation equivariant and permutation equivariant (since translation is a special kind of permutation, any permutation equivariant layer is also translation equivariant).

motivation.text: A generally good strategy is to select layers that reflect the symmetries in your data or task: in object detection, translation equivariance makes sense because, roughly, a bird is a bird no matter where it appears in an image.

concepts.title: Tokenization as Convolution

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Tokenization in transformers can be implemented as a convolutional layer where the kernel size and stride are both equal to the patch size $K$.
concepts.content:
The first step in working with transformers is to tokenize the input. The most basic way to do this is to chop up the input image into non-overlapping patches of size $K \times K$, then convert these patches to vectors via a linear projection. This operation can be written as a convolution with kernel size and stride both equal to $K$:

$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf{T}[n(N/K)+m,c_{\texttt{2}}] = \nonumber\\
&b[c_{\texttt{2}}] +  \sum_{c_{\texttt{1}}=1}^{C_{\texttt{in}}} \sum_{k_1,k_2=-K}^K w[c_{\texttt{1}},c_{\texttt{2}},k_1,k_2] x_{\texttt{in}}[c_{\texttt{1}},K n-k_1,K m-k_2] \quad \triangleleft \quad \text{(tokenization)}
\end{aligned}$$

where, for RGB images, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N \times M}$, $C_{\texttt{in}}=3$, and $C_{\texttt{out}}=d$ (the token dimensionality). This assumes $N$ and $M$ are evenly divisible by $K$. In code, this is a `conv` operator:

```python
T = conv(x_in, channels_in=3, channels_out=d, kernel=K, stride=K) # tokenize
```
concepts.motivation_md: Representing tokenization as a convolution allows the initial processing of an image into discrete tokens to be performed efficiently using standard deep learning hardware and operations.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokenization is equivalent to a convolution with kernel size and stride equal to the patch size $K$.

key_passage.text: this form of tokenization can be written as a convolutional layer with kernel size and stride both equal to $K$

motivation.text: The most basic way to do this is to chop up the input image into non-overlapping patches of size $K \times K$, then convert these patches to vectors via a linear projection. You might already have noticed that this operation can be written as convolution; after all we said the whole idea of CNNs is to chop the signal into patches.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Projections as Convolutions

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: The query, key, and value projections in attention layers are equivalent to multichannel convolutions with a kernel size of 1.
concepts.content: The query, key, and value projections in attention layers apply the same linear transformation to each token vector. Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does. Specifically, the query operation $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}$ can be written as convolving the set of $N$ $d$-channel tokens with a filter bank of $m$ filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of $N$ $m$-channel tokens. This equivalence is visualized in (see figure: The query, key, and value projections in transformers can be written either as a convolution or a matrix multiply.). Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing projections as $1 \times 1$ convolutions highlights the architectural similarity between transformers and CNNs, showing that transformers use standard local operations to prepare data for global attention.
concepts.recap_md: - Query, key, and value projections are mathematically equivalent to $1 \times 1$ convolutions.

key_passage.text: the query operation can be written as convolving the set of N d-channel tokens with a filter bank of m filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of N m-channel tokens. Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.

motivation.text: Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does.

concepts.title: Matrix Product as Convolution

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Every matrix product can be interpreted as a convolution of a multichannel filter bank with a signal.
concepts.content: Convolution appears throughout linear algebra; in fact, every matrix product can be written as a convolution. Whenever you see a product $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$, you can think of it as the convolution of a multichannel filter bank $\mathbf{B}$ (where each row is a filter with kernel size 1) with the signal $\mathbf{A}$ (where time indexes the rows and channels are in the columns).
concepts.motivation_md: This conceptual bridge simplifies the relationship between dense linear layers and convolutional layers, showing that convolution is a more general framework for matrix operations.
concepts.recap_md: - A matrix product $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$ is equivalent to a convolution with a kernel size of 1.

key_passage.text: every matrix product can be written as a convolution! Whenever you see a product $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$, you can think of it as the convolution of a multichannel filter bank $\mathbf{B}$ (one filter in each row; kernel size 1) with the signal $\mathbf{A}$ (time indexes rows, channels in the columns).

motivation.text: Convolution actually appears all over in linear algebra, and in fact every matrix product can be written as a convolution!

concepts.title: Tokenwise MLP as CNN

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A tokenwise MLP layer in a transformer can be mathematically represented as a series of $1 \times 1$ convolutions interleaved with neuronwise nonlinearities, effectively forming a CNN.
concepts.content: A token-wise MLP applies the same MLP $F_{\theta}$ to each token in a sequence. This $F_{\theta}$ consists of linear layers and pointwise nonlinearities. The linear layers take the form $\mathbf{t}_{\texttt{out}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{t}_{\texttt{in}}$. When applied to the entire sequence, this becomes $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{T}}$. This operation is identical to the query projection and can be written as a convolution with kernel size 1. Since the pointwise nonlinearities in the MLP function identically to the pointwise nonlinearities in CNNs, a token-wise MLP can be written as a series of convolutions interleaved with neuronwise-nonlinearities—that is, a CNN.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing tokenwise MLPs as CNNs helps unify the theory of different neural network architectures, demonstrating that transformers heavily utilize convolutional principles for local feature transformation.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokenwise MLPs are equivalent to CNNs using $1 \times 1$ kernels.

key_passage.text: Therefore, the same result holds: the linear layers of the token-wise MLP can all be written as convolutions with kernel size 1. Now the pointwise nonlinearities in the MLP are applied neuronwise, so these layers function identically to the pointwise nonlinearity in CNNs. This is the full set of layers in the MLP, and therefore we have that a token-wise MLP can be written as a series of convolutions interleaved with neuronwise-nonlinearities, i.e. a CNN.

motivation.text: A token-wise MLP applies the same MLP to each token in a sequence.

concepts.title: Similarities between CNNs and Transformers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Most layers in transformers, including tokenization and tokenwise MLPs, are essentially convolutional, sharing common components like normalization and residual connections with CNNs.
concepts.content: Most layers in transformers are convolutional. These layers break up the signal processing problem into chunks, then process each chunk independently and identically. Other operations in transformers—such as normalization layers and residual connections—are also common in CNNs. Breaking a problem into chunks is a fundamentally useful idea known as factorizing a problem into smaller pieces.
concepts.motivation_md: Comparing these architectures reveals that the primary innovation of transformers is not the absence of convolutions, but how they combine convolutional-style local processing with global attention mechanisms.
concepts.recap_md: - Transformers and CNNs both rely on factorizing signals into independently processed chunks.

key_passage.text: As we have now seen, most layers in transformers are convolutional. These layers break up the signal processing problem into chunks, then process each chunk independently and identically.

question.text: So what is different between transformers and CNNs?

motivation.text: Breaking up into chunks is such a fundamentally useful idea that it shows up in many different fields under different names.

concepts.title: Natural Image
concepts.one_liner: A natural image is a sample from the extremely small subset of all possible pixel arrays that represent real-world visual scenes.
concepts.content:
A natural image is a specific type of high-dimensional array of pixels $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. The space of all possible images is incredibly large; for example, even $32\times32$ color thumbnails with 8 bits per channel allow for more than $10^{7,398}$ possible combinations. However, most of these possible images consist of random noise. The set of natural images occupies only a very small part of this total space. A typical sample from the set of all possible images consists of pixels independently sampled from a uniform distribution, whereas a natural image contains structured visual information.

(see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32\times32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the concept of a natural image is fundamental to computer vision and image processing. It establishes that real-world images are not random but follow specific structural patterns, allowing us to distinguish meaningful visual data from noise and build models that can compress, enhance, or generate realistic scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Natural images represent a tiny fraction of the mathematically possible combinations of pixel values.

key_passage.text: An image is a very high dimensional array of pixels ℓ[n,m] and therefore, the space of all possible images is very large.

concepts.title: Visual Worlds
concepts.one_liner: Visual worlds are distinct sets of images characterized by specific visual properties, ranging from synthetic noise to real-world scenes.
concepts.content:
Images can be categorized into different visual worlds, each possessing unique visual characteristics. We can differentiate images as belonging to various worlds—such as white noise, Gabor patches, Mondrian patterns, stars, clouds, line drawings, or computer-generated imagery (CGI)—even if those worlds do not resemble our everyday environment. Defining the exact characteristics that distinguish the set of real images from these other synthetic or abstract visual worlds is a complex task.

(see figure: Different visual worlds, some real, some synthetic. (a) White noise. (b) Gabor patches. (c) Mondrian. (d) Stars. (e) Clouds. (f) Line drawing. (g) Computer graphic imagery (CGI). (h) A real street...)
concepts.motivation_md: By categorizing images into different 'worlds,' researchers can isolate specific visual features and study how human or machine vision systems process different types of structure, from pure randomness to complex 3D geometry.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual worlds are defined by distinct statistical or structural characteristics.

key_passage.text: Each world has different visual characteristics. We can clearly differentiate images as belonging to any of these eight worlds, even if those visual worlds look like nothing we normally see when walking around.

motivation.text: Explaining what makes images in the set of real images different to images in the other sets is not a simple task.

concepts.title: Telling Noise from Texture

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Distinguishing noise from texture involves determining whether visual randomness is an artifact of the imaging process or a physical property of the scene's surfaces.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Telling noise from surface texture. Which one is which?)

How do we tell noise from texture? One might encounter a scene where an image is corrupted with additive stationary noise, or a scene containing an object textured with a pattern that looks like noise. To distinguish them, we look at how the pattern behaves. Stationary image noise is independent of the content of the scene: it is not affected by object boundaries, it does not deform according to the 3D orientation of surfaces, and its frequency does not change with the distance between the camera and the scene. If such noise were actually part of the physical world, it would require a distribution that perfectly conspires with the observer's viewpoint to appear stationary.

The original images from (Figure 1.1.6):

[FIGURE:680c813998d8644a | @fig-noiseInTheWorld (b) has noise added]
concepts.motivation_md: This distinction is crucial for image restoration. If a pattern is identified as noise, it should be removed; if it is identified as texture, it must be preserved as it provides information about the object's material and geometry.
concepts.recap_md: - Stationary noise remains uniform regardless of the 3D geometry or distance of objects in the scene.

key_passage.text: Stationary image noise is independent of the content of the scene, it is not affected by the object boundaries, it does not deform following the three-dimensional (3D) orientation of the surfaces, and it does not change frequency with distance between the camera and the scene.

concepts.title: Stationary Image Noise

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Stationary image noise is additive noise with statistical properties that are independent of location and scene content.
concepts.content: Stationary image noise is independent of the content of the scene. It is not affected by object boundaries, does not deform following the three-dimensional (3D) orientation of the surfaces, and does not change frequency with distance between the camera and the scene. If the noise were actually in the world, stationary noise would require a special noise distribution that conspires with the observer's viewpoint to appear stationary. Additive stationary noise is specifically defined as noise with statistical properties independent of location that is added to an observation.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining noise as stationary allows for the use of powerful statistical tools and filters (like Gaussian models) to remove artifacts without needing to model the complex, varying content of the underlying image.

concepts.title: Image Denoising

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Image denoising is the process of automatically removing noise from an image by separating the uncorrupted content from the noise component.
concepts.content: Noise is a process independent from image content, and the human visual system does not perceive it as a physical part of the scene (like paint). Image denoising is the task of automatically removing this noise. This process is equivalent to separating an image into two distinct components: one representing a clean, uncorrupted picture and the other containing only the noise. Statistical image models are often employed to achieve this separation.
concepts.motivation_md: Denoising is essential for improving the quality of images captured in low-light conditions or with low-quality sensors, ensuring that subsequent analysis or human viewing is not hindered by artifacts.
concepts.recap_md: - Denoising aims to decompose a noisy image into a clean image and a noise-only component.

key_passage.text: Image denoising consists in removing the noise from an image automatically. This is equivalent to being able to separate the image into two components, one looking like a clean uncorrupted picture and the second image containing only noise.

motivation.text: One important task in image processing is image denoising. Noise is an independent process from the image content, and our visual system does not perceive noise as a strange form of paint.

concepts.title: Independent Pixel Model
concepts.one_liner: The independent pixel model assumes that every pixel's intensity is drawn independently from a single stationary distribution.
concepts.content:
The simplest image model assumes that all pixels are independent and their intensity values are drawn from a stationary distribution, meaning the distribution is independent of the pixel's location. The probability $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell)$ of an image $\ell[n,m]$ of size $N \times M$ is given by:

$$p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{m=1}^{M} p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$$

Here, $\theta$ represents the parameters of the model, which can be fitted to data using maximum likelihood. For a discrete gray-scale image with 256 levels, $\theta$ is a vector of 256 probabilities (a histogram). For color images, it involves $256^3$ bins. 

(see figure: Fitting a statistical image model to a set of training images. Once the model is learned we can use the model to sample new images.)

To assess the model, one can sample new images from it. In a multinomial model, the probability of a pixel at $(n,m)$ having value $k$ is $p_{\theta}(\ell [n,m] = k) = \theta_k$. While this model can somewhat approximate images of stars, it fails to reproduce the structure of most other visual worlds because treating pixels as independent observations ignores the inherent spatial correlations in natural images.

(see figure: Estimation of the image model parameters using one image, and then sampling a new image by sampling pixels independently using the histogram of the training image.)

(see figure: Examples of images and corresponding random samples with the same distribution of pixel intensities. Only the image with stars (a) has some visual similarity with the randomly sampled image.)
concepts.motivation_md: This model serves as a baseline in statistical image processing. While it fails to capture spatial structure, it introduces the concept of using probability distributions and histograms to characterize image content.
concepts.recap_md: - The model treats an image as a collection of independent random variables.

key_passage.text: The simplest image model will consist in assuming that all pixels are independent and their intensity value is drawn from some stationary distribution (i.e., the distribution of pixel intensities is independent of the location in the image).

motivation.text: One way of assessing the accuracy of a statistical image model is to sample from the model and view the images it produces. The failure of color histograms as a generative model of images should not be surprising as treating pixels as independent observations is clearly not how images work.

concepts.title: Histogram Matching
concepts.one_liner: Histogram matching is a pixelwise transformation that adjusts one image's intensity distribution to match that of another image.
concepts.content:
Histogram matching is a useful operation where, given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ with histograms $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2$, we seek a pixelwise transformation $f\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$ such that the histogram of the transformed image $f\left(\ell_1 [n,m] \right)$ matches $\mathbf{h}_2$. A common choice is a transformation that preserves the relative ordering of pixel intensities.

This technique has significant perceptual importance. For example, by swapping the histograms of two spheres rendered under different illumination models (such as a campus photograph versus pink noise), the perceived material of the sphere can be transformed from shiny to matte. This demonstrates that simple histogram manipulations can fundamentally change the perception of surface gloss and material properties.

(see figure: Perceptual importance of simple histogram manipulations. Figure from @Fleming2001)
concepts.motivation_md: Histogram matching is used for color correction, normalizing images taken under different lighting conditions, and artistic style transfer by forcing the tonal distribution of one image onto another.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses a pixelwise function to align the intensity distributions of two images.

key_passage.text: Given two images ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ with histograms h₁ and h₂, we look for a pixelwise transformation f(ℓ[n,m]) so that the histogram of the transformed image, f(ℓ₁[n,m]), matches the histogram of ℓ₂. There are many ways in which histograms can be transformed. One natural choice is a transformation that preserves the ordering of pixels intensities.

motivation.text: Manipulating image histograms is a very useful operation. This is an example that illustrates the perceptual importance of simple histogram manipulations.

concepts.title: Pink Noise
concepts.one_liner: Pink noise is random noise characterized by a power spectrum that is inversely proportional to the sum of the squared spatial frequencies.
concepts.content: Pink noise is a type of random noise defined by its power spectrum. Specifically, it has a $\frac{1}{|w_x^2+w_y^2|}$ power spectrum, where $w_x$ and $w_y$ represent the spatial frequencies. It is often used in visual experiments and rendering to simulate certain types of naturalistic but random textures.
concepts.motivation_md: Pink noise is frequently used in image processing and vision science because its statistical properties more closely resemble the spatial frequency distributions found in natural scenes compared to white noise.
concepts.recap_md: - Pink noise has a power spectrum of $\frac{1}{|w_x^2+w_y^2|}$.

key_passage.text: Pink noise is random noise with a $\frac{1}{|w_x^2+w_y^2|}$ power spectrum, where $w_x$ and $w_y$ are the spatial frequencies.

concepts.title: Parametric texture models
concepts.one_liner: Parametric texture models represent a texture image using a small vector of parameters, typically around 1,000 dimensions.
concepts.content: Parametric texture models represent a texture image with a small vector of parameters, usually around 1,000 dimensions.
concepts.motivation_md: These models aim to compress the complex visual information of a texture into a low-dimensional representation for efficient storage and synthesis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Represent textures using a small vector of parameters.
- Typically use approximately 1,000 dimensions.

key_passage.text: Parametric texture models represent a texture image with a small vector of parameters, usually around 1,000 dimensions

concepts.title: Nonparametric Texture Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Nonparametric texture models are a class of image models that became dominant after 2000, preceding the emergence of neural generative models.
concepts.content: Nonparametric texture models became the dominant approach to texture modeling after 2000. They remained the primary method until generative models using neural networks emerged around 2014.
concepts.motivation_md: Nonparametric models were developed to overcome the limitations of fixed-parameter models by using the data itself to represent the texture.
concepts.recap_md:
- Became the dominant texture modeling approach after 2000.
- Preceded the rise of neural network generative models in 2014.

key_passage.text: nonparametric texture models became dominant until generative models with neural networks emerged around 2014.

motivation.text: nonparametric texture models became dominant until generative models with neural networks emerged around 2014.

concepts.title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Nonparametric Markov random field image models define a pixel's probability distribution based on its surrounding neighborhood.
concepts.content: Nonparametric Markov random field image models define the probability distribution of a pixel as dependent on the neighborhood around that pixel. If the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. This image model can be used as a powerful texture synthesis model.
concepts.motivation_md: By assuming that local neighborhoods contain all the information necessary to predict a pixel, these models simplify the complex task of modeling global image statistics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pixel probability depends only on its local neighborhood.
- Provides a powerful framework for texture synthesis.
- Assumes conditional independence from distant pixels given enough local context.

key_passage.text: Nonparametric Markov random field image models define the probability distribution of a pixel as dependent of neighborhood around the pixel. As we said before, if the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image.

motivation.text: This image model can be used as a powerful texture synthesis model.

concepts.title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an iterative texture synthesis method that grows new textures by matching local neighborhoods from an input example.
concepts.content:
As with other texture synthesis algorithms, the input to the Efros-Leung algorithm is an example of the texture to be synthesized, and the output is an image of more of that texture. It is an iterative algorithm as shown in (see figure: In the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99).

At each iteration, we have synthesized pixels in the neighborhood of the pixel to be synthesized. We look through the input image for examples of similar configurations of pixel values as the current local neighborhood, having a sum of squared intensity differences from the local neighborhood lower than some threshold. Randomly select one of the matching instances, and copy the value of the pixel into the pixel to be synthesized. Repeat for all pixels to be synthesized. It can be natural to synthesize the pixels in a raster-scan ordering. Image pixels without sufficient neighboring pixels for context can be randomly sampled from the input texture.

In this nonparametric model, the representation of a texture is the reference image itself. There is not a low-dimensional representation as is the case with parametric texture models. The advantage is that no information is lost in this representation.









Synthesized texture from the Efros-Leung algorithm as a function of size of the context region. A very small context region only covers parts of features (like circles) and fails to complete them, while larger regions maintain individual features, and even larger regions enforce all spatial regularities of the input texture.

(see figure: Image synthesis results from the Efros-Leung algorithm. The small crops are used to synthesize the larger texture regions. Input images are 128 $\times$ 128 pixels, and the outputs are 256 $\times$...) 

While the model works remarkably well, artifacts like oversized features can occur. Increasing the neighborhood size can remove those issues, while decreasing it can help remove unwanted repetitions of reference elements.
concepts.motivation_md: This algorithm solves the problem of generating large, realistic texture regions from a small sample without needing a complex mathematical model of the texture's parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Synthesizes textures iteratively by matching local pixel neighborhoods to an input sample.
- Uses the reference image itself as the texture representation (nonparametric).
- Results depend heavily on the size of the context region used for matching.

key_passage.text: At each iteration, we have synthesized pixels in the neighborhood of the pixel to be synthesized. We look through the input image for examples of similar configurations of pixel values as the current local neighborhood, having a sum of squared intensity differences from the local neighborhood lower than some threshold. Randomly select one of the matching instances, and copy the value of the pixel into the pixel to be synthesized.

motivation.text: In this nonparametric model, the representation of a texture is the reference image itself. There is not a low-dimensional representation as it is the case of parametric texture models. The advantage is that no information is lost in this representation.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Model
concepts.one_liner: An autoregressive model is a class of models, including the Efros-Leung algorithm, that predicts future values based on past values in a sequence.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an autoregressive model. This class of models can be used in conjunction with deep networks to model data sequences or images by predicting the next element based on previous ones.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models provide a structured way to generate data sequentially, ensuring that each new piece of data is consistent with what has already been generated.
concepts.recap_md:
- Predicts the next value in a sequence based on previous values.
- The Efros-Leung algorithm serves as a classic example of this model type.

key_passage.text: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an autoregressive model.

concepts.title: Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models are generative models that use an iterative denoising process to transform noise into structured images.
concepts.content: Diffusion models follow a strategy where an iterative process, similar to the denoising in the Heeger-Bergen algorithm, starts with a noise image and gradually transforms it into a structured image, such as a texture.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models allow for the generation of high-quality, complex data by breaking the generation process into many small, manageable denoising steps.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses an iterative denoising process to generate images.
- Starts with random noise and transforms it into a structured output.

key_passage.text: diffusion models, which follow this same strategy.

motivation.text: The iterative optimization of the Heeger-Bergen algorithm is a type of denoising process: it starts with a noise image and little by little transforms it into an image of a texture. This general idea reappears in diffusion models, which follow this same strategy.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are models that learn to generate images matching the statistics of a set of exemplars using a discriminator network.
concepts.content: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) create images that have the same statistics as a set of exemplars. Unlike earlier methods like the Heeger-Bergen algorithm which use hand-defined subband statistics, GANs use a learned discriminator neural network to determine the statistics that need to be matched.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs automate the discovery of relevant features and statistics in data, allowing for the generation of highly realistic images without manual feature engineering.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generates images by matching the statistics of exemplar sets.
- Uses a discriminator neural network to learn which statistics to match.
- Contrast with hand-defined statistical methods like Heeger-Bergen.

key_passage.text: A GAN also makes images that have the same statistics as a set of exemplars; however, the statistics we seek to match are learned (by a so-called discriminator neural net) rather than hand-defined to be subband statistics.

motivation.text: The Heeger-Bergen algorithm is also connected to generative adversarial networks (GANs), which we will encounter in subsequent sections. The objective of Heeger-Bergen is to make a texture that has the same histogram statistics as an exemplar.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way to make complex visual modeling computations tractable.
concepts.content: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way that allows us to reason about the visual world even when we're modeling very complicated situations. These models are useful in vision, where we often need to exploit modularity to make computations tractable.
concepts.motivation_md: They provide a formal framework to handle uncertainty and complexity in computer vision by breaking down large problems into smaller, interacting components.
concepts.recap_md:
- Represent joint probability distributions using modular structures.
- Enable tractable computation in complex modeling scenarios.
- Widely used in computer vision for reasoning about the visual world.

key_passage.text: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way that allows us to reason about the visual world even when we're modeling very complicated situations.

motivation.text: These models are useful in vision, where we often need to exploit modularity to make computations tractable.

concepts.title: Tokenizing Data

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Tokenization is the process of converting raw input data, such as image patches, into a set of vectors called tokens.
concepts.content: The first step to working with tokens is to tokenize the raw input data. Once this is done, all subsequent layers operate over tokens until the output layer makes a prediction. To tokenize an image, we represent each patch of pixels with a token. The token vector is either the vectorized patch (stacking the three color channels) or a lower-dimensional projection of that vectorized patch. With each patch represented by a token, the full image corresponds to an array of tokens. (see figure: Tokenization: converting an image to a set of vectors. $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$ is a learnable linear projection from the dimensionality of the vectorized crops to $d$ dimensions. This is...)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard neural networks operate on individual pixels (neurons), but complex data like images or text often contain local structures that are more meaningful when processed as units. Tokenization groups raw data into these higher-level vector representations, allowing subsequent layers to model relationships between meaningful entities rather than just individual scalars.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokenization converts raw input data into a sequence or set of vector-valued tokens.

key_passage.text: To tokenize an image, we may simply represent each patch of pixels in the image with a token. The token vector is the vectorized patch (stacking the three color channels one after the other), or a lower-dimensional projection of the vectorized patch.

motivation.text: The first step to working with tokens is to tokenize the raw input data. Once we have done this, all subsequent layers will operate over tokens, until the output layer, which will make some decision or prediction as a function of the final set of tokens.

concepts.title: Token Matrix Notation

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A sequence of tokens is represented by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ where each row is a transposed token vector.
concepts.content:
A sequence of tokens is denoted by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, in which each token in the sequence, $\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N$, is transposed to become a row of the matrix:

$$\mathbf{T} = 
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\
    \vdots \\
    \mathbf{t}_N^\mathsf{T}\\
\end{bmatrix}$$

Graphically, $\mathbf{T}$ is constructed from $\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N$ as shown in (see figure: In this chapter, we will represent a set of tokens as a matrix whose rows are the token vectors.).

Transformers are invariant to permutations of the input sequence, so groups of tokens should be thought of as sets rather than ordered sequences. This notation implies that tokens are to transformers as neurons are to neural nets. While neural net layers operate over arrays of neurons (column vectors), transformers operate over arrays of tokens represented by the matrix $\mathbf{T}$. Although we primarily consider vector-valued tokens, tokens could theoretically be any structured group as long as basic operators like summation are defined.
concepts.motivation_md: To process groups of vectors efficiently using linear algebra, we need a standardized mathematical representation. Organizing tokens as rows in a matrix allows us to use matrix multiplication to perform operations on all tokens simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokens are represented as rows in a matrix $\mathbf{T}$ of size $N \times d$.

key_passage.text: A sequence of tokens will be denoted by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, in which each token in the sequence, $\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N$, is transposed to become a row of the matrix.

motivation.text: The idea of this notation is that tokens are to transformers as neurons are to neural nets. A matrix $\mathbf{T}$ is just a convenient representation of 1D array of vector-value tokens.

concepts.title: Mixing Tokens

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Mixing tokens involves taking a linear combination of vector-valued tokens, analogous to how neural nets take weighted sums of scalar neurons.
concepts.content:
Once data is converted to tokens, we define operations for transforming them, starting with the linear combination of tokens. Unlike a fully connected layer in a standard neural net that sums scalar neurons, this operation takes a weighted sum of vector-valued tokens. (see figure: Linear combination of neurons versus tokens.)

The general form for these equations is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}[i,:]&= \sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[j,:]\\
     \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}
\end{aligned}$$

Operations over tokens are defined similarly to operations over neurons, but with vector values. For example, a fully connected layer (fc layer) over tokens maps $N_1$ input tokens to $N_2$ output tokens using a weight matrix $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_2 \times N_1}$ and optional token biases $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_2 \times d}$:

$$\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$$
concepts.motivation_md: To share information across different parts of an input (like different patches of an image), the network must be able to combine information from multiple tokens. Linear mixing provides a mathematically simple way to aggregate these features.
concepts.recap_md: - Mixing tokens uses a weighted sum of vectors rather than scalars.

key_passage.text: A linear combination of tokens is not the same as a fully connected layer in a neural net. Instead of taking a weighted sum of scalar neurons, it takes a weighted sum of vector-valued tokens.

motivation.text: Once we have converted our data to tokens, we now need to define operations for transforming these tokens and eventually making decisions based on them. The first operation we will define is how to take a linear combination of tokens.

concepts.title: Modifying Tokens

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Tokenwise operators apply nonlinear transformations to each token individually and independently, allowing the model to represent complex, non-linear functions.
concepts.content:
Linear combinations only allow for linear mixing; to model nonlinear functions, we introduce tokenwise operators. These functions apply a nonlinear transformation $F_{\theta}: \mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$ to each token individually and independently. A tokenwise nonlinearity layer is expressed as:

$$\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= 
        \begin{bmatrix}
        F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[0,:]) \\
        \vdots \\
        F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[N-1,:]) \\
        \end{bmatrix}$$

This generalizes pointwise nonlinearities in regular neural nets (like ReLU). A key difference is that while standard neuronwise nonlinearities like ReLU usually have no learnable parameters, the tokenwise function $F_{\theta}$ is often a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with its own learnable weights and biases, making these operations highly expressive.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers alone cannot solve complex problems because the composition of linear functions is still linear. Tokenwise nonlinearities allow the network to learn complex features within each token's vector space.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokenwise operators apply a function $F_{\theta}$ to each token independently.

key_passage.text: Given a nonlinear function $F_{\theta}: \mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$, a tokenwise nonlinearity layer, taking input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$, can be expressed as a per-token nonlinearity where $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= \begin{bmatrix} F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[0,:]) \\ \vdots \\ F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[N-1,:]) \end{bmatrix}$

motivation.text: Linear combinations only let us linearly mix and recombine tokens, and stacking linear functions can only result in another linear function. To get around this limitation, we added pointwise nonlinearities to our neural nets.

concepts.title: Token Nets

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Token nets are computation graphs that use vector-valued tokens as primary nodes instead of scalar neurons.
concepts.content: Token nets refer to computation graphs where tokens, rather than neurons, serve as the primary nodes. These nets alternate between layers that mix nodes in linear combinations (such as fully connected or convolutional layers) and layers that apply pointwise nonlinearities to each node (such as per-token MLPs). Since tokens are essentially groups of neurons, every token net is also a neural net, but viewed as a "net of subnets." (see figure: Neural nets versus token nets. The arrows here represent any functional dependency between the nodes (note that different arrows represent different types of functions).)
concepts.motivation_md: Thinking in terms of tokens rather than individual neurons provides a higher-level abstraction that is more natural for data with inherent grouping, like words in a sentence or patches in an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Token nets use tokens as nodes and alternate between mixing and nonlinear layers.

key_passage.text: We will use the term **token nets** to refer to computation graphs that use tokens as the primary nodes, rather than neurons.

motivation.text: Token nets are just like neural nets, alternating between layers that mix nodes in linear combinations (e.g., fully connected linear layers, convolutional layers, etc.) and layers that apply a pointwise nonlinearity to each node (e.g., relus, per-token MLPs).

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Query-key-value attention is the specific attention allocation function used in transformer architectures.
concepts.content: Query-key-value attention is the particular version of the attention allocation function $f$ that appears in transformers.
concepts.motivation_md: To dynamically determine which parts of an input are relevant to others, we need a mechanism that can compare a 'request' (query) against 'labels' (keys) to retrieve 'content' (values).
concepts.recap_md: - QKV attention is the standard attention mechanism in transformers.

key_passage.text: We will focus on the particular version of $f$ that appears in transformers, which is called **query-key-value attention**.

concepts.title: Self-Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Self-attention is an architecture where every token in a layer submits a query and computes a weighted sum over all tokens in that same layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Self-attention removes the need for hand-designed interaction rules between different types of data (like text and images) by allowing every element in a set to dynamically determine which other elements are most relevant to its own representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Every token acts as a query, a key, and a value simultaneously.

key_passage.text: Self-attention is just such an architecture. The idea is that on a self-attention layer, all tokens submit queries, and for each of these queries, we take a weighted sum over all tokens in that layer.

question.text: But can we come up with a more generic architecture where we don't have to hand design which tokens interact in which ways?

motivation.text: The next question we will consider is which tokens should be doing the querying and which should we be matching against? In the example from the last section, the answer was intuitive because we had a textual question that was asking about content in a visual image, so naturally the text gives the query and we match against tokens that represent the image.

concepts.title: Multihead Self-Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Multihead self-attention (MSA) runs multiple attention layers in parallel to measure token similarity in several different ways simultaneously.
concepts.content:
Multihead self-attention (MSA) addresses the limitation of single-headed attention, which only uses one set of projection matrices to define similarity. By running $k$ attention layers in parallel on the same input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$, the model can measure similarity in multiple ways (e.g., by color, texture, or shape). 

The $k$ output sets of tokens $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1, \ldots, \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k$ are concatenated and projected back to the original dimensionality $d$ using a learnable matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^i &= \texttt{attn}^i(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}) \\
    \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}} &= [\text{concatenation of heads}] \\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}} &= \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}
\end{aligned}$$

In MSA, the value vectors do not need to match the output token dimensionality because the final projection $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$ handles the mapping. This allows the network to add more parallel self-attention layers to increase expressivity.
concepts.motivation_md: A single attention head can only focus on one type of relationship at a time. Multihead attention allows the model to simultaneously attend to different features, such as both the syntax and the semantics of a word, or both the color and the shape of an object.
concepts.recap_md: - MSA runs $k$ independent attention heads in parallel and concatenates their results.

key_passage.text: This method simply consists of running $k$ attention layers in parallel. All these layers are applied to the same input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$. This results in $k$ output sets of tokens, $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1, \ldots, \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k$. To merge these outputs, we concatenate all of them and project back to the original dimensionality of $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$.

question.text: What if we want to measure similarity in more than one way?

motivation.text: A single self-attention layer therefore measures similarity in just one way. What if we want to measure similarity in more than one way?

concepts.title: Markov Random Field (MRF)

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: A Markov random field is an image model where a pixel's probability distribution is independent of other pixels given a sufficient neighborhood of surrounding pixels.
concepts.content: A powerful class of image models is known as Markov random field (MRF) models. The core intuition for these models is that if the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. To fit and sample from the MRF structure requires the mathematical tools of graphical models. This Markov structure can be exploited for texture synthesis, based on the intuition that conditioning on a large enough region of nearby pixels effectively determines the value of the central pixel. This same intuition can be applied to the problem of image denoising.
concepts.motivation_md: MRF models provide a way to capture local spatial dependencies in images. By assuming that a pixel only depends on its immediate neighbors, we can simplify complex global image distributions into manageable local interactions, which is essential for tasks like denoising and texture synthesis.
concepts.recap_md: - A pixel's value is conditionally independent of the rest of the image given its neighbors.

key_passage.text: if the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image.

motivation.text: A powerful class of image models is known as Markov random field (MRF) models. To fit and sample from the MRF structure requires the mathematical tools of graphical models, to be introduced in

concepts.title: Nonlocal Means Denoising

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: Nonlocal means denoising computes a pixel's value as a weighted sum of all other pixels, where weights depend on the similarity of their local neighborhoods.
concepts.content:
The nonlocal means denoising algorithm defines the denoised image as a weighted sum of all other pixels in the image, weighted by the similarity of the local neighborhoods of each pair of pixels. More formally,
$$\ell_{\mbox{NLM}}[n,m] = \sum_{k,l} w_{n,m}[k,l] \ell[k,l]$$ where
$$w_{n,m}[k,l] = \frac{1}{Z_{n,m}} \exp{\frac{- \left| \ell[N_{k,l}] - ℓ[N_{n,m}] \right| ^2}{h^2}},$$
where $N_{i, j}$ denotes an $h \times h$ region of pixels centered at $i, j$, and $Z_{n,m}$ is a normalization constant such that $\sum_{kl} w_{n,m}[k,l] = 1$.

[FIGURE:c5b8102b308188df | Regions of support for the nonlocal means denoising algorithm. Source: Image from @Baudes2005]

The parameter $h$ is typically set to $10 \sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the estimated image noise standard deviation. The weighting function $w_{n,m}[k,l]$ indicates which pixels are averaged together to yield the nonlocal mean value; the algorithm effectively samples from image regions with similar local structure to the position being denoised.

(see figure: Nonlocal means denoising algorithm results. (left) Original image without noise. (middle) Noisy image. (right) Denoised image.Source:Figure from @Baudes2011)
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional denoising filters often blur edges by averaging nearby pixels regardless of content. Nonlocal means improves this by averaging pixels that have similar surrounding patterns, even if they are far apart in the image, preserving repetitive structures and textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Denoising is achieved by a weighted average of pixels based on neighborhood similarity.

key_passage.text: The nonlocal means denoised image is a weighted sum of all other pixels in the image, weighted by the similarity of the local neighborhoods of each pair of pixels.

motivation.text: Baudes, Coll, and Morel made use of that intuition to define the nonlocal means denoising algorithm.

concepts.title: Statistical Image Models Summary
concepts.one_liner: Statistical image models utilize low-level regularities to constrain the space of natural images for tasks like synthesis and denoising.
concepts.content: Statistical image models utilize low-level regularities of images to build a statistical model without trying to understand the high-level content of the pictures. Modeling these statistical regularities enables many tasks, including both image synthesis and image denoising. While these simple models help constrain the space of natural images, they often fail to provide a strong enough model to sample realistic new images. As illustrated in (see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32 \times 32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...), the sequence of models studied only reduces the space of possible images by a small amount.
concepts.motivation_md: Natural images occupy a tiny fraction of the space of all possible pixel combinations. Statistical models attempt to define the boundaries of this 'natural image' space to improve image processing algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - Models use low-level regularities rather than semantic content understanding.

key_passage.text: The models presented in this chapter do not try to understand the content of the pictures, but utilize low-level regularities of images in order to build a statistical model. Modeling these statistical regularities enable many tasks, including both image synthesis and image denoising.

motivation.text: Modeling these statistical regularities enable many tasks, including both image synthesis and image denoising.

concepts.title: Texture
concepts.one_liner: A texture is an image composed of a set of similar looking elements where the representation focuses on statistics rather than individual elements.
concepts.content: Texture is a concept intimately related to human perception. A texture is a type of image that is composed by a set of similar looking elements. A texture representation contains information about the statistics of its constituent elements, but not about the elements individually.
concepts.motivation_md: In many visual scenes, individual details (like blades of grass) are less important than the overall pattern. Defining texture allows us to model these patterns statistically.
concepts.recap_md: - Textures consist of repeating or similar visual elements.

key_passage.text: A texture is a type of image that is composed by a set of similar looking elements. A texture representation contains information about the statistics of its constituent elements, but not about the elements individually.

motivation.text: intimately related to human perception.

concepts.title: Infinite texture generation algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Infinite texture generation can be achieved by cropping pieces from a large sample image, though this provides little insight into human perception.
concepts.content: Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm: if we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images. This is illustrated in (see figure: The infinite texture generation algorithm. If we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images.). However, such an algorithm, although successful in practice, gives little understanding of how human perception works or how to modify textures to create new ones. It also does not help in determining which representations are useful for measuring similarity between textures.
concepts.motivation_md: While simple cropping works for basic synthesis, it doesn't help us understand the underlying mathematical or perceptual structure of textures, which is necessary for more complex editing or recognition tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Simple cropping from a large sample can synthesize new texture instances.

key_passage.text: If we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images.

motivation.text: But such an algorithm, although successful in practice, will give us little understanding on how human perception works and how to modify textures to create new ones. It will also not help us in understanding what representation can be useful to measure similarity between textures.

concepts.title: Perception of sets

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Human vision processes small numbers of objects individually but represents larger groups as a single set.
concepts.content:
When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually and count them in parallel. For displays with one to four elements, the time it takes to report the number of elements does not depend on the count. However, when there are more than four or five objects, we seem to pay attention only to a few and represent the rest as a set. The perception of sets is an important area of study in human visual psychophysics.

(see figure: When looking at these images, we can count the number of circles at a glance if there are less than five circles. When an image has more than five items, we have to count them one by one.)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how the brain transitions from individual object recognition to ensemble (set) perception helps explain how we process complex scenes and textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Small groups (up to 4) are processed in parallel and counted instantly.

key_passage.text: When there are more than four or five objects, we seem to pay attention only to a few of them and represent the rest of them as a set. The perception of sets is an important area of study in human visual psychophysics.

motivation.text: When there are more than four or five objects, we seem to pay attention only to a few of them and represent the rest of them as a set. The perception of sets is an important area of study in human visual psychophysics.

concepts.title: Subitizing

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Subitizing is the ability to instantly determine the number of objects in a display without counting, effective for fewer than five elements.
concepts.content: The ability to know how many objects are in a display without counting them is called subitizing. This phenomenon only works when there are fewer than five elements in a display.
concepts.motivation_md: Subitizing reveals a specific limit in human pre-attentive processing, distinguishing between immediate numerical recognition and the serial process of counting.
concepts.recap_md: - Subitizing is the instant recognition of quantity without serial counting.

key_passage.text: The ability to know how many objects are in a display without counting them is called subitizing. Subitizing only works when there are fewer than five elements in a display.

concepts.title: Crowding

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where objects in peripheral vision become difficult to recognize when surrounded by other similar features.
concepts.content: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where features of objects in the periphery get entangled, making individual recognition difficult. This is illustrated in (see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.). Even if two letters are at the same distance from fixation, a letter surrounded by others (like the B) is harder to read than an isolated one (like the R). This is not due to low resolution, but because the pooling window for image features is larger than the individual objects, causing features to mix. Anything inside these pooling regions will suffer from crowding effects, which are larger than what would be predicted by receptor spacing alone.
concepts.motivation_md: Crowding explains the limitations of peripheral vision and suggests that the brain pools features over large spatial areas in the periphery, which is relevant for understanding how we perceive textures and cluttered scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Peripheral objects are harder to identify when surrounded by other objects.

key_passage.text: As the letter B is surrounded by other letters, the features of the three letters get entangled as if the pooling window for image features was larger than the three letters together.

motivation.text: The reason cannot be due to the low resolution of peripheral vision as both letters are at the same distance from the fixation location. The explanation of this phenomena is due to something called crowding.

concepts.title: Likelihood Term
concepts.one_liner: The likelihood term $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.content: The likelihood term $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In Bayesian inference, the likelihood term is essential for modeling the forward process of how hidden states or scenes produce the data we actually observe.
concepts.recap_md: - The likelihood $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ models the generation of observations from a scene.

key_passage.text: The **likelihood term** $p(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.

concepts.title: Prior Probability
concepts.one_liner: The prior probability, $p(\mathbf{x})$, tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring.
concepts.content: The prior probability, $p(\mathbf{x})$, tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring. For inference, we often ignore the denominator in Bayes' rule as it is constant with respect to the variables we seek to estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: Prior probabilities allow us to incorporate existing knowledge or beliefs about which states of the world are more likely before any data is observed.
concepts.recap_md: - The prior $p(\mathbf{x})$ represents the probability of a scene occurring before considering observations.

key_passage.text: prior probability, p(x), tells the probability of any given scene x occurring.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.one_liner: The evidence $P(\mathbf{y})$ is the denominator in Bayes' rule and is constant with respect to the variables being estimated.
concepts.content: The denominator $P(\mathbf{y})$ is called the evidence. It is constant with respect to the variables we seek to estimate, $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The evidence acts as a normalization constant in Bayes' rule, ensuring that the posterior probability distribution sums to one.
concepts.recap_md: - The evidence $P(\mathbf{y})$ is the marginal probability of the observations.

key_passage.text: denominator, $P(\mathbf{y})$, called the **evidence**, as it is constant with respect to the variables we seek to estimate, $\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Point Estimate
concepts.one_liner: A point estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ is a single best estimate for a hidden variable $\mathbf{x}$ derived from the posterior probability.
concepts.content: Typically, we make many observations, $\mathbf{y}$, of the variables of some system, and we want to find the state of some hidden variable, $\mathbf{x}$, given those observations. The posterior probability, $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})$, tells us the probability for any value of the hidden variables, $\mathbf{x}$. From this posterior probability, we often want some single best estimate for $\mathbf{x}$, denoted $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ and called a point estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: While a posterior distribution provides a full range of probabilities, practical applications often require a single concrete value to act upon.
concepts.recap_md: - A point estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ is a single value chosen to represent the most likely or best state of a hidden variable.

key_passage.text: From this posterior probability, we often want some single *best* estimate for 𝐱, denoted 𝐱̂ and called a point estimate.

motivation.text: The posterior probability, p(𝐱|𝐲), tells us the probability for any value of the hidden variables, 𝐱. From this posterior probability, we often want some single *best* estimate for 𝐱, denoted 𝐱̂ and called a point estimate.

concepts.title: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)
concepts.one_liner: The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})$.
concepts.content: Selecting the best estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ requires specifying a penalty for making a wrong guess. If we penalize all wrong answers equally, the best strategy is to guess the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability, $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})$. This is because any other explanation $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ for the observations $\mathbf{y}$ would be less probable. This value is called the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: The MAP estimate is used when we want the most probable single explanation for our data, effectively treating all incorrect guesses as equally bad.
concepts.recap_md: - The MAP estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ is the mode of the posterior distribution.

key_passage.text: That is called the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate.

motivation.text: If we penalize all wrong answers equally, the best strategy is to guess the value of x that maximizes the posterior probability, p(x | y) (because any other explanation x̂ for the observations y would be less probable).

concepts.title: Minimum Mean Squared Error (MMSE)
concepts.one_liner: The minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate is the point estimate that minimizes the average squared distance from the correct answer.
concepts.content: If we want to penalize wrong answers as a function of how far they are from the correct answer, specifically using the squared distance in $\mathbf{x}$, then the point estimate that minimizes the average value of that error is called the minimum mean squared error estimate (MMSE). To find this estimate, we seek the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that minimizes the squared error, weighted by the probability of each outcome: $$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \mbox{argmin}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} \int_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}) (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}})' (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}) d\mathbf{x}$$ Differentiating with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ to solve for the stationary point, the global minimum for this convex function, we find $$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \int_{\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{x} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}) d\mathbf{x}.$$ Thus, the minimum mean squared error estimate, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE}$, is the mean of the posterior distribution. If $\mathbf{x}$ represents a discretized space, then the marginalization integrals over $d\mathbf{x}$ become sums over the corresponding discrete states of $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The MMSE estimate is ideal when large errors are significantly more costly than small ones, leading to an estimate that represents the average expected value.
concepts.recap_md: - The MMSE estimate is the mean of the posterior distribution.

key_passage.text: Thus, the minimum mean squared error estimate, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE}$, is the mean of the posterior distribution.

motivation.text: But we may want to penalize wrong answers as a function of how far they are from the correct answer. If that penalty function is the squared distance in $\mathbf{x}$, then the point estimate that minimizes the average value of that error is called the minimum mean squared error estimate (MMSE).

concepts.title: Marginal Probability for Discrete Variables
concepts.one_liner: For discrete variables, the marginal probability at a node is computed by summing over the states of all other nodes.
concepts.content: For the case of discrete variables, we compute the marginal probability at a node by summing over the states at all the other nodes, $$p\left(x_i \mid \mathbf{y}\right)=\sum_{\lambda_i} \sum_{x_j} p\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_N \mid \mathbf{y}\right),$$ where the notation $j \backslash i$ means "all possible values of $j$ except for $j = i$."
concepts.motivation_md: Marginalization allows us to focus on the probability distribution of a specific variable of interest by removing the influence of other variables in a joint distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginal probability for a discrete node is found by summing the joint probability over all other variables.

key_passage.text: For the case of discrete variables, we compute the marginal probability at a node by summing over the states at all the other nodes, $$p\left(x_i \mid \mathbf{y}\right)=\sum_{\lambda_i} \sum_{x_j} p\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_N \mid \mathbf{y}\right),$$

concepts.title: Messages

position.section_title: Simple Example of Inference in a Graphical Model

concepts.one_liner: Messages are partial sums that pass information between nodes in a probabilistic graphical model.
concepts.content: Partial sums are named messages because they pass information from one node to another. For example, the message from node 3 to node 2 is defined as $m_{32}(x_2) = \sum_{x_3} \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) m_{63}(x_3)$. Another example is the message from node 2 to node 1: $m_{21}(x_1) = \sum_{x_2} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) m_{52}(x_2) m_{32}(x_2)$. Note that the messages are always about the states of the node that the message is being sent to; that is, the arguments of the message $m_{ij}$ are the states $x_j$ of node $j$. The algorithm corresponding to these calculations is called belief propagation.
concepts.motivation_md: Messages provide a computationally efficient way to perform inference in complex graphical models by breaking down global sums into local computations.
concepts.recap_md: - Messages $m_{ij}$ pass information from node $i$ to node $j$ regarding the states of node $j$.

key_passage.text: The partial sums of equation ( are named **messages** because they pass information from one node to another. Note that the messages are always messages about the states of the node that the message is being sent to, that is, the arguments of the message $m_{ij}$ are the states $x_j$ of node $j$.
