concepts.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent
concepts.one_liner: Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a randomly sampled batch of training data to reduce the computational cost of optimization.
concepts.content:
In large-scale learning, computing the true gradient $
abla_{	heta}J(	heta)$ is expensive because it requires summing gradients over every training point: $$  egin{align} 
abla_{	heta} J(	heta, \{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N) &= 
abla_{	heta}  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)})\ &=  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 
abla_{	heta} \mathcal{L}(f_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}) \end{align} $$. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) addresses this by randomly subsampling a batch of size $B$ and computing an estimate $	ilde{\mathbf{g}} =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{b=1}^B 
abla_{	heta} \mathcal{L}(f_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}^{(b)}), \mathbf{y}^{(b)}) $. This introduces a tradeoff between accuracy and speed controlled by the hyperparameter $B$. (see figure: Stochastic gradient descent algorithm. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a stochastic subset (batch) of the full training data, and makes an update on that basis.) Beyond speed, SGD can jump over small bumps in the loss landscape and provide implicit regularization, often converging to solutions with minimum parameter norms in linear problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Computing gradients on massive datasets is computationally prohibitive; SGD allows for frequent updates and faster convergence by using representative samples.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses a randomly sampled batch of data to estimate the full gradient. - The batch size $B$ balances the tradeoff between computational speed and gradient accuracy. - It provides benefits like escaping local minima and implicit regularization of the model.

key_passage.text: The variant of gradient descent that uses this idea is called stochastic gradient descent (SGD), because each iteration of descent uses a different randomly (stochastically) sampled batch of training data to estimate the gradient.

motivation.text: One problem with the gradient-based methods we have seen so far is that the gradient may in fact be very expensive to compute, and this is often the case for learning problems. This is because learning problems typically have the form that J is the average of losses incurred on each training datapoint.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.one_liner: Overfitting occurs when a model fits properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, resulting in poor generalization.
concepts.content: Overfitting happens when we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data. Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set.
concepts.motivation_md: The goal of machine learning is to perform well on new data, not just memorize the training set; understanding overfitting is crucial for building robust models.
concepts.recap_md: - It is characterized by high training performance but low test performance. - It occurs when a model captures noise or specific artifacts of the training set. - Generalization is the ability of the model to perform well on data it has not seen before.

key_passage.text: When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, we call this overfitting. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data.

motivation.text: Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set. In general it may not, since the test set may have different properties from the training set.

concepts.title: Image Blending
concepts.one_liner: Image blending consists of introducing elements of one image into another by using a mask to specify how the images are combined.
concepts.content: Image blending, or image compositing, consists in introducing elements of one image inside another. Creating convincing composite images is challenging, as the edge between the two images has to be invisible. One way of formalizing the image-blending operation is by defining a mask, $\mathbf{m}$, that specifies how the images will be combined. The mask is used to select which pixels come from each of the two images in order to create the composite image. For example, blending two images using a mask can be visualized as: [FIGURE:1a6744bb03a38c89] [FIGURE:d0117de8048c2287] [FIGURE:0221968e4f64f996]. In this example, the mask indicates that the blended image will combine the half-left of the first image with the right-half of the second image. One naive solution to this problem is to define blending as $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \boldsymbol\ell^A * \mathbf{m} + \boldsymbol\ell^B * (1-\mathbf{m})$, which often results in a sharp, unpleasing transition: (see figure: Resulting blended image from @fig-orange_apple_mask. This result is not very pleasing.). To achieve a seamless merge, Burt and Adelson introduced an image blending algorithm using Laplacian pyramids capable of achieving a smooth transition between the two images.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple image blending often creates sharp, visible edges between combined images. This concept addresses the need for seamless compositing where transitions are invisible to the human eye.
concepts.recap_md: - Image blending uses a mask $\mathbf{m}$ to determine which pixels are taken from each source image. - Naive blending often results in sharp, unnatural transitions at the boundaries. - Advanced techniques like Laplacian pyramids are used to achieve smooth, seamless transitions.

key_passage.text: Image blending (or image compositing) consists in introducing elements of one image inside another. One way of formalizing the image-blending operation is by defining a mask, 𝐦, that specifies how the images will be combined.

motivation.text: Creating convincing composite images is challenging, as the edge between the two images has to be invisible. We would like to be able to merge both images in a seamless way.

concepts.title: Pyramid Blending Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Pyramid blending uses Laplacian pyramids to transition between images across multiple spatial scales for a smooth, seamless result.
concepts.content: Using the Laplacian pyramid, we can transition from one image to the next over many different spatial scales to make a gradual transition between the two images. The algorithm proceeds in four steps. First, build the Laplacian pyramid for the two input images; in this example, seven levels are used along with the last low-pass residual: (see figure: Laplacian pyramids (seven levels and Gaussian residual) for both input images.). Second, build the Gaussian pyramid of the mask: (see figure: Gaussian pyramid of the mask.). Third, combine the three pyramids to compute the Laplacian pyramid of the blended image as $\mathbf{l}_k = \mathbf{l}_k^A * \mathbf{m}_k + \mathbf{l}_i^B * (1-\mathbf{m}_k)$. The same is done for the low-pass residual. Finally, collapse (decode) the resulting pyramid to produce the blended image: (see figure: Image compositing with the Laplacian pyramid. Example inspired by @{Burt83}.). This result has a smooth transition and produces a pleasing blending. The mask does not need to be rectangular, but quality depends on image alignment and scene composition.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard blending creates artifacts at edges. Pyramid blending solves this by performing the blend across multiple frequency scales, ensuring that both fine details and coarse structures transition smoothly.
concepts.recap_md: - The process involves building Laplacian pyramids for images and a Gaussian pyramid for the mask. - Pyramids are combined level-by-level using the mask before being collapsed into a single image. - This multi-scale approach results in a much more pleasing and seamless blend than single-scale methods.

key_passage.text: The Laplacian pyramid of the blended image is obtained as $$\mathbf{l}_k = \mathbf{l}_k^A * \mathbf{m}_k + \mathbf{l}_i^B * (1-\mathbf{m}_k)$$ The same is done for the low-pass residual. Finally, the fourth step consists in collapsing (i.e., decoding) the resulting pyramid to produce the blended image.

motivation.text: Using the Laplacian pyramid, we can transition from one image to the next over many different spatial scales to make a gradual transition between the two images. This method remains one of the most popular methods for image blending due to its simplicity and the quality of the resulting images.

concepts.title: Steerable Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The steerable pyramid is a multiscale oriented representation that adds orientation information to the image decomposition while remaining translation-invariant and self-invertible.
concepts.content: The steerable pyramid is a multiscale oriented representation that is translation-invariant, non-aliased, and self-invertible. It provides a richer representation than the Laplacian pyramid by adding information about image orientation. Ideally, this transformation is shiftable, allowing for interpolations in position, scale, and orientation using linear combinations of a set of basis coefficients. Analysis is performed using a steerable filter bank: (see figure: Oriented filters and the low-pass kernel used in the steerable pyramid.). The decomposition in scale is formed by introducing a low-pass filter and recursively breaking the low-pass filtered component into angular and low-pass frequency components. One block of the steerable pyramid computation is shown here: [FIGURE:23144f4d582c7514]. To ensure reconstruction, filters must be designed so their sums of squared magnitudes tile in the frequency domain. The architecture includes an analysis network (encoder) and a synthesis network (decoder) that reconstructs the input from the representation: (see figure: Steerable pyramid architecture.). The steerable pyramid is a self-inverting overcomplete representation, as seen in this example using four orientations and three scales: (see figure: Steerable pyramid representation (three levels and four orientations). Why is that each orientation subband seems to indicate a different time?).
concepts.motivation_md: While Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids capture scale, they lack orientation information. Steerable pyramids provide a more expressive, oriented representation necessary for tasks like texture analysis and edge detection.
concepts.recap_md: - It decomposes images into multiple scales and orientations using a steerable filter bank. - The representation is overcomplete, meaning it contains more coefficients than the original pixel count. - It is designed for perfect reconstruction, allowing the original image to be synthesized from the coefficients.

key_passage.text: The steerable pyramid adds information about image orientation. Therefore, the steerable representation is a multiscale oriented representation that is translation-invariant. It is non-aliased and self-invertible.

question.text: Why is that each orientation subband seems to indicate a different time?

motivation.text: The Laplacian pyramid provides a richer representation than the Gaussian pyramid. But we would like to have an even more expressive image representation.

concepts.title: Pictorial Summary of Pyramid Representations
concepts.one_liner: Pyramid representations can be visualized as projection matrices that transform input signals into localized, multi-scale, or multi-orientation components.
concepts.content: Pyramid representations can be summarized by their projection matrices $\mathbf{P}$, which are formed by stacking the projection matrices of each pyramid level: (see figure: Visual comparison of linear transform image representations discussed in this chapter. All the transforms are visualized as a matrix where the number of rows is the size of the input, and the number...). For a 1D input signal, a three-level Gaussian pyramid projection matrix is $\mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{I}; \mathbf{G}_0; \mathbf{G}_1]$, where the first block is the identity matrix. For a two-level Laplacian pyramid with a Gaussian residual, the matrix is $\mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{L}_0; \mathbf{L}_1; \mathbf{G}_1]$. Unlike the global Fourier transform, the Gaussian pyramid is a localized transform where output values depend only on pixels in a neighborhood. The Laplacian pyramid is a band-passed representation, except for the low-pass residual layer. For 2D images, the steerable pyramid adds multiple orientations per scale, causing the representation to be very overcomplete and the projection matrix to be much taller than it is wide.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing pyramids as matrices helps compare their mathematical properties, such as locality, overcompleteness, and frequency response, relative to standard transforms like the Fourier transform.
concepts.recap_md: - Gaussian pyramids are localized transforms, while Laplacian pyramids provide band-passed representations. - Steerable pyramids are highly overcomplete due to their multi-orientation and non-aliased subbands. - Projection matrices for these pyramids are "tall," reflecting that they produce more coefficients than input pixels.

key_passage.text: shows a pictorial summary of the different pyramid representations we've discussed in this chapter. The figure shows the projection matrices P for each transformation, both in the 1D case and 2D case. Each projection matrix formed by stacking the projection matrices of each pyramid level.

motivation.text: The Gaussian pyramid is seen to be banded, showing that it is a localized transform where the output values only depend on pixels in a neighborhood. The Laplacian pyramid is a band-passed image representation, except for the low-pass residual layer.

concepts.title: Convolutional Neural Nets
concepts.one_liner: Convolutional neural nets are architectures specifically designed to exploit the spatial structure inherent in visual signals.
concepts.content: Convolutional neural nets, also called convnets or CNNs, are a neural net architecture especially suited to the structure in visual signals. While standard neural nets are designed to process generic data, CNNs are designed to exploit the special structure found in many domains, particularly visual signals.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard neural networks do not inherently account for the spatial relationships in images. CNNs solve this by using architectures that specifically leverage local patterns and spatial hierarchies.
concepts.recap_md: - CNNs are specialized neural networks for processing data with spatial or temporal structures. - They are the primary architecture used for visual signal processing in modern machine learning.

key_passage.text: Convolutional neural nets, also called convnets or CNNs, are a neural net architecture especially suited to the structure in visual signals.

motivation.text: But in many domains, the data has special structure, and we can design neural net architectures that are better suited to exploiting that structure.

concepts.title: CNNs as Patch Processing
concepts.one_liner: CNNs function by processing small patches of an input image independently and identically using a scanning neural network.
concepts.content: The key idea of CNNs is to chop up the input image into little patches and then process each patch independently and identically: [FIGURE:bf2d851dfcb790e1]. CNNs are well suited to processing spatial or temporal signals, such as geospatial data or sounds, where there is a natural way to scan across a signal and process each windowed region separately. Each patch is processed with a classifier module, which is a neural net that scans across the input and classifies each patch. If these predictions are rearranged back into the shape of the input image and color coded, they form an input-output mapping: [FIGURE:18506f1d2dfb020b].
concepts.motivation_md: Processing an entire image at once is computationally expensive and ignores local features. Patch-based processing allows the network to learn features that are valid regardless of their location in the image.
concepts.recap_md: - CNNs treat images as a collection of small patches processed by the same neural network module. - The output of this process is a grid of predictions corresponding to the patches in the input. - This scanning mechanism allows CNNs to handle various signal types, including audio and geospatial data.

key_passage.text: The key idea of CNNs is to chop up the input image into little patches, and then process each patch independently and identically.

motivation.text: CNNs are also well suited to processing many other spatial or temporal signals, such as geospatial data or sounds. If there is a natural way to scan across a signal, processing each windowed region separately, then CNNs may be a reasonable choice.

concepts.title: Semantic Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning a specific class label to every individual pixel in an image.
concepts.content: Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning a class label to each pixel in an image. This can be achieved by chopping up the image into overlapping patches. If done densely, such that each patch is one pixel offset from the last, it produces a full resolution image of predictions: [FIGURE:bc57f84e5eede7f0]. One reason CNNs are powerful is because they can map an input image to an output image with the same shape, rather than outputting a single label.
concepts.motivation_md: Many vision tasks require knowing exactly where objects are and what every pixel represents, rather than just identifying if an object exists anywhere in the image.
concepts.recap_md: - Semantic segmentation produces a label for every pixel, resulting in a dense map of classifications. - CNNs facilitate this by outputting data that maintains the spatial dimensions of the input image.

key_passage.text: This CNN solved a task known as semantic segmentation, which is the task of assigning a class label to each pixel in an image.

motivation.text: One reason CNNs are powerful is because they map an input image to an output image with the same shape, rather than outputting a single label like in the nets we saw in previous chapters.

concepts.title: Feature Map
concepts.one_liner: A feature map is a channel in a neural network's output that highlights specific features, such as edges, found in the input.
concepts.content: Each channel in a convolutional layer is called a feature map, as it shows specific features of the input, such as the location of vertical edges.
concepts.motivation_md: To understand what a network is "seeing," it is useful to separate the different types of information (like edges or textures) into distinct spatial maps.
concepts.recap_md: - Feature maps are the individual channels produced by convolutional filters. - They indicate the presence and location of specific visual features across the input image.

key_passage.text: We call each of these channels a **feature map**, as it shows some features of the input, such as where the vertical edges are.

concepts.title: Imputation

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

concepts.one_liner: Imputation is the process of predicting gaps in measurements, such as filling in missing pixels in a corrupted image.
concepts.content: Imputation is the problem of predicting gaps in measurements. Common examples include filling in missing pixels in a corrupted image or superresolving a movie to play at a higher framerate.
concepts.motivation_md: In real-world data collection, measurements are often incomplete, noisy, or low-resolution. Imputation provides a framework for recovering this missing information by predicting it from the available data.
concepts.recap_md: - Imputation involves predicting missing values or gaps in a dataset.

key_passage.text: to predict gaps in our measurements, a problem known as imputation

motivation.text: Filling in missing pixels in a corrupted image is an example of imputation, as is superresolving a movie to play at a higher framerate.

concepts.title: Autoencoder
concepts.one_liner: An autoencoder is a function that maps data back to itself via a low-dimensional representational bottleneck to learn useful embeddings.
concepts.content:
Autoencoders are one of the oldest and most common kinds of representation learners. An autoencoder is a function that maps data back to itself (hence the "auto"), but via a low-dimensional representational bottleneck.

(see figure: {\small (left) An autoencoder maps from points in data space, to points in representation space, and back. (right) An example of running an autoencoder on an input image of a bird.)

The key trick is to impose constraints on the intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$, so that it becomes useful. The most common constraint is compression: $\mathbf{z}$ is a low-dimensional, compressed representation of $\mathbf{x}$.

To be precise, an autoencoder $F$ consists of two parts, an encoder $f$ and a decoder $g$, with $F = g \circ f$. The encoder, $f: \mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^M$, maps high-dimensional data $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ to a vector embedding $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M$. Typically, $M < N$, performing dimensionality reduction. The decoder, $g: \mathbb{R}^M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$ performs the inverse mapping to $f$, and ideally $g$ is exactly the inverse function $f^{-1}$. Because it may be impossible to perfectly invert $f$, we use a loss function to penalize the distance from perfect inversion, such as the squared error reconstruction loss, $\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{recon}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{x}) = \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2$.

The learning problem is defined as:
$$f^*,g^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{f,g} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}} \left\lVert g(f(\mathbf{x})) - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2 $$

The goal is to find a lower dimensional representation from which we can reconstruct the data. The autoencoder discards redundant features but avoids losing essential information. The choice of loss function determines what information is preserved; for instance, $L_2$ loss focuses on individual pixel intensities, while other loss functions can penalize errors in edges, textures, or perceptual structures.



Autoencoders appear in many forms, such as steerable pyramids or the CycleGAN algorithm. Typically, $f$ and $g$ are deep neural networks trained via gradient descent. After training, the decoder $g$ is often discarded, leaving the learned encoder $f$ for representation learning.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoencoders solve the problem of unsupervised representation learning. By forcing data through a bottleneck and requiring its reconstruction, the model is compelled to discover the most salient, non-redundant features of the data without needing manual labels.
concepts.recap_md: - An autoencoder consists of an encoder $f$ that compresses data and a decoder $g$ that reconstructs it.

key_passage.text: An autoencoder is a function that maps data back to itself (hence the "auto"), but via a low-dimensional representational bottleneck.

motivation.text: The idea is to find a lower dimensional representation of the data from which we are able to reconstruct the data.

concepts.title: Bottleneck
concepts.one_liner: A bottleneck is a low-dimensional representation space that constrains the flow of information in an autoencoder.
concepts.content: A bottleneck is a low-dimensional representational layer in an autoencoder that forces the model to compress the input data into a more compact form.
concepts.motivation_md: Without a bottleneck, an autoencoder could simply learn the identity function, failing to extract any meaningful or useful features. The bottleneck forces the network to prioritize the most important information.
concepts.recap_md: - A bottleneck is a low-dimensional intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$ used to compress data.

concepts.title: Reconstruction Loss
concepts.one_liner: Reconstruction loss is a metric, typically squared error, that measures how accurately an autoencoder reconstructs its input.
concepts.content: Reconstruction loss is a loss function used to penalize how far a reconstructed output is from the original input. A typical choice is the squared error reconstruction loss, defined as $\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{recon}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{x}) = \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2$.
concepts.motivation_md: To train an autoencoder, we need a quantitative measure of how much information was lost during the encoding and decoding process. Reconstruction loss provides this objective function for optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - It measures the error between the original input $\mathbf{x}$ and the reconstructed output $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

key_passage.text: typical choice is the squared error reconstruction loss, $\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{recon}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{x}) = \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2$.

concepts.title: Relationship between Autoencoders and PCA
concepts.one_liner: Linear $L_2$ autoencoders learn an embedding subspace equivalent to that of Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
concepts.content: Autoencoders are closely related to dimensionality reduction algorithms like Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Specifically, an $L_2$ autoencoder where both the encoder $f$ and decoder $g$ are linear functions learns an $M$-dimensional embedding that spans the same subspace as a PCA projection to $M$ dimensions.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the link between autoencoders and PCA helps ground deep learning methods in classical statistical theory, showing that autoencoders can be viewed as a non-linear generalization of PCA.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear autoencoders with $L_2$ loss span the same subspace as PCA.

key_passage.text: an $L_2$ autoencoder, for which both $f$ and $g$ are linear functions, learns an $M$-dimensional embedding that spans the same subspace as a PCA projection to $M$-dimensions

motivation.text: Closely related to autoencoders are other dimensionality reduction algorithms like principle components ananlysis (PCA).

concepts.title: Predictive Encodings
concepts.one_liner: Predictive representation learning uses a prediction task as a pretext to train a useful data encoder.
concepts.content:
In predictive representation learning, the goal is to use prediction as a way to train a useful representation rather than to make predictions themselves. The process involves encoding data into an embedding $\mathbf{z}$, then mapping from that embedding to a target prediction $\mathbf{y}$. This composition of functions can be trained with a prediction task to yield a good data encoder. The prediction task serves as a pretext task for learning representations.

Different prediction tasks induce different properties in the representation. Examples include predicting future frames in a video, predicting the next pixel in an image sequence, or using an image's semantic class as a target. While these tasks resemble supervised learning, they are distinct because the goal is the resulting image encoding rather than the classifier itself.

Formally, let $\mathbf{y}$ be the prediction target. Predictive representation learning is visualized as:

[FIGURE:4b90715c8d8cd84b]

where $D$ is a distance function (e.g., $L_2$). Unlike autoencoders, the relative dimensionalities of the input $N$, embedding $M$, and target $K$ depend on the specific task. For example, in image classification, $N$ is the input pixel count, $M$ is a lower-dimensional embedding, and $K$ is the number of classes.

(see figure: Examples of different pretext tasks.)
concepts.motivation_md: Predictive encodings allow models to learn meaningful features from data by leveraging the inherent structure of the data (like temporal or spatial sequences) as a source of supervision, avoiding the need for expensive manual labeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Predictive learning uses a pretext task to induce useful data representations.

key_passage.text: In predictive representation learning, the goal is not to make predictions per se, but to use prediction as a way to train a useful representation. The way to do this is first encode the data into an embedding z, then map from the embedding to your target prediction.

motivation.text: Neuroscientists think the brain also uses prediction to better encode sensory signals, but focus on a different part of the problem. The idea of predictive coding states that the sensory cortex only transmits the difference between its predictions and the actual observed signal.

concepts.title: Pretext Task
concepts.one_liner: A pretext task is a prediction problem used to train a model to learn useful data representations rather than for the prediction itself.
concepts.content: In predictive representation learning, the goal is to use prediction as a way to train a useful representation. This is achieved by encoding data into an embedding $\mathbf{z}$ and then mapping from that embedding to a target prediction. The prediction task used in this process is called a pretext task, as it serves as a means to obtain a good data encoder.
concepts.motivation_md: Pretext tasks provide a way to perform 'self-supervised' learning, where the data itself provides the labels, allowing models to learn complex features without human-annotated datasets.
concepts.recap_md: - A pretext task is a proxy objective used to learn data embeddings.

key_passage.text: The prediction task is a pretext task for learning good representations.

motivation.text: In predictive representation learning, the goal is not to make predictions per se, but to use prediction as a way to train a useful representation.

concepts.title: Predictive Coding
concepts.one_liner: Predictive coding is the theory that the brain encodes sensory signals by only transmitting the difference between its predictions and actual observations.
concepts.content: Predictive coding is a concept from neuroscience suggesting that the sensory cortex only transmits the difference between its predictions and the actual observed signal. In the context of representation learning, this idea can be used to compress signals by only transmitting the "surprises" or prediction errors.
concepts.motivation_md: Predictive coding explains how biological and artificial systems can achieve high efficiency by focusing computational resources on unexpected information rather than redundant, predictable signals.
concepts.recap_md: - It involves transmitting only the error (difference) between a prediction and the actual signal.

key_passage.text: The idea of predictive coding states that the sensory cortex only transmits the difference between its predictions and the actual observed signal.

motivation.text: Neuroscientists think the brain also uses prediction to better encode sensory signals, but focus on a different part of the problem. Predictive coding focuses on one thing you can do with such a representation: use it to compress future signals by just transmitting the surprises.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message
concepts.one_liner: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$ from node $i$ to node $j$ is the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree leaving node $i$ that excludes node $j$.
concepts.content: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is defined as the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$.
concepts.motivation_md: In graphical models, calculating marginal probabilities directly is often computationally expensive. Belief propagation messages serve as partial sums that allow for efficient, local computation of these marginals by summarizing information from subtrees.
concepts.recap_md: - A message $m_{ij}$ represents the summarized probability information from the subtree rooted at $i$ (excluding $j$).

key_passage.text: A message $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message Update Rule
aliases: recursive belief propagation message update rule
concepts.one_liner: The belief propagation update rule computes messages by multiplying incoming messages with pairwise compatibility functions and marginalizing over the sending node's states.
concepts.content:
The belief propagation message update rule is derived by passing summations over node states through nodes that are constant over those summations, resulting in a recursive factorization. As illustrated in (see figure: Example motivating belief propagation update rule. (a) Marginalization of a graph with no loops. (b) Shows how the partial sums at $x_j$ distribute over nodes.), messages such as $m_{j+1,j}$ and $m_{kj}$ correspond to partial sums over specific nodes in the graph. Marginalization over the states of all nodes leaving node $j$, not including node $i$, leads to the belief propagation message passing rule.

To compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

1. Multiply together all messages (independent probabilities) coming in to node $j$, except for the message from node $i$ back to node $j$.
2. Multiply by the pairwise compatibility function $\psi_{ij}(x_i, x_j)$.
3. Marginalize over the variable $x_j$.

These steps are summarized in the following equation to compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

$$m_{j i}\left(x_i\right)=\sum_{x_j} \psi_{i i}\left(x_i, x_j\right) \prod_{k \in \eta(j) \backslash i} m_{k j}\left(x_j\right)$$

where $\eta(j) \backslash i$ denotes the neighbors of node $j$ except for node $i$. (see figure: Pictorial depiction of belief propagation message passing rules of equation (@eq-bpupdate), where $\odot$ indicates elementwise multiplication (i.e., the Hadamard product).) Any local potential functions $\phi_{j}(x_j)$ are treated as an additional message into node $j$, such that $m_{0j}(x_j) = \phi_{j}(x_j)$. For continuous variables, the sum over the states of $x_j$ is replaced by an integral over the domain of $x_j$.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule allows for the recursive calculation of marginals in a tree-structured graph by breaking down a global summation into local, modular computations that can be passed between neighbors.
concepts.recap_md: - To send a message to node $i$, node $j$ combines all incoming messages from its other neighbors with its local compatibility function.

key_passage.text: To compute the message from node j to node i: Multiply together all messages (independent probabilities) coming in to node j, except for the message from node i back to node j, Multiply by the pairwise compatibility function ψij(xi, xj) (also independent of the other multiplicands), Marginalize over the variable xj.

motivation.text: Remembering that the message from node j to node i is the sum over the tree leaving node j, we can then read-off the recursive belief propagation message update rule by marginalizing over the state probabilities at node j.

concepts.title: Nosey Neighbor Rule
concepts.one_liner: The 'nosey neighbor rule' describes how BP messages represent a neighbor's belief about a node's state based on all the information they have gathered.
concepts.content: Belief propagation messages are partial sums in the marginalization calculation, where the arguments of messages are always the state of the node that the message is going to. This follows the "nosey neighbor rule" (from Brendan Frey, Univ. Toronto): Every node is a house in some neighborhood. Your nosey neighbor says to you, "Given what I've seen myself and everything I've heard from my neighbors, here's what I think is going on inside your house."
concepts.motivation_md: This metaphor provides an intuitive way to understand the directionality and content of messages in the belief propagation algorithm.
concepts.recap_md: - Messages are always functions of the state of the receiving node.

key_passage.text: BP follows the "nosey neighbor rule" (from Brendan Frey, Univ. Toronto): Every node is a house in some neighborhood. Your nosey neighbor says to you, "Given what I've seen myself and everything I've heard from my neighbors, here's what I think is going on inside your house."

concepts.title: Marginal Probability in Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: In a loopless network, the marginal probability at a node is the product of all its incoming messages.
concepts.content:
(see figure: To compute the marginal probability at node $i$, we multiply together all the incoming messages at that node: $p_{i}$ as another message.)

The marginal probability at a node $i$ is the sum over the joint probabilities of all states except those of $x_i$. In a network with no loops, the conditional independence structure ensures that the marginal probability at node $i$ is the product of the sum of all states of all nodes in each subtree connected to node $i$. Because the subtrees are independent when conditioned on node $i$, the marginal probability is simply the product of all incoming messages:

$$p_{i}(x_i) = \prod_{j\in \eta(i)}  m_{ji}(x_i)$$

This product includes the local clique potential at node $i$, $\psi_i(x_i)$, which is treated as one of the incoming messages.
concepts.motivation_md: The primary goal of belief propagation is to compute these marginal probabilities efficiently without performing an exhaustive summation over the entire joint distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - The marginal probability $p_i(x_i)$ is the product of all messages $m_{ji}(x_i)$ entering node $i$.

key_passage.text: the marginal probability at a node $i$ is the product of all the incoming messages: $$p_{i}(x_i) = \prod_{j\in \eta(i)} m_{ji}(x_i)$$

motivation.text: Because we assume the network has no loops, the conditional independence structure assures us that marginal probability at a node $i$ is the product of the sum of all states of all nodes in each subtree connected to node $i$: Conditioned on node $i$, the probabilities within each subtree are independent.

concepts.title: Message Update Protocols
concepts.one_liner: Message update protocols like depth-first and parallel updates determine the sequence in which belief propagation messages are calculated across a network.
concepts.content:
To find all messages, the recursive BP update rule is applied whenever all required incoming messages are defined. The process starts at leaf nodes, which can send messages because they have no incoming messages other than from the recipient node. Two natural protocols are used:

1. **Depth-first update**: One node is chosen as the root. Messages are passed from the leaves up to the root, and then back down from the root to the leaves.
2. **Parallel update**: At each step, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has already received the necessary incoming messages.

[FIGURE:05fcd402b5e6435d]
[FIGURE:642603864966b118]
[FIGURE:8a28a6db9b463c3e]
**Synchronous parallel update schedule**: Each node sends an outgoing message as soon as it receives the necessary incoming messages.

[FIGURE:25f610399a220f05]
[FIGURE:9560b6515cfb38e6]
[FIGURE:455ef9a295437c12]
[FIGURE:a33008ecd7f522ba]
**Depth-first BP message passing schedule**: Select a root node, start at leaves, proceed to root, perform an outgoing sweep, and end at leaf nodes.

A single sweep through all nodes allows the calculation of the marginal at any node. A second sweep (from root back to leaves) calculates all messages needed for marginals at every node, requiring only twice the computation of a single-node marginal.
concepts.motivation_md: Efficiently computing marginals for all nodes in a graph requires a systematic way to order message updates so that dependencies are met and computations are reused.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth-first updates use a root-based two-pass sweep (leaves-to-root and root-to-leaves).

key_passage.text: Two natural message passing protocols are consistent with that rule: depth-first update, and parallel update. In depth-first update, one node is arbitrarily picked as the root. Messages are then passed from the leaves of the tree (leaves, relative to that root node) up to the root, then back down to the leaves. In parallel update, at each turn, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has received all the necessary incoming messages.

motivation.text: Note that when computing marginals at many nodes, we reuse messages with the BP algorithm. A single message-passing sweep through all the nodes lets us calculate the marginal at any node (using the depth-first update rules to calculate the marginal at the root node). A second sweep from the root node back to all the leaf nodes calculates all the messages needed to find the marginal probability at every node. It takes only twice the number of computations to calculate the incoming messages to every node, and thus the marginal probabilities everywhere, as it does to calculate the incoming messages for the marginal probability at a single node.

concepts.title: Loopy Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Loopy belief propagation applies standard BP update rules to graphs with cycles, often providing useful local approximations despite the lack of global guarantees.
concepts.content:
The BP message update rules provide exact marginals only when the network topology is a tree or a chain. For graphs with loops, exact computation depends on the treewidth, which can be intractably large in fields like computer vision. However, applying BP update rules locally as a heuristic is often effective. This is known as the **loopy belief propagation algorithm**:

1. Convert the graph to pairwise potentials.
2. Initialize all messages to all ones, or to random values between 0 and 1.
3. Run the belief propagation update rules until convergence.
concepts.motivation_md: Many real-world problems, such as image processing, involve graphs with many loops where exact inference is impossible; loopy BP provides a practical, though approximate, alternative.
concepts.recap_md: - Loopy BP is a heuristic that applies tree-based update rules to cyclic graphs.

key_passage.text: Here is the algorithm, also know as loopy belief propagation algorithm: 1. Convert graph to pairwise potentials. 2. Initialize all messages to all ones, or to random values between 0 and 1. 3. Run the belief propagation update rules until convergence.

motivation.text: Message update rules are described locally, and one might imagine that it is a useful local operation to perform, even without the global guarantees of ordinary BP. It turns out that is true.

concepts.title: Treewidth
concepts.one_liner: Treewidth is a graph-theoretic quantity that determines the complexity of exact marginal probability computation in graphs with loops.
concepts.content: The BP message update rules only work to give the exact marginals when the topology of the network is that of a tree or a chain. In general, exact computation of marginal probabilities for graphs with loops depends on a graph-theoretic quantity known as the **treewidth** of the graph.
concepts.motivation_md: Treewidth helps characterize the computational difficulty of performing exact inference on a specific graph structure.
concepts.recap_md: - Treewidth dictates the feasibility of exact inference in cyclic graphical models.

key_passage.text: In general, one can show that exact computation of marginal probabilities for graphs with loops depends on a graph-theoretic quantity known as the treewidth of the graph.

motivation.text: The BP message update rules only work to give the exact marginals when the topology of the network is that of a tree or a chain.

concepts.title: Max-Product Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Max-product belief propagation is a variation of the BP algorithm that finds the state configuration maximizing the joint probability.
concepts.content: Instead of summing over the states of other nodes, we are sometimes interested in finding the configuration $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the joint probability. Because the argmax operator passes through constant variables in the same way the summation sign does, an alternate version of the BP algorithm can be used. In this **max-product** version of belief propagation, the summation in the update rule is replaced with an argmax. This algorithm computes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate of the hidden states.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard BP finds marginal probabilities, max-product BP is used when the goal is to find the single most likely global state of the system.
concepts.recap_md: - Max-product BP replaces the summation in the update rule with an argmax.

key_passage.text: This is called the max-product version of belief propagation, and it computes an MAP estimate of the hidden states.

motivation.text: Instead of summing over the states of other nodes, we are sometimes interested in finding the x that maximizes the joint probability.

concepts.title: Affordance
concepts.one_liner: An affordance is a property of an environment or object that offers an observer possibilities for action, such as a path affording locomotion.
concepts.content: Introduced by Gibson in 1966, an affordance is what an environment or object offers an observer. For example, a path affords locomotion, an obstacle affords collision, and a stairway affords both descent and ascent. An object's affordance is generally a direct consequence of its properties, such as a hollow object affording containment or a sharp edge affording cutting. Animate objects afford social interaction.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how we perceive the environment not just as physical shapes, but as opportunities for action, simplifying the link between perception and behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Affordances are the action possibilities provided by the environment or objects to an observer. - These possibilities are often direct consequences of physical properties, such as a hollow object affording containment. - Animate objects are unique in that they afford social interaction.

key_passage.text: A *path* affords locomotion from one point to another, an *obstacle* affords collision, and a *stairway* affords both descent and ascent. An *object* is a substance enclosed by a surface. The affordance of an object is generally a direct consequence of its properties: a hollow object can contain substances, a detached object affords carrying, an object with a sharp edge affords cutting, and so on.

concepts.title: Direct Perception
concepts.one_liner: Direct perception is the process of picking up information directly from a rich ambient optic array without the need for additional mental processing.
concepts.content: Gibson's theory of visual perception postulates that the ambient optic array is very rich and contains all the information needed to perceive the environment. Direct perception is the process of information pickup directly from this ambient array. This is in contrast with other theories of visual perception that assume input stimuli are impoverished and that perception is indirect, requiring additional processes. A richer input might allow for a simpler solution to the perception problem.
concepts.motivation_md: It challenges the idea that the brain must perform complex computations to 'fill in' missing data, suggesting instead that the environment provides sufficient information for immediate understanding.
concepts.recap_md: - Direct perception involves the immediate pickup of information from the ambient optic array. - It assumes the environment provides rich enough information that additional cognitive processing is unnecessary. - This approach suggests that richer sensory input can simplify the overall problem of perception.

key_passage.text: Direct perception is the process of information pickup directly from the ambient array.

motivation.text: The richer the input is, one might hope that the solution to the perception problem will be simpler.

concepts.title: Information Pickup
concepts.one_liner: Information pickup is the process by which an observer directly extracts environmental information from the rich ambient optic array.
concepts.content: In Gibson's theory of visual perception, the ambient optic array is considered rich and contains all the information needed to perceive the environment. Information pickup is the process of direct perception where this information is gathered directly from the ambient array. This contrasts with indirect theories which assume that sensory input is impoverished and requires additional processes.
concepts.motivation_md: This term describes the mechanism of direct perception, emphasizing that the observer is an active gatherer of existing environmental information rather than a passive receiver of stimuli.
concepts.recap_md: - Information pickup is the core mechanism of direct perception from the ambient optic array. - It relies on the premise that the environment provides a rich, complete set of information for the observer. - It contrasts with indirect theories that view sensory input as impoverished.

key_passage.text: Direct perception is the process of information pickup directly from the ambient array.

motivation.text: Gibson's theory of visual perception postulates that the ambient optic array is very rich and contains all the information needed to perceive the environment.

concepts.title: Indirect Perception
concepts.one_liner: Indirect perception is the theory that sensory input is impoverished and must be complemented by additional internal processes to achieve environmental understanding.
concepts.content: Indirect perception is a theory of visual perception that assumes input stimuli are very impoverished. In this view, perception is considered indirect because it must be complemented by additional processes to be complete. This is the most common theory of perception, though it stands in contrast to Gibson's theory of direct information pickup from a rich ambient array.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept represents the traditional view of vision, explaining why many researchers believe complex brain computations are necessary to interpret sensory data.
concepts.recap_md: - Indirect perception assumes that sensory stimuli are too poor to provide a full understanding of the environment. - It requires additional internal processes to complement and interpret the raw input. - It is currently the most common theory in visual perception studies.

key_passage.text: The indirect theory of perception is the most common one.

motivation.text: when building a perceptual system, the richer the input is, one might hope that the solution to the perception problem will be simpler.

concepts.title: Gibson's View on Stimuli
concepts.one_liner: Gibson critiqued the term 'stimuli' because it implies the environment acts upon a passive observer rather than the observer actively picking up information.
concepts.content: Gibson critiqued the term 'stimuli' because it implied that the environment stimulates the observer. For Gibson, it was important to emphasize that the observer is not a passive recipient but is actively picking up information from the environment.
concepts.motivation_md: This critique highlights the shift from seeing the brain as a reactive machine to seeing the observer as an active participant in the environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Gibson rejected the term 'stimuli' to avoid the implication of a passive observer. - He emphasized the active role of the observer in 'picking up' environmental information.

key_passage.text: Gibson did not like the term stimuli because it implied that the environment stimulates the observer. For Gibson, it is important to stress that the observer is only picking up information.

motivation.text: Gibson did not like the term stimuli because it implied that the environment stimulates the observer.

concepts.title: Neural Mechanisms of Visual Perception
concepts.one_liner: Neuroscience seeks to understand vision by reverse engineering how the brain's networks of interconnected cells solve perceptual tasks.
concepts.content: Neuroscience has significantly influenced computer vision through concepts like RGB encoding, neural networks, and attention modulation. A core premise in computational neuroscience is that vision can be understood by reverse engineering how the brain solves tasks. Historically, Santiago Ramón y Cajal proved in 1890 that the brain is composed of networks of interconnected cells, rather than a continuous mass, as shown in his work on the anatomy of the retina. ![Drawing of the retina by Santiago Ramón y Cajal.](figures/taxonomy/cajal.png)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the biological hardware of vision provides a blueprint for creating artificial vision systems and explains the physical basis of perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision can be understood by reverse engineering the brain's biological solutions to perceptual tasks. - Santiago Ramón y Cajal proved the brain consists of networks of interconnected cells rather than a continuous mass. - This discovery laid the foundation for modern neural network models and computational neuroscience.

key_passage.text: It was in 1890 that Santiago Ramón y Cajal, using Golgi's stain, isolated individual neurons and proved that the brain is composed by networks of interconnected cells as shown in his work on the anatomy of the retina. This was the first time that networks were observed.

motivation.text: Neuroscience has greatly contributed to our understanding of how vision works and has inspired a large number of computer vision approaches: red-green-blue (RGB) encoding of images, filter based image representations, neural networks, and attention modulation. Studies on the neural mechanisms of visual perception had a lasting impact.

concepts.title: The Retina
concepts.one_liner: The retina is a neural structure that transforms light into electrical impulses and performs the initial stages of visual processing.
concepts.content: ![Drawing of the retina by Santiago Ramón y Cajal.](figures/taxonomy/cajal.png) The drawing of the retina (@fig-cajal) shows the first layers of neurons that process visual input. The retina transforms light into electrical impulses, starting with photoreceptors (rods and cones) and continuing through layers of amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells. Ganglion cells then transmit the output through the optic nerve to the rest of the brain. While Ramón y Cajal revealed this circuitry, his work did not fully explain the functional behavior of these circuits.
concepts.motivation_md: The retina acts as the primary transducer for vision, converting physical light into a language the brain can understand and performing initial data compression.
concepts.recap_md: - The retina transforms light into electrical signals using photoreceptors like rods and cones. - Information is processed through layers of amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells before leaving via the optic nerve. - It represents the first stage of neural circuitry in the visual processing stream.

key_passage.text: The retina is an amazing piece of the brain that transforms light into impulses. Light is first transformed into electric signal by the photoreceptors (rods and cones) and is then processed by a few layers formed by several types of neurons (amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells).

motivation.text: The retina is an amazing piece of the brain that transforms light into impulses. Finally, ganglion cells transmit the output of the retina through the optic nerve to the rest of the brain.

concepts.title: Receptive Field
concepts.one_liner: A receptive field is the specific region of the input stimulus space that must be stimulated to produce a response in a particular neuron.
concepts.content: The retina was one of the first visual structures studied from a functional perspective. In 1938, Haldan Keffer Hartline popularized the concept of the receptive field, which corresponds to the region of the input stimulus space—the retina—that must be stimulated to produce a response in a neuron. Most neurons in the visual processing stream are activated only when light shines on a precise portion of the retina. Only stimulation within the receptive field (RF) produces a response. [FIGURE:542154188035b8df]
concepts.motivation_md: This concept allows researchers to map how specific neurons correspond to specific parts of the environment, explaining how the brain organizes spatial information.
concepts.recap_md: - A receptive field is the area of the sensory surface where a stimulus triggers a neuronal response. - Visual neurons typically respond only to light within a specific, precise portion of the retina. - This concept is fundamental to understanding how the visual system processes spatial information.

key_passage.text: The receptive field of a neuron corresponds to the region of the input stimulus space (the retina in the case of a visual neuron) that has to be stimulated in order to produce a response in the neuron.

motivation.text: Most neurons in the visual processing stream are activated only when light shines on a precise portion of the retina.

concepts.title: Handling Boundaries in Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Implementing a convolution requires deciding how to handle image boundaries, often by padding the input to maintain the output size.
concepts.content:
When implementing a convolution, one must decide how to handle image boundaries. One solution is omitting pixels affected by the boundary, but this causes the output size to differ from the input and can result in significant data loss for large kernels.

[FIGURE:6b79adcf26f0dfd2]

Only the green region contains values that can be computed without boundary handling. The most general approach is extending the input image by adding $N$ pixels left and right and $M$ pixels at the top and bottom for a kernel with support $\left[ -N, N \right] \times \left[-M, M\right]$. Typical padding choices include:

- Zero padding: Set pixels outside the boundary to zero or another constant like the mean image value.
- Circular padding: Replicate pixels from the opposite side, transforming the signal into a periodic infinite signal: $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[(n)_P,(m)_Q\right]$.
- Mirror padding: Reflect valid image pixels over the boundary; this often yields the best results.
- Repeat padding: Set the value to that of the nearest valid output image pixel.

(see figure: Each row shows: (a) Different types of boundary extension. The last image shows the ground truth. (b) The output of convolving the image with a uniform kernel of size $11 \times 11$ with all the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution kernels require a neighborhood of pixels to compute a value; at the edges, some neighbors are missing, requiring a strategy to avoid data loss or size reduction.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Boundary handling prevents the output image from shrinking by extending the input with additional pixels.", "- Common padding methods include zero padding, circular padding, mirror padding, and repeat padding." ]

key_passage.text: The most general approach consists in extending the input image by adding additional pixels so that the output can have the same size as the input. So, for a kernel with support $\left[ -N, N \right] \times \left[-M, M\right]$, one has to add $N$ additional pixels left and right of the image and $M$ pixels at the top and bottom.

motivation.text: When implementing a convolution, one is confronted with the question of what to do at the image boundaries. There's really no satisfactory answer for how to handle the boundaries that works well for all applications.

concepts.title: Circular Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Circular convolution is a special case of convolution that uses circular padding, treating the input signal as an infinite periodic extension.
concepts.content:
[FIGURE:adb812066d7186ad]

Circular convolution is an analytically useful technique that uses circular padding to extend a signal beyond its boundaries. The circular convolution of two signals $h$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ of length $N$ is defined as:

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =  \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$

In this formulation, the signal $h \left[ (n)_N \right]$ is the infinite periodic extension, with period $N$, of the finite length signal $h \left[n \right]$. The output is also a periodic signal with period $N$, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[(n)_N \right]$. Circular convolution shares the same properties as standard convolution, such as commutativity.
concepts.motivation_md: Circular convolution is analytically convenient for reducing boundary artifacts and is a fundamental operation when working with periodic signals or Fourier transforms.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Circular convolution treats finite signals as periodic by using modulo indexing.", "- The output of a circular convolution is itself a periodic signal with the same period as the inputs." ]

key_passage.text: The circular convolution of two signals, $h$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, of length $N$ is defined as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$

motivation.text: This trick is also very useful analytically and conduces to a special case of the convolution: the circular convolution uses circular padding. When convolving a finite length signal with a kernel, we have seen that it can be convenient to extend the signal beyond its boundary to reduce boundary artifacts.

concepts.title: Convolution in the Continuous Domain
concepts.one_liner: Continuous convolution defines the interaction of two continuous signals by replacing the discrete sums of standard convolution with integrals.
concepts.content:
The convolution in the continuous domain is defined similarly to discrete signals but replaces sums with integrals. Given two continuous signals $h(t)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, the convolution operator is defined as:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$

The properties of continuous domain convolution are analogous to discrete convolution, with commutative, associative, and distributive relationships still holding. We can also define the impulse, $\delta (t)$, in the continuous domain such that $\ell(t) \circ \delta(t) = \ell(t)$. The impulse is zero everywhere except at the origin, where it takes an infinitely high value so that its integral is equal to 1:
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) dt = 1$$
The impulse function is also called the impulse distribution or the Dirac delta function.

[FIGURE:3bb6012ff85cabfe]
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous convolution extends the mathematical framework of filtering and signal interaction from discrete digital samples to continuous physical signals.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Continuous convolution uses an integral to combine two functions, mirroring the discrete summation process.", "- The Dirac delta function acts as the identity element for continuous convolution." ]

key_passage.text: The convolution in the continuous domain is defined in the same way as with discrete signals but replacing the sums by integrals. Given two continuous signals $h(t)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, the convolution operator is defined as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$

concepts.title: Cross-Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Cross-correlation is a translation-invariant operator used to locate templates in an image, differing from convolution by not inverting the kernel.
concepts.content:
The cross-correlation operator provides a technique to locate a template in an image and is closely related to convolution. The cross-correlation $\star$ between an image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and a kernel $h$ with square support $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$ is:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\star h =  \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$

Unlike convolution, where the kernel is inverted left-right and up-down, cross-correlation does not invert the kernel. For example, convolving an upward-pointing triangle kernel with impulses results in upward-pointing triangles, whereas cross-correlation results in downward-pointing triangles. While convolution outputs maximum values for inverted matches, cross-correlation outputs maximum values at the center of direct template matches.

(see figure: Cross-correlation versus convolution. (a) Kernel. (b) and (e) are two input images. (c) and (f) are the output convolution with the kernel (a). (d) and (g) are the cross-correlation output with the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-correlation provides a simple technique to locate a template in an image by measuring similarity without the kernel inversion required by convolution.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Cross-correlation is similar to convolution but does not involve flipping the kernel before the sliding sum.", "- It is primarily used as a template matching technique to locate specific patterns within an image." ]

key_passage.text: The cross-correlation operator (denoted by $\star$) between the image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and the kernel $h$ is written as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\star h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$ where the sum is done over the support of the filter $h$, which we assume is a square $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$. In the convolution, the kernel is inverted left-right and up-down, while in the cross-correlation is not.

motivation.text: The cross-correlation provides a simple technique to locate a template in an image.

concepts.title: Normalized Cross-Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Normalized cross-correlation improves template matching by normalizing the kernel and scaling the output by the local standard deviation of the image.
concepts.content:
Normalized cross-correlation at location $(n,m)$ is the dot product between a template $h$ (normalized to zero mean and unit norm) and a local image patch $p$ of the same size, also normalized to unit norm. First, the kernel $h$ is normalized to $\hat{h}$. The output is then calculated as:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \frac{1}{\sigma \left[n,m \right]} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] \hat{h} \left[k,l \right]$$

The output is scaled by the local standard deviation $\sigma[n,m]$ of the image patch centered at $(n,m)$. The local mean $\mu[n,m]$ and variance $\sigma^2[n,m]$ are computed over the kernel's support $(2N+1)^2$. While this method can correctly detect templates like the letter 'a' in @fig-normcorr, it is fragile and only useful under limited conditions, as it is not robust to rotation, scaling, or changes in appearance like font variations.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard cross-correlation is sensitive to changes in local image brightness and contrast; normalization makes the matching process more robust to these variations.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Normalized cross-correlation accounts for local brightness and contrast by using the local mean and standard deviation.", "- Although robust to intensity changes, the method remains sensitive to geometric transformations like scaling and rotation." ]

key_passage.text: The normalized cross-correlation, at location $(n,m)$, is the dot product between a template, $h$, (normalized to be zero mean and unit norm) and the local image patch, $p$, centered at that location and with the same size as the kernel, normalized to be unit norm.

motivation.text: Normalized correlation will detect the object independently of location, but it will not be robust to any other changes such as rotation, scaling, and changes in appearance.

concepts.title: Impulse Response
concepts.one_liner: The impulse response is the output of a linear time-invariant system when the input is a single impulse.
concepts.content: For a linear time-invariant (LTI) filter with kernel $h\left[n\right]$, the output from an impulse $\delta[n]$ is $y\left[n\right] = h\left[n\right]$. Similarly, the output of a translated impulse $\delta \left[n -n_0 \right]$ is $h \left[n -n_0 \right]$. Because the kernel $h\left[n\right]$ defines the system's response to an impulse, it is also called the impulse response of the system.
concepts.motivation_md: The impulse response allows us to characterize the entire behavior of a linear system by knowing only how it reacts to a single point input.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- The impulse response $h[n]$ is the kernel that defines a linear time-invariant (LTI) system.", "- Knowing the impulse response allows for the calculation of the system's output for any arbitrary input via convolution." ]

key_passage.text: This is why the kernel that defines an LTI system, $h\left[n\right]$, is also called the impulse response of the system.

motivation.text: For an LTI filter with kernel $h\left[n\right]$, the output from an impulse is $y\left[n\right] = h\left[n\right]$. The output of a translated impulse $\delta \left[n -n_0 \right]$ is $h \left[n -n_0 \right]$.

concepts.title: Spatial Frequency
concepts.one_liner: Spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space, providing a precise language for analyzing image components like sharpness and blur.
concepts.content: Spatial frequency provides a precise language to describe image components and the effects of linear filters, moving beyond informal terms like "sharp" or "blurry." By analogy with temporal frequencies that describe variation over time, a spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space. The Fourier transform allows a signal to be represented as a sum of complex exponentials, each corresponding to a different spatial frequency.
concepts.motivation_md: We need a more precise language to talk about the effect of linear filters, and the different image components, than to say "sharp" and "blurry" parts of the image.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Spatial frequency quantifies the rate of change in an image's intensity across its dimensions.", "- High spatial frequencies correspond to sharp edges and fine details, while low frequencies correspond to smooth gradients." ]

key_passage.text: By analogy with temporal frequencies, which describe how quickly signals vary over time, a spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space. The Fourier transform lets us describe a signal as a sum of complex exponentials, each of a different spatial frequency.

motivation.text: We need a more precise language to talk about the effect of linear filters, and the different image components, than to say "sharp" and "blurry" parts of the image. The Fourier transform provides that precision.

concepts.title: Image Transforms as Representation Change
concepts.one_liner: Image transforms convert pixel data into alternative representations to reveal properties useful for solving vision tasks.
concepts.content: Image transforms convert pixel data into alternative representations that can reveal properties useful for solving vision tasks. A linear image transform of the form $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ changes the initial pixel representation into an intermediate representation $\mathbf{x}$, which may not be an image. Such representations are particularly valuable when they are invertible, allowing the original pixels to be recovered via $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}= \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{x}$. The Fourier transform is a prominent example of a representation that offers properties not immediately available in the original pixel data.
concepts.motivation_md: Sometimes it is useful to transform the image pixels into another representation that might reveal image properties that can be useful for solving vision tasks.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Transforms map images into new mathematical spaces to highlight specific characteristics like frequency or orientation.", "- Invertible transforms allow for processing in the transform domain followed by a return to the original pixel space." ]

key_passage.text: Linear image transforms with the form $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ can be thought of as a way of changing the initial pixels representation of $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ into a different representation in $\mathbf{x}$.

motivation.text: Sometimes it is useful to transform the image pixels into another representation that might reveal image properties that can be useful for solving vision tasks. A useful representation $\mathbf{x}$ should have a number of interesting properties not immediately available in the original pixels of $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$.

concepts.title: Affinity-Based Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Affinity-based segmentation uses a distance metric to group similar patterns into segments, often by learning embeddings where high-affinity data points are clustered together.
concepts.content:
Affinity-based segmentation methods are based on the idea of affinity, where a distance metric models whether two items should be grouped. This metric usually measures how similar two patterns are or how likely they are to be part of the same object. For example, a simple affinity function over pixel pairs could be the Euclidean distance between their color values. Pixels with high affinity should belong to the same group, while pixels with low affinity should belong to different groups. Methods using this idea include graph cuts, spectral clustering, and Markov random field (MRF)-based clustering.

In modern practice, contrastive learning is a common way to implement this approach. Contrastive methods learn an embedding in which data points with high affinity are nearby and those with low affinity are far apart. Once this embedding is learned, clustering can be performed using a simple quantization method like $k$-means. This entire pipeline is shown in (see figure: Image segmentation using $k$-means over DINO @caron2021emerging features), using DINO as the particular contrastive embedding.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional clustering often struggles with complex visual data. Affinity-based segmentation provides a way to define similarity (affinity) specifically for the task, allowing for more flexible grouping. By leveraging contrastive learning, we can automatically learn these similarity metrics from data, making segmentation more robust than using simple hand-defined pixel distances.
concepts.recap_md: - Affinity serves as a distance metric measuring the likelihood that two items belong to the same object.

key_passage.text: Other clustering methods are based on the idea of affinity, where we try to model a distance metric (the affinity) that tells us whether two items should be grouped. The distance metric usually measures how similar two patterns are, or how likely they are to be part of the same object.

motivation.text: pixels with high affinity should belong to the same group and pixels with low affinity should belong to two different groups. Contrastive learning is a perfect fit for affinity-based segmentation because contrastive methods learn from similarities (positive pairs) and differences (negative pairs), and this is what an affinity metric gives us!

concepts.title: Affinity
concepts.one_liner: Affinity is a distance metric that measures how similar two patterns are or how likely they are to be part of the same object.
concepts.content: Affinity is a concept used in clustering methods where a distance metric is modeled to determine whether two items should be grouped together. This metric usually measures the similarity between two patterns or the likelihood that they belong to the same object.
concepts.motivation_md: To group data points effectively, we need a mathematical way to express 'belonging together.' Affinity provides this formal measure of similarity or grouping likelihood.
concepts.recap_md: - Affinity acts as a distance metric for grouping items.

key_passage.text: where we try to model a distance metric (the affinity) that tells us whether two items should be grouped. The distance metric usually measures how similar two patterns are, or how likely they are to be part of the same object.
