concepts.title: Edge Detection
concepts.one_liner: Edge detection aims to create a compact representation of an image's content using sparse, stable boundaries that relate to scene geometry.
concepts.content: Edge detection is an early vision technique based on the idea that edges form a good, compact representation of an image's content. Edges are relatively sparse and remain stable despite nuisances like noise and lighting. Different kinds of edge structures are connected to scene geometry; for instance, an edge representing an occluding contour indicates a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw pixel data is redundant and sensitive to noise. Edge detection extracts the most essential structural information, providing a stable foundation for understanding scene geometry and object boundaries.
concepts.recap_md: - Edges provide a sparse and stable representation of image content.

key_passage.text: edge detection, where the idea was that the edges in an image should form a good, compact representation of the image's content, because edges are relatively sparse, and they are stable with respect to nuisances like noise and lighting.

motivation.text: edges are relatively sparse, and they are stable with respect to nuisances like noise and lighting. Subsequent work identified connections between different kinds of edge structure and scene geometry; for example, an edge that represents an occluding contour indicates that there is a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.

concepts.title: Occluding Contour
concepts.one_liner: An occluding contour is an edge that indicates a depth discontinuity in a scene.
concepts.content: An occluding contour is a specific kind of edge structure that represents a boundary where one object blocks another. In terms of scene geometry, the presence of an occluding contour indicates that there is a depth discontinuity at that location.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding which edges represent object boundaries versus surface markings is crucial for depth perception and navigating a 3D environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Occluding contours signal depth discontinuities in a scene.

key_passage.text: an edge that represents an occluding contour indicates that there is a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.

concepts.title: Line Drawings
concepts.one_liner: Line drawings represent the edge structure of an image and are highly intuitive for human perception.
concepts.content: Line drawings are a way of representing the edge structure in an image. They are of high interest to humans, suggesting that representing images via edge structure is a useful approach. While there is research in computer graphics regarding the modeling of line drawings, it remains unclear if this representation will eventually be as compelling for machine vision as it is for human vision.
concepts.motivation_md: Humans can recognize complex objects from just a few strokes. Studying line drawings helps researchers understand the minimal information required for visual recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Line drawings capture the essential edge structure of an image.

key_passage.text: Line drawings are another way of representing the edge structure in an image, and they seem to be of high interest to humans.

motivation.text: This suggests that there may be something useful about representing images in terms of their edge structure.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Representation (2.5D)
concepts.one_liner: Layer-based or 2.5D representations capture aspects of depth by modeling the world as a series of layers rather than a full 3D space.
concepts.content: Layer-based representations are used in computer vision to capture aspects of depth without the computational expense of modeling a fully 3D world. These layers, and other related pseudo-3D representations, are often referred to as 2.5D representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Full 3D modeling is often computationally expensive and unnecessary for tasks like occlusion handling. 2.5D layers provide a middle ground that captures depth relationships efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Layer-based representations are also known as 2.5D representations.

key_passage.text: layer-based representations like this have been popular as a way of capturing some aspects of depth without the expense of modeling a fully 3D world; sometimes layers and other related pseudo-3D representations are called 2.5D representations.

motivation.text: layer-based representations like this have been popular as a way of capturing some aspects of depth without the expense of modeling a fully 3D world

concepts.title: Ordinal Structure
concepts.one_liner: Ordinal structure refers to the relative ordering of objects, such as which item is on top of another.
concepts.content: Ordinal structure refers to the relative depth ordering of objects rather than their exact positions in metric space. For example, in a pile of paper, the ordinal structure tells us which piece is on top, which is often the most important information for interaction.
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world tasks, knowing the exact distance to an object is less important than knowing its relative order (e.g., 'A is in front of B').
concepts.recap_md: - Ordinal structure captures the relative depth ordering of objects.

key_passage.text: Layers capture ordinal structure and often this is the structure we care about

motivation.text: for example, if we want to pick up a piece of paper in our pile, the main thing that matters is if it is on top.

concepts.title: Emergent Groups
concepts.one_liner: In modern vision systems, perceptual structures like objects and contours often emerge within hidden layers rather than being explicitly designed.
concepts.content: While explicit edge detection and bottom-up segmentation are less common in modern computer vision, perceptual organization remains present. Current systems still process the world in terms of objects, contours, and layers, but these structures are emergent in their hidden layers rather than being made explicit by human design. For example, object detectors have been observed to emerge inside neural networks trained for tasks like colorization.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why classical vision topics are still relevant: even if we don't program them explicitly, deep learning models often 'rediscover' these fundamental structures to solve complex tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptual structures emerge naturally in the hidden layers of neural networks.

key_passage.text: But this doesn't mean that perceptual organization is absent from current systems. These systems still see the world in terms of objects, contours, layers, and so forth, but those structures are emergent in their hidden layers rather than made explicit by human design.

motivation.text: Edge detection and bottom-up segmentation are not the workhorses they once were. But this doesn't mean that perceptual organization is absent from current systems.

concepts.title: Alignment
concepts.one_liner: Alignment is the property that two views in a positive pair map to the same point in an embedding space.
concepts.content: Wang and Isola showed that the contrastive loss (specifically the InfoNCE form) encourages two simple properties of the embeddings: alignment and uniformity. Alignment is the property that two views in a positive pair will map to the same point in the embedding space, meaning the mapping is invariant to the difference between the views.
concepts.motivation_md: Alignment ensures that different versions of the same data point (positive pairs) are treated as semantically identical by the model, which is a core goal of contrastive learning.
concepts.recap_md: - Alignment requires that positive pairs map to the same embedding point.

key_passage.text: alignment is the property that two views in a positive pair will map to the same point in embedding point, that is, the mapping is invariant to the difference between the views.

motivation.text: the contrastive loss (specifically the InfoNCE form) encourages two simple properties of the embeddings: alignment and uniformity.

concepts.title: Uniformity
concepts.one_liner: Uniformity encourages embeddings to spread out evenly across the surface of a hypersphere.
concepts.content: Uniformity comes from the negative term in the contrastive loss, which encourages embeddings to spread out and tend toward an evenly spread, uniform distribution. For this to work out mathematically, the embeddings must be normalized; specifically, each embedding vector must be a unit vector. Without normalization, the negative term can push embeddings toward being infinitely far apart. In practice, $L_2$ normalization is applied so that embeddings tend toward a uniform distribution over the surface of the $M$-dimensional hypersphere, where $M$ is the dimensionality of the embeddings.
concepts.motivation_md: Uniformity prevents the model from collapsing all data points into a single point, ensuring that the embedding space is used efficiently to distinguish between different data points.
concepts.recap_md: - Uniformity encourages embeddings to spread out toward a uniform distribution.

key_passage.text: Uniformity comes from the negative term, which encourages embeddings to spread out and tend toward an evenly spread, uniform distribution. Importantly, for this to work out mathematically, the embeddings must be normalized, that is, each embedding vector must be a unit vector. The result is that the embeddings will tend toward a uniform distribution over the surface of the M-dimensional hypersphere, where M is the dimensionality of the embeddings.

motivation.text: Otherwise, the negative term can push embeddings toward being infinitely far apart from each other. Fortunately, it is standard practice in contrastive learning (and many other forms of representation learning) to apply L_2 normalization to the embeddings.

concepts.title: Decomposing Contrastive Learning into Alignment and Uniformity
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive learning can be explicitly decomposed into separate loss functions for alignment and uniformity.
concepts.content:
A result of this analysis is that we may explicitly decompose contrastive learning into one loss for alignment and another for uniformity, with the following forms:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) &= \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+) \sim p_{\texttt{pos}}} [\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^+)\right\rVert_2^{\alpha}]\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}(f;t) &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}, \, \mathbf{x}^- \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [e^{-t\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^-)\right\rVert_2^2}]\\
    \mathcal{L}(f;\alpha,t,\lambda) &= \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}
\end{aligned}$$

where $p_{\texttt{pos}}$ is the distribution of positive pairs and $\alpha$, $t$, and $\lambda$ are hyperparameters of the losses.
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing the loss allows researchers to analyze and tune the two fundamental goals of contrastive learning—feature invariance and feature diversity—independently.
concepts.recap_md: - The total loss is a weighted sum of alignment and uniformity components.

key_passage.text: A result of this analysis is we may explicit decompose contrastive learning into one loss for alignment and another for uniformity, with the following forms: $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) &= \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+) \sim p_{\texttt{pos}}} [\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^+)\right\rVert_2^{\alpha}]\\ \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}(f;t) &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}, \, \mathbf{x}^- \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [e^{-t\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^-)\right\rVert_2^2}]\\ \mathcal{L}(f;\alpha,t,\lambda) &= \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}} \end{aligned}$$ where $p_{\texttt{pos}}$ is the distribution of positive pairs and $\alpha$, $t$, and $\lambda$ are hyperparameters of the losses.

concepts.title: Tradeoffs in Visual Representations
concepts.one_liner: Every representation involves tradeoffs, where a good representation for one task may be poor for another.
concepts.content: Different representations make different problems easy or hard. It is important to remember that every representation involves a set of tradeoffs: a good representation for one task may be a bad representation for another task. One of the current goals of computer vision research is to find general-purpose representations. This does not mean the representation will be good for all tasks, but rather that it will be effective for the wide variety of tasks that humans care about, which is a small subset of all possible tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that no single representation is perfect for every problem helps in designing specialized features or seeking general-purpose embeddings that align with human needs.
concepts.recap_md: - Representations involve inherent tradeoffs between different tasks.

key_passage.text: every representation involves a set of tradeoffs: a good representation for one task may be a bad representation for another task.

motivation.text: Different representations make different problems easy, or hard. One of the current goals of computer vision research is to find general-purpose representations, and what this means is not that the representation will be good for all tasks but that it will be good for a wide variety of the tasks that humans care about, which is a very tiny subset of all possible tasks.

concepts.title: Perceptual Group
concepts.one_liner: A perceptual group is a visual representation where primitive elements are organized into meaningful structures like contours or objects.
concepts.content: A perceptual group is a particular kind of visual representation. While a camera sees raw RGB pixel values, the human mind sees structures such as contours, surfaces, objects, and events. (see figure: A few kinds of perceptual organization in the human visual system.) Many of these perceptual structures can be thought of as groups of primitive elements: a contour is a group of points forming a line, and an object is a group of parts forming a cohesive whole. Identifying these meaningful groups is a longstanding area of interest in both human and computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: Grouping raw pixels into higher-level structures is necessary for an agent to understand and interact with the world in terms of objects and events rather than just light intensities.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptual groups organize primitive elements into cohesive wholes like objects.

key_passage.text: Many of these perceptual structures can be thought of as *groups of primitive elements*: a contour is a group of points that form a line, an object is a group of parts that form a cohesive whole, and so on.

question.text: What a camera sees is the raw RGB pixel values of the photo. But what your mind sees is rather different. What are some structures you can name?

motivation.text: Because of this, understanding how humans, and machines, can identify meaningful perceptual groups has been a longstanding area of interest in both human and computer vision.

concepts.title: Why Group?
concepts.one_liner: Grouping provides a powerful substrate for downstream analysis by discovering language-like structures from unsupervised principles.
concepts.content: Grouping is a special case of representation learning, and the reasons to group are the same: groups provide a good substrate for downstream analysis and processing. Perceptual organization—the identification of objects, relationships, shapes, and events—is similar to describing an image in text. While mapping images to text is a common trend, perceptual organization aims to discover these language-like structures from bottom-up grouping rules and unsupervised principles rather than human-language supervision. Furthermore, perceptual groups can go beyond the limits of language, representing coherent structures in our minds that may be hard to name. (see figure: How many objects do you see?)
concepts.motivation_md: By discovering structure without explicit supervision, grouping allows for the emergence of semantic concepts like 'object' from raw data, facilitating reasoning and communication.
concepts.recap_md: - Grouping serves as a foundation for high-level reasoning and downstream tasks.

key_passage.text: Grouping is a special case of representation learning, and the reasons to group are the same as the reasons to do representation learning: groups are a good substrate for downstream analysis and processing.

question.text: What exactly is an object?

motivation.text: groups are a good substrate for downstream analysis and processing. To get an intuition for why this is, consider how you might describe the scene around you.

concepts.title: Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities.
concepts.content: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities. There is no single definition of what constitutes a coherent entity; it varies by task and could correspond to a nameable object, a material region, or a distinct piece of geometry (see Figure 1.1.6). Segmentation can be framed as a clustering problem where each pixel is assigned to one of $k$ clusters. Two common approaches include assigning similar pixels to the same cluster or assigning pixels to the same cluster if no boundary exists between them. (see figure: There are multiple ways you might segment any given image, and each way will highlight different world properties. This cactus branch could be viewed as (a) a single segment (the "branch"), (b) two...)
concepts.motivation_md: Segmentation simplifies image analysis by breaking down a complex scene into its constituent parts, allowing algorithms to process individual objects or regions independently.
concepts.recap_md: - Segmentation partitions an image into task-dependent coherent regions.

key_passage.text: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities.

motivation.text: Segmentation can be framed as a clustering problem: assign each pixel in an image to one of k clusters.

concepts.title: K-Means Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: K-means segmentation partitions an image by clustering pixels based on their color features.
concepts.content: $K$-means is a simple clustering algorithm that can be applied to image segmentation. To use it, each pixel is treated as a datapoint and its color is used as its feature vector. For example, using $ab$ color values allows an image to be represented as a scatter plot of color distributions. (see figure: Different regions of coherent color in the image correspond to clusters in the scatter plot of all the $ab$-values of the image's pixels. In general, segmentation can be reduced to the problem of...) The algorithm finds clusters in this color space and assigns each pixel to a cluster based on its color. (see figure: $K$-means segmentation on the fruits example.) This approach effectively segments regions of constant color, such as a zebra from its background, but it fails to group complex patterns that are not defined by color similarity. (see figure: (top row): $k$-means segmentation succeeds on a seemingly hard image. *Photo source*: Fredo Durand. (bottom row): $k$-means fails on an image that, to our eye, looks no more complex.)
concepts.motivation_md: K-means provides a computationally efficient baseline for segmentation by exploiting the fact that many objects are characterized by relatively uniform color distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - K-means segments images by clustering pixels in a color feature space.

key_passage.text: K-means tries to find clusters in this scatter plot (and, if you prefer a probabilistic interpretation, it can be thought of as fitting a mixture of Gaussians to the datapoints, which aims to approximate the distribution from which these pixels were sampled). We can segment via k-means by simply assigning each pixel to the cluster assignment of its color value.

motivation.text: K-means, which we covered in is one of the simplest and most useful clustering algorithms, so let's try it for segmentation.

concepts.title: Residual Block
concepts.one_liner: A residual block is a neural network component where a skip connection adds the input directly to the output of a block of layers.
concepts.content: In the context of ResNets, skip connections are called residual connections. This kind of skip connection is added to the output of a block of layers $F$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{residual block} \end{aligned}$$ In a residual block, you can think of $F$ as a residual that additively perturbs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ to transform it into an improved $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$. If $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ does not have the same dimensionality as $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$, then a linear mapping can be added to convert the dimensions: $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Residual blocks allow for training much deeper networks by making it easier for layers to learn identity mappings, which helps mitigate the vanishing gradient problem and simplifies optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - Residual connections add the input of a block to its output to create a residual mapping.

key_passage.text: In a residual block like this, you can think of F as a residual that additively perturbs x_in to transform it into an improved x_out.

motivation.text: In the context of ResNets, skip connections are called residual connections. This kind of skip connection is added to the output of a block of layers F.

concepts.title: Ubiquity of CNN Principles
concepts.one_liner: The core principles of CNNs, such as local processing and global information integration, are ubiquitous across many modern architectures like transformers.
concepts.content: While architectures like transformers may appear to replace CNNs in vision problems, the underlying principles of CNNs remain ubiquitous in sensory processing. Transformers also include stages that process each patch identically and independently, but they interleave these stages with other stages that globalize information across patches. Whether these newer architectures are called convolutional is a matter of debate; however, learning the principles allows one to recognize them in all systems regardless of their names.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the fundamental principles of CNNs is more important than the specific architecture, as these concepts of local and global processing reappear in many state-of-the-art models.
concepts.recap_md: - CNN principles like independent patch processing are found in diverse architectures including transformers.

key_passage.text: The reason we cover CNNs is not because the exact architecture presented here will last, but because the underlying principles it embodies are ubiquitous in sensory processing. The two key properties mentioned in are in fact present in transformers and many other architectures beyond CNNs: transformers also include stages that process each patch identically and independently, but they interleave these stages with other stages that globalize information across patches.

motivation.text: if we learn the principles we can recognize them in all the systems we encounter and need not get hung up on names.

concepts.title: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
concepts.one_liner: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are architectures for sequential computation that use feedback connections to create cycles in their computation graphs.
concepts.content: RNNs are a neural net architecture for modeling sequences, performing sequential rather than parallel computation. Unlike feedforward architectures represented by directed acyclical computation graphs, RNNs are neural nets with feedback connections. A feedback connection defines a recurrence in the computational graph, meaning the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of a timestep, where one timestep corresponds to one functional call to each layer, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs. (see figure: Basic RNN with one hidden layer.) (see figure: RNN with multidimensional inputs, hidden states, and outputs.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard feedforward networks are limited to fixed-size inputs and outputs; RNNs solve this by using internal state to process sequences of arbitrary length.
concepts.recap_md: - RNNs use feedback connections to process sequential data through time.

key_passage.text: RNNs are a neural net architecture for modeling sequences---they perform sequential computation (rather than parallel computation). These architectures can be represented by directed acyclical computation graphs. (RNNs), are neural nets with feedback connections.

motivation.text: A feedback connection defines a recurrence in the computational graph. Their computation graphs have cycles. That means that the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline.

concepts.title: Recurrent Layer
concepts.one_liner: A recurrent layer uses a state variable to maintain memory, updating its state based on current input and previous state to produce an output.
concepts.content: A recurrent layer is defined by the following equations: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= f(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]) &\triangleleft \quad\quad \text{update state based on input and previous state}\\ \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]&= g(\mathbf{h}_t) &\triangleleft \quad\quad \text{produce output based on state} \end{aligned}$$ This is a layer that includes a state variable, $\mathbf{h}$. The operation of the layer depends on its state, and the layer updates its state every time it is called; therefore, the state acts as a kind of memory.
concepts.motivation_md: Recurrent layers allow a network to maintain information about previous inputs, enabling the model to learn dependencies across time in sequential data.
concepts.recap_md: - The hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$ acts as a memory that is updated at each timestep.

key_passage.text: This is a layer that includes a state variable, $\mathbf{h}$. The operation of the layer depends on its state. The layer also updates its state every time it is called, therefore the state is a kind of memory.

concepts.title: Simple Recurrent Network (SRN)
concepts.one_liner: A Simple Recurrent Network (SRN) is a recurrent layer where the state update and output are computed using linear layers followed by pointwise nonlinearities.
concepts.content: One common kind of recurrent layer is the Simple Recurrent Network (SRN), defined by Elman. For this layer, $f$ is a linear layer followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, and $g$ is another linear layer. The full computation is defined by the following equations: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= \sigma_1(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]+ \mathbf{b})\\ \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]&= \sigma_2(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c}) \end{aligned}$$ where $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are pointwise nonlinearities. In SRNs, tanh is the common choice for the nonlinearity, but ReLUs and other choices may also be used.
concepts.motivation_md: SRNs provide a basic framework for capturing temporal patterns by combining current inputs with a linear transformation of the previous hidden state.
concepts.recap_md: - SRNs update the hidden state using a linear combination of the previous state and current input.

key_passage.text: For this layer, $f$ is a linear layer followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, and $g$ is another linear layer. The full computation is defined by the following equations: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= \sigma_1(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]+ \mathbf{b})\\ \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]&= \sigma_2(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c}) \end{aligned}$$ where $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are pointwise nonlinearities.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through Time (BPTT)
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through Time (BPTT) is a technique for training RNNs by unrolling them into a directed acyclic graph over a fixed number of timesteps.
concepts.content: Backpropagation is only defined for DAGs, and since RNNs are not DAGs, we apply backpropagation by unrolling the net for $T$ timesteps. This creates a DAG representation of the truncated RNN, known as Backpropagation through Time (BPTT). This approach yields exact gradients when $T$ equals the total number of timesteps; otherwise, it is an approximation that ignores dependencies longer than $T$. (see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN.) For a total cost $J$ summed over losses at each timestep, the gradient is: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial [\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}]} = \sum_{t=0}^T \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t], \mathbf{y}_t)}{\partial [\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}]} \end{aligned}$$ The backpropagation graph has a branching structure where gradients summate wherever the forward pass branches. (see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN with a loss at each timestep.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard backpropagation cannot handle cycles in a computation graph; BPTT resolves this by treating the sequence as a deep feedforward network where each layer represents a timestep.
concepts.recap_md: - BPTT unrolls the RNN into a DAG to allow the application of standard backpropagation.

key_passage.text: To apply backpropagation to RNNs, we unroll the net for T timesteps, which creates a DAG representation of the truncated RNN, and then do backpropagation through that DAG. This is known as BPTT.

question.text: What about the gradient of the total cost with respect to the parameters, ∂J/∂[W, U, V]?

motivation.text: Backpropagation is only defined for DAGs and RNNs are not DAGs. To apply backpropagation to RNNs, we unroll the net for T timesteps, which creates a DAG representation of the truncated RNN, and then do backpropagation through that DAG.

concepts.title: The Problem of Exploding and Vanishing Gradients
concepts.one_liner: RNNs suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients because the gradient computation involves a long product of matrices that can grow or shrink exponentially over time.
concepts.content: (see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN with a loss at each timestep.) Running an RNN for many timesteps creates very large computation graphs where gradient computation involves a series of matrix multiplies of length $\mathcal{O}(T)$. For example: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[0]} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]}{\partial \mathbf{h}_T} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_T}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{T-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_1}{\partial \mathbf{h}_0} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_0}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[0]} \end{aligned}$$ With ReLU nonlinearities, this can result in a product of $T$ matrices $\mathbf{W}$. If values in $\mathbf{W}$ are large, the gradient will explode; if they are small, the gradient will vanish, making the system numerically unstable.
concepts.motivation_md: This problem identifies a fundamental limitation of simple RNNs, explaining why they struggle to learn long-term dependencies and motivating the development of gated architectures like LSTMs.
concepts.recap_md: - Gradients in RNNs involve a chain of matrix multiplications proportional to the sequence length.

key_passage.text: In a worst-case scenario (for numerics), suppose all the relu are active; then we have a product of T matrices W, which means the gradient is W^T (T is an exponent here, not a transpose). If values in W are large, the gradient will explode. If they are small, the gradient will vanish.

motivation.text: The gradient computation involves a series of matrix multiplies that is O(T) in length. One solution to this problem is to use RNN units that have better numerics, an example of which we will give subsequently.

concepts.title: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
concepts.one_liner: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a recurrent module designed to maintain persistent memories and avoid gradient problems using a gated cell state.
concepts.content: LSTMs are special recurrent modules designed to avoid the vanishing and exploding gradients problem. An LSTM acts as a memory controller with a cell state $\mathbf{c}$, a vector it can read from and write to, storing persistent memories. It takes a hidden state $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$ and observation $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]$ to produce an updated $\mathbf{h}_t$. Internally, subcomponents decide what to delete, write, and read. The forget gate is: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_f\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_f) \end{aligned}$$ The write components are: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_i\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_i)\\ \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t &= \texttt{tanh}(\mathbf{W}_C\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_c\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_c) \end{aligned}$$ The cell state update is: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{c}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{t} \end{aligned}$$ Finally, the output is determined by: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_o\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_o)\\ \mathbf{h}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t \odot \texttt{tanh}(\mathbf{c}_t) \end{aligned}$$ This architecture allows information to propagate through an identity connection, similar to skip connections in ResNets.
concepts.motivation_md: LSTMs were created to solve the vanishing gradient problem in standard RNNs, allowing the network to learn dependencies over much longer time intervals by protecting the cell state.
concepts.recap_md: - The cell state $\mathbf{c}_t$ allows for long-term information storage via an additive update rule.

key_passage.text: An LSTM is like a little memory controller. It has a cell state, $\mathbf{c}$, which is a vector it can read from and write to. The cell state can record memories and retrieve them as needed. The cell state plays a similar role as the hidden state, $\mathbf{h}$, from regular RNNs---both record memories---but the cell state is built to store persistent memories that can last a long time (hence the name long short-term memory).

motivation.text: LSTMs are a special kind of recurrent module, that is designed to avoid the vanishing and exploding gradients problem described in recurrent neural networks backpropagation through time.

concepts.title: Diffusion Model
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models are a class of generative models that learn to create data by reversing a signal corruption process.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models are a class of model that uses a strategy of breaking a complex task into many simple pieces. Unlike autoregressive models that remove pixels one by one, diffusion models use a signal corruption process. Starting with an uncorrupted image $\mathbf{x}_0$, they add noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ to result in a noisy version $\mathbf{x}_1$. This process is repeated, adding noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to produce an even noisier signal $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on. Most commonly, the noise used is isotropic Gaussian noise.

(see figure: An autoregressive sequence in reverse is a corruption process that removes one pixel at a time.)

(see figure: Forward diffusion process.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generating complex structured data like images directly from noise is difficult. Diffusion models solve this by breaking the generation task into a sequence of small, manageable denoising steps, using a controlled corruption process to create the necessary training data.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models generate data by iteratively reversing a multi-step corruption process.

key_passage.text: Diffusion models are another class of model that uses this same strategy. Diffusion models instead use the following corruption process: starting with an uncorrupted image, $\mathbf{x}_0$, they add noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ to this image, resulting in a noisy version of the image, $\mathbf{x}_1$. Then they repeat this process, adding noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to produce an even noisier signal $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on.

motivation.text: The idea of diffusion models is that this is not the only corruption process we could have used, and maybe not the best.

concepts.title: Forward Diffusion Process
concepts.one_liner: The forward diffusion process iteratively adds noise to an image until it becomes indistinguishable from pure Gaussian noise.
concepts.content:
The forward diffusion process is a signal corruption method where, starting with an uncorrupted image $\mathbf{x}_0$, noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ is added to produce a noisy version $\mathbf{x}_1$. This is repeated to produce increasingly noisier signals $\mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_T$. Most commonly, isotropic Gaussian noise is used.

(see figure: Forward diffusion process.)

After $T$ steps, the image $\mathbf{x}_T$ looks like pure noise if $T$ is large enough. Specifically, if the following noise process is used, then $\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$ as $T \rightarrow \infty$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_t &= \sqrt{(1-\beta_t)}\mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\mathbf{\epsilon}_t\\ \epsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) \end{aligned}$$
The $\beta_t$ values are typically $\leq 1$ and can be fixed for all $t$ or set according to a schedule that changes the amount of noise added over time.
concepts.motivation_md: This process provides a systematic way to transform structured data into noise, which serves as the foundation for creating training examples for the reverse (generative) process.
concepts.recap_md: - Forward diffusion transforms data into noise by adding Gaussian noise at each step $t$.

key_passage.text: starting with an uncorrupted image, 𝐱₀, they add noise 𝛆₀ to this image, resulting in a noisy version of the image, 𝐱₁. Then they repeat this process, adding noise 𝛆₁ to produce an even noisier signal 𝐱₂, and so on.

motivation.text: The idea of diffusion models is that this is not the only corruption process we could have used, and maybe not the best.

concepts.title: Reverse Diffusion Process
concepts.one_liner: The reverse diffusion process uses a trained neural network to iteratively remove noise and recover a clean image from a noisy signal.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models train a neural net $f_{\theta}$ to reverse the corruption process. This is achieved via supervised learning on sequences of images that get progressively noisier. By flipping these sequences in time, we obtain training examples for the mapping $\mathbf{x}_t \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$, which are then fit by the predictor $f_{\theta}$.

(see figure: Reverse diffusion process. The forward process creates supervision to train the reverse process.)

The model $f_{\theta}$ acts as a denoiser that learns to remove a small amount of noise. When applied repeatedly starting from pure noise, the process coalesces into a noise-less image resembling the training data. Training involves two main steps:
1. Generate training data by corrupting images (forward process).
2. Train a neural net to invert each corruption step (reverse process).
concepts.motivation_md: While turning data into noise is easy, turning noise into data is hard. This process enables generation by learning to perform the difficult task of denoising in small, incremental steps.
concepts.recap_md: - The reverse process uses a neural network to map a noisy image $\mathbf{x}_t$ back to a cleaner version $\mathbf{x}_{t-1}$.

key_passage.text: diffusion models train a neural net, $f_{\theta}$, to reverse this process. It can be trained via supervised learning on examples sequences of different images getting noisier and noisier. If we apply this denoiser over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of our training examples.

motivation.text: If we apply this denoiser over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of our training examples.

concepts.title: Denoiser
concepts.one_liner: A denoiser is a neural network trained to remove a small amount of noise from an image.
concepts.content: A denoiser, denoted as $f_{\theta}$, is a neural network that learns to remove a little bit of noise from an image. If this denoiser is applied over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of the training examples.
concepts.motivation_md: The denoiser is the core functional component of a diffusion model, responsible for the actual generation of structured data from noise.
concepts.recap_md: - A denoiser $f_{\theta}$ performs the mapping from a noisy state to a less noisy state.

key_passage.text: We call $f_{\theta}$ a **denoiser**; it learns to remove a little bit of noise from an image. If we apply this denoiser over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of our training examples.

motivation.text: If we apply this denoiser over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of our training examples.

concepts.title: Training Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Training diffusion models involves teaching a neural network to predict either the less noisy image or the noise itself at specific time steps.
concepts.content:
To improve predictions, the denoising function can observe the time step $t$ as an input: $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$. Knowing $t$ helps the denoiser distinguish between a corrupted scene (likely at large $t$) and a naturally chaotic texture (likely at small $t$).

(see figure: Training a diffusion model consists of first producing training pairs of the form {noisy image, less noisy image}. Then do supervised learning on these pairs.)

The denoiser is trained using a loss $\mathcal{L}$, such as $L_2$ distance. While some models output Gaussian density parameters for probabilistic interpretations, others use various prediction models for $f_{\theta}$. A common reparameterization trick is to train the model to predict the noise $\epsilon_t$ rather than the signal:
$$\begin{aligned} f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) &= \epsilon_t \\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} &= \mathbf{x}_t + \epsilon_t \end{aligned}$$
Ultimately, diffusion models turn images into noise to create training sequences for a process that turns noise back into data.
concepts.motivation_md: Providing the time step $t$ and reparameterizing the model to predict noise are techniques that make the optimization problem easier and more stable for the neural network.
concepts.recap_md: - Training uses pairs of {noisy image, less noisy image} generated by the forward process.

key_passage.text: Training a diffusion model consists of first producing training pairs of the form {noisy image, less noisy image}. Then do supervised learning on these pairs.

motivation.text: One way to look at diffusion models is that we want to learn a mapping from pure noise (e.g., $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$) to data. It is very hard to figure out how to create structured data out of noise, but it is easy to do the reverse, turning data into noise.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
concepts.one_liner: A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) is a system that synthesizes data in a single step using a generator and a discriminator.
concepts.content: A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a model that attempts to directly output samples from a complex distribution in one step. The core idea is that synthetic data looks like real data if a classifier cannot distinguish between them. GANs consist of two neural networks: the generator, $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, which synthesizes data from noise, and a discriminator, $d_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^1$, which tries to classify between synthesized and real data.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs were designed to generate high-quality samples in a single forward pass, avoiding the iterative sampling required by autoregressive or diffusion models.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs use a competitive framework between a generator and a discriminator.

key_passage.text: GANs consist of two neural networks, the generator, g_θ: Z → X, which synthesizes data from noise, and a discriminator, d_φ: X → Δ¹, which tries to classify between synthesized data and real data.

motivation.text: Autoregressive models and diffusion models sample simple distributions step by step to build up a complex distribution. Could we instead create a system that directly, in one step, outputs samples from the complex distribution.

concepts.title: Generator (GAN)
concepts.one_liner: The generator is the component of a GAN that synthesizes data from noise.
concepts.content: In the context of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), the generator is a neural network $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$ that synthesizes data from noise.
concepts.motivation_md: The generator's role is to learn the mapping from a simple latent distribution to the complex distribution of the real data.
concepts.recap_md: - The generator $g_{\theta}$ maps noise $\mathcal{Z}$ to data space $\mathcal{X}$.

key_passage.text: GANs consist of two neural networks, the generator, g_θ: Z → X, which synthesizes

concepts.title: Discriminator (GAN)
concepts.one_liner: The discriminator is the component of a GAN that attempts to distinguish between real and synthetic data.
concepts.content: In a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), the discriminator is a neural network $d_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^1$ that tries to classify between synthesized data and real data.
concepts.motivation_md: The discriminator provides the training signal for the generator by acting as an adaptive loss function that measures how 'realistic' the generated samples are.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator $d_{\phi}$ acts as a classifier to identify synthetic versus real data.

key_passage.text: a discriminator, $d_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^1$, which tries to classify between synthesized data and real data.

concepts.title: Object Detectors Emerge from Scene-Level Supervision
concepts.one_liner: Object detectors can emerge in the hidden layers of a convolutional neural network trained only for scene-level classification tasks.
concepts.content:
The real power of pretext tasks lies in acquiring useful image embeddings $\mathbf{z}$ as a byproduct. This $z$-space may have emergent structure that was not explicit in the raw training data or the pretext task. For example, a convolutional neural net (CNN) trained to perform scene classification (identifying rooms like kitchens or bedrooms) develops hidden neurons that fire selectively for specific object classes, such as staircases or rafts.

(see figure: Visualizing two neural receptive fields in a scene classifier neural net. Images taken from @zhou2014object)

These neurons, located on convolutional layers, act as filter responses where highlighted regions indicate feature map thresholds. This demonstrates that object detectors emerge in hidden layers even when the network is only supervised for scene classification. This suggests that identifying constituent objects is a necessary step for recognizing scenes and provides evidence that CNNs may internally parse scenes in a manner similar to human perception.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how high-level semantic understanding (like identifying specific objects) can arise automatically from broader supervision (like identifying scenes). It justifies why pretext tasks are effective for representation learning: the network must learn to detect objects as a prerequisite for solving the more general task.
concepts.recap_md: - Object-specific neurons emerge in CNNs trained on scene-level labels without explicit object-level supervision.

key_passage.text: object detectors, that is, neurons that selectively fire when they see a particular object class, emerge in the hidden layers of a CNN trained only to perform scene classification.

motivation.text: how else would the net recognize scenes if not first by identifying their constituent objects?

concepts.title: Self-Supervision
concepts.one_liner: Self-supervision is the process of creating prediction targets directly from raw data rather than relying on external labels.
concepts.content:
Predictive learning is effective when prediction targets induce good representations. When labeled targets are unavailable, we can create targets out of the raw data itself. This idea is called self-supervision.

[FIGURE:62baf82aec2fdf08]

In this framework, $V_1$ and $V_2$ are two different functions of the full data tensor $\mathbf{X}$. For example, $V_1$ might represent the left side of an image $\mathbf{X}$ while $V_2$ represents the right side; the pretext task is then to predict the right side from the left. Common examples include predicting a future video frame from past frames or predicting the next pixel in a raster-order sequence.
concepts.motivation_md: Labeled data is expensive and scarce. Self-supervision allows models to learn from the vast amounts of unlabeled data available by turning the data itself into a supervised learning problem.
concepts.recap_md: - Self-supervision generates labels from the data tensor $\mathbf{X}$ using functions $V_1$ and $V_2$.

key_passage.text: Instead we could try to cook up targets out of the raw data itself; for example, we could decide that the top right pixel's color will be the "label" of the image. This idea is called self-supervision. It looks like this: where V_1 and V_2 are two different functions of the full data tensor X. For example, V_1 might be the left side of the image X and V_2 could be the right side, so the pretext task is to predict the right side of an image from its left side.

motivation.text: Predictive learning is great when we have good prediction targets that induce good representations. What if we don't have labeled targets provided to us?

concepts.title: Emergence of Perceptual Groups from Pretext Tasks
concepts.one_liner: Object detectors emerge as a byproduct of various pretext tasks, suggesting that 'objects' are fundamental structures for any visual system understanding the world.
concepts.content:
Object detectors emerge not only from scene classification but also as a byproduct of training a net for tasks like colorization. This is illustrated by the receptive fields found in colorization models.

(see figure: Visualizing two neural receptive fields in the colorization model from @zhang2016colorful. Images generated by Andrew Owens and Richard Zhang.)

In fact, object detectors emerge in CNNs for almost any reasonable pretext task, including scene recognition, colorization, and inpainting missing pixels. This suggests that "objects" are not just a peculiarity of human perception but map onto fundamentally useful structures in the world. Any visual system tasked with understanding the world likely arrives at a similar representation, carving the sensory array into objects and other perceptual groups.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the universality of object-centric representations. It suggests that certain ways of organizing visual information are mathematically or structurally optimal for many different tasks, reinforcing the value of pretext tasks in learning robust features.
concepts.recap_md: - Object detectors emerge from diverse pretext tasks like colorization and inpainting.

key_passage.text: What may be going on is that these things we call "objects" are not just a peculiarity of human perception but rather map onto some fundamentally useful structure out there in the world, and any visual system tasked with understanding our world would arrive at a similar representation, carving up the sensory array into objects and other kinds of perceptual groups.

question.text: What do you think emerges as a byproduct of training a net to perform colorization?

motivation.text: In fact, object detectors emerge in CNNs for just about any reasonable pretext task: scene recognition, colorization, inpainting missing pixels, and more.

concepts.title: Abstract Pretext Tasks
concepts.one_liner: Abstract pretext tasks involve predicting semantic or geometric regularities, such as image rotation or the relative position of patches.
concepts.content: Other varieties of self-supervised learning set up abstract prediction problems rather than predicting missing data. For example, a model may be tasked with predicting if an image has been rotated 90 degrees or determining the relative position of two image patches based on their appearance. These pretext tasks induce effective visual representations because solving them requires the model to learn semantic and geometric regularities of the world, such as the fact that clouds appear at the top of images or tree trunks appear below branches.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple data reconstruction might not capture high-level logic. Abstract tasks force the model to understand global structure and semantic relationships, leading to more sophisticated representations.
concepts.recap_md: - Abstract tasks include predicting image rotation or the relative spatial arrangement of image patches.

key_passage.text: Other varieties of self-supervised learning set up more abstract prediction problems, rather than just aiming to predict missing data. For example, we may try to predict if an image has been rotated 90 degrees, or we may aim to predict the relative position of two image patches given their appearance.

motivation.text: These pretext tasks can induce effective visual representations because solving them requires learning about semantic and geometric regularities in the world, such as that clouds tend to appear near the top of an image or that the trunk of a tree tends to appear below its branches.

concepts.title: Clustering
concepts.one_liner: Clustering is the process of quantizing a signal into discrete categories by mapping dataset members to a set of integer classes.
concepts.content:
Clustering is a method of signal compression that quantizes data into discrete categories. Mathematically, clustering is a function $f: \{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N \rightarrow \{1,\dots,k\}$, which maps members of a dataset to $k$ integer classes (where $k$ can be unbounded). Using one-hot codes to represent these integers, clustering can be visualized as a form of self-discovered labeling.

(see figure: You can think of clustering as being just like image labeling, except that that labels are self-discovered rather than being predefined.)
concepts.motivation_md: Clustering allows us to simplify complex, continuous data into a manageable number of discrete categories, making it easier to organize, summarize, and reason about large datasets without human-provided labels.
concepts.recap_md: - Clustering maps a dataset to $k$ discrete integer classes.

key_passage.text: Mathematically, clustering is a function $f: \{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N \rightarrow \{1,\dots,k\}$, that is, a mapping from the members of a dataset $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ to $k$ integer classes ($k$ can potentially be unbounded).

motivation.text: Another way is to quantize the signal into discrete categories, an operation known also as clustering.

concepts.title: Vector Quantization
concepts.one_liner: Vector quantization is another term for clustering, emphasizing the compression of signals into discrete category labels for abstracted reasoning.
concepts.content:
Vector quantization is a term for clustering common in representation learning literature.

(see figure: You can think of clustering as being just like image labeling, except that that labels are self-discovered rather than being predefined.)

Clustering follows the principle of compression: summarizing a signal with a discrete category label provides a lightweight and abstracted substrate for further reasoning. This is analogous to how natural language uses words like "antelope" or "zebra" as discrete labels to summarize vast, diverse conceptual sets. In this sense, words are clusters—mappings from data to integers—and clustering is the process of creating new words for things. Just as words gain structure through grammar, visual clusters can have additional structure added to them.
concepts.motivation_md: By treating data points as members of discrete groups, we can perform high-level reasoning and communication using 'tokens' or 'words' rather than raw, high-dimensional vectors.
concepts.recap_md: - Vector quantization treats discrete category labels as compressed summaries of complex data.

key_passage.text: Another name for clustering, more common in the representation learning literature, is vector quantization.

motivation.text: Clustering follows from the principle of compression: if we can well summarize a signal with just a discrete category label, then this summary can serve as a lighter weight and more abstracted substrate for further reasoning.

concepts.title: Code Vectors and Cluster Centers
concepts.one_liner: A code vector is a representation of the data within a cluster, most commonly defined as the cluster center or mean value.
concepts.content: Many clustering algorithms compute a representation for the data within each cluster, known as a code vector. The most common code vector is the cluster center, $\mu$, which is the mean value of all datapoints assigned to that cluster. While clusters can be represented by other statistics like variance or arbitrary embeddings, the set of cluster centers $\{\mu_i\}_{i=1}^k$ serves as a summary of the main modes of behavior in the entire dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Code vectors provide a concrete 'prototype' for each cluster, allowing us to represent any member of that cluster with a single, representative vector.
concepts.recap_md: - A code vector (often the cluster center $\mu$) represents the average or typical member of a cluster.

key_passage.text: Many clustering algorithms not only partition the data but also compute a representation of the data within each cluster; this representation is sometimes called a code vector. The most common code vector is the cluster center, μ, that is, the mean value of all datapoints assigned to the cluster.

motivation.text: The set of cluster centers, {μi}i=1k, is a representation of a whole dataset. They summarize the main modes of behavior in the dataset.

concepts.title: K-Means Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: K-means is a clustering algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by minimizing the distance between datapoints and their assigned cluster code vectors.
concepts.content:
K-means is a popular clustering algorithm that partitions data into $k$ clusters. Each datapoint $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ is assigned an integer index $a_i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, and each cluster is associated with a code vector $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M$. The objective is to minimize the distance between each datapoint and its assigned code vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{kmeans}} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_{a_i} - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert^2_2
\end{aligned}
$$

This ensures the code vector is a good approximation of the datapoints in its cluster, providing a compressed representation of the dataset. The algorithm optimizes two sets of parameters: cluster assignments (represented by an encoder function $f$) and code vectors (represented by a decoder function $g$).

[FIGURE:83e2c20af43a1fa5]

While the structure resembles an autoencoder, the bottleneck is discrete. Because the parameters of $f$ are discrete, the gradient $\frac{\partial f}{\partial a_i}$ is undefined, making standard gradient descent unsuitable for optimizing assignments.
concepts.motivation_md: K-means provides a simple, iterative way to find natural groupings in data and reduce the complexity of a dataset to $k$ representative points.
concepts.recap_md: - K-means minimizes the sum of squared distances between points and their cluster centers.

key_passage.text: K-means is a clustering algorithm that partitions the data into k clusters. Each datapoint x^(i) is assigned to a cluster indexed by an integer a_i ∈ {1, …, k}. Each cluster is given a code vector z ∈ ℝ^M. The k-means objective is to minimize the distance between each datapoint and the code vector of the cluster it is assigned to.

motivation.text: This way, the code vector assigned to each datapoint will be a good approximation to the value of that datapoint, and we will have a faithful, but compressed, representation of the dataset.

concepts.title: Generator
concepts.one_liner: A generator is a function that produces a synthetic output, such as an image, by mapping a randomized input vector and an optional label to the output space.
concepts.content:
One way to make a function stochastic is to make it a deterministic function of a stochastic input. We define $g$ as a function, called a **generator**, that takes a randomized vector $\mathbf{z}$ as input along with the label/description $\mathbf{y}$, and produces an image $\mathbf{x}$ as output, that is, $g: \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Then this function can output a different image $\mathbf{x}$ for each different setting of $\mathbf{z}$. The generative process is as follows. First sample $\mathbf{z}$ from a prior $p(Z)$, then deterministically generate an image based on $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{y}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} \sim p(Z)\\
    \mathbf{x} = g(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}
$$

Graphical model for generating $X \| Y, Z$.

[FIGURE:b59cceb106ac5b5a]

This procedure is shown in @fig-generative_models-image_generation_with_z:

(see figure: Making a generator stochastic by conditioning on a random variable.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generators allow us to model complex, high-dimensional probability distributions (like the space of all natural images) by transforming simple, well-understood noise distributions through a deterministic function.
concepts.recap_md: - A generator $g$ transforms a random latent vector $\mathbf{z}$ and a label $\mathbf{y}$ into a synthetic sample $\mathbf{x}$.

key_passage.text: We define $g$ as a function, called a **generator**, that takes a randomized vector $\mathbf{z}$ as input along with the label/description $\mathbf{y}$, and produces an image $\mathbf{x}$ as output, that is, $g: \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Then this function can output a different image $\mathbf{x}$ for each different setting of $\mathbf{z}$.

motivation.text: One way to make a function stochastic is to make it a deterministic function of a stochastic input, and this is how most of the generative models in this chapter will work.

concepts.title: Latent Variables
concepts.one_liner: Latent variables are unobserved inputs to a generator that specify attributes of the output not determined by the explicit label.
concepts.content: Usually we draw $\mathbf{z}$ from a simple distribution such as Gaussian noise, that is, $p(Z) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1})$. The way to think of $\mathbf{z}$ is that it is a vector of **latent variables**, which specify all the attributes of the images other than those determined by the label. These variables are called latent because they are not directly observed in the training data (it just consists of images $\mathbf{x}$ and their labels $\mathbf{y}$). In our example, $\mathbf{y}$ tells $g$ to make a bird but the $\mathbf{z}$-vector is what specifies exactly which bird. Different dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ specify different attributes, such as the size, color, pose, background, and so on; everything necessary to fully determine the output image.
concepts.motivation_md: Latent variables provide a way to capture the underlying factors of variation in data that aren't explicitly labeled, allowing a model to generate diverse outputs for the same class.
concepts.recap_md: - Latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ represent unobserved attributes like pose, color, or background.

key_passage.text: The way to think of z is that it is a vector of latent variables, which specify all the attributes of the images other than those determined by the label. These variables are called latent because they are not directly observed in the training data (it just consists of images x and their labels y).

motivation.text: In our example, y tells g to make a bird but the z-vector is what specifies exactly which bird. Different dimensions of z specify different attributes, such as the size, color, pose, background, and so on; everything necessary to fully determine the output image.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: A conditional generative model is a model used to represent any conditional distribution $p(X \mid Y)$.
concepts.content: A **conditional generative model** is a model of any conditional distribution $p(X \mid Y)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional generative models allow for controlled synthesis, where the user can specify certain desired characteristics (like a class label) while the model generates the remaining details.
concepts.recap_md: - These models represent the conditional distribution $p(X \mid Y)$ rather than just the marginal $p(X)$.

key_passage.text: conditional generative model for a model of any conditional distribution p(X | Y)

concepts.title: Sampling from a Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of querying a learned generator with new, randomized latent vectors to produce novel outputs.
concepts.content:
How can we learn to synthesize images that look realistic? The machine learning way to do this is to start with a training set of *examples* of real images, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Recall that in supervised learning, an *example* was defined as an {`input`, `output`} pair; here things are actually no different, only the `input` happens to be the null set. We feed these examples to a learner, which spits out a generator function. Later, we may query the generator with new, randomized $\mathbf{z}$-vectors to produce novel outputs, a process called **sampling** from the model. This two-stage procedure is shown in @fig-generative_models-gen_model_training_vs_sampling:

(see figure: Learning and using a generator.)
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling allows us to use a trained model to create new, never-before-seen data points that share the characteristics of the training set.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling involves passing a random vector $\mathbf{z}$ through the generator to create a new output.

key_passage.text: Later, we may query the generator with new, randomized z-vectors to produce novel outputs, a process called sampling from the model.

motivation.text: How can we learn to synthesize images that look realistic? The machine learning way to do this is to start with a training set of examples of real images, and feed these examples to a learner, which spits out a generator function.

concepts.title: Objective of Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The goal of generative modeling is to create a generator that produces synthetic data identically distributed to the true training data.
concepts.content:
The objective of the learner is to create a generator that produces *synthetic* data, $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, that looks like the *real* data, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. There are a lot of ways of define "looks like" and they each result in a different kind of generative model. Two examples are:

1. Synthetic data looks like real data if matches the real data in terms of certain marginal statistics, for example, it has the same mean color as real photos, or the same color variance, or the same edge statistics.

2. Synthetic data looks like real data if it has high probability under a density model fit to the real data.

The first approach works well when we only want to match certain properties of the training data. The second approach is better when we want to produce synthetic data that matches *all* statistics of the training examples. In practice, we may not be able to match all statistics, due to limits of the model's capacity. To be precise, the goal of deep generative models is to produce synthetic data that is *identically distributed* as the training data, that is, we want $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ where $p_{\texttt{data}}$ is the true process that produced the training data.
concepts.motivation_md: By aiming to match the true data distribution, generative models can create realistic synthetic examples that can be used for data augmentation, simulation, or creative content generation.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to produce synthetic data $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ such that $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$.

key_passage.text: The objective of the learner is to create a generator that produces synthetic data, that looks like the real data. To be precise, the goal of the deep generative models we consider in this chapter is to produce synthetic data that is identically distributed as the training data, that is, we want $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ where $p_{\texttt{data}}$ is the true process that produced the training data.

motivation.text: The second approach, which is the main focus of this chapter, is better when we want to produce synthetic data that matches all statistics of the training examples.

concepts.title: Generalization vs. Memorization in Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: A good generative model must generalize by producing novel samples that look real without simply memorizing the training data.
concepts.content: What if our model just memorizes all the training examples and generates random draws from this memory? Indeed, memorized training samples perfectly satisfy the goal of making synthetic data that looks real. A second, sometimes overlooked, property of a good generative model is that it be a simple, or smooth, function, so that it generalizes to producing synthetic samples that look like the training data but are not identical to it. A generator that only regurgitates the training data is overfit in the same way a classifier that memorizes the training data is overfit. In both cases, the true goal is to fit the training data and to do so with a function that generalizes.
concepts.motivation_md: Generalization ensures that the model has learned the underlying structure of the data rather than just recording specific instances, allowing it to create truly novel content.
concepts.recap_md: - A generator should produce novel samples, not just regurgitate training data.

key_passage.text: A second, sometimes overlooked, property of a good generative model is that it be a simple, or smooth, function, so that it generalizes to producing synthetic samples that look like the training data but are not identical to it.

motivation.text: A generator that only regurgitates the training data is overfit in the same way a classifier that memorizes the training data is overfit. In both cases, the true goal is to fit the training data and to do so with a function that generalizes.

concepts.title: Direct Approach (Implicit Model)
concepts.one_liner: The direct approach to generative modeling involves learning a function that maps latent vectors directly to the data space.
concepts.content: The direct approach to forming data generators involves learning the function $G: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach is efficient for sampling because it provides a straightforward mapping from a simple noise distribution to the complex data distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Learns a direct mapping $G$ from latent space $\mathcal{Z}$ to data space $\mathcal{X}$.

key_passage.text: Direct approach: learn the function $G: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$.

concepts.title: Indirect Approach
concepts.one_liner: The indirect approach involves learning a scoring function and generating samples by finding data points that achieve high scores.
concepts.content: The indirect approach to forming data generators involves learning a function $E: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and generating samples by finding values for $\mathbf{x}$ that score highly under this function.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach focuses on modeling the energy or density of the data, which can be useful for tasks like anomaly detection or denoising.
concepts.recap_md: - Learns a scoring function $E$ over the data space $\mathcal{X}$.

key_passage.text: learn a function $E: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and generate samples by finding values for $\mathbf{x}$ that score highly under this function.

concepts.title: Block Coordinate Descent for K-Means
concepts.one_liner: $K$-means uses block coordinate descent to alternate between minimizing the objective with respect to cluster assignments and cluster means.
concepts.content:
$K$-means uses an optimization algorithm called **block coordinate descent**. This algorithm splits up the optimization parameters into multiple subsets (blocks) and alternates between fully minimizing the objective with respect to each block of parameters. In $k$-means, there are two parameter blocks: the assignments of datapoints to clusters, denoted as $\{a_i\}_{i=1}^N$, and the code vectors (cluster means), denoted as $\{\mathbf{z}_j\}_{j=1}^k$.

The update rules for these blocks are as follows:

$$\begin{aligned} a_i &\leftarrow \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,k\}} \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_j - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2 \end{aligned}$$
This step assigns each datapoint to its nearest cluster mean.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{z}_j &\leftarrow \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}(a_i = j)\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \end{aligned}$$
This step sets each code vector to be the mean of all datapoints currently assigned to that cluster.

These steps are repeated until a fixed point is reached, which occurs when all datapoints are closest to their assigned cluster's code vector. The first update is a brute force enumeration of all $k$ possible assignments. The second update finds the optimal codes given the current assignments; because the point that minimizes the sum of squared distances from a dataset is the mean of that dataset, the optimal code vectors are the cluster means.
concepts.motivation_md: The $k$-means objective function is difficult to minimize for all parameters simultaneously. Block coordinate descent simplifies the problem by breaking it into two sub-problems—assignment and averaging—each of which has a simple, closed-form optimal solution.
concepts.recap_md: - The algorithm alternates between assigning each point to the nearest cluster center and recomputing centers as the mean of assigned points.

key_passage.text: This algorithm splits up the optimization parameters into multiple subsets (blocks). Then it alternates between *fully* minimizing the objective with respect to each block of parameters. In $k$-means there are two parameter blocks: $\{a_i\}_{i=1}^N$ and $\{\mathbf{z}_j\}_{j=1}^k$.

motivation.text: $K$-means uses an optimization algorithm called **block coordinate descent**. This algorithm splits up the optimization parameters into multiple subsets (blocks).

concepts.title: K-Means from Multiple Perspectives
concepts.one_liner: $K$-means can be viewed as a representation learning algorithm, a simple generative model, or a vanilla form of a Gaussian mixture model.
concepts.content: $K$-means can be viewed from multiple complementary perspectives. While presented here as a representation learning algorithm—specifically an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck—it can also be viewed as a way of interpreting data or as a simple generative model. $K$-means is a vanilla form of a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). These relationships form a rich tapestry: autoencoders and variational autoencoders (VAEs) are continuous versions of $k$-means and GMMs, respectively. While GMMs and VAEs are formal probabilistic models, $k$-means and standard autoencoders do not typically come with probabilistic semantics. Identifying the "delta" or difference between a new model and models you already know is a useful exercise for understanding the connections between different methods in machine learning.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding $k$-means from multiple perspectives helps connect simple clustering to more complex topics like generative modeling, Gaussian mixture models, and variational autoencoders.
concepts.recap_md: - $K$-means is functionally equivalent to an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck.

key_passage.text: These views are all complementary and all simultaneously true. Here we showed that k-means is like an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck. K-means can also be viewed as a vanilla form of a GMM.

question.text: Which one is correct?

motivation.text: It can be confusing at first to see multiple different perspectives on the same method: Which one is correct? But rarely is there a single correct perspective. It is useful to identify the delta between each new model you encounter and all the models you already know.

concepts.title: Perceptual Grouping
concepts.one_liner: Perceptual grouping is the process by which humans organize visual elements into structures like contours, surfaces, and objects.
concepts.content: In vision, the problem of clustering is related to the idea of **perceptual grouping**. Humans see the world as organized into different levels of perceptual structure, such as contours and surfaces, or objects and events. These structures are groupings, or clusters, of related visual elements. For example, a contour is a group of points that form a line, and an object is a group of parts that form a cohesive, nameable whole. Algorithms like $k$-means, when applied in a suitable feature space, can discover these structures.
concepts.motivation_md: Clustering algorithms provide a computational way to mimic the human ability to organize raw sensory data into meaningful, high-level structures.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptual grouping organizes visual elements into higher-level structures like objects and contours.

key_passage.text: We humans see the world as organized into different levels of perceptual structure: contours and surfaces, objects and events. These structures are groupings, or clusters, of related visual elements: a contour is a group of points that form a line, an object is a group of parts that form a cohesive, nameable whole, and so on.

concepts.title: Contrastive Learning
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive learning supervises representations to be invariant to certain transformations by ensuring similar datapoints have similar embeddings.
