concepts.one_liner: Structured prediction methods model the joint dependencies between output variables rather than treating them as independent.
concepts.content: Methods that model joint structure in the output space are called structured prediction methods. They are characterized by the fact that they don't factorize the output into independent potentials conditioned on the input.
concepts.motivation_md: In tasks like language translation or image generation, the output is a complex object where the parts must fit together. Structured prediction ensures the model respects these internal relationships.
concepts.recap_md: - Structured prediction avoids the assumption of conditional independence among output variables.

key_passage.text: Methods that model joint structure in the output space are called structured prediction methods---they don't factorize the output into independent potentials conditioned on the input.

concepts.title: Backtranslation
concepts.one_liner: Backtranslation is the application of cycle-consistency within the field of natural language processing.
concepts.content: In natural language processing, the idea of cycle-consistency is known as **backtranslation**.
concepts.motivation_md: Backtranslation provides a way to enforce consistency in translation tasks by ensuring that a sentence translated into a target language and then back to the source language remains unchanged.
concepts.recap_md: - Backtranslation is the NLP equivalent of cycle-consistency.

key_passage.text: In natural language processing, the idea of cycle-consistency is known as backtranslation.

concepts.title: CycleGAN
concepts.one_liner: CycleGAN is a generative model that translates between two domains using a cycle-consistent objective to ensure mappings are reversible and realistic.
concepts.content:
Adding the cycle-consistency loss to the conditional generative model learning problem yields the complete CycleGAN objective: 

$$ 
\begin{aligned} 
    \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{	heta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\ 
    \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big] 
\end{aligned} 
$$ 

This model translates from domain $X$ to domain $Y$ and back, such that the outputs in domain $Y$ look realistic according to a domain $Y$ discriminator, and vice versa for domain $X$. The mappings are cycle-consistent: one complete cycle from $X$ to $Y$ and back should arrive where it started (and vice versa). A diagram for this whole process is given in @fig-conditional_generative_models-cyclegan_schematic:

(see figure: CycleGAN schematic. Figure derived from @CycleGAN2017)
concepts.motivation_md: CycleGAN allows for image-to-image translation between two domains without requiring paired training examples, relying instead on the assumption that the mapping should be reversible.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses two pairs of generators and discriminators to translate between domains $X$ and $Y$.

key_passage.text: This model translates from domain X to domain Y and back, such that the outputs in domain Y look realistic according to a domain Y discriminator, and vice versa for domain X, and the mappings are cycle-consistent: one complete cycle from X to Y and back should arrive where it started (and, again, vice versa).

concepts.title: Limitations of Cycle-Consistency
concepts.one_liner: Cycle-consistency encourages one-to-one mappings but can be confounded by permutations that satisfy the objective while producing incorrect results.
concepts.content: The cycle-consistency losses encourage that the translation is a one-to-one function, and thereby reduce the number of valid solutions. This is a good idea when the true solution is indeed one-to-one, as is often the case in translation problems. However, other symmetries still exist and may confound methods like CycleGAN: if we permute the correct $X$-to-$Y$ mapping and apply the inverse permutation to the $Y$-to-$X$ mapping, then CycleGAN will still be satisfied but the mapping will now be incorrect.
concepts.motivation_md: While cycle-consistency constrains the search space for mappings, it is important to understand its failure modes, such as when the model learns a consistent but semantically incorrect permutation.
concepts.recap_md: - Cycle-consistency assumes the underlying translation is a one-to-one function.

key_passage.text: if we permute the correct X-to-Y mapping and apply the inverse permutation to the Y-to-X mapping, then CycleGAN will still be satisfied but the mapping will now be incorrect.

motivation.text: The cycle-consistency losses encourage that the translation is a one-to-one function, and thereby reduce the number of valid solutions. This is a good idea when the true solution is indeed one-to-one, as is often the case in translation problems.

concepts.title: Trend toward General-Purpose Modeling
concepts.one_liner: A current trend in artificial intelligence is replacing bespoke, task-specific systems with general-purpose conditional generative models.
concepts.content: Many problems in vision can be phrased as structured prediction, and conditional generative models are a great approach to these problems. They provide a unified and simple solution to a diverse array of problems. A current trend in computer vision (and all of artificial intelligence) is to replace bespoke systems for specific kinds of structured prediction—object detectors, image captioning systems, and so on—with general-purpose conditional generative models. This trend toward general-purpose modeling tools is why modern study focuses less on special-purpose systems for specific vision problems.
concepts.motivation_md: General-purpose models simplify the AI landscape by providing a single framework capable of solving many different tasks that were previously handled by specialized architectures.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditional generative models offer a unified solution for diverse structured prediction problems.

key_passage.text: A current trend in computer vision (and all of artificial intelligence) is to replace bespoke systems for specific kinds of structured prediction---object detectors, image captioning systems, and so on---with general-purpose conditional generative models.

motivation.text: Many problems in vision can be phrased as structured prediction, and conditional generative models are a great approach to these problems. They provide a unified and simple solution to a diverse array of problems.

concepts.title: Data Bias and Shift
concepts.one_liner: Failures in machine learning often stem from the discrepancy between the theoretical assumption of identically distributed data and the reality of data shift.
concepts.content: The goal of learning is to acquire rules from past data that work well on future data. In the theory of machine learning, it is almost always assumed that the future is *identically distributed* as the past. In reality, it is almost always the case that this is not true. Many of the failures of machine learning in industry and in society are due to this discrepancy between theory and practice. It is critical to understand what happens when a learned system is deployed on data that is unlike what it was trained on.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding data bias and shift is essential for building robust models that can handle real-world scenarios where future data inevitably differs from training data.
concepts.recap_md: - Machine learning theory often assumes training and test data are identically distributed.

key_passage.text: In the theory of machine learning, it is almost always assumed that the future is identically distributed as the past. In reality, it is almost always the case that this is not true.

question.text: What happens when a learned system is deployed on data that is unlike what it was trained on?

motivation.text: Many of the failures of machine learning in industry and in society are due to this discrepancy between theory and practice.

concepts.title: Dataset Bias
concepts.one_liner: Dataset bias occurs because every dataset offers a different and biased sample of the visual world based on its collection strategy.
concepts.content: Bias is present in all datasets. Even datasets that try to cover the same aspect of the world collect data with different styles and strategies that reflect on the statistics of the dataset. In the case of image datasets for computer vision, the goal is to represent the visual world with all its complexity and diversity. Despite that there is a single visual world, different computer vision datasets offer a different, and biased, sample of that world.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing dataset bias is the first step in understanding why models trained on one dataset may fail to generalize to others, even if they target the same domain.
concepts.recap_md: - All datasets contain inherent biases based on their collection strategies.

key_passage.text: bias is present in all datasets. Even datasets that try to cover the same aspect of the world, they collect data with different styles and strategies that will reflect on the statistics of the dataset.

motivation.text: In the case of image datasets for computer vision, the goal is to represent the visual world with all its complexity and diversity. Despite that there is a single visual world, different computer vision datasets offer a different, and biased, sample of that world.

concepts.title: Annotation Bias
concepts.one_liner: Annotation bias arises from the choices annotators make regarding which images to label and which language to use.
concepts.content: When annotating images, image annotators will choose which images to annotate and which labels to use. This will also correlate with viewpoint preferences and other photographer biases, as those images might be easier to annotate and segment, risking a compounding effect with photographer bias. Annotations require making language choices that are an important source of bias, especially social bias.
concepts.motivation_md: Annotation bias highlights how human subjectivity in the labeling process introduces systematic errors and social biases into machine learning models.
concepts.recap_md: - Annotator choices regarding images and labels introduce systematic bias.

key_passage.text: When annotating images, image annotators will choose which images to annotate and which labels to use. This will also correlate with viewpoint preferences and other photographer biases as those images might be easier to annotate and segment, and this has the risk of compounding with the photographer bias.

motivation.text: Annotations will require making language choices and that are an important source of bias, especially social bias.

concepts.title: Social Bias
concepts.one_liner: Social bias refers to the different and often stereotypical ways groups of people are reflected in data and labels.
concepts.content: Social bias refers to biases associated with how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. This type of bias can affect both the images and the associated labels. Social biases can originate from the data collection protocol or from existing social biases; for example, images may be captured in certain world regions or contain stereotypes. Labels can also reflect social assumptions, such as a dataset that associates doctors with males and nurses with females. These biases can have a negative social impact once models are deployed, making it important to incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Addressing social bias is crucial for ensuring that AI systems are fair, ethical, and do not reinforce harmful stereotypes when deployed in society.
concepts.recap_md: - Social bias stems from data collection protocols and existing societal stereotypes.

key_passage.text: Social bias refers to biases associated to how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. Social biases can be originated by the data collection protocol or by existing social biases.

motivation.text: These types of biases, besides impacting the overall model performance, can have a negative social impact once they are deployed. It is important to be aware of those biases, and incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects.

concepts.title: GAN Minimax Game and Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks are trained through a minimax game where a generator and discriminator compete to respectively synthesize and detect realistic data.
concepts.content:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) consist of a generator $g_{\theta}$ and a discriminator $d_{\phi}$ that play an adversarial game. The generator $g_{\theta}$ tries to become better at generating synthetic images, while $d_{\phi}$ tries to become better at detecting errors $g_{\theta}$ is making. The learning problem is written as a minimax game:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\theta\max_\phi \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Schematically, the generator synthesizes images that are fed as input to the discriminator. The discriminator tries to assign a high score to generated images (classifying them as synthetic) and a low score to real images from a training set.

(see figure: Architecture of a GAN being trained to generate images of flamingos. The synthetic image in this example is generated by BigGAN @brock2018large)

Although called an adversarial game, the discriminator helps the generator improve by pointing out its current errors. This is analogous to a student (generator) and a teacher (discriminator) in a painting class; the teacher provides feedback on specific errors, such as shading or variety, until the student produces paintings as good as the teacher's. 

From the discriminator's perspective, given a generator $g_{\theta}$, $d_{\phi}$ tries to maximize its ability to discriminate between real and synthetic images. This objective is logistic regression between real data $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and synthetic data $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{(i)})$. The optimal discriminator $d_{\phi}^*$ is defined as:

$$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

From the generator's perspective, given $d_{\phi}^*$, $g_{\theta}$ tries to solve:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}^*(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Because $d_{\phi}^*$ depends on the current $g_{\theta}$, updating the generator requires re-solving for the optimal discriminator. In practice, optimization alternates between taking one gradient step for the generator and $K$ gradient steps for the discriminator (where $K=1$ is often sufficient).
concepts.motivation_md: GANs solve the problem of learning complex, high-dimensional data distributions (like natural images) without requiring a hand-defined loss function. By using a neural network as a learned discriminator, the model can discover and correct subtle statistical discrepancies between real and synthetic data that simple mathematical metrics might miss.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs use a minimax objective where the generator minimizes the probability that the discriminator correctly identifies synthetic data.

key_passage.text:
The learning problem can be written as a minimax game: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\theta\max_\phi \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))]
\end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: The generator tries to become better and better at generating synthetic images while the discriminator tries to become better and better at detecting any errors the generator is making.

concepts.title: GANs as Statistical Image Models
concepts.one_liner: GANs are learned statistical image models that amortize the optimization process by learning a mapping from latent noise to data samples.
concepts.content: GANs are related to classical image and texture models, such as the Heeger-Bergen model, which synthesize images by matching statistics of a source texture. In such models, optimization adjusts image pixels until specific statistics (like subband histograms) match the training data. In GAN terminology, the loss checking for this match acts as a discriminator. However, unlike GANs, these discriminators are hand-defined rather than learned. Furthermore, GANs amortize the optimization via learning: they learn a mapping $g_{\theta}$ from latent noise to samples, rather than performing a fresh optimization process from scratch for every new sample.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional statistical image models require manually identifying which features (like histograms) are important. GANs improve on this by learning the relevant statistics automatically and providing a fast way to generate new samples through a learned generator function.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs replace hand-defined statistical matches with a learned discriminator network.

key_passage.text: GANs are related to the image and texture models we saw in statistical image models. For example, in the Heeger-Bergen model, we synthesize images with the same statistics as a source texture. This can be phrased as an optimization problem in which we optimize image pixels until certain statistics of the images match those same statistics measured on a source (training) image.

motivation.text: In the Heeger-Bergen model the objective is to match subband histograms. In the language of GANs, the loss that checks for such a match is a kind of discriminator; it outputs a score related to the difference between a generated image's statistics and the real image's statistics.

concepts.title: The Relationship between Generative Modeling and Representation Learning
concepts.one_liner: Generative modeling and representation learning are essentially inverse problems, mapping between raw data and simple underlying embeddings.
concepts.content:
Generative modeling and representation learning are closely related fields that learn mappings both to and from data. Generative models map a simple base distribution (noise) to data, while representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations called embeddings. These two problems are essentially inverses of each other, and solving one can often inform the solution to the other.

In deep learning, neural networks can be viewed from two perspectives. Moving from raw data to abstracted representations layer-by-layer highlights representation learning. Conversely, moving backward from abstracted representations to concrete data highlights generative modeling. Both directions are valid and form a full picture of the relationship between data and embeddings.

(see figure: The relationship between representation learning and generative modeling. Here we label one side as "Data" and the other as "Embedding"; but what's the precise difference between these two things?...)

While backpropagation also moves backward through a network, it computes the gradient $\nabla f$, whereas generative modeling focuses on the inverse function $f^{-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the symmetry between generation and representation allows researchers to build models that not only create realistic data but also understand the underlying structure of that data, leading to more robust and interpretable AI.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models map noise to data; representation learning maps data to embeddings.

key_passage.text: The intuition is that generative models map a simple base distribution (i.e., noise) to data, whereas representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations (embeddings). These two problems are, essentially, inverses of each other.

motivation.text: Many algorithms explicitly treat them as inverse problems, where solving the problem in one direction can inform the solution in the other direction.

concepts.title: Embeddings
concepts.one_liner: Embeddings are simple underlying representations of data produced by representation learning.
concepts.content: Representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations known as embeddings. This process is essentially the inverse of generative modeling, which maps a simple base distribution (noise) to data. Many algorithms treat these as inverse problems where solving one direction informs the other.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw data is often high-dimensional and noisy. Embeddings provide a compressed, meaningful representation that makes it easier for machines to process, categorize, and manipulate information.
concepts.recap_md: - Embeddings are the output of representation learning that capture the essence of data in a simpler form.

key_passage.text: representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations (**embeddings**)

motivation.text: These two problems are, essentially, inverses of each other. Many algorithms explicitly treat them as inverse problems, where solving the problem in one direction can inform the solution in the other direction.

concepts.title: Latent Variables as Representations
concepts.one_liner: Latent variables in generative models serve as complete representations of the data, capturing all unobserved factors that affect the output.
concepts.content: In generative models, latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ specify all unobserved factors that affect the model's output. For example, in a model predicting the color of a black and white photo ($g: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$), $\mathbf{x}$ is the input image and $\mathbf{z}$ represents information that cannot be inferred from the input alone, such as the specific color of a shirt. In unconditional generative models, latent variables act as a complete representation of the data, meaning all information in the generated data is controlled by and represented within these variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Latent variables allow models to handle ambiguity and variety. By treating these variables as representations, we can manipulate specific features of generated data by simply changing the underlying latent code.
concepts.recap_md: - Latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ represent unobserved factors or features of the data.

key_passage.text: latent variables are representations of the data. In the case of an unconditional generative model, the latent variables are a complete representation of the data: all information in the data is represented in the latent variables.

motivation.text: In the context of generative models, the role of the latent variable was to specify all unobserved factors that might affect the output of a model. For example, if the model predicts the color of a black and white photo, it is a mapping g: x, z → y, with x being the black and white input, y being the color output and z being any other information that needs to be known in order to make the mapping completely deterministic; for example, the color of a t-shirt which cannot be inferred solely from the black and white input.

concepts.title: Marginal Likelihood
concepts.one_liner: The marginal likelihood is the probability of the data under a model, calculated by integrating over all unobserved latent variables.
concepts.content:
The data log likelihood function $L(\{\mathbf{x}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta)$ measures the log likelihood of the data under a model $p_{\theta}$:

$$\begin{aligned} L(\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$

To compute $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$, we can express it as the marginal likelihood, which marginalizes over all unobserved latent variables $\mathbf{z}$:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$

This approach reduces the modeling problem to learning the conditional distribution $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z})$, assuming $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ is known. For instance, the conditional distribution can be modeled as a unit Gaussian centered on the output of a function $g(\mathbf{z})$, such that $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu = g(\mathbf{z}), \sigma = \mathbf{1})$.
concepts.motivation_md: In models with hidden factors, we cannot observe the latent variables directly. Marginal likelihood allows us to evaluate how well our model fits the observed data by accounting for all possible states of those hidden factors.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginal likelihood integrates the conditional probability $p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})$ over the distribution of latent variables $p(\mathbf{z})$.

key_passage.text: One way to express this function is as the marginal likelihood of $\mathbf{x}$, marginalizing over all unobserved latent variables $\mathbf{z}$: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: The advantage of expressing $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ in this way is that, assuming we know $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, the rest of the modeling problem is reduced to learning the conditional distribution $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z})$, which itself can be straightforwardly modeled using $g$.

concepts.title: Variational Autoencoder (VAE)
concepts.one_liner: A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) turns a standard autoencoder into a generative model by regularizing the latent space and adding noise to the encoder.
concepts.content:
A variational autoencoder (VAE) is a model that transforms an autoencoder into a generative model capable of synthesizing data. In a standard autoencoder, the decoder maps a representation $\mathbf{z}$ back to the data $\mathbf{x}$, functioning much like a generator.

(see figure: The relationship between an autoencoder and a generative model.)

However, a standard autoencoder does not provide a distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ for sampling new images. Sampling a random $\mathbf{z}$ (e.g., from a unit Gaussian) might result in out-of-distribution inputs that the decoder cannot map to natural-looking images. The latent space of a vanilla autoencoder can be as complex as the data space itself.

(see figure: The latent space of an autoencoder can be just as complex as the data space.)

VAEs solve this by regularizing the latent distribution to fit a base distribution (like a Gaussian) and adding noise to the encoder's output. This ensures the model maximizes data likelihood under a formal probabilistic framework and allows for effective sampling.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard autoencoders are good for compression but bad for generation because their latent spaces are often disjointed. VAEs enforce a continuous, smooth latent space, making it possible to sample new, realistic data points.
concepts.recap_md: - VAEs regularize the latent space into a standard distribution to enable data synthesis.

key_passage.text: Variational autoencoders VAEs are a way to turn an autoencoder into a proper generative model, which can be sampled from and which maximizes data likelihood under a formal probabilistic model. The trick is very simple: just take a vanilla autoencoder and (1) regularize the latent distribution to squish it into a Gaussian (or some other base distribution), (2) add noise to the output of the encoder.

question.text: You might ask, what if, after training an autoencoder, you just sample a random z, say from a unit Gaussian, and feed it through the decoder?

motivation.text: One goal of generative modeling is to be able to make up random images from scratch. So we need a distribution from which we can sample different z from scratch, that is, we need p_z. An autoencoder doesn't directly give us this.

concepts.title: Mixture Model
concepts.one_liner: Mixture models are probability models defined as a weighted sum of component distributions.
concepts.content: Mixture models are probability models of the form $P(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i w_ip_i(\mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple distributions like Gaussians often cannot capture the complexity of real-world data. Mixture models allow for more flexible modeling by combining multiple simple distributions to represent data with multiple clusters or modes.
concepts.recap_md: - A mixture model represents a population as a combination of several distinct sub-distributions.

key_passage.text: Mixture models are probability models of the form $P(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i w_ip_i(\mathbf{x})$.

concepts.title: Amortized Inference

position.section_title: Conditional Generative Models Solve Multimodal Structured Prediction

concepts.one_liner: Amortized inference is a technique where a model learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs through a neural network to approximate the results of iterative inference algorithms.
concepts.content: Amortized inference refers to a "thinking fast" approach to prediction where inference is performed through a single forward pass of a neural network. This contrasts with models like conditional random fields (CRFs) that "think slow" by running iterative algorithms such as belief propagation for each query. In amortized inference, the computational cost of inference is amortized over a training phase. This phase learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs that approximates the solution that would have been obtained through exact inference on that input.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional probabilistic models often require expensive iterative algorithms to make predictions at test time. Amortized inference solves this by shifting the computational burden to the training phase, allowing for nearly instantaneous predictions during deployment by using a neural network to approximate the inference process.
concepts.recap_md: - It replaces iterative inference algorithms with a single forward pass of a neural network.

key_passage.text: Sometimes the thinking fast approach is referred to as amortized inference, where the idea is that the cost of inference is amortized over a training phase. This training phase learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs that approximates the solution we would have gotten if we did exact inference on that input.

motivation.text: The conditional generative models in this section think fast: they do inference through a single forward pass of a neural net. This contrasts with CRFs which make predictions via thinking slow: given a query observation, you run belief propagation or another iterative inference algorithm to arrive at a prediction.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks extend GANs by providing conditioning information to both the generator and the discriminator to model specific conditional distributions.
concepts.content: A generative adversarial network (GAN) can be made conditional by adding $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to both the generator and the discriminator: $$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) \big] \end{aligned}$$ This modification changes the discriminator's task from identifying real versus synthetic outputs to identifying real versus synthetic input-output pairs. An input-output pair is considered synthetic if the output looks synthetic or if the output does not match the input. If both issues are avoided, the produced samples are $iid$ with respect to the true conditional distribution of the data $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard GANs generate samples from a general distribution but offer no control over the specific characteristics of the output. Conditional GANs allow users to direct the generation process by providing specific input data, enabling tasks like generating an image from a specific class or label.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator evaluates the validity of the input-output pair $(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$ rather than just the output.

key_passage.text: We can make a generative adversarial network (GAN) conditional simply by adding $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to both the generator and the discriminator. What this does is change the job of the discriminator from asking "is the output real or synthetic?" to asking "is the input-output *pair* real or synthetic?"

motivation.text: An input-output pair can be considered synthetic for two possible reasons: The output looks synthetic or the output does not match the input. If both reasons are avoided, then it can be shown that the produced samples are iid with respect to the true conditional distribution of the data $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x})$.

concepts.title: Conditional Variational Autoencoders

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional Variational Autoencoders model conditional distributions by marginalizing over latent variables that are independent of the conditioning inputs.
concepts.content:
A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) defines a conditional distribution as the marginal over a latent variable: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$ In cVAEs, we restrict attention to latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ that are independent of the inputs $\mathbf{x}$, resulting in the likelihood model: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$ This corresponds to the following graphical model:
[FIGURE:184e45370a8359cb]

The latent variable $\mathbf{z}$ should encode information about $\mathbf{y}$ that is independent of what $\mathbf{x}$ already provides. For example, if predicting the next frame $\mathbf{y}$ of a bouncing ball from a frame $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}$ provides color and position, while $\mathbf{z}$ might capture the unknown velocity. Marginalizing over $\mathbf{z}$ allows the model to place maximum likelihood on the data. (see figure: A scenario where a yellow ball is moving across a plane. The observation, $\mathbf{x}$, is a static frame. From that observation, we know what will be the color and rough position of the ball in the...)

Like regular VAEs, cVAEs use an encoder to predict the importance sampling distribution $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$. During training, both the encoder and decoder take the conditioning information $\mathbf{x}$ as input. (see figure: cVAE architecture. The dotted lines indicate that the *target encoder* is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard VAEs learn to represent data in a latent space but cannot easily generate data conditioned on specific external information. cVAEs allow for structured generation where the model uses the conditioning input to handle known features and the latent space to handle remaining uncertainty.
concepts.recap_md: - The latent variable $\mathbf{z}$ is assumed to be independent of the conditioning input $\mathbf{x}$.

key_passage.text: In conditional VAEs (cVAEs), we restrict our attention to latent variables z that are independent of the inputs we are conditioning on, so we have: p_θ(y|x) = ∫_z p_θ(y|z,x)p_z(z)dz

motivation.text: The idea is that z should only encode bits of information about y that are independent from whatever x already tells us about y.

concepts.title: Conditional Autoregressive Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional autoregressive models treat conditioning inputs as a prefix to the sequence being modeled, factorizing the probability into a series of conditional predictions.
concepts.content: Autoregressive models naturally model sequences of conditional distributions. To condition them on inputs $\mathbf{x}$, we can concatenate $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the sequence of $y$ values, creating the sequence $[x_1, \ldots, x_m, y_1, \ldots, y_n]$. The probability model factorizes as: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p_{\theta}(y_i \bigm | y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, x_1, \ldots, x_m) \end{aligned}$$ Each term in the product predicts the next item given all previous items, including the conditioning prefix. Because this structure is identical to unconditional autoregressive modeling, the same implementation and tools can be used for both cases, simply by choosing whether or not to prefix the sequence.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models are powerful for sequence generation but need a way to incorporate context. By treating the context as a prefix, we can leverage existing sequence modeling architectures to generate outputs that are consistent with given constraints or history.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is achieved by prefixing the target sequence with the conditioning variables $\mathbf{x}$.

key_passage.text: To condition them on some inputs $\mathbf{x}$, we can simply concatenate $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the sequence of $y$ values we are modeling, yielding the new sequence: $[x_1, \ldots, x_m, y_1, \ldots, y_n]$.

motivation.text: Each distribution in this product is a prediction of the next item in a sequence given the previous items, which is no different than what we had for unconditional autoregressive models. Therefore, the tools for modeling unconditional autoregressive distributions are also appropriate for modeling conditional autoregressive distributions.

concepts.title: Conditional Diffusion Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models incorporate conditioning variables into the denoising function to guide the generative process toward specific outputs.
concepts.content: Diffusion models can be made conditional by concatenating the conditioning variables $\mathbf{x}$ into the input of the denoising function: $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$ Both diffusion and autoregressive models convert generative modeling into a sequence of supervised prediction problems. Conditioning is achieved by augmenting the training pairs from $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ to $\{[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{c}^{(i)}], \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\mathbf{c}$ represents additional paired observations. For example, in text-to-image synthesis, providing a text description as an additional input to $f_{\theta}$ allows the model to denoise toward an image that matches that text. (see figure: Text-conditional diffusion model.)
concepts.motivation_md: Unconditional diffusion models generate high-quality but random samples. By adding conditioning variables like text or class labels to the denoising step, we can steer the model to generate specific content that satisfies user-provided constraints.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is implemented by adding the variable $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to the denoising function $f_{\theta}$.

key_passage.text: All we need to do is concatenate the conditioning variables, $\mathbf{x}$, into the input to the denoising function: $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x})$

motivation.text: The intuition is that if we give $f_{\theta}$ a description of the image as an additional input, then it can do a better job at solving its prediction task. Because of this, $f_{\theta}$ will become sensitive to the text command, and if you give different text it will denoise toward a different image---an image that matches that text!

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation is the task of mapping an input image from one representation or domain to another, such as converting a sketch into a photograph.
concepts.content: Image-to-image problems are mapping tasks where both the input and output are images, defined as arrays of size $N \times M \times C$ (height by width by channels). These problems are common in computer vision and include tasks such as colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation. This perspective treats these tasks as translating from one view of the data to another; for instance, semantic segmentation translates a color-based view of the world into a semantic-based view. The goal of image-to-image translation is to learn these mappings, such as translating from pixels to semantics or from a photograph to a painting.
concepts.motivation_md: Many computer vision tasks share a common structure: they require transforming an input image into a different but spatially aligned output image. Defining these as 'translation' allows for a unified framework to solve diverse problems like segmentation, colorization, and style transfer.
concepts.recap_md: - It involves mapping an input image to an output image of the same or similar spatial dimensions.

key_passage.text: Image-to-image problems are mapping problems where the input is an image and the output is also an image, where we will here think of an image as any array of size N × M × C (height by width by number of channels). This perspective yields the problem of image-to-image translation; just like we can translate from English to French, can we translate from pixels to semantics, or perhaps from a photographic depiction of scene to a painting of that same scene?

question.text: just like we can translate from English to French, can we translate from pixels to semantics, or perhaps from a photographic depiction of scene to a painting of that same scene?

motivation.text: These problems are very common in computer vision. Examples include colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation (a per-pixel label map is also an image, just with K channels, one for each label, rather than three channels, one for each color channel).

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN
concepts.one_liner: The pix2pix method uses a conditional GAN with a U-Net generator and a CNN discriminator to perform image-to-image translation.
concepts.content: One approach to image-to-image translation is using a conditional GAN, as popularized by the "pix2pix" paper. In this framework, the generator maps an input image (such as a facade layout map) to an output image (such as a matching photo). The generator typically uses an image-to-image architecture like a U-Net, which is a CNN with accordion-shaped skip connections. The discriminator is a regular CNN that maps the output image to a scalar score representing whether the input-output pair is real or synthetic. (see figure: The pix2pix @pix2pix2017 model applied to translating a facade layout map into a photo of the facade. The model was trained on the CMP Facades Database @Tylecek13 and the input and ground truth...)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard supervised learning for image translation often results in blurry outputs because simple loss functions like MSE average over possible outcomes. Using a GAN loss forces the model to produce sharp, realistic images that are indistinguishable from real data.
concepts.recap_md: - It utilizes a U-Net architecture for the generator to preserve spatial information through skip connections.

key_passage.text: One approach to image-to-image translation is to use a conditional GAN, as was popularized in the "pix2pix" paper. The generator therefore maps an image to an image so we will implement it with an image-to-image neural architecture.

motivation.text: To illustrate this approach, we will look at the problem of translating a facade layout map into a photo. In this setting, the conditioning information (input) is a layout map showing where all the architectural elements are positioned on the facade (i.e., a semantic segmentation image of the facade, with colors indicating where the windows, doors, and so on are located), and the output is a matching photo.

concepts.title: Omitting Noise in Conditional GANs
concepts.one_liner: In some conditional GAN implementations, the noise input is omitted because the input image provides sufficient entropy for the generator.
concepts.content: In certain conditional GAN settings, noise inputs are omitted, and the generator takes only the image $\mathbf{x}$ as input. This is done because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ often contains enough entropy by itself, making additional noise unnecessary for creating variety in the model's outputs. However, the downside to this approach is that the model becomes deterministic, providing only one prediction $\mathbf{y}$ for each input $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: While GANs are theoretically designed to map noise to data, in conditional tasks like image-to-image translation, the network often learns to ignore the noise. Omitting it simplifies the architecture when a single high-quality mapping is preferred over a variety of outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - The generator relies on the entropy of the input image $\mathbf{x}$ instead of an explicit noise vector.

key_passage.text: Notice that we have omitted the noise inputs here; instead the generator only takes as input the image $\mathbf{x}$. It turns out that in this setting the noise is not really a necessary input, and many implementations omit it. This is because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ has enough entropy by itself, and you don't necessarily need additional noise to create variety in the outputs of the model.

motivation.text: This is because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ has enough entropy by itself, and you don't necessarily need additional noise to create variety in the outputs of the model.

concepts.title: Mixture of Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: A mixture of Gaussians is a classical model that represents a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian distributions.
concepts.content:
VAEs are mixture models, and the most common kind of VAE is a mixture of Gaussians. The mixture of Gaussians model is a classical model that represents a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian distributions:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^k w_i \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{\mu}_i, \mathbf{\Sigma}_i) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{mixture of Gaussians} \end{aligned}$$

where the parameters are $\theta = \{\mathbf{\mu}_i, \mathbf{\Sigma}_i\}_{i=1}^k$, representing the mean and variance of all Gaussians in the mixture.
concepts.motivation_md: Mixture models allow for the representation of complex, multi-modal data distributions by combining several simpler distributions (like Gaussians), providing more flexibility than a single distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents a probability density as a weighted sum of $k$ Gaussian components.

key_passage.text: The mixture of Gaussians model is in fact classical model that represents a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian distributions: p_θ(x) = Σ(i=1 to k) w_i N(x; μ_i, Σ_i)

motivation.text: VAEs are mixture models, and the most common kind of VAE is a mixture of Gaussians.

concepts.title: Infinite Mixture of Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: An infinite mixture of Gaussians models a distribution by integrating over a continuous set of Gaussian components parameterized by a function.
concepts.content:
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) use an infinite mixture of Gaussians, where the number of components $k \rightarrow \infty$. To parameterize an infinite mixture, the mean and variance are treated as functions of an underlying continuous variable $\mathbf{z}$. You can think of a function as the infinite set of values a variable takes on over some domain.

The function used by the VAE is $g_{\theta}$, decomposed into $g_{\theta}^{\mu}$ and $g_{\theta}^{\Sigma}$ to separately model the means and variances. By choosing a unit Gaussian distribution as the continuous domain to integrate over, the infinite mixture is described as:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} \underbrace{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; g^{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}), g^{\Sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}))}_{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z})}\underbrace{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})}_{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}d\mathbf{z} \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{VAE hypothesis space} \end{aligned}$$

This models an infinite mixture as an integral that marginalizes over a continuous latent variable. This can be viewed as transforming a base distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ to a modeled distribution $p_{\theta}$ by applying a deterministic mapping $g_{\theta}$ and adding Gaussian probability around each point in the range.

(see figure: From a finite mixture of Gaussians to an infinite mixture.)

While this example uses Gaussians, VAEs can be constructed using other base distributions, making mixture models metamodels whose components can be any density model.
concepts.motivation_md: Finite mixtures are limited by a fixed number of components; infinite mixtures provide a more powerful "metamodel" capable of representing highly complex data by marginalizing over a continuous latent space.
concepts.recap_md: - Extends Gaussian mixtures to the limit where the number of components $k$ approaches infinity.

key_passage.text: We can't learn an infinite set of means and variances. The trick we will use is to make the mean and variance be *functions* of an underlying continuous variable. What we have done is model an infinite mixture as an integral that marginalizes over a continuous latent variable.

question.text: But wait, how can we parameterize an infinite mixture?

motivation.text: Gaussian mixture models, VAEs use an *infinite* mixture of Gaussians, that is, $k \rightarrow \infty$.

concepts.title: The Challenge of Optimizing VAEs
concepts.one_liner: The VAE objective is intractable because its exact computation requires integrating over an infinite set of deep network forward passes.
concepts.content:
The VAE's objective is intractable because its exact computation requires integrating over an infinite set of deep net forward passes. The difficulty of optimizing VAEs lies in approximating this intractable objective. Once an approximation is derived, optimization can be performed using backpropagation on the approximate loss.

With the objective and hypothesis given, the VAE learning problem is defined as:

$$\begin{aligned} \theta^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\theta} L(\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta)\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N \log \int_{\mathbf{z}} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}; g^{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}), g^{\Sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$

where the integral represents the marginal likelihood $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard deep learning optimization requires a computable gradient; since the VAE marginal likelihood involves an intractable integral, we must find ways to approximate it to enable training.
concepts.recap_md: - The VAE objective involves an integral over latent space that cannot be computed analytically.

key_passage.text: The difficulty of optimizing VAEs lies in the difficulty of approximating this intractable objective. Once we derive our approximation, optimization again will be easy: just apply backpropagation on this approximate loss.

question.text: Wait, a whole section on optimization? Didn't this book say that general-purpose optimizers (like backpropagation) are often sufficient in the deep learning era?

motivation.text: The issue here is that the VAE's objective is intractable. Its exact computation requires integrating over an infinite set of deep net forward passes.

concepts.title: Monte Carlo Estimation of the VAE Objective
concepts.one_liner: Monte Carlo estimation approximates the intractable VAE likelihood integral by averaging the likelihood over a finite set of random latent samples.
concepts.content:
Because the integral for $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ may not have a closed form for complex functions $g_{\theta}$, it must be approximated numerically. A Monte Carlo estimate approximates the integral as an expectation over the latent distribution:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) &= \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z}\\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}[p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})]\\ &\approx \frac{1}{M} \sum_{j=1}^M p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(j)}), \quad \mathbf{z}^{(j)} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}} \end{aligned}$$

This allows the learning problem to be written in a closed differentiable form. In practice, for each iteration of backpropagation, a batch of random samples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}$ is collected from the training set and a batch of random latents $\{\mathbf{z}^{(j)}\}$ is sampled from the unit Gaussian. Each $\mathbf{z}$ is passed through the network $g_{\theta}$ to evaluate the log probabilities of the $\mathbf{x}$ samples, followed by a backward pass to update parameters $\theta$.

(see figure: Fitting an infinite mixture of Gaussians whose means and variances are parameterized by a generator function $g_\theta$)
concepts.motivation_md: Monte Carlo methods provide a general-purpose way to approximate expectations and integrals that are otherwise impossible to solve analytically, enabling the use of gradient-based optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - Approximates the marginal likelihood integral using the empirical mean of samples from the prior.

key_passage.text: The first trick we will use is a Monte Carlo estimate of this integral: p_θ(x) = ∫_z p_θ(x | z)p_z(z)dz = E_{z∼p_z(z)}[p_θ(x | z)] ≈ 1/M ∑_{j=1}^M p_θ(x | z^{(j)}), z^{(j)} ∼ p_z

motivation.text: The integral for p_θ(x^{(i)}) does not necessarily have a closed form since g_θ may be an arbitrarily complex function. Therefore, we need to approximate this integral numerically.

concepts.title: Importance Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Importance sampling is a technique for approximating expectations by sampling from a biased distribution and applying a correction factor.
concepts.content:
Monte Carlo estimation does not scale well to high dimensions because many samples from $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ are needed to accurately estimate the integral. In a VAE, most terms $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z}^{(j)})$ are near zero because a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$ only has substantial probability under Gaussians whose means are near $\mathbf{x}$.

(see figure: To estimate $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ we only need to consider the Gaussian components (gray circles) that place significant probability on $\mathbf{x}$.)

Importance sampling addresses this by sampling from a different density $q_{\mathbf{z}}$ that focuses on regions where $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z})$ is large, then multiplying by a correction factor $\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}$:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) d\mathbf{z} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\mathbf{z}}}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big] \end{aligned}$$

The optimal distribution to sample from is $q^* = p_{\theta}(Z | \mathbf{x})$, which minimizes the variance of the estimator. This allows for a good approximation of the data likelihood with far fewer samples.

(see figure: Optimal importance sampling estimates $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ by drawing samples from $p_{\theta}(Z \| \mathbf{x})$.)
concepts.motivation_md: In high-dimensional spaces, random sampling is inefficient because most samples contribute nothing to the integral; importance sampling focuses computation on the most relevant regions of the latent space.
concepts.recap_md: - Reduces estimator variance by sampling from a distribution $q$ that targets high-probability regions.

key_passage.text: Rather than sampling $\mathbf{z}^{(i)} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}$, we sample from some other density $\mathbf{z}^{(i)} \sim q_{\mathbf{z}}$, and multiply by a correction factor $\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}$ to account for the fact that we are sampling from a biased distribution.

motivation.text: The reason is that in order for our Monte Carlo estimate of the integral to be accurate, we may need many samples from $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, and the higher the dimensionality of $\mathbf{z}$, the more samples we will typically need.

concepts.title: Variational Inference
concepts.one_liner: Variational inference approximates an intractable density by finding the closest tractable distribution within a parameterized family, typically by minimizing KL divergence.
concepts.content:
Variational inference is a strategy used to approximate an intractable density $p$ by finding the nearest density in a tractable family $q_{\psi}$. In VAEs, the ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z | \mathbf{x})$ is approximated by a Gaussian $q_{\psi} = \mathcal{N}(f_{\psi}^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\psi}^{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}))$, where $f_{\psi}$ acts as a probabilistic encoder.

(see figure: A VAE's encoder, $f_{\psi}$, models $p(Z \| \mathbf{x})$ as a Gaussian parameterized by $f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})$.)

The goal is to choose $q_{\psi}$ to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to the true posterior. This leads to the maximization of the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), denoted as $J$:

$$\begin{aligned} J = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) \Big] - \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid \mathbf{x}) \| p_{\mathbf{z}}\right) \end{aligned}$$

This objective $J$ is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood $J_p = \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$. By maximizing $J$, we simultaneously optimize the model parameters $\theta$ and the variational parameters $\psi$. The first term of the ELBO measures the reconstruction likelihood, while the second term measures the gap between the approximate posterior and the prior.
concepts.motivation_md: The true posterior distribution in complex models is often impossible to compute; variational inference turns this estimation problem into an optimization problem that can be solved with gradient descent.
concepts.recap_md: - Approximates the posterior $p(Z|X)$ using a tractable distribution $q(Z|X)$.

key_passage.text: The idea of variational inference is to approximate an intractable density $p$ by finding the nearest density in a tractable family $q_{\psi}$, parameterized by $\psi$. In VAEs, we approximate our ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ with a $q_{\psi}$ in a family we can efficiently sample from; the most common choice is to again use a Gaussian, conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$: $q_{\psi} = \mathcal{N}(f_{\psi}^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\psi}^{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}))$.

motivation.text: Now we know what distribution we *should* be sampling $\mathbf{z}$ from: $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$. The only remaining problem is that this distribution may be complicated and hard to sample from.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Encoder
concepts.one_liner: A probabilistic encoder is a function that maps an input to the parameters of a probability distribution over a latent space.
concepts.content:
In VAEs, the ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z | \mathbf{x})$ is approximated with a tractable family $q_{\psi}$. The most common choice is a Gaussian conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$: $q_{\psi} = \mathcal{N}(f_{\psi}^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\psi}^{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}))$. The function $f_{\psi}$ maps from the input $\mathbf{x}$ to the parameters (mean and variance) of a distribution over the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$. This function $f_{\psi}$ is known as a probabilistic encoder.

(see figure: A VAE's encoder, $f_{\psi}$, models $p(Z \| \mathbf{x})$ as a Gaussian parameterized by $f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})$.)

In the VAE architecture, $f$ plays the role of the encoder while the generator function $g$ plays the role of the decoder.
concepts.motivation_md: Instead of mapping an input to a single point in latent space, a probabilistic encoder maps it to a distribution, allowing the model to capture uncertainty and providing a principled way to perform importance sampling.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps input data $\mathbf{x}$ to the parameters of a latent distribution $q(Z|X)$.

key_passage.text: The $f_{\psi}$ is a function that maps from $\mathbf{x}$ to parameters of a distribution over $\mathbf{z}$; in other words, $f_{\psi}$ is a probabilistic encoder!

motivation.text: In VAEs, we approximate our ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ with a $q_{\psi}$ in a family we can efficiently sample from; the most common choice is to again use a Gaussian, conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Jensen's Inequality
concepts.one_liner: Jensen's inequality is used in VAEs to establish that the ELBO is a lower bound on the marginal log-likelihood.
concepts.content:
Jensen's inequality is used to show that the VAE objective $J$ is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood $J_p = \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$:

$$\begin{aligned} J_p &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big]\\ &\geq \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log \big(\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\big)\Big] \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{Jensen's inequality}\\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[-\log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) + \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) + \log p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}) \Big]\\ &= J \quad\quad\triangleleft\quad\text{VAE objective}\\ &\Rightarrow \quad J \leq J_p \end{aligned}$$

This inequality allows us to maximize a tractable expectation $J$ instead of the intractable log-likelihood $J_p$.
concepts.motivation_md: Jensen's inequality provides the mathematical justification for replacing a difficult 'log of an expectation' with a simpler 'expectation of a log', which is essential for deriving the ELBO in variational inference.
concepts.recap_md: - Proves that $\log \mathbb{E}[f(z)] \geq \mathbb{E}[\log f(z)]$ for positive functions.

key_passage.text: Jensen's inequality: $$\begin{aligned} J_p &= \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\\ &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big]\\ &\geq \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log \big(\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\big)\Big]

motivation.text: The fact that $J$ is a lower-bound on $J_p$ follows from Jensen's inequality

concepts.title: Linear probes
concepts.one_liner: Linear probes are lightweight linear modules added to a computation graph to repurpose a network for new tasks or to assess the knowledge represented in feature maps.
concepts.content: A model can be adapted by changing its parameters or by adding new modules to the computation graph. One important kind of new module is a read out module that takes features from the computation graph as input and produces a new prediction as output. When these modules are linear, they are called linear probes. These modules are relatively lightweight, having few parameters, and can be optimized with tools from linear optimization where closed form solutions are often available. Because of this, linear probes are very popular as a way of repurposing a neural net to perform a new task. These modules are also useful as a way of assessing what kind of knowledge each feature map in the original network represents; if a feature map can linearly classify some attribute of the data, then that feature map contains information about that attribute. In this usage, linear probes are probing the knowledge represented in some layer of a neural net.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear probes provide a computationally efficient way to adapt large pre-trained models to new tasks without retraining the entire network. They also serve as a diagnostic tool for researchers to interpret what specific layers of a neural network have learned about the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear probes are linear read-out modules added to a network to generate new predictions.

key_passage.text: When these modules are linear, they are called linear probes. These modules are relatively lightweight (few parameters) and can be optimized with tools from linear optimization (where there are often closed form solutions).

motivation.text: Because of this, linear probes are very popular as a way of repurposing a neural net to perform a new task. These modules are also useful as a way of assessing what kind of knowledge each feature map in the original network represents, in the sense that if a feature map can linearly classify some attribute of the data, then that feature maps knows something about that attribute.

concepts.title: Learning from a teacher
concepts.one_liner: Learning from a teacher involves a student model observing a well-trained teacher model to imitate its outputs or match its intermediate processing.
concepts.content:
Supervised learning is often described as learning from examples, where a learner is given a dataset of input-output pairs to infer a relationship. This can be visualized as:

[FIGURE:bf8fbd1d5fd5a3e3]

This kind of learning is like having a teacher who provides an answer key but no explanations. Alternatively, we can consider a more instructive setting where the teacher is a well-trained model $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ that maps input queries to output answers. The student (the learner) observes both data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ and has access to the teacher model $t$. The student can learn to imitate the teacher's outputs or can learn to match how the teacher processes the queries by matching intermediate activations of the teacher model.

[FIGURE:872a10889f557ebb]

Learning from examples can be considered a special case of learning from a teacher where the teacher is the world and our only access is observing the outputs $y$ that match each input $x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard supervised learning is limited to observing final labels. By treating a trained model as a teacher, a student model can leverage richer information, such as the teacher's internal logic or confidence levels, to learn more efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - The student model learns by imitating the teacher model's outputs or intermediate activations.

key_passage.text: One way of formalizing this setting is to consider the teacher as a well-trained model $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ that maps input queries to output answers. The student (the learner) observes both data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ and has access to the teacher model $t$. The student can learn to imitate the teacher's outputs or can learn to match *how the teacher processes the queries*, matching intermediate activations of the teacher model.
