This results in an augmented dataset of the form $\{T_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), T_{\mathcal{Y}}(\mathbf{y}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^M$. This requires that $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$ express an equivariance between the two domains, defined as $T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x),\theta_{\mathcal{Y}}) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x,\theta_{\mathcal{X}})) \quad \forall \theta$. This is standard when $\mathbf{y}$ has spatial or temporal structure aligned with $\mathbf{x}$, such as semantic segmentation. For instance, if we apply a random crop to an image $\mathbf{x}$, we must apply the same crop to the label map $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple invariance is insufficient for tasks like segmentation or object detection where the label is spatially dependent on the input. Equivariance ensures that when the input is moved or altered, the label is updated accordingly to maintain correctness.
concepts.recap_md: - Transforms both inputs and outputs to maintain the relationship $T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x)) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x))$.

key_passage.text: For this to make sense, we require that $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$ express an **equivariance** between the two domains, which means, $$\begin{aligned} T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x),\theta_{\mathcal{Y}}) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x,\theta_{\mathcal{X}})) \quad \forall \theta \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{$y$ equivariant with respect to $T_\mathcal{X}, T_\mathcal{Y}$} \end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: To handle the case where $y(\mathbf{x}) \neq y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$, we may use a more advanced kind of data augmentation, where we transform the $\mathbf{y}$ values at the same time as we transform the $\mathbf{x}$ values, using transforms $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$.

concepts.title: Out-of-distribution
concepts.one_liner: Test data is out-of-distribution when it differs significantly from the training data in characteristics like resolution, category, or feature space.
concepts.content: Data augmentation works by broadening the distribution of training data, which can reduce the gap between training and test data. When test images look quite different from training data—for example, having lower resolution or containing different object categories—we say the test data are out-of-distribution relative to the training data. This effect is illustrated in (Figure 1.1.6), where training data from Caltech256 is compared to test data from CIFAR100. By adding variation through augmentation (like mirroring, cropping, or color jitter), the training distribution broadens so that the test data become more in-distribution relative to the training set.
concepts.motivation_md: Models often fail when they encounter data that looks different from what they saw during training. Understanding out-of-distribution data helps researchers use augmentation to bridge the gap and improve real-world generalization.
concepts.recap_md: - Refers to test data that differs significantly from the training distribution.

key_passage.text: We say that the test data are **out-of-distribution** relative to the training data.

motivation.text: Data augmentation adds variation to the training data, which broadens the training distribution. The result is that the test data become more in-distribution, compared to the training data.

concepts.title: Learned data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Learned data augmentation uses algorithms to automatically discover complex transformations, such as pose variations, that are difficult to implement manually.
concepts.content: While simple transformations like mirror flipping or cropping are easy to implement, they represent only a few of the possible transformations a model might need to be invariant to. For complex tasks like pedestrian detection, we may want the model to be invariant to pose variation. Because such variations are difficult to code by hand, we can use learning algorithms to learn how to augment our data and achieve the desired invariances or equivariances automatically.
concepts.motivation_md: Manual augmentation is limited to simple geometric or color shifts. Learning the augmentations allows for more complex, domain-specific variations that better reflect the real-world challenges a model will face.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses algorithms to learn optimal data transformations instead of manual coding.

key_passage.text: Instead we can use learning algorithms to learn how to augment our data and achieve the invariances we would like.

motivation.text: But these are just a few of all possible transformations that we might want to be invariant to. Imagine if we are building a pedestrian detector. Then we would probably like it to be invariant to pose variation in the pedestrian.

concepts.title: Generative data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Generative data augmentation uses models like GANs or VAEs to create new training examples by perturbing latent variables.
concepts.content: One method for learned augmentation is using generative models, such as GANs or VAEs. These models are suitable because their latent variables can control different factors of variation. Given a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, an encoder $f_{\phi}$, and a generator $g_{\theta}$, we can create an augmented copy as $\mathbf{x} = g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{w})$, where $\mathbf{w}$ is a small perturbation to the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$. Using various settings for $\mathbf{w}$, such as Gaussian perturbations $\mathbf{w} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, results in a set of output images that are slight variations of one another. (see figure: Generative data augmentation `genaug`)
concepts.motivation_md: Generative models can capture complex, high-level variations in data that simple rotations or crops cannot, allowing for the creation of diverse and realistic training samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Employs GANs or VAEs to generate augmented data via latent space manipulation.

key_passage.text: Given a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, an encoder $f_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, and a generator $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, we can create an augmented copy of $\mathbf{x}$ as, $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x} = g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{w}) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{generative data augmentation via latent manipulation} \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathbf{w}$ is a small perturbation to the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$.

motivation.text: One way to do this is to use generative models. Latent variable generative models like generative adversarial networks (GANs) or variational autoencoders (VAEs) are especially suitable, because the latent variables can be used to control different factors of variation in the generated data.

concepts.title: Robust optimization
concepts.one_liner: Robust optimization is a general approach in optimization literature that includes techniques like adversarial training to improve model performance under competition or uncertainty.
concepts.content: Adversarial training is a specific application of a broader approach known in the optimization literature as robust optimization. This general framework is used for various purposes beyond standard classification, including training generative adversarial networks, training agents to explore in reinforcement learning, and training agents that compete against other agents.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard optimization may produce models that are fragile to small changes. Robust optimization provides a mathematical framework to ensure models remain effective even under worst-case perturbations or adversarial conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - A general optimization framework for training resilient models.

key_passage.text: This general approach is also known as robust optimization in the optimization literature.

motivation.text: Adversarial training has many other uses as well, beyond the scope of the current chapter- it is used for training generative adversarial networks, for training agents to explore in reinforcement learning, and for training agents that compete against other agents.

concepts.title: Multitask training
concepts.one_liner: Multitask training involves sharing data between different tasks by defining a broader metatask that encompasses them as special cases.
concepts.content: Because data for any single task is often finite, multitask training allows for sharing data between tasks. The approach involves broadening the task itself by defining a new metatask, $AB$, for which tasks $A$ and $B$ are special cases. For example, data imputation is a metatask that includes both colorization (predicting missing color channels) and inpainting (predicting masked-out pixels). A joint colorization-inpainting model can be trained on data from both specific tasks by treating them as general data imputation.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique addresses data scarcity. By training on multiple related tasks simultaneously, a model can learn more robust and generalizable features than it would from a single task alone.
concepts.recap_md: - Shares data across tasks by defining a generalized metatask.

key_passage.text: The idea is to define a new task, AB, for which tasks A and B are special cases. Then we can train AB on both the data for task A and for task B.

motivation.text: Because we have finite data for any given task, it can help to share data between tasks. In line with the theme of this chapter, one approach is to not just broaden the data but to also broaden the task.

concepts.title: One-shot learning
concepts.one_liner: One-shot learning is the ability to learn to recognize a new concept after seeing it just once.
concepts.content: Deep learning systems are often criticized for being data hungry, requiring thousands of labeled examples to learn a concept like "dog." In contrast, humans possess the ability to learn to recognize a new kind of animal after seeing it just once. This ability is known as one-shot learning.
concepts.motivation_md: The goal of one-shot learning is to reduce the massive data requirements of neural networks, making AI more efficient and capable of learning from limited information, similar to human cognition.
concepts.recap_md: - The ability to learn a concept from a single labeled example.

key_passage.text: humans can learn to recognize a new kind of animal after seeing it just once, an ability known as one-shot learning.

motivation.text: A common criticism of deep learning systems is that they are data hungry. To learn a new concept (e.g., "is this a dog?") may require showing a deep net thousands of labeled examples of that concept.

concepts.title: Testing and Benchmark Bias
concepts.one_liner: Biases in the test set can negatively impact system behavior because researchers use them to decide which algorithms or data collections are most effective.
concepts.content: Biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on final system behavior than training bias. The test set is what researchers and engineers use to decide which algorithm is best, or what data collection is more effective for training. However, there might be little correlation between the performance measured on the test set and the final performance of the system during deployment. In particular, if we compare two training datasets, one biased and another less biased, by evaluating the performance of a system trained on them using a biased test dataset, we could reach the conclusion that the biased dataset is better.
concepts.motivation_md: Evaluation metrics are only as reliable as the data they are measured on. If a test set is biased, it can mislead developers into choosing models that perform well on the benchmark but fail in real-world deployment.
concepts.recap_md: - Biased test sets can lead to incorrect conclusions about which training data or algorithms are superior.

key_passage.text: if we compare two training datasets, one biased and another less biased, by evaluating the performance of a system trained on them using a biased test dataset, we could reach the conclusion that the biased dataset is better.

motivation.text: One usually thinks about the biases in the training set, but biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on the final system behavior than the training bias. The test set is what researchers and engineers use to decide which algorithm is best, or what data collection is more effective for training.

concepts.title: Adversarial attacks
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks involve adding imperceptible noise to data to force a neural network to produce a specific, incorrect output.
concepts.content: Adversarial attacks occur when an attacker adds imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking completely innocuous to a human. The noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires. The adversary can do this by optimizing the noise pattern to cause the network to make a particular output, while restricting the noise to be very subtle, typically within a small $r$-radius ball around the original image. For example, to cause an image classifier $f$ to think the cat in (see figure: An adversarial attack that adds subtle changes to the cat photo to make a neural net classify it instead as an ostrich. The noise image color values are scaled 20x for visualization.) is an ostrich, the attacker could find the noise pattern via the following optimization: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{\epsilon}} H(\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}, f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{\epsilon})), \quad\quad \text{subject to} \quad\quad \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r \end{aligned}$$ where $H$ is the cross-entropy loss and $\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}$ is a one-hot code for the ostrich class.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks are often sensitive to small, targeted perturbations that humans cannot see. Understanding these attacks is crucial for building secure systems that cannot be easily manipulated by malicious actors.
concepts.recap_md: - Adversarial attacks use optimized, subtle noise to manipulate model outputs.

key_passage.text: These are called adversarial attacks because we suppose the attacker, who adds the noise, is an adversary that wants to fool or manipulate your system. The adversary can do this by simply optimizing the noise pattern to cause the network to make a particular output, while restricting the noise to be very subtle (within an small r-radius ball around the original image).

motivation.text: This was famously demonstrated by Szegedy et al., who showed that one can add imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking completely innocuous to a human. In fact, the noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires.

concepts.title: Adversarial robustness
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial robustness refers to a system's ability to minimize worst-case error rather than just the average error over training data.
concepts.content: Adversarial analysis is worst-case analysis. Typically, systems are trained to minimize empirical risk, defined as the mean error over the training data. Because the focus is only on the mean, the worst case might be arbitrarily bad. Alternative approaches try to minimize worst-case error, which can result in systems that are more adversarially robust.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard training focuses on average performance, which leaves models vulnerable to specific, targeted failures. Robustness aims to guarantee a certain level of performance even under the most difficult or manipulated conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - Adversarial robustness focuses on minimizing the worst-case error rather than the mean empirical risk.

key_passage.text: Alternative approaches try to minimize worst-case error, and this can result in systems that are more adversarially robust.

motivation.text: Because we only focus on the mean, the worst case might be arbitrarily bad.

concepts.title: Adversarial training
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial training is a technique that increases model robustness by training on worst-case transformations rather than random ones.
concepts.content: Adversarial training can be used to increase the robustness of models to adversarial attacks. While standard data augmentation applies random transformations to the data to do well in expectation, adversarial training considers augmenting with worst-case transformations that incur the highest loss possible for a given training example: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\theta \in \Theta}[\mathcal{L}(f(T(\mathbf{x};\theta)),\mathbf{y})]] \end{aligned}$$ This increases the robustness of the learned function $f$ to perturbations that may occur at test time. In the context of adversarial robustness, one form of this is to set $T$ to be an epsilon-ball attack, where $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\mathbf{\epsilon} \, s.t. \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r}[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}),\mathbf{y})]] \end{aligned}$$ This can increase robustness against the kinds of epsilon-ball attacks seen in adversarial analysis.
concepts.motivation_md: To defend against adversarial attacks, models must be exposed to them during training. By solving a minimax problem, the model learns to handle the most difficult perturbations it might encounter.
concepts.recap_md: - Adversarial training replaces random data augmentation with worst-case perturbations.

key_passage.text: Instead of doing random transformations, we could instead consider augmenting with worst case transformations, applying those transformations that incur the highest loss possible for a given training example.

motivation.text: One of its effects is that it can increase the robustness of the learned function f to perturbations that may occur at test time (like those we saw in the previous chapter).

concepts.title: Model adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Model adaptation, also known as transfer learning, is a strategy for dealing with dataset bias and shift by adjusting a model to new domains.
concepts.content: There are two general ways of dealing with dataset bias and shift. The first is called domain randomization, or data augmentation. The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation.
concepts.motivation_md: When a model is trained on one distribution but must perform on another, model adaptation provides a way to bridge the gap without starting training from scratch.
concepts.recap_md: - Model adaptation is a primary strategy for addressing dataset shift and bias.

key_passage.text: The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation.

motivation.text: There are two general ways of dealing with dataset bias and shift.

concepts.title: Data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Data augmentation increases the size and diversity of a dataset by adding synthetic pairs created through random transformations of the original data.
concepts.content: Data augmentation is a method for dealing with dataset bias and shift by adding random transformations of each datapoint. For example, common augmentations can be applied to an image, as shown in (see figure: A few common types of data augmentation.). By mapping from a smaller dataset to a larger one, it simulates the effect of adding more real data. For each $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}$ pair in the original dataset, you add $M$ new synthetic pairs $\{T(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^M$, where $T$ is a transformation function with stochastic parameters $\theta \sim p_{\theta}$. For instance, if $T$ is a `crop` function, $\theta$ would be the coordinates specifying where to apply the crop.
concepts.motivation_md: Machine learning models require large amounts of data to generalize well. Data augmentation allows practitioners to artificially expand their datasets, improving model performance and robustness to variations.
concepts.recap_md: - Data augmentation creates synthetic training examples using stochastic transformations like cropping or rotating.

key_passage.text: augments a dataset by adding random transformations of each datapoint. When you do this for every image in a dataset, you are essentially mapping from a smaller dataset to a larger dataset. The way data augmentation works is that for each pair in your original dataset, you add M new synthetic pairs, where T is a data transformation function with stochastic parameters.

motivation.text: We know that more data is usually better, so this is a way to simulate the effect of adding more real data to your dataset. Data augmentation is like a philosopher's stone of machine learning: it converts lead (small data) into gold (big data).

concepts.title: Domain randomization
concepts.one_liner: Domain randomization is a technique used with simulators to randomize parameters, creating a broader set of experiences for a learner.
concepts.content: Domain randomization is an idea analogous to data augmentation used when data is generated by a simulator rather than a static dataset. Instead of adding random transformations to points in a dataset, we randomize the parameters of the simulator so that each interaction with the simulation will look slightly different. For example, lighting conditions may be randomized. This converts a narrow set of experiences, such as a simulation with one kind of lighting condition, to a much broader set of experiences to learn from.
concepts.motivation_md: Simulators often fail to capture the complexity of the real world. By randomizing simulation parameters, models can learn to be invariant to factors like lighting or texture, easing the transfer to reality.
concepts.recap_md: - Domain randomization applies the principles of data augmentation to simulated environments.

key_passage.text: Here, rather than adding random transformations to points in a dataset, we instead randomize the parameters of the simulator, so that each interaction with the simulation will look slightly different, for example, the lighting conditions may be randomized.

motivation.text: There are two general ways of dealing with dataset bias and shift. The first is called domain randomization, or data augmentation. The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation.

concepts.title: Transfer learning
concepts.one_liner: Transfer learning uses prior knowledge from previously solved problems to accelerate learning on new, related tasks.
concepts.content: Transfer learning, also known as model adaptation, is a general way of dealing with dataset bias and shift. It provides the means to use priors to accelerate learning and deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly.
concepts.motivation_md: Training models from scratch is computationally expensive and requires massive datasets. Transfer learning allows us to leverage existing models to solve new problems with less data and time.
concepts.recap_md: - Transfer learning utilizes knowledge from one domain to improve learning in another.

key_passage.text: Transfer learning deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly.

motivation.text: There are two general ways of dealing with dataset bias and shift. The first is called domain randomization, or data augmentation. The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation.

concepts.title: Harris Corner Detector
concepts.one_liner: The Harris corner detector identifies image points that are easy to localize by evaluating how the sum of squared intensity differences over an image patch changes under small translations.
concepts.content:
Good image features are positions in the image that are easy to localize given only the image intensities. The Harris corner detector identifies these points by evaluating how the sum of squared intensity differences over an image patch change under a small translation of the image. If the squared intensity changes quickly with patch translation in every direction, then the region contains a good image feature.

To derive the detector, we treat an image as a continuous function $\ell(x,y)$. For a small translation $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$, the squared intensity difference $E(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ summed over a small image patch $P$ is:
$$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) = \sum_{(x, y) \in P} \left( \ell(x,y) - \ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) \right)^2$$

Expanding $\ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y)$ using a Taylor series about $\ell(x, y)$ yields:
$$\ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) \approx \ell(x, y) + \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \Delta x + \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \Delta y$$

Substituting this into the energy equation and writing it in matrix form gives:
$$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) \approx \left[ \Delta x ~~ \Delta y \right] \mathbf{M} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Delta x \\ \Delta y \end{array} \right]$$
where
$$\mathbf{M} = \sum_{(n, m) \in P} \begin{bmatrix} (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x})^2 & \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} & (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y})^2 \end{bmatrix}$$

The smallest eigenvalue, $\lambda_{\mbox{min}}$, of the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ indicates the smallest possible change of image intensities under translation in any direction. To detect corners, one identifies points where $\lambda_{\mbox{min}} > \lambda_c$ for a chosen threshold $\lambda_c$.

[FIGURE:f0a494b7b289ab61]

[FIGURE:c647fcb81431db39]

[FIGURE:c1856c0bb1300e0f]
concepts.motivation_md: In computer vision, we need to find points in an image that can be reliably matched across different views. The Harris corner detector solves this by finding regions where the image intensity changes significantly in all directions, making them uniquely localizable.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies features by measuring intensity change under small translations in all directions.

key_passage.text: The smallest eigenvalue, λ_min of the matrix, M, indicates the smallest possible change of image intensities under translation of the patch in any direction. Thus, to detect good corners, one can identify all points for which λ_min > λ_c, for some threshold λ_c.

motivation.text: Good image features are positions in the image that are easy to localize, given only the image intensities. The Harris corner detector identifies image points that are easy to localize by evaluating how the sum of squared intensity differences over an image patch change under a small translation of the image.

concepts.title: SIFT Image Descriptors
concepts.one_liner: SIFT uses histograms of oriented filter responses to create image descriptors that are sensitive to local structure but robust to lighting and location changes.
concepts.content:
Matching corresponding image features requires a local description of the image region to allow matching like regions across two images. SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) uses histograms of oriented filter responses to create an image descriptor that is sensitive to local image structure, but insensitive to minor changes in lighting or location which may occur across the two images of a stereo pair.

Local orientation is a powerful representation because images of the same object under different lighting conditions can look quite different in pixel intensities but very similar in their local orientation. SIFT descriptors exploit this by taking histograms of local orientation over local spatial regions, which further allows the descriptors to be robust to small image translations.

[FIGURE:faa7107c0d4f9db0]

[FIGURE:d0b75366352a79a7]
concepts.motivation_md: Raw pixel values are highly sensitive to lighting and viewpoint changes. SIFT provides a robust way to describe local image patches so they can be accurately matched even when the environment or camera position changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses histograms of oriented gradients to describe local image patches.

key_passage.text: SIFT uses histograms of oriented filter responses to create an image descriptor that is sensitive to local image structure, but that is insensitive to minor changes in lighting or location which may occur across the two images of a stereo pair.

motivation.text: Matching corresponding image features require a local description of the image region to allow matching like regions across two images.

concepts.title: Interpolation between feature matches
concepts.one_liner: Depth between matched feature points can be interpolated using probabilistic methods or dynamic programming to approximate a global solution for stereo shape inference.
concepts.content:
Methods to interpolate depth between the depths of matched points include probabilistic methods such as belief propagation. Under assumptions about the local spatial relationships between depth values, optimal shapes can be inferred provided the spatial structure over which inference is performed is a chain or a tree. 

Another approach uses dynamic programming, which has the same constraints on spatial structure for exact inference. An example is semiglobal matching (SGM), which applies one-dimensional processing over many different orientations to approximate a global solution to the stereo shape inference problem.
concepts.motivation_md: Feature matching only provides depth at specific points. To create a dense depth map, we need techniques to intelligently fill in the gaps between these points based on spatial consistency.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses belief propagation or dynamic programming to infer depth between sparse matches.

key_passage.text: Methods to interpolate depth between the depths of matched points include probabilistic methods such as belief propagation, discussed in Under assumptions about the local spatial relationships between depth values, optimal shapes can be inferred provided the spatial structure over which inference is performed is a chain or a tree.

motivation.text: Under assumptions about the local spatial relationships between depth values, optimal shapes can be inferred provided the spatial structure over which inference is performed is a chain or a tree.

concepts.title: Epipolar plane
concepts.one_liner: The epipolar plane is the plane containing the two camera origins and a specific 3D point in the world.
concepts.content:
The epipolar plane is defined within the geometry of a stereo pair. Given a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, in the world, the epipolar plane is the plane that contains the two camera origins and that 3D point.

(see figure: Geometry of a stereo pair and terminology. The figure shows the epipolar plane, epipolar lines, and epipoles ($e_1$ and $e_2$), for a given point $\mathbf{P}$. As we move the point $\mathbf{P}$, only...)
concepts.motivation_md: Defining the epipolar plane helps simplify the 3D search for matching points into a 2D geometry problem, which is fundamental for stereo vision algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - Defined by the two camera centers and a 3D point.

key_passage.text: The epipolar plane is the plane that contains the two camera origins and a 3D point, 𝐏.

concepts.title: Epipolar lines
concepts.one_liner: Epipolar lines are the intersections of the epipolar plane with the camera planes.
concepts.content:
The epipolar lines are the intersection between the epipolar plane and the camera planes. When the point $\mathbf{P}$ moves in space, the epipolar plane and epipolar lines change accordingly.

(see figure: Geometry of a stereo pair and terminology. The figure shows the epipolar plane, epipolar lines, and epipoles ($e_1$ and $e_2$), for a given point $\mathbf{P}$. As we move the point $\mathbf{P}$, only...)
concepts.motivation_md: Epipolar lines restrict the search for a matching point in one image to a single line in the other image, drastically reducing computational complexity in stereo matching.
concepts.recap_md: - Formed by the intersection of the epipolar plane and the image planes.

key_passage.text: The epipolar lines are the intersection between the epipolar plane and the camera planes.

concepts.title: Epipoles
concepts.one_liner: Epipoles are the points where the line connecting camera origins intersects the camera planes.
concepts.content:
The epipoles are the intersection points between the line that connects both camera origins and the camera planes. Unlike the epipolar plane and lines, the epipoles' location does not depend on the point $\mathbf{P}$. Consequently, all epipolar lines for any point in the scene intersect at these same epipoles.

(see figure: Geometry of a stereo pair and terminology. The figure shows the epipolar plane, epipolar lines, and epipoles ($e_1$ and $e_2$), for a given point $\mathbf{P}$. As we move the point $\mathbf{P}$, only...)
concepts.motivation_md: The epipoles represent the projection of one camera's center onto the other camera's image plane, serving as a fixed reference point for all possible epipolar lines.
concepts.recap_md: - Fixed points where the baseline between cameras intersects the image planes.

key_passage.text: The **epipoles** are the intersection points between the line that connects both camera origins and the camera planes. The epipoles' location does not depend on the point $\mathbf{P}$. Therefore, all the epipolar lines intersect at the same epipoles.

concepts.title: Essential matrix
concepts.one_liner: The essential matrix relates the 3D coordinates of a point viewed by two cameras, capturing the relative rotation and translation between them.
concepts.content:
The essential matrix $\mathbf{E}$ relates the coordinates of a 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ as seen by two cameras. If $\mathbf{P}_1$ and $\mathbf{P}_2$ are the coordinates in the first and second camera systems respectively, they are related by $\mathbf{P}_2 = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_1 + \mathbf{T}$. 

By taking the cross product with $\mathbf{T}$ and the dot product with $\mathbf{P}_2$, we derive the relationship:
$$\mathbf{P}_2^\mathsf{T}\left( \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} \right) \mathbf{P}_1 = 0$$

The essential matrix is defined as $\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{T}_{\times} \mathbf{R}$, where $\mathbf{T}_{\times}$ is the skew-symmetric matrix representing the cross product with $\mathbf{T}$. This leads to the epipolar constraint for image coordinates $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ (assuming focal length $f=1$):
$$\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$$

Properties of the essential matrix:
- It has five degrees of freedom (three for rotation, three for translation, minus one for global scaling).
- It has rank 2.
- It has two identical non-zero singular values and one zero singular value.
concepts.motivation_md: The essential matrix provides a mathematical way to enforce the geometric constraints of a stereo system using only the relative pose of the cameras, allowing us to relate points in one view to lines in another.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates calibrated camera coordinates via the constraint $\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$.

key_passage.text: The matrix $\mathbf{E}$ is called the **essential matrix** and it corresponds to: $$\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{T}_{\times} \mathbf{R}$$ This results in the relationship: $$\mathbf{P}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{P}_1 = 0$$

motivation.text: This equation relates the coordinates of the two projections of a 3D point into two cameras. If we fix the coordinates from one of the cameras, the equation reduces to the equation of a line for the coordinates of the other camera, which is consistent with the geometric reasoning that we made before.

concepts.title: Fundamental matrix
concepts.one_liner: The fundamental matrix relates pixel coordinates between two images in a stereo pair, incorporating both extrinsic and intrinsic camera parameters.
concepts.content:
The fundamental matrix $\mathbf{F}$ relates image coordinates in pixels (homogeneous coordinates $\mathbf{c}=[n,m,1]^\mathsf{T}$) between two cameras. It incorporates intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$ (such as pixel size and origin) into the epipolar constraint. The relationship is expressed as:
$$\mathbf{c}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F} \mathbf{c}_1 = 0$$

The fundamental matrix is related to the essential matrix $\mathbf{E}$ via the intrinsic matrix:
$$\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{K}^{\mathsf{T}}$$

Like the essential matrix, the fundamental matrix has rank 2. It has 7 degrees of freedom: out of 9 total elements, one is lost to scale ambiguity and one is lost because the determinant must be zero.
concepts.motivation_md: While the essential matrix works with calibrated camera coordinates, the fundamental matrix allows us to relate raw pixel coordinates directly, which is essential when the internal camera parameters are known but not yet removed from the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates raw pixel coordinates across two views using $\mathbf{c}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F} \mathbf{c}_1 = 0$.

key_passage.text: The equation relating image coordinates in both cameras has the same algebraic form as in equation ( $$\mathbf{c}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F} \mathbf{c}_1 = 0$$ where $\mathbf{F}$ is the **fundamental matrix**.

motivation.text: If we want to use image coordinates, in homogeneous coordinates, $\mathbf{c}=[n,m,1]^\mathsf{T}$, we need to also incorporate the intrinsic camera parameters (which will also incorporate pixel size and change of origin).

concepts.title: Conditional GAN as a Learned Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: A conditional GAN can be viewed as a regression problem where the discriminator acts as a learned loss function that adapts to the data structure and generator behavior.
concepts.content: One way to think about this setup is that it is a regression problem with a *learned loss function* $d_{\phi}$, a view shown in (see figure: The discriminator of a GAN as a learned loss function.). This loss function adapts to the structure of the data and the behavior of the generator to penalize just the relevant errors the generator is currently making. It can help to also add a conventional regression loss, such as the $L_1$ loss, to stabilize the optimization process, yielding the following objective: $$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_G\max_D \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert_1 \big] \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional loss functions like L1 or L2 often fail to capture complex data structures in image-to-image tasks. Using a GAN discriminator as a learned loss allows the model to adaptively penalize errors based on the data's underlying distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator $d_{\phi}$ serves as a learned loss function that adapts to the generator's specific errors.

key_passage.text: One way to think about this setup is that it is a regression problem with a learned loss function $d_{\phi}$, a view shown in This loss function adapts to the structure of the data and the behavior of the generator to penalize just the relevant errors the generator is currently making.

motivation.text: This loss function adapts to the structure of the data and the behavior of the generator to penalize just the relevant errors the generator is currently making. It can help to also add a conventional regression loss, such as the $L_1$ loss, to stabilize the optimization process.

concepts.title: PatchGAN Discriminator
concepts.one_liner: The PatchGAN is a discriminator architecture that scores individual image patches as real or fake and averages these scores to determine the total loss.
concepts.content: One popular architecture for image-to-image tasks is a **PatchGAN** discriminator, in which we score each *patch* in the output image as real or fake and take the average over patch scores as our total loss: $$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i=0}^N \sum_{j=0}^M d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}(\mathbf{x}[i:i+k,j:j+k], \mathbf{y}[i:i+k,j:j+k]) \end{aligned}$$ where $k \times k$ is the patch size. This operation is equivalent to the sliding window action of a CNN, so $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ can simply be implemented as a CNN that outputs a $2 \times N \times M$ feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores. Naturally, patches can be sampled at different strides and resolutions, depending on the exact architecture of the CNN $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard discriminators that score an entire image can be difficult to train and require many parameters. PatchGAN focuses on local structure, making the learning task more manageable and statistically efficient.
concepts.recap_md: - PatchGAN evaluates local $k \times k$ patches rather than the entire image to calculate a total loss.

key_passage.text: One popular architecture for image-to-image tasks is a PatchGAN discriminator, in which we score each patch in the output image as real or fake and take the average over patch scores as our total loss.

motivation.text: One of the main levers we have is the architecture of $d_{\phi}$; different architectures will have the capacity, and/or inductive bias, to penalize different kinds of errors.

concepts.title: Analysis of PatchGAN Patch Sizes
concepts.one_liner: PatchGAN discriminators offer statistical advantages by using fewer parameters on more data, though their effectiveness depends heavily on the chosen patch size.
concepts.content: The PatchGAN strategy has two advantages over scoring the whole image: it can be easier to model if a patch is real or synthetic ($d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ needs fewer parameters), and there are more patches in the training data than there are images. These properties give PatchGAN discriminators a statistical advantage. The disadvantage is that the PatchGAN only has the capacity to penalize errors observable within a single patch, as shown in (see figure: Varying the receptive field (patch size) of the convolutional discriminator affects what kinds of structure the discriminator enforces. These results are from @pix2pix2017). A $1\times1$ discriminator cannot penalize errors in joint pixel statistics like edge structure, resulting in blurry results. Larger receptive fields enforce higher order patch realism but cannot model structure larger than the patch size, potentially causing tiling artifacts. Quality may degrade with very large discriminators (e.g., $286\times286$) because the task becomes too hard given limited training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the trade-offs of patch sizes helps in designing discriminators that balance local detail with global structure while remaining computationally and statistically efficient.
concepts.recap_md: - Patch-based discriminators benefit from having fewer parameters and more training samples compared to whole-image discriminators.

key_passage.text: A 1×1 discriminator can only observe a single pixel at a time and cannot penalize errors in joint pixel statistics such as edge structure, hence the blurry results. Larger receptive fields can enforce higher order patch realism, but cannot model structure larger than the patch size (hence the tiling artifacts that are occur with a period roughly equal to the patch size).

motivation.text: The disadvantage is that the PatchGAN only has the architectural capacity to penalize errors that are observable within a single patch. This can be seen by training models with different discriminator patch sizes and observing the results.

concepts.title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired image-to-image translation is the task of learning to map between two domains without direct correspondence between specific training instances.
concepts.content: In many settings, paired training data $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ is hard to obtain. For example, translating a photo into a Cezanne painting (see figure: A style transfer example from the CycleGAN paper @CycleGAN2017 *Input photo source*: Alexei A. Efros.) would require the artist to paint specific scenes for our training set. However, humans can imagine these changes because we understand the general style of the target domain without needing exact pairs. This is the **unpaired translation** setting, distinguished from **paired translation** as shown in (see figure: (left) An example of paired image-to-image translation (colorization) versus (right) unpaired translation (photo to Cezanne). Figure adapted from @CycleGAN2017).
concepts.motivation_md: Paired datasets are often expensive or impossible to create. Unpaired translation allows models to learn mappings between domains using only independent sets of examples from each domain.
concepts.recap_md: - Unpaired translation maps between domains without requiring specific ground-truth pairs for training.

key_passage.text: We call this setting the unpaired translation setting, and distinguish it from paired translation as indicated in

question.text: How could this be done?

motivation.text: Unfortunately, very often, paired training data is hard to obtain. For example, consider the task of translating a photo into a Cezanne painting

concepts.title: Emergent Pairing in GANs
concepts.one_liner: In GANs, the specific mapping between input noise and output data is not predetermined but emerges during training to satisfy the objective of matching the data distribution.
concepts.content: GANs train a mapping from a noise distribution to a data distribution $p(Z) \rightarrow p(X)$. They do this without knowing the pairing between $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ values in the training data. Instead this pairing is *emergent*. Which $\mathbf{z}$-vector corresponds to which $\mathbf{x}$ is not predetermined but self-organizes to satisfy the GAN objective: all $\mathbf{z}$-vectors should map to realistic images, and, collectively they should map to the data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: This self-organizing property is what allows GANs to be applied to problems where explicit supervision of individual correspondences is unavailable.
concepts.recap_md: - The correspondence between input vectors and output samples in a GAN is not fixed beforehand.

key_passage.text: They do this without knowing the pairing between z and x values in the training data. Instead this pairing is emergent. Which z-vector corresponds to which x is not predetermined but self-organizes to satisfy the GAN objective.

motivation.text: GANs have a very useful property that makes them well-suited to solving this task. GANs train a mapping from a noise distribution to a data distribution p(Z) → p(X).

concepts.title: Symmetries in Unpaired Learning
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired learning problems contain many symmetries where different mappings achieve the same loss because the GAN objective only evaluates the output distribution, not individual instance matches.
concepts.content: A GAN may learn the correct mapping from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{y}$, but there are many symmetries in this learning problem where different mappings achieve equivalent loss. For example, any permutation in the mapping does not affect the output *distribution*, and the GAN objective only cares about the output distribution. Put another away, the GAN discriminator is different than a normal loss function. Rather than checking if the output matches a target *instance* (that $g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ matches $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$), it checks if the output is part of an admissible set of realistic $\mathbf{y}$ values. This property makes GANs perfect for working with unpaired data, where we don't have instance-level supervision but only have set-level supervision.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that standard GAN losses only enforce distribution matching explains why additional constraints are needed to ensure the learned mapping is meaningful and not just a random permutation.
concepts.recap_md: - The GAN objective is satisfied as long as the set of generated outputs matches the target distribution.

key_passage.text: This is because any permutation in the mapping does not affect the output distribution, and the GAN objective only cares about the output distribution.

motivation.text: This property makes GANs perfect for working with unpaired data, where we don't have instance-level supervision but only have set-level supervision.

concepts.title: Unpaired Learning
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired learning uses labels to identify which set a datapoint belongs to, providing set-level supervision rather than instance-level correspondence.
concepts.content: We call this **unpaired** learning rather than **unsupervised** because we still have supervision in the form of labels indicating which *set* each datapoint belongs to. That is, we know whether each image is an $\mathbf{x}$ or a $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between "unpaired" and "unsupervised" clarifies that the model still utilizes domain-level information to guide the learning process.
concepts.recap_md: - Unpaired learning is distinct from unsupervised learning because it utilizes domain labels.

key_passage.text: We call this unpaired learning rather than unsupervised because we still have supervision in the form of labels indicating which set each datapoint belongs to.

motivation.text: That is, we know whether each image is an x or a y.

concepts.title: Cycle-Consistency
concepts.one_liner: Cycle-consistency is a constraint requiring that a sample translated from one domain to another and back again should return to its original state.
concepts.content: A regular GAN objective for mapping $X$ to $Y$ does not distinguish between the correct mapping and others that achieve the same output distribution. To break the symmetry we need to add additional constraints like **cycle-consistency**. The idea is that if we translate from $X$ to $Y$ and then back to $X$, we should arrive where we started. In natural language processing, this is known as **backtranslation**. Cycle-consistency losses are regularizers that encourage a learned mapping to be roughly one-to-one. The cycle-consistency losses from CycleGAN are: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{x};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1\\ \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{y};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \end{aligned} $$
concepts.motivation_md: Without cycle-consistency, unpaired translation models can learn arbitrary mappings that satisfy the discriminator but lose the content of the input. This constraint ensures the mapping is reversible and preserves information.
concepts.recap_md: - Cycle-consistency requires that $f(g(x)) \approx x$ and $g(f(y)) \approx y$.

key_passage.text: The idea of cycle-consistency is that if we translate from X to Y and then translate back (from Y to X) we should arrive where we started.

motivation.text: a regular GAN objective, applied to mapping from X to Y, solves the unpaired translation problem, but it does not distinguish between the correct mapping and the many other mappings that achieve the same output distribution. To break the symmetry we need to add additional constraints or inductive biases.

concepts.title: Disparity vs Depth Representation
concepts.one_liner: Estimating 3D structure can be done via disparity or depth, with disparity often being easier to model due to its independence from camera parameters and uniform noise characteristics.
concepts.content: When estimating the 3D structure of a scene, we can represent the output as either disparity or depth. Disparity is often easier to estimate because it is independent of camera parameters. Furthermore, modeling noise is more straightforward with disparity, as we can assume noise is independent of the disparity value itself. In contrast, when using depth, the estimation error tends to increase for more distant points.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing between disparity and depth is a fundamental design decision in stereo vision. Disparity is preferred for its mathematical simplicity and stable noise properties, whereas depth is the ultimate physical quantity of interest but suffers from increasing error at a distance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Disparity is independent of camera parameters and has noise characteristics that are easier to model.
 - Depth estimation error increases for points that are further away from the camera.

key_passage.text: We can estimate the disparity or the depth. Disparity might be easier to estimate as it is independent of the camera parameters. It is also easier to model noise, as we can assume that noise is independent of disparity. However, when using depth, estimation error will be larger for distant points.

question.text: One important question is how we want to represent the output.

motivation.text: We are ultimately interested in estimating the 3D structure of the scene.

concepts.title: Disparity Regularization for Planar Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: For flat surfaces, the second-order derivative of disparity along any spatial direction is zero, a property that does not hold for depth.
concepts.content: An interesting property of disparity is that for flat surfaces, the second-order derivative along any spatial direction, $\mathbf{x}$, is zero: $$\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2}  = 0.$$ This equality does not hold for depth. This property allows for the introduction of a simple regularization term that favors planarity in the estimated scene.
concepts.motivation_md: This mathematical property provides a simple way to enforce a 'smoothness' or 'planarity' constraint in computer vision algorithms, helping to resolve ambiguities in disparity estimation for flat objects.
concepts.recap_md:
- The second-order derivative of disparity is zero for planar surfaces.
 - This property allows for simple regularization to favor planarity, which is not possible using depth directly.

key_passage.text: Another interesting property of disparity is that for flat surfaces, the second-order derivative along any spatial direction, $\mathbf{x}$, is zero: $$\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2} = 0.$$ This equality does not hold for depth.

motivation.text: This property allows introducing a simple regularization term that favors planarity.

concepts.title: Converting Disparity to Depth
concepts.one_liner: Depth is calculated by taking the inverse of the disparity value for a given pixel.
concepts.content: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity: $$\begin{aligned} z \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{ d \left[n,m \right] } \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: While algorithms often compute disparity for numerical stability, humans and robots require depth (actual distance) to navigate or interact with the 3D world.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth $z$ is the reciprocal of disparity $d$.
 - The conversion is performed per-pixel using the formula $z = 1/d$.

key_passage.text: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity, that is $z \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{ d \left[n,m \right] }$

concepts.title: Recovering World Coordinates from Depth
concepts.one_liner: World coordinates in the camera frame are recovered by multiplying the pixel's depth by the inverse of the intrinsic camera matrix.
concepts.content: To recover the world coordinates for every pixel, we assume a pinhole camera model. Using the depth $z \left[n,m \right]$ and the intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$, we obtain the 3D coordinates for a pixel with image coordinates $[n,m]$ in the camera reference frame as: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = z\left[n,m \right] \times \mathbf{K}^{-1} \times \begin{bmatrix} n \\ m \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ Note that $\mathbf{K}$ represents the intrinsic camera parameters for the reference image.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the 3D location of objects relative to the camera is essential for tasks like mapping, obstacle avoidance, and 3D modeling.
concepts.recap_md:
- 3D coordinates are recovered using depth and the inverse intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}^{-1}$.
 - The calculation transforms 2D image coordinates $[n, m]$ into 3D camera-frame coordinates $[X, Y, Z]$.

concepts.title: Two-Stage Neural Networks for Stereo
concepts.one_liner: Two-stage stereo networks use shared-weight feature extraction followed by a 3D convolutional neural net to aggregate matching costs and estimate disparity.
concepts.content:
Given two images, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$, the disparity at each location can be computed by a function $\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$. The objective is to minimize the difference between estimated disparities $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$ and ground truth $\mathbf{d}$, often using a loss function such as $J(\theta) = \sum_t \left| \mathbf{d} - f_{\theta} (\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) \right|^2$. 

When matching and filtering are implemented separately, a common formulation uses one neural network $g$ to extract features from both images and another network $c$ to compute matching costs: $f(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) = c \left( g(\mathbf{v}_1), g(\mathbf{v}_2) \right)$. A typical approach involves:
- Rectifying the stereo pair so scanlines align.
- Extracting features using a pair of networks with shared weights.
- Forming a 3D cost volume representing visual evidence of matches for each pixel and possible disparity.
- Applying a 3D convolutional neural net (CNN) to aggregate costs over the volume to estimate the best disparity for each pixel. This replaces traditional regularization steps like SGM with improved performance.

(see figure: Block diagram of CNN stereo processing, abstracted from the block diagrams of @Chang2018, @Zhang2019GANet, @Kendall2017)
concepts.motivation_md: Modern deep learning approaches improve upon traditional stereo matching by learning complex feature representations and cost aggregation strategies directly from data, leading to higher accuracy in challenging scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Stereo pairs are rectified and processed through shared-weight networks for feature extraction.
 - A 3D cost volume is formed and processed by a 3D CNN to estimate the final disparity map.
 - This neural approach effectively performs the role of regularization in traditional stereo algorithms.

key_passage.text: When matching and filtering are implemented separately, one common formulation is to use one neural network to extract features from both images, g(i₁) and g(i₂), and one neural network to compute the matching cost and estimate the disparities at every pixel.

motivation.text: The objective is that the estimated disparities, d̂, should be close to ground truth disparities, d.

concepts.title: Scenarios for Homography: Planar Scenes and Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a simple geometric transformation that maps pixels between images when the scene is planar or the camera undergoes pure rotation.
concepts.content:
In general, mapping pixels between two images from different viewpoints requires knowing the 3D scene structure and relative camera motion. However, in specific scenarios, a simple transformation called a homography can warp one image into another without 3D knowledge. This occurs when the scene is planar or when the two cameras are related only by a rotation. 

[FIGURE:d89ebe83f072de38]

[FIGURE:4c2d17b07db71aed]

These two images are (approximately) related by an homography. Homographies are used in applications such as perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, and creating bird's-eye views.
concepts.motivation_md: Homographies simplify image alignment by removing the need for complex 3D reconstruction in common cases like stitching panoramas or correcting the perspective of a flat document.
concepts.recap_md:
- Homographies apply when the scene is planar or the camera motion is pure rotation.
 - They allow image warping without requiring explicit 3D scene structure.
 - Common applications include image stitching and perspective correction.

key_passage.text: there are a few scenarios where we can find a simple transformation that allows warping one image into another image corresponding to a new camera location without requiring knowing the 3D scene structure: this will happen when the scene is planar or when the two cameras are related just by a rotation. In those two cases the coordinates of corresponding points across the two images are related by a homography.

motivation.text: Homographies can be used in applications such as perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, creating bird's-eye views, correcting keystone distortions for projected images, and many others.

concepts.title: Definition of Homography (Projective Transformation)
concepts.one_liner: A homography, or projective transformation, is a geometric transformation that preserves the collinearity of points and can be represented by a 3x3 matrix multiplication in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
A homography (or projective transformation) is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines. It is a function $h$ that maps points such that if points $\mathbf{p}_1$, $\mathbf{p}_2$, and $\mathbf{p}_3$ are collinear, their transformed versions $h(\mathbf{p}_1)$, $h(\mathbf{p}_2)$, and $h(\mathbf{p}_3)$ are also collinear. In homogeneous coordinates, this mapping $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$ is expressed as a product with a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{H}$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This is written compactly as $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$, where $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{p}'$ are 2D points in homogeneous coordinates.

(see figure: Homography. Colinear points remain colinear after transformation. Angles between lines are not preserved.)
concepts.motivation_md: Defining homographies mathematically using matrices allows us to use linear algebra to efficiently transform images and solve for camera parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- A homography preserves straight lines (collinearity) but not necessarily angles.
 - It is represented by a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{H}$ acting on homogeneous coordinates.
 - The transformation is defined by the linear relation $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$.

key_passage.text: A homography (or projective transformation) is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines. The homography is a function h that maps points into points, p' = h(p), with the property that if points p₁, p₂, and p₃ are colinear, then the transformed points h(p₁), h(p₂), and h(p₃) are also colinear.

concepts.title: Proof of Collinearity Preservation under Homography
concepts.one_liner: Collinearity is preserved under homography because the linear equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates remains a linear equation after the transformation.
concepts.content: To prove that collinear points remain collinear after a homography, we use the equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates, $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$. Given the homography relation $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$, we can express the original points as $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$. Substituting this into the line equation yields $(\mathbf{H} ^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$. This result is itself the equation of a line for the projected points $\mathbf{p}'$, confirming that they remain collinear.
concepts.motivation_md: This proof validates the fundamental property of homographies, ensuring that straight edges in the real world (like building corners) remain straight in warped images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The proof uses the homogeneous line equation $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$.
 - Substituting $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$ shows the transformed points satisfy a new line equation.
 - This confirms that projective transformations are indeed linear mappings in homogeneous space.

key_passage.text: To prove that colinear points remain colinear after the homography we can use the equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates, $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$. Replacing the last equality into the equation of the line gives $(\mathbf{H} ^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$, which corresponds to the equation of the line for the projected points $\mathbf{p}'$.

concepts.title: Measuring Heights Using Parallel Lines
concepts.one_liner: The height of an object can be estimated from a single image by projecting its vertical segment onto a reference object of known height using vanishing points and the cross-ratio invariant.
concepts.content:
To measure the height of an object (e.g., a desk) given a reference object (e.g., a bookshelf) in a scene, we must account for perspective projection which prevents direct comparison of 2D image distances. (see figure: Given the height of a reference object, the location of the horizon line and one vanishing point, how can we estimate the height of other objects in the scene?)

First, we project the desk height onto the bookshelf using the following steps in homogeneous coordinates:
1. Estimate the line $\boldsymbol{l}_1 = \mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b$ passing through the ground points of the desk $\mathbf{g}_d$ and bookshelf $\mathbf{g}_b$.
2. Compute the intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ with the horizon line $\mathbf{h}$ to find the vanishing point $\mathbf{a} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \mathbf{h}$.
3. Compute the line $\boldsymbol{l}_2 = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{t}_d$ passing through $\mathbf{a}$ and the top of the desk $\mathbf{t}_d$. Lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ are parallel in 3D and vertically aligned.
4. Find the intersection $\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol{l}_2 \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$, where $\mathbf{b}$ represents the top of the desk if it were moved into contact with the bookshelf.

The segment between $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{g}_b$ is the projection of the desk height on the bookshelf. Because of perspective foreshortening, we use the cross-ratio invariant between the four collinear points (top of bookshelf $\mathbf{t}_b$, projected desk top $\mathbf{b}$, ground $\mathbf{g}_b$, and vertical vanishing point $\mathbf{v}_3$) to relate image distances to 3D heights:
$$\frac{h_{\text{bookshelf}}}{h_{\text{desk}}} = \frac{\left| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{v}_3 \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{g}_b \right| }{\left| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{g}_b \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{v}_3  \right|}$$
Solving this equality allows for the estimation of the unknown height $h_{\text{desk}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In single-view metrology, we cannot directly compare the sizes of objects at different depths because perspective projection causes distant objects to appear smaller. This technique solves the problem of measuring an unknown height by geometrically 'moving' it to a reference location where its size can be compared to a known standard using projective invariants.
concepts.recap_md: - Project the target height onto a reference object by finding a common vanishing point on the horizon line.

key_passage.text: Lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ are parallel on 3D and vertically aligned. In order to use the cross-ratio invariant we need two sets of four colinear points related by a projective geometry.

question.text: Can we use this information together with the geometry of the scene to estimate the height of the desk, $h_{\text{desk}}$?

motivation.text: Due to perspective projection, we can not directly compare the relative height of the desk with respect to the height of the bookshelf using distances measured over the image. In order to be able to compare 3D distances using 2D image distances both objects need to be put in correspondence first.

concepts.title: Projective Invariants
concepts.one_liner: Projective invariants are geometric measures that remain unchanged after a perspective projection.
concepts.content: Projective invariants are measures that do not change after perspective projection. The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.
concepts.motivation_md: Perspective projection distorts lengths and angles, making it difficult to recover 3D information from 2D images. Projective invariants provide a mathematical way to identify properties that stay constant despite this distortion, enabling 3D reconstruction and measurement.
concepts.recap_md: - Invariants are properties that are preserved under perspective transformations.

key_passage.text: Projective invariants are measures that do not change after perspective projection. The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.

concepts.title: Height Propagation to Supported Objects
concepts.one_liner: Height information can be propagated from objects on the ground to objects supported by them to measure heights not in contact with the ground plane.
concepts.content: The method of measuring heights relies on using vertical lines in contact with the ground plane to propagate information from one point in space to another. While this method requires establishing the vertical projection of a point onto a reference plane (like the ground), it can be extended. Once the height of objects in contact with the ground is estimated, that information can be used to propagate 3D measurements to other objects that are not directly on the ground, provided they are supported by objects of known height.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard single-view metrology often requires objects to touch the ground plane to establish a reference. This technique allows for the measurement of 'floating' or stacked objects by treating the supporting object as a secondary reference plane.
concepts.recap_md: - Vertical projection to a reference plane is required to propagate measurements between points.

key_passage.text: once we have estimated the height of objects that are in contact with the ground, we can use them to propagate 3D information to other objects not directly on top of the ground. We can estimate the height of objects that are not in contact with the ground if they are on top of objects of known

motivation.text: The method can not work if we can not establish the vertical projection of a point into the ground plane (or any other plane of reference). But once we have estimated the height of objects that are in contact with the ground, we can use them to propagate 3D information to other objects not directly on top of the ground.

concepts.title: Supported-by hierarchy
concepts.one_liner: The supported-by hierarchy is the structural parsing of which objects in a scene provide physical support for others.
concepts.content: This procedure highlights the importance of the correct parsing of the supported-by hierarchy between objects in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: To measure objects not touching the ground, a vision system must understand the physical relationships between objects—specifically, which object supports another—to correctly propagate height measurements upward from the ground plane.
concepts.recap_md: - Correct parsing of object support relationships is essential for 3D scene measurement.

key_passage.text: This procedure highlights the importance of the correct parsing of the supported-by hierarchy between objects in the scene.

concepts.title: 3D Metrology from a Single View
concepts.one_liner: 3D metrology from a single view uses reference objects and vanishing points to extract 3D locations and measurements from a 2D image.
concepts.content: 3D metrology involves using a reference object to measure other objects and establishing a general framework to locate 3D points. In a typical scene, the axes of a 3D coordinate frame can be aligned with the three dominant orthogonal orientations, which in turn align with the image's vanishing points. (see figure: Can we find out where to put the ticks in the world-coordinate axes as seen by the camera so that they correspond to calibrated measurements? Simply placing them at evenly spaced intervals along the...) By calibrating the projected world-coordinate axes in the image plane, we can transport points into the 3D world axes to measure object sizes and point locations.
concepts.motivation_md: Normally, a single 2D image loses depth information, making 3D measurement impossible. Single-view metrology recovers this information by exploiting geometric constraints like vanishing points and known reference dimensions.
concepts.recap_md: - Vanishing points and reference objects allow for the calibration of 3D axes in a 2D image.

key_passage.text: We will show how can we use the world-coordinates in order to extract 3D object locations from a single image.

question.text: Can we find out where to put the ticks in the world-coordinate axes as seen by the camera so that they correspond to calibrated measurements?

motivation.text: In the previous section we showed how to use a reference object to measure other objects. Let's now discuss a more general framework to locate 3D points.

concepts.title: Calibration of the Projected World Axis
concepts.one_liner: Calibrating projected world axes involves using the cross-ratio and reference measurements to place non-linearly spaced tick marks along image axes.
concepts.content: To calibrate world-coordinate axes in an image, one must determine the correct positions for tick marks (e.g., 1m, 2m). Due to perspective distortion, these marks are not evenly spaced in the image plane. The calibration process uses the cross-ratio invariant, the horizon line of a reference plane, the position of orthogonal vanishing points, and the known real-world measurement of at least one object. (see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.) By using reference measurements (such as a bookshelf height or table radius), we can solve for the image locations of specific units (e.g., $\alpha_X=\alpha_Y=\alpha_Z=1$ m). (see figure: Calibrated world axes. Each axis is calibrated using the measurement of a scene element parallel to the world-coordinate axis. In this example, we used the bookshelf height (197 cm) and the radius of...) Once the system is calibrated, one can read 3D information directly, such as the camera height, which corresponds to the horizon line location in a horizontal ground plane scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Because of perspective foreshortening, a pixel distance at the bottom of an image represents a different physical distance than the same pixel distance near the horizon. Calibrating the axes allows us to map these non-linear image coordinates back to linear real-world measurements.
concepts.recap_md: - Perspective distortion prevents even spacing of coordinate ticks in the image plane.

key_passage.text: We will use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane. For doing this we will need the location of the horizon line of a reference plane (i.e. the ground plane), the position of the orthogonal vanishing point and the real measure of one object in the scene.

question.text: Where should we position the tick marks that correspond to 1, 2, 3, ... meters from the origin on each axis in

motivation.text: Due to geometric distortion introduced by perspective projection, the tick marks are not evenly spaced within the image plane. This distortion affects each axis in a distinct manner.

concepts.title: Locating a 3D Point
concepts.one_liner: A 3D point's coordinates can be recovered from a single view by using its projection onto the ground plane and its relationship to calibrated world axes.
concepts.content:
While a single point $\mathbf{P}$ cannot be localized in 3D from a single view without context, the presence of objects and known geometry allows for 3D estimation. If a point $\mathbf{P}$ belongs to an object in contact with the ground, we can identify its ground projection $\mathbf{G}$. (see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...)

Once $\mathbf{G}$ is located, it can be projected onto the world-coordinate axes. To find the $Y$-coordinate, we find the line $\boldsymbol{l}_3$ through $\mathbf{G}$ and the origin, find its intersection $\mathbf{v}$ with the horizon, and then find the intersection of line $\boldsymbol{l}_4$ (connecting $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{P}$) with the $Y_w$-axis. The $P_x$ and $P_z$ coordinates are found by connecting $\mathbf{G}$ to the vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.
concepts.motivation_md: Recovering 3D coordinates from a 2D image is an ill-posed problem because many 3D points project to the same 2D pixel. By assuming the point is part of an object on a known plane (like the ground), we can resolve this ambiguity.
concepts.recap_md: - Projecting a point onto the ground plane is the key step to resolving its 3D position.

key_passage.text: It suffices to know that the point P belongs to an object that is in contact with the ground and the geometry of this object provides the information to localize the projection of the point P on the ground plane, which we denote with G. Once we know the image location of the projection of the 3D point P to the ground, G, we can project this point to the world-coordinate axis.

motivation.text: In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of a single point P from a single view. But real world scenes are composed by a multitude of objects providing context, which allows solving the 3D estimation problem even with just a single image.

concepts.title: Camera Calibration from Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: Camera intrinsics can be estimated from three orthogonal vanishing points by solving for the conic matrix under the constraint of 3D orthogonality.
concepts.content:
Camera parameters can be extracted using only vanishing points, provided certain conditions are met. In scenes with many parallel lines aligned with the world coordinate system, the three vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_i$ correspond to three orthogonal 3D directions $\mathbf{D}_i$. The relationship between these is given by $\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i$. Because the directions are orthogonal ($\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$), we derive a constraint that depends only on the intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{K}$:
$$\mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j = 0$$
We define the conic matrix $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$. Assuming the camera skew is zero, $\mathbf{W}$ has a specific structure with four unknown values. These values can be solved as a system of linear equations $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{w} = 0$ using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Finally, $\mathbf{K}$ is recovered from $\mathbf{W}$ via Cholesky factorization and normalization.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional camera calibration requires specialized patterns or known 3D point correspondences.
