This method allows for 'self-calibration' using only the geometric structure (parallel and orthogonal lines) naturally present in man-made environments like offices or city streets.
concepts.recap_md: - Orthogonal vanishing points provide linear constraints on the camera's intrinsic matrix.

key_passage.text: We will use the vanishing points to derive a set of constraints on the projection matrix. To do this, we start by inverting equation: $\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i$ Because the vectors $\mathbf{D}_i$ are orthogonal, we have that $\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$.

motivation.text: Here we will see a different method that uses only the vanishing points to extract the camera parameters; note that this method will only work under some conditions.

concepts.title: Rigidity assumption

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Any set of elements undergoing a 2D transformation with a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion.
concepts.content: The rigidity assumption, introduced by Shimon Ullman in 1979, states: "Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion." This principle is fundamental to the problem of structure from motion (SFM), allowing for the 3D reconstruction of objects based on their movement.
concepts.motivation_md: The rigidity assumption provides a necessary constraint to solve the otherwise ill-posed problem of recovering 3D structure from 2D motion. Without assuming objects are rigid, an infinite number of non-rigid deformations could explain any 2D image sequence.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes that 2D transformations representing a possible rigid 3D motion should be interpreted as such.

key_passage.text: Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion.

motivation.text: the rigidity assumption introduced by Shimon Ullman in 1979 where he writes: "Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion."

concepts.title: Tomasi and Kanade SFM algorithm

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: An early structure from motion algorithm that uses keypoint trajectories under parallel projection to recover 3D point locations.
concepts.content: One of the first algorithms for structure from motion for rigid bodies was introduced by Tomasi and Kanade. For simplicity, their approach assumed parallel projection (orthographic camera) instead of perspective projection. The algorithm takes as input a video sequence captured by a moving camera looking at a static scene. The video is first processed by extracting keypoints and tracking them over time. The input to the reconstruction algorithm is the keypoint trajectories and the output is the 3D locations of those points with respect to a reference world-coordinate system, usually defined by the first frame in the video. This model was later extended by Sturm and Triggs to handle perspective projection.
concepts.motivation_md: This algorithm was developed to provide a systematic way to recover 3D scene geometry from a continuous video stream by tracking specific points over time.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses keypoint trajectories from a video sequence as input.

key_passage.text: One of the first algorithms for structure from motion for rigid bodies was introduced by Tomasi and Kanade. For simplicity, their approach assumed parallel projection (orthographic camera) instead of perspective projection. The algorithm took as input a video sequence captured by a moving camera looking at a static scene. The video was first processed by extracting keypoints and tracking them over time. The input to the reconstruction algorithm was the keypoint trajectories and the output was the 3D locations of those points with respect to a reference world-coordinate system (usually defined by the first frame in the video).

concepts.title: General Multiview SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: General SFM reconstructs 3D scenes from multiple images taken by different cameras without assumptions about camera placement.
concepts.content: The task of SFM became more general, and instead of focusing on one moving camera, SFM was applied to the problem of reconstructing the 3D scene even from multiple images taken by different cameras and making no assumption about the placement of the cameras. Work by Snavely et al. showed how one could produce spectacular registrations and camera pose estimates of images taken with many different cameras, such as reconstructing famous buildings from pictures taken by tourists.
concepts.motivation_md: General multiview SFM allows for 3D reconstruction from unstructured image collections, such as internet photo sets, where camera parameters and positions are unknown and inconsistent.
concepts.recap_md: - Reconstructs 3D scenes from multiple, uncoordinated cameras.

key_passage.text: SFM was applied to the problem of reconstructing the 3D scene even from multiple images taken by different cameras and making no assumption about the placement of the cameras.

motivation.text: The task of SFM became more general, and instead of focusing on one moving camera, SFM was applied to the problem of reconstructing the 3D scene even from multiple images taken by different cameras and making no assumption about the placement of the cameras.

concepts.title: Sparse SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Sparse SFM recovers the 3D structure of a scene and camera locations from a set of images with overlapping content.
concepts.content:
Given a set of $M$ images with overlapping content, the goal of sparse SFM is to recover the 3D structure of the scene and the location of the camera for each image. 

[FIGURE:add3ece10bc2f8e3 | ]

[FIGURE:a44c3c8790d4afeb | ]

[FIGURE:cfac5559fd2fbafc | ]

[FIGURE:754710267c564352 | ]

[FIGURE:f92487351d88e5fd | ]

[FIGURE:849fc092066afb75 | ]

[FIGURE:97d38dd3274f362c | ]

[FIGURE:4419d604d757ae28 | ]

[FIGURE:38cd2d42f4569d8c | ]

[FIGURE:e356046160152df4 | ]

[FIGURE:c3ad7e7def8df202 | ]

[FIGURE:7584772085ce40bb | ]

Twelve viewpoints of a sugar bowl we had at home. Although it is not a fancy object, it is useful to start with a simple shape to check what happens on every step. The bowl has a rough texture that might also allow for enough keypoints to be present along its surface. The images have $3,024 \times 4,032$ pixels.

[FIGURE:650332b40afe8612 | ]

[FIGURE:75a0127601cdecc8 | ]

[FIGURE:2c89fbe1dc622d06 | ]

[FIGURE:9326a080edd0d9c2 | ]

[FIGURE:48d19a31f0eb162b | ]

[FIGURE:db2e3b3cb4baa606 | ]

[FIGURE:e527b7ec74b0fa55 | ]

[FIGURE:11392eedbcfc69c0 | ]

Eight pictures taken in a plaza in Palma de Mallorca, Spain. The images have $3,024 \times 4,032$ pixels.

In the sparse SFM problem, we consider that in the scene there are $N$ distinct points (where $N$ is smaller than the number of pixels on each image) that are matched across $M$ different views. We denote the $N$ 3D points as $\mathbf{P}_i$. For each of the $M$ views, we denote the projection of point $\mathbf{P}_i$ as seen by camera $j$ by $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$. Each view has camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$, and ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$. The goal is to recover 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$, the intrinsic camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, and the extrinsic camera parameters ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$ and ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$ for each camera $j$ given the set of corresponding 2D points $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$.

Assuming calibrated cameras where ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$ is known, we have $3N$ unknowns for the 3D points and $6(M-1)-1$ unknowns for the extrinsic parameters of $M-1$ cameras (assuming the first camera is at the origin). With $2NM$ observations, a solution is possible when $$2NM \geq 3N + 6(M-1)-1$$
concepts.motivation_md: Sparse SFM provides a mathematical framework to reconstruct 3D geometry using only a small set of identifiable feature points rather than every pixel, making the computation more efficient and robust to noise.
concepts.recap_md: - Recovers 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}, {\mathbf R}^{(j)}, {\mathbf T}^{(j)}$ from 2D correspondences $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$.

key_passage.text: In the sparse SFM problem, we consider that in the scene there are N distinct points (with N smaller than the number of pixels on each image) that are matched across M different views (we will consider later that not all points may be visible across all images).

motivation.text: The goal of the SFM problem is, given the set of corresponding 2D points p^(j)_i, recover 3D points P_i, the intrinsic camera parameters, K^(j), and the extrinsic camera parameters R^(j) and T^(j), for each camera j.

concepts.title: Scale drift

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The accumulation of slight numerical errors in scale factor when adding new images to a 3D reconstruction over time.
concepts.content: When every point is not visible in every view, each new image added to a structure from motion (SFM) reconstruction must be triangulated with respect to its closest image. In doing so, slight numerical errors may occur, causing the new frame to have an ever-so-slightly different scale factor with respect to the reconstruction. This error accumulates over time, causing scale drift.
concepts.motivation_md: Scale drift is a critical problem in incremental SFM and SLAM because it leads to geometric inconsistencies where the reconstructed scene's size and distances become distorted over long sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Occurs when new frames are triangulated with slight numerical errors in scale.

key_passage.text: when doing so, we may have a slight numerical error, and this new frame may end up having an ever-so-slightly different scale factor with respect to the reconstruction. This accumulates over time, causing scale drift.

motivation.text: if the visibility criteria isn't met, for each new image we are adding in to SFM, we will need to triangulate it with respect to its closest image

concepts.title: Bundle adjustment

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The process of optimizing the 'bundle of rays' connecting camera centers and 3D point coordinates to minimize reprojection error.
concepts.content: Bundle adjustment refers to the process of optimizing the "bundle of rays" connecting the camera centers and the coordinates of the 3D points. It is also described as the optimization of the reprojection error.
concepts.motivation_md: Bundle adjustment is used to refine initial 3D reconstructions and camera poses, ensuring that the final model is as consistent as possible with all observed 2D image data.
concepts.recap_md: - Optimizes the reprojection error of a 3D reconstruction.

key_passage.text: The term bundle adjustment refers to the process of optimizing the "bundle of rays" connecting the camera centers and the coordinates of the 3D points.

motivation.text: of the reprojection error is also called bundle adjustment.

concepts.title: Interest points

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Image locations that are likely to be stable under different geometric transformations and illumination changes.
concepts.content: The goal of finding image features is to locate image locations that are likely to be stable under different sets of geometric transformations (translation, scaling, rotation, skew, and projective) and illumination changes. These stable regions are called interest points.
concepts.motivation_md: Interest points provide reliable landmarks in an image that can be matched across different views, which is a prerequisite for tasks like 3D reconstruction and object recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Stable image regions used as features for matching across views.

key_passage.text: These stable regions are called interest points.

motivation.text: The goal of finding image features is to locate image locations that are likely to be stable under different sets of geometric transformations (translation, scaling, rotation, skew, and projective), and illumination changes.

concepts.title: Moving element

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: An early term for interest points, referring to any image point that could be identified and followed over time.
concepts.content: Initially, interest points were called moving elements. A moving element was defined as any image point that could be identified and followed over time, such as a corner, a line termination point, or a texture element.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept was developed in early computer vision to describe the basic primitives needed to track motion and infer structure from temporal sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - An early name for interest points.

key_passage.text: A moving element was any image point that could be identified and followed over time such as a corner, a line termination point, or a texture element

concepts.title: Homography from Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The coordinates of corresponding points across images taken from the same point by rotating the camera are related by a homography, independently of their distance.
concepts.content:
When three images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera with no translation between positions, the coordinates of corresponding points are related by a homography. This relationship holds independently of how far the points are from the camera. 

[FIGURE:1db46673e5bbe185]

[FIGURE:8267e250a2c64ddf]

[FIGURE:83ad2f9f3b5c333e]

Setting the world coordinate system to align with camera 1, the projection of a 3D point $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$ into the camera 1 plane (with zero translation) is:
$$\lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}$$

Projecting the same point into camera 2 with rotation $\mathbf{R}$ and zero translation gives:
$$\lambda_2 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: Camera rotation generates two images related by a homography.)

By inverting these projections, we find the relationship between corresponding image points in homogeneous coordinates:
$$\lambda_2 / \lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This can be written as $\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, where $\mathbf{H}$ is a $3\times3$ matrix. This relationship also holds if the two cameras have different intrinsic parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how images can be perfectly aligned or stitched together when the camera only rotates. It proves that for a purely rotating camera, the transformation between views is a simple linear mapping in homogeneous coordinates, which is essential for creating panoramas from a single tripod location.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure camera rotation (zero translation) results in image coordinates related by a $3\times3$ homography matrix.

key_passage.text: the coordinates of the corresponding points across each pair of images are related by a homography independently of how far they are from the camera.

motivation.text: The three images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera. There is no translation between the three camera positions as the photographer took the three images by keeping the camera origin static when moving the camera. Under this condition, the coordinates of the corresponding points across each pair of images are related by a homography independently of how far they are from the camera.

concepts.title: Homography from Planar Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points inside that plane are related by a homography.
concepts.content:
When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points across the two views for points inside that plane are related by a homography. 

[FIGURE:8d12e88a6496cd81]

[FIGURE:d33152acf9add1c2]

To prove this, we place the world-coordinate system on the plane such that $Z=0$. 

(see figure: Geometry of a the projection of a planar scene. The origin of the world-coordinates system is placed inside the plane and the $Z$-axis is perpendicular to it.)

The projection equation for a camera is:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

By setting $Z=0$ for points on the plane, the equation simplifies to:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 &\mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

where $\mathbf{c}_i$ is the $i$-th column of the rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$. Since this is a product of two $3 \times 3$ matrices, it can be written as $\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Because this holds for any camera, the relationship between corresponding points in two cameras viewing the same plane is also a homography.
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world scenes, such as buildings or roads, the geometry is dominated by flat surfaces. Understanding that planar surfaces map between views via a homography allows for tasks like perspective correction, document scanning, and augmented reality overlays on flat surfaces.
concepts.recap_md: - Points on a 3D plane map to image coordinates via a homography.

key_passage.text: This last result shows that the coordinates of points on the plane are related to the corresponding points in the image plane by a homography.

motivation.text: A second case is when two cameras observe a 2D plane. In that case, the coordinates of corresponding points across the two camera views, for points inside the plane, are related by a homography.

concepts.title: Homography vs Epipolar Constraint
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint but only applies under specific conditions.
concepts.content: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint between corresponding points across two camera views. However, the homography only applies under certain conditions—such as a purely rotating camera or a planar scene—while the epipolar constraint always holds for any general motion and scene geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: It is important to distinguish between general geometric constraints (epipolar) and specific geometric constraints (homography). Knowing when to use a homography allows for more precise modeling when the scene is planar or the camera motion is restricted.
concepts.recap_md: - Homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint.

key_passage.text: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint between corresponding points across two camera views. However, the homography only applies under certain conditions as we have seen, while the epipolar constraint always holds.

concepts.title: Direct Linear Transform (DLT) for Homography Estimation
concepts.one_liner: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) estimates a homography matrix from a set of point correspondences by solving a linear system.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Two overlapping images and some found correspondences using SURF descriptors. A random set of four correspondences are highlighted.)

Given a set of point correspondences across two cameras, we can compute the homography relating the locations of imaged points using the direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm. This results in a linear set of equations for the parameters of the homography matrix in the form $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is a $2N \times 9$ matrix for $N$ corresponding pairs. 

The vector $\mathbf{h}$ contains the 9 elements of the matrix $\mathbf{H}$ stacked as a column vector. Since $\mathbf{h}$ has only 8 degrees of freedom (due to global scaling), at least four correspondences are required for estimation. The solution is the eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$ corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue, which minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$. In practice, it is useful to further minimize the reprojection error after initialization with DLT, as the algebraic residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$ lacks geometric meaning.
concepts.motivation_md: To align images or map points between views, we need a mathematical method to calculate the transformation matrix. DLT provides a direct, linear way to solve for this matrix using simple point matches.
concepts.recap_md: - DLT solves $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$ to estimate the $3 \times 3$ homography matrix.

key_passage.text: To estimate the homography we can use the direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm, as we did for the camera calibration problem in This will give us a linear set of equations for the parameters of the homography matrix with the form: $$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is a$2N \times 9$ matrix, when given $N$ corresponding pairs.

motivation.text: Given a set of point locations, and their correspondences across the two cameras, we can compute the homography relating the locations of imaged points within the two cameras.

concepts.title: RANSAC (Random Sampling with Consensus)
concepts.one_liner: RANSAC is a robust model-fitting algorithm that uses random sampling and consensus to handle data containing outliers.
concepts.content:
RANSAC, which stands for random sampling with consensus, is an algorithm used to fit models to data robustly, particularly when feature point detection is noisy or contains mismatches. 

The procedure is as follows:
1. Randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of a model (such as a line or a homography).
2. Compute the model parameters from this randomly sampled set.
3. Identify the inliers in the dataset—datapoints that fit the model within a specified tolerance.
4. Repeat this procedure $N$ times.
5. Compute a final model using the set of inliers corresponding to the largest consensus set found across all iterations.
concepts.motivation_md: In real-world computer vision, many point matches are incorrect (outliers). Standard least-squares methods fail in the presence of even a few outliers; RANSAC allows us to find the correct model by ignoring the 'noise'.
concepts.recap_md: - RANSAC fits models by repeatedly sampling small subsets of data and checking for consensus.

key_passage.text: First, randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of some model. Then, compute the model parameters from the randomly sampled set of points. Compute the inliers in the dataset, that is, the datapoints that fit the model (or achieve consensus) to within some tolerance. Repeat that procedure some number of times, N. Compute a final model from the set of inlier points corresponding to the largest number of inlier datapoints.

motivation.text: Because the detection of the feature points can be noisy, the homography fitting needs to be robust against inevitable feature mismatches between images. A good algorithm to fit models to data robustly is RANSAC, which stands for random sampling with concensus.

concepts.title: Heuristic for RANSAC Sample Count
concepts.one_liner: The number of RANSAC iterations required to find a good fit depends on the probability of selecting inliers and the desired confidence level.
concepts.content:
A heuristic can be derived for the number of samples $k$ required to ensure a good model fit with probability $p$. Let $n$ be the number of datapoints required to specify the model, and $w$ be the estimated probability that any selected datapoint is an inlier. 

The probability that all selected points in one trial are inliers is $w^n$, and the probability that at least one is an outlier is $1 - w^n$. The probability that only bad models are selected in $k$ trials is $(1 - w^n)^k$. Setting this equal to $1-p$ and solving for $k$ gives:
$$k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$$

For example, if $w=0.18$ and $n=2$, achieving 95% accuracy requires $k=91$ trials. In practice, points should be selected without replacement to avoid degenerate fits, though the analysis assumes selection with replacement. This assumption is valid when the number of selected points is small relative to the total dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Running RANSAC indefinitely is inefficient. This heuristic provides a mathematical way to determine the minimum number of iterations needed to be confident that we have found the correct model.
concepts.recap_md: - The number of iterations $k$ is calculated based on the inlier ratio $w$ and model size $n$.

key_passage.text: Taking the logarithm of both sides lets us solve for k, the number of RANSAC iterations required to find a good fit, with probability p: k = log(1-p)/log(1-w^n)

motivation.text: The paper derives a heuristic for the number of samples, S, required to be assured a good model fit.

concepts.title: Homography Estimation using RANSAC
concepts.one_liner: Homography estimation using RANSAC involves repeatedly sampling four point correspondences to robustly calculate the transformation matrix via DLT.
concepts.content: In the case of homography estimation, eight equations are required to use the DLT algorithm to estimate $\mathbf{H}$. Since each point correspondence contributes two equations, a minimum of four corresponding points is needed. To perform robust estimation, multiple sets of four points are randomly selected, and RANSAC is used to determine the homography that best fits the majority of the correspondences between two images.
concepts.motivation_md: Because feature matching often produces 'false positives' (points that look similar but aren't the same physical point), combining DLT with RANSAC is the standard way to reliably estimate a homography in real-world images.
concepts.recap_md: - Estimating a homography requires a minimum of four point correspondences.

key_passage.text: We can sample multiple randomly selected sets of four points and use RANSAC to estimate the homography between two images.

motivation.text: In the case of the homography estimation, we need eight equations to use the DLT algorithm to estimate H. As each point contributes two equations, we need four corresponding points.

concepts.title: Image Stitching
concepts.one_liner: Image stitching uses estimated homographies to align and warp multiple overlapping images into a single panoramic view.
concepts.content:
Using DLT and RANSAC, the homography between each pair of images can be computed to align them with respect to a reference image. These estimated homographies allow for warping all images into a single camera view to create a panoramic image.

(see figure: Panoramic image composed by the three overlapping images from @fig-example_three_images)
concepts.motivation_md: Image stitching is the technology behind panoramic photos on smartphones. It allows a narrow field-of-view camera to capture wide-angle scenes by combining multiple overlapping shots.
concepts.recap_md: - Homographies are used to warp and align multiple images into a common reference frame.

key_passage.text: Using DLT and RANSAC with can compute the homography between each pair of images in figure and align them with respect to a reference image (in this example we pick the middle image as a reference). We can use the estimated homographies to warp all of the images into a single camera view as shown in fig-panorama.

concepts.title: The Plenoptic Function
concepts.one_liner: The plenoptic function is a full description of all light rays traveling across space, defining intensity based on position, direction, wavelength, and time.
concepts.content:
The plenoptic function describes what can potentially be seen by capturing the information about the world contained in the light filling a region of space. Given a scene, it provides a full description of all the light rays that travel across the space. The function tells us the light intensity of a light ray passing through the three-dimensional (3D) point $(X, Y, Z)$ from the direction given by the angles $(\psi, \phi)$, with wavelength $\lambda$, at time $t$: $$L(X, Y, Z, \psi, \phi, \lambda, t)$$ In practice, time is often ignored and continuous wavelength is replaced by three color channels. The function can be represented in a parametric form $L_{\theta}$ where the parameters $\theta$ are adapted to represent each specific scene.

(see figure: Plenoptic function @Adelson91. The figure shows a slice of the plenoptic function at four locations. Two of the locations are in free space, and two other locations are inside a pinhole camera.)

An image is formed by summing all the light rays that reach each sensor on a camera, which corresponds to summing over a section of the plenoptic function. Inside a pinhole camera, the plenoptic function has most values set to zero, with non-zero values only at specific directions at each location to form an image of the exterior.
concepts.motivation_md: The plenoptic function provides a unified mathematical framework to describe all available visual information in a scene. It serves as the theoretical foundation for computer vision and graphics, allowing researchers to treat image formation as the process of sampling a subset of this high-dimensional light field.
concepts.recap_md: - The plenoptic function $L(X, Y, Z, \psi, \phi, \lambda, t)$ describes the intensity of every light ray in a volume.

key_passage.text: Given a scene, the plenoptic function is a full description of all the light rays that travel across the space. The plenoptic function tells us the light intensity of a light ray passing through the three-dimensional (3D) point (X, Y, Z) from the direction given by the angles (ψ, φ), with wavelength λ, at time t: L(X, Y, Z, ψ, φ, λ, t)

question.text: What information about the world is contained in the light filling a region of space?

motivation.text: A radiance field can be considered as a way to represent a portion of the plenoptic function.

concepts.title: Radiance Field
concepts.one_liner: A radiance field is a function that assigns color and volumetric density to every point in space, often including viewing direction.
concepts.motivation_md: Radiance fields allow for the representation of complex 3D geometry and appearance (like transparency and specularity) in a continuous format that is well-suited for differentiable rendering and neural optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - A radiance field maps spatial coordinates and viewing angles to RGB color and density $\sigma$.

key_passage.text: A radiance field is a representation of part of the plenoptic function, based on the idea that the optical content of a scene can be modeled as a cloud of colorful particles with different levels of transparency. We will presently define a radiance field $L$ as a mapping from the coordinates in a scene to color and density (i.e. transparency) values of the scene content at those coordinates.

motivation.text: Such a representation can be rendered into images using volume rendering, which we will learn about in The angular coordinates $\psi$ and $\phi$ allow that an object's color be different depending on the angle we look at it, which is the case for shiny surfaces and many other materials.

concepts.title: Vector Fields
concepts.one_liner: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space.
concepts.content: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space. For example, a vector field might be defined as $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$, where $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are spatial coordinates and $v_1$ and $v_2$ are the resulting values. Radiance fields are a specific application of vector fields used to represent scenes.
concepts.motivation_md: Vector fields provide a general mathematical language for describing spatially varying properties, such as fluid flow, electromagnetic forces, or, in this context, the visual properties of a 3D scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Vector fields map spatial coordinates to a vector of values.

key_passage.text: Radiance fields are an example of vector fields, which are functions that assign a vector to each position in space.

motivation.text: they turn out to be a very important way of representing scenes

concepts.title: Voxel Fields
concepts.one_liner: Voxel fields are discrete 3D grids that represent values like spatial occupancy or color, functioning as 3D versions of pixels.
concepts.content: Voxel fields, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow \mathbf{v}$, are discrete fields that represent values $\mathbf{v}$ such as spatial occupancy, flux, or color within a volume. They are essentially 3D pixels. Like pixels, they possess the property of being piecewise constant over cubes defined by their resolution.
concepts.motivation_md: Voxels provide a straightforward way to discretize 3D space for storage and computation, making them useful for medical imaging, 3D modeling, and physical simulations.
concepts.recap_md: - Voxels are discrete 3D units that are piecewise constant over their resolution.

key_passage.text: Voxel fields, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow \mathbf{v}$ are discrete fields that can represent values $\mathbf{v}$ like spatial occupancy, flux, or color in a volume.

concepts.title: Signed Distance Functions (SDFs)
concepts.one_liner: A signed distance function (SDF) represents the distance from any point in space to the closest surface of an object.
concepts.content: Signed distance functions (SDFs), $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface from a given point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$. This is a useful representation for defining and manipulating 3D geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: SDFs are highly efficient for determining surface intersections and performing geometric operations like boolean unions or subtractions in computer graphics.
concepts.recap_md: - An SDF maps a 3D point to its distance from the nearest surface.

key_passage.text: Signed distance functions (SDFs), $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface to point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$.

motivation.text: This is a useful representation of geometry.

concepts.title: Implicit Representation of Fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Implicit representations define a field using a function and a finite set of parameters rather than explicitly storing values at every coordinate.
concepts.content: An implicit representation of a field does not explicitly store values at all coordinates. Instead, it records a finite set of parameters for a function that can calculate the field's value at any given coordinate.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit representations allow for infinite resolution and significantly lower memory usage compared to explicit grids (like voxels) by leveraging the predictive power of functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Implicit representations use parameterized functions instead of explicit data grids.

key_passage.text: Sometimes this is called an implicit representation of the field, since we don't explicitly store the values of the field at all coordinates. Instead we just record a finite set of parameters of a function that can tell us the value of the field at any coordinate.

motivation.text: the field at that location

concepts.title: Parameterized Radiance Fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Parameterized radiance fields use differentiable function approximators to represent the mapping from coordinates to color and density.
concepts.content:
There are many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ that can represent a target radiance field $L$. Examples include neural networks or mixtures of Gaussians. The essential property of these functions is that $L_{\theta}$ is differentiable with respect to its parameters $\theta$. This differentiability allows the use of gradient-based optimization to find parameters that best fit the field to a set of images. Regardless of the specific function family used, the module takes coordinates as input and produces colors and densities as output.

(see figure: Module for a parameterized radiance field. We use $\mathbf{R}$ to denote the vector of coordinates $L_\theta$ takes as input.)

Because these are differentiable functions, they can be treated as modules within a larger differentiable computation graph, optimized via backpropagation.
concepts.motivation_md: By parameterizing radiance fields with differentiable functions, we can use standard machine learning optimization techniques to reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md: - Parameterized radiance fields must be differentiable to allow for gradient-based optimization.

key_passage.text: There are many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ that could represent our target radiance field $L$. We could use a neural net (e.g., mildenhall2020nerf), or a mixture of Gaussians (e.g., kerbl20233d), or any number of other function approximators. The important property we seek is that the field $L_{\theta}$ is a differentiable function of the parameters $\theta$, hence we can use gradient-based optimization to find a setting of the parameters that yields a desirable field.

motivation.text: we can use gradient-based optimization to find a setting of the parameters that yields a desirable field (we will use this property when we fit a radiance field to images). Later we will put together multiple such modules and use backpropagation to optimize the whole system to fit the field to a set of images.

concepts.title: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) use neural networks, typically multilayer perceptrons, to model the radiance field of a scene.
concepts.content:
Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model a radiance field $L$ using a neural network $L_{\theta}$. While the original NeRF architecture uses a multilayer perceptron (MLP), other architectures are possible. In the MLP formulation, evaluating the color and density at a single coordinate involves a single forward pass through the network.

To create an explicit representation of the field's values on a grid, the field can be queried at multiple coordinate locations. In this context, a NeRF behaves like a convolutional neural network (CNN) with 1x1 filters, as the MLP is applied to each position in the input grid.

(see figure: NeRF architecture for computing the values at each position in an entire radiance field, sampled on a grid. The $\texttt{pos\_enc}$ refers to positional encoding. You can consider this architecture...)

As established in the original NeRF work, the output layer typically uses a $\texttt{relu}$ activation to ensure density $\sigma$ is non-negative, and a $\texttt{sigmoid}$ activation to ensure $r,g,b$ values fall within the $[0,1]$ range.
concepts.motivation_md: NeRFs provide a powerful way to synthesize novel views of complex scenes by encoding the entire scene's geometry and appearance into the weights of a neural network.
concepts.recap_md: - NeRFs use MLPs to map coordinates to color and density.

key_passage.text: NeRFs model the radiance field $L$ with a neural network $L_{\theta}$. The neural network architecture in the original NeRF is a multilayer perceptron (MLP), but other architectures could be used as well. For the MLP formulation, evaluating the color-density at a single coordinate corresponds to a single forward pass through an MLP.

concepts.title: Interest point detection

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Interest point detection identifies image regions that are distinct from their surroundings and stable under geometric transformations to facilitate stereo matching and 3D reconstruction.
concepts.content:
Interest point detection identifies image regions, such as corners, that are likely to be distinct from their surroundings and stable under geometric transformations. Classical methods include the Harris corner detector, local extrema of the Laplacian pyramid across space and scale, Harris-Laplace, and maximally stable regions. 

More recently, detecting points of interest has been formulated as a learning problem. Given a set of manually annotated examples, a classifier can be trained to automatically label image patches as being centered on a keypoint or not. Examples of learning-based approaches include Quad-Networks and SuperPoint. 

(see figure: Keypoint detector formulated as a patch classification problem. The classifier labels the patch as containing a keypoint in the center or not.)

(see figure: All the detected keypoints in three views from the sugar bowl. But the images look rather textureless; what is the keypoint detector finding interesting in these images?)

Training a classifier often involves using synthetic images where keypoints are unambiguously defined or augmenting real images with random geometric transformations to create robust ground truth. As shown in the sugar bowl and plaza examples, keypoint detectors find image regions with strong spatial changes, such as window corners, bricks, or even small surface irregularities on seemingly textureless objects.

[FIGURE:20cc53bc83ed338f]

[FIGURE:549e4ecf64ea35ae]

While hand-engineered detectors are derived from first principles and require no training data, learning-based detectors can leverage unsupervised learning to achieve state-of-the-art performance.
concepts.motivation_md: To perform 3D reconstruction or stereo matching, a system must first identify specific locations in an image that can be reliably found again from a different perspective. Interest point detection solves this by finding 'anchors' like corners or textures that remain recognizable despite changes in camera angle or lighting.
concepts.recap_md: - Interest points are image regions, such as corners, that are distinct and stable under geometric transformations.

key_passage.text: Corners are examples of image regions that are likely to be distinct from the image surroundings and also be stable under geometric transformations (i.e., corners remain corners under a number of transformations).

question.text: what is the keypoint detector finding interesting in these images?

motivation.text: The keypoint detector finds image regions with strong spatial changes. Those regions are also likely to be found on images of the same object but under different viewpoints.

concepts.title: Local image descriptors

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Local image descriptors are numerical vectors extracted at keypoint locations to uniquely identify and match those points across different images.
concepts.content:
Once a keypoint detector finds stable image regions, a local image descriptor is extracted at each location to allow finding the same keypoint across different images. Classical hand-engineered descriptors include SIFT, SURF, and ORB. 

(see figure: Examples of descriptors for three keypoints. For each keypoint, the figure shows the corresponding image patch and the computed descriptor. Each descriptor has a length of 256 values.)

These descriptors represent the image patch around a keypoint as a vector (e.g., of length 256). This representation allows for matching keypoints even under different viewpoints and illumination conditions. For instance, a descriptor can identify the same window corner or surface irregularity across multiple views of a scene.

[FIGURE:867b7d3bf524344c]

[FIGURE:79782851e8d2b5ec]
concepts.motivation_md: Detecting a keypoint is not enough; the system needs a way to 'describe' that point so it can be mathematically compared to points in other images. Descriptors provide a unique signature for each point, enabling the matching process required for 3D reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Descriptors are vectors that characterize the visual information in an image patch around a keypoint.

key_passage.text: Once we have trained a keypoint detector that finds image regions that are distinct and likely to be stable under geometric transformations, we run the detector in the set of images we want to match. We need now to extract at each location a descriptor that will allow finding the same keypoint across the different images.

motivation.text: We need now to extract at each location a descriptor that will allow finding the same keypoint across the different images. As shown in the keypoint detector and descriptor finds image regions and its matches even under different viewpoints and illumination conditions.

concepts.title: Brute-force matching

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Brute-force matching compares features from one image with features from every other image in a dataset.
concepts.content: Brute-force matching is a procedure where features from one image are matched with features from every other image in the set. This approach is typically used when the total number of images is small. Modern implementations may utilize graph network-based matchers, such as SuperGlue, to perform the actual matching of these features.
concepts.motivation_md: When the relationship between images is unknown, the simplest way to find correspondences is to compare every feature in one image against every feature in all others. This ensures no potential matches are missed when the dataset size allows for such computation.
concepts.recap_md: - Matches features by comparing every image pair in the dataset.

key_passage.text: We perform brute-force matching, that is, match features from one image with features from every other image because we have a small number of images.

motivation.text: because we have a small number of images

concepts.title: Incremental Structure from Motion Optimization

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Incremental Structure from Motion builds a 3D reconstruction by starting with an image pair and sequentially adding images while refining camera poses and point locations.
concepts.content:
Incremental Structure from Motion (SFM) minimizes reprojection error by building a reconstruction step-by-step. The process typically starts with a pair of images, using their matches to compute fundamental and essential matrices while accounting for outliers via RANSAC. An initial 3D reconstruction is created through triangulation. 

Additional images are then added sequentially, repeating the matching and triangulation process until all images are incorporated. This results in an initial set of approximated camera poses and 3D locations for keypoints. Finally, the camera poses, 3D locations, and intrinsics are refined using bundle adjustment, often employing a robust cost function like the Huber kernel to handle errors.
concepts.motivation_md: Solving for all camera positions and 3D points simultaneously is computationally difficult and prone to failure. By starting small and adding images one by one, the system can maintain a stable estimate of the scene and filter out errors early in the process.
concepts.recap_md: - Starts with a base image pair to establish an initial 3D triangulation.

key_passage.text: One standard approach is to do it incrementally starting with only a pair of images. We use the matches between those two images to compute the fundamental and essential matrices, while accounting for outliers using RANSAC. We can then compute an initial 3D reconstruction of the matched points using triangulation as we have already discussed in Then, we add another image and we repeat the same process until we have incorporated all the images.

motivation.text: To find the final set of 3D points, the camera poses and the 3D locations of the keypoints are then further refined by bundle adjustment (camera intrinsics are refined too, if needed).

concepts.title: Batch-mode Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Batch-mode Structure from Motion computes the entire scene structure and camera poses offline after all input images have been processed.
concepts.content: Batch-mode Structure from Motion (SFM) is an offline approach that computes the scene structure after processing all input images. In this mode, bundle adjustment is typically run only once, though it must handle a potentially large number of cameras and 3D points simultaneously. This approach leverages information from all available viewpoints from the start. However, a significant drawback is that if new images are added to the set, the entire SFM pipeline must be rerun from the beginning.
concepts.motivation_md: Batch-mode SFM is ideal for situations where all images are available upfront (like a photo collection) and the highest possible global consistency is desired, as it optimizes all parameters together rather than sequentially.
concepts.recap_md: - Processes all images simultaneously to compute scene structure.

key_passage.text: the batch model offline or batch-mode SFM approaches, which compute the scene structure after processing all input images. In this mode, bundle adjustment will only need to be run once, albeit across a potentially large number of cameras and 3D points.

motivation.text: This mode allows leverages images from all available viewpoints right from the outset. However, if new images are added the entire SFM pipeline needs to be rerun.

concepts.title: Incremental-mode Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Incremental-mode Structure from Motion estimates scene structure and camera parameters sequentially as new images arrive.
concepts.content: Incremental-mode Structure from Motion (SFM), also known as online SFM, attempts to estimate scene structure and camera parameters as each new image arrives. In this mode, bundle adjustment is performed periodically whenever a sufficient number of new points have been added. This approach is particularly useful for applications where the full set of images is not available beforehand or where real-time performance is a requirement.
concepts.motivation_md: For applications like robotics or augmented reality, the system cannot wait for all data to be collected. Incremental SFM allows the reconstruction to grow and update dynamically as the camera moves through an environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Updates the 3D model and camera parameters as new images are provided.

key_passage.text: Online, or incremental-mode SFM approaches attempt to estimate scene structure and camera parameters as and when a new image arrives. In this mode, bundle adjustment is run periodically, whenever a sufficient number of points have been newly added.

motivation.text: Incremental-mode SFM is often used in applications where all images are not available a priori, or where real-time performance is desired.

concepts.title: Sparse Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Sparse Structure from Motion computes 3D reconstructions for a small subset of distinct, reliably detectable image pixels.
concepts.content: Sparse Structure from Motion (SFM) is a feature-based variant where 3D reconstruction is computed only for a small subset of image pixels. These pixels correspond to distinct points that can be detected reliably and repeatably across different camera poses. While some approaches attempt to use lines, planes, or objects, point-based features remain the most popular choice due to their geometric simplicity and the wide availability of robust detectors and descriptors.
concepts.motivation_md: Computing 3D coordinates for every single pixel is computationally expensive and often unnecessary. Sparse SFM focuses only on the most 'reliable' points (like corners), which provides enough information to determine camera motion and the basic geometry of the scene efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Reconstructs only a subset of distinct points rather than the full image.

key_passage.text: In sparse SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed only for a small subset of the image pixels --- distinct points that may be detected reliably and repeatably across camera pose variations.

motivation.text: Point-based features remain the most popular choice due to their geometric simplicity, and the availability of a wide range of point feature detectors and descriptors.

concepts.title: Dense Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Dense Structure from Motion computes a 3D reconstruction for nearly every pixel in an image by optimizing photometric error.
concepts.content:
In dense Structure from Motion (SFM), 3D reconstruction is computed for every (or most) image pixels, resulting in rich and visually informative models useful for robot navigation or mixed reality. Unlike sparse methods that minimize 3D reprojection error of features, dense SFM approaches usually optimize photometric error—the difference in intensity (grayscale or RGB) of corresponding pixels across images. 

These techniques are generally slower than sparse methods and require more assumptions, such as the scene being Lambertian (intensity is invariant to viewing direction). They also typically handle smaller baseline motions between images compared to point feature-based approaches.
concepts.motivation_md: While sparse SFM gives a 'skeleton' of a scene, dense SFM provides a complete surface reconstruction. This is essential for tasks like obstacle avoidance in robotics or placing virtual objects in mixed reality where the full geometry of the environment matters.
concepts.recap_md: - Computes 3D data for almost every pixel to create detailed reconstructions.

key_passage.text: In dense SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed for every (or most) of the image pixels. The resulting 3D reconstructions are rich and visually informative, and are useful in applications like robot navigation or mixed reality.

motivation.text: The resulting 3D reconstructions are rich and visually informative, and are useful in applications like robot navigation or mixed reality.

concepts.title: Conic Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The conic matrix $\mathbf{W}$ is defined as $\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$ and possesses various mathematical properties.
concepts.content: It is useful to define the matrix $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$. This is known as the conic matrix and it has many different properties.
concepts.motivation_md: The conic matrix is a mathematical construct used in computer vision to relate camera intrinsics to the geometry of conics in the image plane, facilitating tasks like camera calibration.
concepts.recap_md: - The conic matrix is defined by the formula $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$.

key_passage.text: It is useful to define the following matrix: $$\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$$ This is also known as the conic matrix and it has lots of different properties

concepts.title: Monocular Depth Cues

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Monocular depth cues are image features, such as shading and texture gradients, used by the human visual system to interpret 3D structure from a single picture.
concepts.content: Monocular depth cues are image features used by the human visual system to interpret the 3D structure of a picture. Shading refers to changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation, light intensity, and the relative angle between light and the surface normal. Shape from shading studies how to recover shape by inverting rendering equations. Texture gradients provide 3D information because distant objects appear smaller; measuring the relative size of textural elements allows for coarse estimates of scene structure [FIGURE:74c32638e485d003]. Shadows and interreflections also inform the location and geometry of objects. Aerial perspective, or atmospheric perspective, occurs when distant objects have lower contrast due to atmospheric dispersion, especially in fog [FIGURE:52838648eb2a6dee]. Additionally, detecting familiar objects with known sizes can provide absolute depth measurements, and linear perspective provides strong cues for 3D reconstruction.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding monocular depth cues is essential for developing computational methods that can reconstruct 3D scenes from single 2D images, mimicking human visual perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Shading and texture gradients allow the brain to infer surface orientation and relative distance.

key_passage.text: Shading refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation.

motivation.text: Before delving into the subject of this chapter, let's quickly review some of the image features that are used by the human visual system to interpret the 3D structure of a picture.

concepts.title: Shading and Shape from Shading

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Shading refers to image intensity changes caused by surface orientation, which can be used to recover 3D shape by inverting rendering equations.
concepts.content: Shading refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation. Shape from shading studies how to recover shape by inverting the rendering equations.
concepts.motivation_md: Shading provides a direct link between 2D pixel intensities and 3D surface geometry, allowing for the reconstruction of detailed surface contours from a single viewpoint.
concepts.recap_md: - Intensity changes are a function of surface albedo, light intensity, and surface normal orientation.

key_passage.text: Shading refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. Shape from shading studies how to recover shape by inverting the rendering equations.

motivation.text: The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation.

concepts.title: Texture Gradients

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Texture gradients provide 3D scene structure estimates by measuring the relative size of textural elements that appear smaller as they recede into the distance.
concepts.content: Texture gradients are a source of 3D information based on the principle that distant things appear smaller than closer things. By measuring the relative size between textural elements that appear in different image regions, we can get a coarse estimate of the 3D scene structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Texture gradients allow for depth estimation in scenes with repetitive patterns or surfaces, providing a geometric cue for distance without requiring multiple viewpoints.
concepts.recap_md: - Distant textural elements appear smaller than those closer to the camera.

key_passage.text: As far things appear smaller than closer things, by measuring the relative size between textural elements that appear in different image regions we can get a coarse estimate of the 3D scene structure

motivation.text: Another source of 3D information are texture gradients.

concepts.title: Aerial Perspective

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Aerial perspective is a depth cue where distant objects exhibit lower contrast due to atmospheric dispersion or fog.
concepts.content: When looking at large landscapes, like a mountain range, mountains that are far away have lower contrast due to dispersion by the atmosphere. This effect gets accentuated when there is fog. Therefore, contrast can be used as a cue to infer relative distances between objects. This depth cue is called aerial perspective or atmospheric perspective.
concepts.motivation_md: Aerial perspective provides a way to estimate depth over very long distances where other cues like binocular parity or texture gradients might fail.
concepts.recap_md: - Atmospheric dispersion causes distant objects to appear with lower contrast.

key_passage.text: contrast can be used as a cue to infer relative distances between objects. This depth cue is called aerial perspective or atmospheric perspective.

motivation.text: When looking at large landscapes, like a mountain range, mountains that are far away have lower contrast due to dispersion by the atmosphere.

concepts.title: Depth Map Representation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: A depth map is a dense representation where each pixel value corresponds to the distance from the camera to the scene surface.
concepts.content: Depth maps (or disparity maps) represent the distance to objects in a scene. Most depth sensors capture aligned RGB images and dense depth maps $z[n,m]$ [FIGURE:baae76d353508145] [FIGURE:4ecc5be8314ca221]. Given a dense depth map and the intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$, the depth can be translated into a 3D point cloud. Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation for each pixel is $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$, where $\mathbf{p}$ are pixel coordinates and $\mathbf{P}$ are 3D point coordinates. In heterogeneous coordinates, this can be rewritten as: $X[n,m] = (n-c_x) \frac{z[n,m]}{a}$, $Y[n,m] = (m-c_y) \frac{z[n,m]}{a}$, and $Z[n,m] = z[n,m]$, where $a, c_x, c_y$ are intrinsic camera parameters. Depth maps are usually visualized using the turbo colormap to differentiate them from natural gray-scale images [FIGURE:5e64d445bf392d94].
concepts.motivation_md: Depth maps provide a computationally efficient way to store 3D information in a 2D grid format, allowing standard image processing techniques to be applied to spatial data.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth maps store the distance $z$ for every pixel $(n,m)$ in an image.

key_passage.text: Given a dense depth map, we can translate the depth into a 3D point cloud if we know the intrinsic camera parameters, K, of the sensor.

motivation.text: Most depth sensors capture aligned RGB images, ℓ[n,m], and dense depth maps, z [n,m], as shown in

concepts.title: Point Cloud

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: A point cloud is a collection of isolated 3D points without any inherent connectivity or grouping.
concepts.content: In a point cloud, there is no notion of grouping of 3D points. 3D points are isolated and are not connected to each other.
concepts.motivation_md: Point clouds are the most direct output of many 3D scanning technologies, providing a raw set of spatial coordinates before any surface reconstruction occurs.
concepts.recap_md: - Points in a point cloud are isolated and lack connectivity.

key_passage.text: In a point cloud, there is no notion of grouping of 3D points. 3D points are isolated and are not connected to each other.

concepts.title: Mesh

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: A mesh is a 3D representation that connects points with triangles to represent surfaces or objects in contact.
concepts.content: A mesh connects points with triangles. It is used to connect points that belong to the same surface or that are in contact, which involves solving a perceptual organization problem.
concepts.motivation_md: Meshes are used to create continuous surfaces from discrete points, which is essential for realistic rendering and physical simulations in 3D environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Meshes use triangles to connect discrete 3D points into surfaces.

key_passage.text: A mesh connects points with triangles, but only makes sense to connect points that belong to the same surface or that are in contact.

concepts.title: Optimization via Volume Rendering

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering enables gradient-based optimization by ensuring that small changes to scene content yield small, non-zero changes to the loss function.
concepts.content: After approximately 2,500 steps of gradient descent, the optimization arrives at a fairly accurate representation of the scene. At this point, object densities are high enough that volume rendering essentially amounts to ray casting, which finds the color of the first surface hit. The primary reason for using volume rendering, even in scenes without volumetric effects, is to facilitate optimization. Volume rendering provides the property that small changes to scene content yield small changes to the loss, resulting in small but non-zero gradients. In contrast, ray casting is an all-or-none operation where small changes to scene content, such as an occluder suddenly revealing an object, can yield drastic changes to rendered images. This makes gradient-based optimization difficult with ray casting but achievable with volume rendering. This benefit is the second major advantage of volume rendering, alongside the ability to model translucency and subsurface effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard ray casting creates discontinuous jumps in pixel values when objects move or appear, making gradient-based optimization nearly impossible. Volume rendering smooths these transitions, providing the non-zero gradients necessary for neural networks to learn 3D geometry from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md: - Volume rendering provides a continuous loss function where small scene changes result in small gradient updates.

key_passage.text: With volume rendering, we have the property that small changes to the scene content yield small changes to our loss; that is, we have small but non-zero gradients. Ray casting, in contrast, is an all or none operation, and therefore small changes to scene content can yield drastic changes to the rendered images.

motivation.text: Not because we care about volumetric effects; in this scene there are none. Rather because it makes it possible for optimization to find the ray casting solution. With volume rendering, we have the property that small changes to the scene content yield small changes to our loss; that is, we have small but non-zero gradients. Ray casting, in contrast, is an all or none operation, and therefore small changes to scene content can yield drastic changes to the rendered images.

concepts.title: The Rendering Equation

position.section_title: Beyond Radiance Fields: The Rendering Equation

concepts.one_liner: The rendering equation is a general formalism for image rendering that models light scattering off surfaces to handle multi-bounce effects.
concepts.content:
The rendering equation, introduced by Kajiya in 1986, provides a formalism for image rendering by directly modeling light scattering off the surfaces in a scene. The equation is written as:

$$L(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = g(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') \left[ e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') + \int_S \rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}) L(\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}) d\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime} \right]$$

In this equation, $L(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$ represents the intensity of the light ray passing from point $\mathbf{x}'$ to point $\mathbf{x}$. The function $e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$ denotes the light emitted from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$, representing light sources. The function $\rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime})$ is the intensity of light scattered from $\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}$ to $\mathbf{x}$ by a surface patch at location $x'$, which is related to the bidirectional reflectance distribution function. The variables $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}'$, and $\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}$ represent world coordinate vectors. The term $g(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')$ is a visibility function encoding scene geometry and occlusions; it is 0 if points are not visible to each other, and $1/\lVert \mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}' \rVert ^2$ otherwise to model energy propagation. Essentially, the transport intensity of light between two surface points is the sum of emitted light and the total light intensity scattered toward the destination from all other surface points.
concepts.motivation_md: To accurately simulate how light behaves in a complex environment, researchers needed a mathematical framework that accounts for light sources, surface reflections, and the way light bounces between multiple objects.
concepts.recap_md: - The equation models light intensity as the sum of emitted light and light scattered from all other points in the scene.

key_passage.text: L(x,x') = g(x,x') [ e(x,x') + ∫_S ρ(x,x',x'') L(x',x'') dx'' ] where L(x,x') is the intensity of light ray that passes from point x' to point x, the function e(x,x') is the light emitted from x' to x, and the function ρ(x,x',x'') is the intensity of light scattered from x'' to x by a patch of surface at location x'.

motivation.text: The goal was to introduce a new formalism for image rendering by directly modeling the light scattering off the surfaces composing a scene.

concepts.title: Apparent Motion

position.section_title: Motion Perception in the Human Visual System

concepts.one_liner: Apparent motion is the illusion of continuous movement created by displaying a sequence of static images.
concepts.content: Apparent motion refers to the phenomenon where the human visual system perceives continuous motion from a sequence of static images. This discovery from cognitive psychology has significantly impacted imaging technology, most notably in the creation of movies.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how the brain perceives motion allows engineers to create fluid visual experiences, like film and video, using only a series of still frames.
concepts.recap_md: - Apparent motion is the psychological phenomenon of perceiving movement in a sequence of static frames.

key_passage.text: The fact that we learned to create the illusion of continuous motion by displaying a sequence of static images (a phenomenon called apparent motion) was a remarkable discovery.

motivation.text: Much is known and many advances from cognitive psychology have impacted imaging technology. One example is movies.

concepts.title: Waterfall Illusion

position.section_title: Motion Perception in the Human Visual System

concepts.one_liner: The waterfall illusion is a motion aftereffect where staring at constant motion causes a subsequent static texture to appear to drift in the opposite direction.
concepts.content: The waterfall illusion is a famous visual illusion associated with motion perception. When an observer looks at constant motion, such as a waterfall, the brain adapts to that motion. If the observer immediately looks at a static texture after this adaptation, the texture appears to drift in the opposite direction. This phenomenon was known to the ancient Greeks and was reported by Aristotle.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion provides insight into how the brain's motion detectors adapt to stimuli, helping researchers understand the underlying neural mechanisms of vision.
concepts.recap_md: - The illusion occurs when the brain adapts to constant motion, causing static objects to appear to move in the opposite direction.

key_passage.text: When looking at a constant motion (such as a waterfall) our brain adapts to the motion in such a way that if, immediately after adaptation, we look at a static texture we will see it drifting in the opposite direction.

motivation.text: There are a number of visual illusions associated with motion perception that are intriguing and offer a window into how motion perception is implemented in the brain.

concepts.title: Rotating Snakes Illusion

position.section_title: Motion Perception in the Human Visual System

concepts.one_liner: The Rotating Snakes illusion uses static images with specific patterns to produce a sensation of motion.
concepts.content: The Rotating Snakes visual illusion, created by cognitive psychologist Akiyoshi Kitaoka, demonstrates that static images can produce a sensation of motion. (see figure: Motion-induced visual illusion, after @Murakami2010. The illusion becomes stronger when viewed peripherally rather than looking directly at the image. Changing the contrast of this image can change...) The effect uses simple elements to induce the illusion and typically becomes more intense as the viewer moves their eyes to explore different parts of the image or views it peripherally.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion demonstrates that motion perception is not just about tracking moving objects, but can be triggered by specific spatial patterns and eye movements.
concepts.recap_md: - This illusion creates a perceived sense of rotation from a completely static image.

key_passage.text: One beautiful example is the Rotating Snakes visual illusion created by cognitive psychologist Akiyoshi Kitaoka. It is possible to create static images that produce the sensation of motion.

motivation.text: Another remarkable and surprising visual illusion is that it is possible to create static images that produce the sensation of motion.

concepts.title: Hassenstein-Reichardt Model
concepts.one_liner: The Hassenstein-Reichardt model is an early computational model of motion perception based on the fly's visual system.
concepts.content: The Hassenstein-Reichardt model is one of the earliest computational models of motion perception. It was proposed by Hassenstein and Reichardt in 1956 following their studies of motion detectors within the visual system of flies.
concepts.motivation_md: By studying simpler biological systems like the fly, researchers could develop the first mathematical frameworks for how neurons might detect the direction and speed of motion.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a foundational computational model for biological motion detection.

key_passage.text: One of the early computational models of motion perception was proposed by Hassenstein and Reichardt when studying the motion detectors in the fly's visual system.

concepts.title: Adelson-Bergen Energy Model
concepts.one_liner: The Adelson-Bergen energy model is a computational framework for human motion perception.
concepts.content: The energy model proposed by Adelson and Bergen in 1985 is a computational model designed to explain human motion perception. It is often discussed in the context of filter banks and how the visual system extracts motion energy from stimuli.
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a way to understand how the human brain processes motion as a spatiotemporal energy signal, rather than just tracking discrete features.
concepts.recap_md: - The model characterizes motion perception through the lens of spatiotemporal energy filters.
