concepts.title: Matching-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Matching-based motion estimation computes pixel displacement between video frames by finding corresponding color patches.
concepts.content: Matching-based motion estimation computes the displacement of pixels between two video frames by finding correspondences. (see figure: Frame 1) (see figure: Frame 2) Because individual pixel colors are often not distinctive enough, each pixel is represented by a color patch of size $C=3\times(2s+1)\times(2s+1)$ centered on the pixel. For a pixel at $(n,m)$ in image $\boldsymbol\ell$, the patch is $\boldsymbol\ell[n-s:n+s, m-s:m+s]$. Small values of $s$ may be less distinctive, while large values may fail if there is significant geometric distortion. To simplify matching, we often assume small motion and search only within a neighborhood of size $L \times L$ in the second frame. The algorithm computes the Euclidean distance between patches and selects the one with the smallest distance. (see figure: Patch matching motion estimation. The algorithm starts by chopping the two frames into overlapping patches. Then, for every patch from the first frame, we compute the distance to all the nearby...) (see figure: Two frames and best match for an input patch from frame 1 within frame 2. Search is done only within a small neighborhood.) The choice of patch size $s$ is critical: very small patches result in noisy motion fields, while very large patches can cause motion to 'bleed' across object boundaries. (see figure: Effect of the choice of the patch size parameter, $s$, on the estimated optical flow. When the patch size is just one pixel ($s=0$), the approach fails as there are many similar pixels that...) This approach is independent of object types and can serve as a cue for grouping, though it typically lacks subpixel accuracy and struggles at motion discontinuities.
concepts.motivation_md: Estimating how objects move between frames is fundamental for video compression, tracking, and autonomous navigation. Patch matching provides a straightforward way to estimate this motion without needing to pre-segment objects.
concepts.recap_md: - Motion is estimated by finding the best-matching patch in a subsequent frame using Euclidean distance.

key_passage.text: Under this formulation, the task of motion estimation consists of finding, for each pixel in frame 1, the location of the corresponding pixel in frame 2. Just as in the chapter on stereo matching, we need first to define how we will compare pixels to find correspondences.

question.text: How can we compute the motion between the two frames?

motivation.text: One way of representing the motion is by computing the displacement for each pixel between the two frames.

concepts.title: Free Fusion
concepts.one_liner: Free fusion consists in making the eyes converge or diverge in order to fuse a stereogram without needing a stereoscope.
concepts.content: Free fusion consists in making the eyes converge or diverge in order to fuse a stereogram without needing a stereoscope. Making it work requires practice. Try it in @fig-random_dot_stereogram.
concepts.motivation_md: Free fusion allows a person to experience 3D depth from 2D images without requiring specialized optical hardware like a stereoscope.
concepts.recap_md: - Free fusion is the technique of manually adjusting eye convergence to perceive depth in a stereogram.

key_passage.text: Free fusion consists in making the eyes converge or diverge in order to fuse a stereogram without needing a stereoscope.

motivation.text: Making it work requires practice.

concepts.title: Random Dot Stereograms
concepts.one_liner: Random dot stereograms demonstrate that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features even in the absence of other depth cues.
concepts.content:
Random dot stereograms, introduced by Bela Julesz, are a beautiful demonstration that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features across two views even in the absence of any other depth cues. The random images contain no recognizable features and are quite different from the statistics of the natural world. But this seems not to affect our ability to compute the displacements between the two images and perceive 3D structure.

(see figure: Random dot stereogram. Both images are almost identical. The difference is that there is a square in the middle that is displaced by a few pixels left-right between the two images. When each image it...)
concepts.motivation_md: These stereograms prove that the human brain can extract 3D information purely from binocular disparity, even when individual images lack recognizable objects or textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Random dot stereograms contain no recognizable features, yet allow for 3D perception through feature displacement.

key_passage.text: Random dot stereograms are a beautiful demonstration that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features across two views even in the absence of any other depth cues.

motivation.text: The random images contain no recognizable features and are quite different from the statistics of the natural world. But this seems not to affect our ability to compute the displacements between the two images and perceive 3D structure.

concepts.title: Anaglyph Pinhole Camera
concepts.one_liner: An anaglyph pinhole camera captures stereo images in a single shot by using two pinholes with different color filters.
concepts.content:
A stereo pinhole camera can be built to produce anaglyph images, like the one in @fig-titanic, in a single shot by making two pinholes instead of just one. By placing different color filters on each hole, the camera produces an image that is the superposition of two images taken from slightly different viewpoints, each with a different color. To see the 3D image, the picture is viewed by placing the same color filters in front of the eyes, such as red and blue glasses.

(see figure: One way of playing with pinhole cameras is to build an anaglyph pinhole camera. The anaglyph pinhole camera captures stereo images by projecting an anaglyph image on the projection plane.)

Experimental results show that the distance between pinholes affects 3D perception; for example, a 1.5 in distance may be easier to fuse than 3 in. Because filters reduce the light entering the camera, longer exposure times are required to maintain image quality. While increasing the distance between pinholes increases the parallax effect and the range of 3D information, if the images are too far apart, the visual system will not be able to fuse them.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique provides a simple way to capture 3D depth information in a single exposure by encoding two different perspectives into distinct color channels.
concepts.recap_md: - An anaglyph pinhole camera uses two holes with color filters to capture two perspectives simultaneously.

key_passage.text: We can transform the pinhole camera into an anaglyph pinhole camera by making two holes and placing different color filters on each hole. This will produce an image that will be the superposition of two images taken from slightly different viewpoints. Each image will have a different color. Then, to see the 3D image we can look at the picture by placing the same color filters in front of our eyes.

motivation.text: One interesting aspect of pinhole cameras is that you can build different types of cameras by playing with the shape of the pinhole. In particular, we can build a camera that produces anaglyph images in a single shot by making two pinholes instead of just one.

concepts.title: Stereo Triangulation
concepts.one_liner: Stereo triangulation estimates the depth of points in the world by comparing images from two spatially offset cameras.
concepts.content:
The task of stereo is to triangulate the depth of points in the world by comparing the images from two spatially offset cameras. To triangulate depth, we must describe how image positions in the stereo pair relate to depth in the 3D world. In a simple setting where two identical, calibrated cameras are translated horizontally with parallel optical axes, a 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ projects to $[x_L,y_L]^\mathsf{T}$ in the left camera and $[x_R,y_R]^\mathsf{T}$ in the right camera. Because of the horizontal alignment, $y_L=y_R$. Using similar triangles, the depth $Z$ can be calculated as:

$$Z =  \frac{fT}{x_L-x_R}$$

where $f$ is the focal length and $T$ is the horizontal offset (baseline) between the cameras. The difference in horizontal position $x_L - x_R$ is called the disparity, which is inversely proportional to the depth $Z$.
concepts.motivation_md: Triangulation provides the mathematical basis for recovering 3D scene structure from 2D images by exploiting the geometric relationship between multiple viewpoints.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth is calculated using similar triangles based on camera focal length and the baseline distance between cameras.

key_passage.text: A simple way to triangulate the depth, Z, of a point visible in both images is through similar triangles. The two triangles (yellow triangle and yellow+orange triangle) shown in (b) are similar, and so the ratios of their height to base must be the same.

motivation.text: The task of stereo is to triangulate the depth of points in the world by comparing the images from two spatially offset cameras. To triangulate depth, we need to describe how image positions in the stereo pair relate to depth in the 3D world.

concepts.title: Multiview Stereo
concepts.one_liner: Multiview stereo is the task of triangulating depth using more than two cameras.
concepts.content: If more than two cameras are used to triangulate the depth of points in the world, the task is referred to as multiview stereo.
concepts.motivation_md: Using more than two cameras increases the accuracy of depth estimation and helps resolve occlusions that might be problematic in a standard two-camera setup.
concepts.recap_md: - Multiview stereo extends basic stereo triangulation to configurations involving three or more cameras.

key_passage.text: If more than two cameras are used, the task is referred to as multiview stereo.

concepts.title: Disparity
concepts.one_liner: Disparity is the difference in horizontal position of a world point as seen in the left and right camera images.
concepts.content: The difference in horizontal position of any given world point, $\mathbf{P}$, as seen in the left and right camera images, $x_L - x_R$, is called the disparity. For a configuration of two cameras with parallel orientation, disparity is inversely proportional to the depth $Z$ of the point $\mathbf{P}$. The task of inferring depth in a stereo pair reduces to measuring this disparity everywhere.
concepts.motivation_md: Disparity is the fundamental observable quantity in stereo vision that allows for the calculation of distance to objects in a scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Disparity is defined as the shift $x_L - x_R$ between corresponding points in a stereo image pair.

key_passage.text: The difference in horizontal position of any given world point, P, as seen in the left and right camera images, x_L - x_R, is called the disparity, and is inversely proportional to the depth Z of the point P for this configuration of the two cameras--parallel orientation.

concepts.title: The Stereo Matching Problem
concepts.one_liner: Stereo matching is the problem of identifying which points in one image correspond to the same 3D point in another image.
concepts.content:
The stereo matching problem involves determining which points in one camera's image correspond to the same 3D point in another camera's image. This is the crux of the stereo problem, as images are complex and correspondences are not immediately known. 

[FIGURE:5b3ceb105441e961]

[FIGURE:8bc44da026c71495]

A naive algorithm searching for pixels of the same intensity often fails due to factors like lack of texture, image noise, specularities, and occlusions. Effective approaches often involve finding features and matching them across images, then interpolating or filtering these matches to obtain a reliable disparity estimate everywhere. These two steps are often referred to as matching and filtering.
concepts.motivation_md: Solving the matching problem is a prerequisite for calculating disparity; without accurate correspondences, depth cannot be triangulated in complex scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Stereo matching identifies corresponding features between two views to calculate disparity.

key_passage.text: The task of finding disparity at each point is often broken into two parts: (1) finding features, and matching the features across images, and (2) interpolating between, or adjusting, the feature matches to obtain a reliable disparity estimate everywhere.

motivation.text: But in reality the two images will be complex and we will not know which points in one camera correspond to the same 3D point on the other camera. This requires solving the stereo matching problem.

concepts.title: Disparity Space Image
concepts.one_liner: A disparity space image represents matching errors for a range of disparity offsets across horizontal positions.
concepts.content: The disparity space image is a configuration where matching errors, such as the squared difference of intensity differences from offset versions of the same row in a stereo pair, are plotted for a range of disparity offsets. These offsets are typically plotted vertically as a function of horizontal position. This representation helps identify the best matches, though raw intensity matches can be noisy and may require edge-preserving filters to produce reliable results.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a structured way to evaluate matching costs across all possible disparities, facilitating the use of optimization techniques to find the most likely depth estimates.
concepts.recap_md: - The disparity space image maps horizontal image position and disparity offset to a matching cost.

key_passage.text: The disparity space image, a configuration for plotting disparity offsets vertically from a left-eye image of the stereo pair.

concepts.title: When Optical Flow and Motion Flow Are Not the Same
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow and physical motion flow can differ when image brightness changes do not correspond to the actual movement of 3D points in a scene.
concepts.content:
There are a number of scenarios where motion in the image brightness does not correspond to the motion of the 3D points in the scene. Examples where the definition of motion is unclear include:

- A rotating Lambertian sphere with static illumination produces no image changes, while a static sphere with a moving light source produces perceived motion.
- Moving in front of a textureless wall produces no change in the image.
- Waves in water appear to move along the surface, but the actual motion of the water is primarily up and down.
- A rotating mirror or any surface with a specular component will produce the appearance of faster motion.
- A camera moving in front of a specular planar surface will not produce a motion field corresponding to a homography.

Ideally, motion estimation should assign the physical cause to each source of variation in the image, rather than just measuring pixel motion.
concepts.motivation_md: In computer vision, we often assume that changes in pixel intensity represent physical movement. However, lighting changes, reflections, and lack of texture can create 'optical flow' that does not match the actual 'motion field' of objects, necessitating a distinction between the two.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow is the apparent motion of brightness patterns, while motion flow is the actual 3D movement of scene points.

key_passage.text: There are a number of scenarios where motion in the image brightness does not correspond to the motion of the 3D points in the scene.

motivation.text: Motion estimation should not just measure pixel motion, it should also try to assign to each source of variation in the image the physical cause for that change.

concepts.title: The Aperture Problem
concepts.one_liner: The aperture problem occurs when observing a 1D structure through a limited window, making it impossible to determine the true motion direction.
concepts.content:
One classical example of the limitations of motion estimation from images is the aperture problem. The aperture problem happens when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame, as shown in (see figure: Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what...). If none of the termination points are in view within the observation window (i.e., the aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. Only the component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

The Barber-pole illusion is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

[FIGURE:62969696d2b66d2a]
concepts.motivation_md: Local sensors or small image windows often lack enough context to determine global motion. Understanding the aperture problem is essential for developing algorithms that combine local measurements into a consistent global motion estimate.
concepts.recap_md: - The aperture problem prevents measuring motion parallel to a 1D structure if its endpoints are hidden.

Only the component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

concepts.title: Barber-pole Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The Barber-pole illusion is a visual phenomenon where a rotating pole induces a perceived downward motion due to the aperture problem.

The Barber-pole illusion is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

concepts.title: Representation of Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Motion can be represented either as dense optical flow images or as a sparse set of moving point tracks.
concepts.content:
Motion over time can be modeled as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) ight]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. A limitation of this formulation is the lack of an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by specific scene points over time, as a location $(x,y)$ may correspond to different scene elements as time changes.

An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This requires establishing the correspondence of the same scene point over time (tracking). This can be challenging because the appearance of a 3D point changes due to perspective projection and illumination variations. Consequently, most point-based representations use a sparse set rather than a dense array.

Choosing between these representations depends on the application, and for complex flows like smoke or water, the ideal representation remains an open question.
concepts.motivation_md: Different computer vision tasks require different ways of describing motion; dense flow is useful for video compression or stabilization, while sparse tracks are better for 3D reconstruction and object tracking.
concepts.recap_md: - Dense optical flow assigns a velocity vector to every pixel in the image.

key_passage.text: We can model motion over time as a sequence of dense optical flow images: [u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t)] The quantities u(x,y,t)and v(x,y,t) indicate that a pixel at image coordinates (x,y) at time t moves with velocity (u,v).

question.text: For instance, what representation would be the most appropriate to describe the flow of smoke or water over time?

motivation.text: The problem with this formulation is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by points in the scene over time. As time t changes, the location (x,y) might correspond to different scene elements.

concepts.title: Dense Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Dense optical flow models motion as a velocity vector for every pixel in an image sequence.
concepts.content: Motion over time can be modeled as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. The problem with this formulation is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by points in the scene over time. As time $t$ changes, the location $(x,y)$ might correspond to different scene elements.
concepts.motivation_md: Dense flow provides a complete map of apparent motion across the entire image, which is necessary for tasks like motion-compensated frame interpolation.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents motion as a velocity field $[u, v]$ defined at every pixel $(x, y)$.

key_passage.text: We can model motion over time as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$.

motivation.text: The problem with this formulation is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by points in the scene over time.

concepts.title: Sparse Set of Moving Points (Tracks)
concepts.one_liner: A sparse set of moving points models motion by tracking the trajectories of specific scene points over time.
concepts.content: An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This has the challenge that we have to establish the correspondence of the same scene point over time (tracking). The appearance of a 3D scene point will change over time due to perspective projection and other variations such as illumination changes over time. It might be difficult to do this on a dense array. Therefore, most representations of motion as sets of moving points use a sparse set of points.
concepts.motivation_md: Tracking specific points (like corners or features) is more computationally efficient and robust for tasks like Structure from Motion (SfM) than trying to track every single pixel.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents motion as a collection of discrete point trajectories or tracks.

key_passage.text: An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): { P_t^(i) }_{i=1}^N

motivation.text: This has the challenge that we have to establish the correspondence of the same scene point over time (tracking). Therefore, most representations of motion as sets of moving points use a sparse set of points.

concepts.title: Brightness Constancy Assumption
concepts.one_liner: The brightness constancy assumption states that the captured brightness of a scene element remains constant as it moves.
concepts.content:
The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time. Mathematically, this assumption translates into the following relationship, given a sequence $\ell(x,y,t)$:

$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  = \ell(x,y,t)$$

where $u$ and $v$ are the element displacement over one unit of time and are functions of pixel location $u(x,y)$ and $v(x,y)$. This is equivalent to saying that $\ell(x, y, t + 1) = \ell(x-u,y-v,t)$. (see figure: Translation to the right of a simple $6 \times 6$ size image.)

The constant brightness assumption only approximately holds in reality. For it to be exact, the scene should have Lambertian objects illuminated from a light source at infinity, with no occlusions, shadows, or interreflections. In reality, pixels might be occluded in one frame or new pixels might appear at boundaries and behind occlusions.
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption provides the fundamental constraint needed to solve for motion: it links the spatial gradients of an image to its temporal changes, allowing us to estimate velocity.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes $\ell(x + u, y + v, t + 1) = \ell(x, y, t)$ for moving scene elements.

key_passage.text: The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time.

motivation.text: The constant brightness assumption only approximately holds in reality. For it to be exact, we should have a scene with Lambertian objects illuminated from a light source at infinity, with no occlusions, no shadows, and no interreflections.

concepts.title: Domain adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa, to make their distributions identical.
concepts.content: Often, the data we train on comes from a different distribution, or domain, than the data we will encounter at test time. For example, a recognition system might be trained on internet photos but deployed on a self-driving car, where the imagery looks very different. Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa. One option is to adapt the test data, ${\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N$, to look more like the training data so that the model $f$ works well on both. Alternatively, we can adapt the training data to look like the test data before training $f$. In either case, the goal is to make the distribution of test and train data identical, so that a method that works on one will work just as well on the other.
concepts.motivation_md: Machine learning models often fail when the 'domain' of the deployment data differs from the training data. Domain adaptation provides a framework to bridge this gap, ensuring that models remain effective even when the environment or data source changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Domain adaptation aligns the distributions of training and test data to improve model generalization.

key_passage.text: Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa.

motivation.text: Often, the data we train on comes from a different distribution, or domain, than the data we will encounter at test time. For example, maybe we have trained a recognition system on internet photos and now we want to deploy the system on a self-driving car.

concepts.title: Unsupervised domain adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised domain adaptation aligns training and test distributions using unlabeled test inputs when labels are only available during training.
concepts.content:
Commonly, we only have access to labels at training time, but may have plentiful unlabeled inputs ${\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_i}_{i=1}^N$ at testing time. This setting is known as unsupervised domain adaptation. In this case, we cannot make use of test labels, but we can still align the test inputs to look like the training inputs (or vice versa). One way to do so is to use a generative adversarial network (GAN) that translates the data in one domain to look identically distributed as the data in the other domain.

(see figure: Unpaired domain adaptation via adversarial translation.)
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world applications, it is easy to collect large amounts of data in a new environment but very expensive to label it. Unsupervised domain adaptation allows models to leverage this unlabeled data to adapt to new domains.
concepts.recap_md: - This method performs domain alignment using only unlabeled inputs from the target test domain.

key_passage.text: Commonly, we only have access to labels at training time, but may have plentiful unlabeled inputs at testing time. This setting is sometimes referred to as unsupervised domain adaptation. Here we cannot make use of test labels but we can still align the test inputs to look like the training inputs (or vice versa).

motivation.text: Commonly, we only have access to labels at training time, but may have plentiful unlabeled inputs at testing time. Here we cannot make use of test labels but we can still align the test inputs to look like the training inputs (or vice versa).

concepts.title: Using generative models as data sources
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can serve as data sources for transfer learning by providing an unbounded supply of synthetic, manipulatable data.
concepts.content: Generative models produce synthetic data that looks like real data, an ability that is highly useful for transfer learning. Generative data is not just a cheap copy of real data; it can be "more" data and "better" data. It is "more" because we can draw an unbounded number of samples that interpolate and remix training data in novel ways. It is "better" because the data comes coupled with a generation procedure that has structure, such as latent variables, which can be exploited to manipulate the data distribution. For example, if a model is pretrained to produce images, one can edit its latent variables to generate specific scenarios—like cows on beaches—to adapt training data for new applications. In this usage, knowledge about data is transferred to accelerate learning for a new problem, leveraging the generative model's understanding of how the world looks.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard datasets are often limited or biased. Generative models allow us to synthesize an infinite variety of training examples, including rare edge cases, by manipulating the underlying variables of the data generation process.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models provide an infinite source of synthetic data that goes beyond simple replication of training sets.

key_passage.text: generative data (i.e., synthetic data sampled from a generative model) is not just a cheap copy of real data. It can be more data, and it can be better data. It can be more data because we can draw an unbounded number of samples from a generative model.

question.text: Why use fake data if you have access to the real thing?

motivation.text: In this usage, you are transferring knowledge about data, to accelerate learning to solve a new problem. The function being learned can be trained from scratch, but it is leveraging the generative model's knowledge about what images look like and how the world works.

concepts.title: Generative data
concepts.one_liner: Generative data is synthetic data sampled from a generative model that can interpolate and remix training data in novel ways.
concepts.content: Generative data refers to synthetic data sampled from a generative model. It is not just a cheap copy of real data; it can be "more" data and "better" data. It is "more" data because an unbounded number of samples can be drawn from a generative model, which can interpolate and remix the training data in novel ways. Generative models can also produce "better" data because the data comes coupled with a procedure that generated it, providing structure that can be exploited to understand and manipulate the data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Generative data solves the problem of data scarcity and lack of diversity by allowing for the creation of targeted, high-quality synthetic samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative data consists of synthetic samples that can be produced in unbounded quantities.

key_passage.text: generative data (i.e., synthetic data sampled from a generative model) is not just a cheap copy of real data. It can be more data, and it can be better data.

motivation.text: It can be more data because we can draw an unbounded number of samples from a generative model. Generative models can also produce better data because the data comes coupled with a procedure that generated it, and this procedure has structure that can be exploited to understand and manipulate the data distribution.

concepts.title: Learned loss

position.section_title: Other Kinds of Knowledge that Can Be Transferred

concepts.one_liner: A learned loss is a loss function that is itself pretrained to define the objective for a learning task.
concepts.content: A learned loss refers to the pretraining of the component that defines the loss function. Instead of using a standard, manually defined loss, this component is learned to optimize the training of a model.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard loss functions like MSE or Cross-Entropy may not be optimal for every task. Learning the loss function allows the system to discover a more effective objective for training.
concepts.recap_md: - A learned loss is a pretrained objective function used to guide the training of other models.

key_passage.text: The term for this is a learned loss

motivation.text: picked the line that defines the loss function; that can be pretrained!

concepts.title: Learned optimizer

position.section_title: A Combinatorial Catalog of Transfer Learning Methods

concepts.one_liner: A learned optimizer is an optimization algorithm that is pretrained to update model parameters more effectively than standard algorithms.
concepts.content: A learned optimizer is a component that defines the optimizer (such as SGD) and can be pretrained. While it is currently less common to adapt these modules—they are usually pretrained and then held fixed—there is no reason why they cannot be adapted in principle.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional optimizers use fixed rules. A learned optimizer can discover specialized update strategies that lead to faster or more stable convergence for specific types of neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Learned optimizers are pretrained modules that replace or augment standard optimization algorithms like SGD.

key_passage.text: the optimizer can also be pretrained. This is called a **learned optimizer**

motivation.text: It's currently less common to *adapt* modules like these (they are usually just pretrained and then held fixed), but in principle there is no reason why you can't.

concepts.title: Transfer learning as empirical risk minimization

position.section_title: A Combinatorial Catalog of Transfer Learning Methods

concepts.one_liner: Many transfer learning methods can be framed as empirical risk minimization (ERM) where different components are optimized during pretraining or adaptation.
concepts.content:
Many transfer learning methods follow a similar format: pretrain one component of the system, then adapt that component and/or other components. These methods can be related by framing them as empirical risk minimization (ERM) with different components optimized during pretraining and/or during adaptation.

| Method | Learning | Inference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Generative data | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{{rgb}{0.8, 0.0, 0.2}}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{x},\textcolor{pretrained_color}{y}}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(\textcolor{pretrained_color}{x}), \textcolor{pretrained_color}{y})]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Distillation | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x), \textcolor{pretrained_color}{t}(x))]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Prompting | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\epsilon}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x \oplus \textcolor{adapted_color}{\epsilon}), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x \oplus \textcolor{adapted_color}{\epsilon})$ |
| Finetuning | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{both_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{both_color}{\theta}}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{both_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Probes / heads | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(h_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\phi}}(f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x)), y)]$ | $h_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\phi}}(f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x))$ |
| Learned loss | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\mathcal{L}}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Learned optimizer | $\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\arg\min}_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |

Note: The $\oplus$ symbol indicates concatenation or addition. Domain adaptation does not map neatly to ERM and is omitted here.
concepts.motivation_md: Providing a unified mathematical framework for transfer learning allows researchers to categorize and compare diverse techniques like prompting and distillation using the common language of optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - Transfer learning methods can be unified as ERM problems where different parts (model, loss, optimizer) are pretrained or adapted.

key_passage.text: we present the relationship these methods by framing them all as empirical risk minimization with different components optimized during pretraining and/or during adaptation.

motivation.text: Many of the methods we introduced previously follow a similar format: Pretrain one component of the system. Adapt that component and/or other components.

concepts.title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

position.section_title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

concepts.one_liner: Sequence models like RNNs can be viewed as adaptation algorithms that update their behavior based on previously seen items in a sequence.
concepts.content: Sequence models, such as CNNs, transformers, and RNNs, can be considered adaptation algorithms because they update their behavior based on the items in the sequence they have already seen. This ability to handle adaptation is clearest with RNNs, which update their hidden states as they process data. These changes in hidden state modify the mapping from input to output, effectively allowing the model to adapt. Since learning is the problem of adapting future behavior as a function of past data, an RNN processing a sequence of training points can be viewed as performing learning.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing sequence modeling as a form of adaptation helps explain how models like RNNs can 'learn' from context during inference, bridging the gap between static prediction and dynamic learning.
concepts.recap_md: - Sequence models adapt their behavior dynamically based on previously processed information in a sequence.

key_passage.text: RNNs update their hidden states as they process a sequence of data. These changes in hidden state change the behavior of the mapping from input to output. Therefore, RNNs adapt as they process data.

motivation.text: Now consider that learning is the problem of adapting future behavior as a function of past data. RNNs can be run on sequences of frames in a movie or on sequences of pixels in an image.

concepts.title: Geons

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Geons are a small set of geometric components, such as blocks and cylinders, used to represent and recognize complex objects.
concepts.content: Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing them into a small set of geometric components, such as blocks, cylinders, and cones, which he called Geons. He derived 36 different Geons that can be discriminated visually. Geons are defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists of a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how the human visual system might simplify complex objects into a finite set of manageable parts, making object recognition more efficient and structured.
concepts.recap_md: - Geons are basic geometric primitives like cones and blocks used as building blocks for object representation.

key_passage.text: Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing the object into a small set of geometric components (e.g., blocks, cylinders, cones, and so on.) that he called Geons. He derived 36 different Geons that we can discriminate visually. Geons we defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature.

motivation.text: An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists in a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.

concepts.title: Compositionality in the Visual World

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Compositionality in vision involves forming objects from simpler, shared elements like Geons, though it is less rigid than compositionality in language.
concepts.content: One important aspect of Biederman's theory is that objects are formed by compositing simpler elements (Geons), which are shared across many different object classes. Compositionality in the visual world is not as strong as that found in language, where a fixed set of words are composed to form sentences with different meanings. In the visual world, components shared across different object classes will have different visual appearances; for example, the legs of tables and chairs share many properties but are not identical. Geons are effective for representing artificial objects like tables, cabinets, and phones, but they fail when applied to represent "stuff" such as grass, clouds, and water, or highly textured objects like trees or food.
concepts.motivation_md: Compositionality explains how a limited set of components can represent a vast array of objects, though it also highlights the limitations of part-based models when dealing with natural textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual compositionality uses shared components across different classes, though their appearance may vary.

key_passage.text: Compositionality in the visual world is not as strong as the one found in language, where a fix set of words are composed to form sentences with different meanings. In the visual world, components shared across different object classes will have different visual appearances (e.g., legs of tables and chairs share many properties but are not identical).

motivation.text: Geons are great to represent artificial objects (e.g., tables, cabinets, and phones) but fail when applied to represent stuff (e.g., grass, clouds, and water) or highly textured objects such as trees or food.

concepts.title: Levels of Categorization

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Categorization occurs at three levels of abstraction: superordinate, basic-level, and subordinate.
concepts.content:
When working on object recognition, a typical task is to train a classifier to categorize images. A category represents a collection of equivalent objects. Categorization is advantageous because it allows an organism to ignore irrelevant differences between stimuli. Eleanor Rosch proposed that categorization occurs at three different levels of abstraction:

1. **Superordinate level**: Very general categories providing a high degree of abstraction (e.g., Furniture, Tree).
2. **Basic level**: The most common level of abstraction (e.g., Chair, Oak).
3. **Subordinate level**: The most specific level of categorization (e.g., Kitchen chair, White oak).

Two objects belonging to the same superordinate category share fewer attributes than two objects belonging to the same subordinate category.
concepts.motivation_md: Categorization helps organisms process information efficiently by grouping similar objects, reducing the cognitive load of treating every unique stimulus as entirely new.
concepts.recap_md: - The basic level is the most common and intuitive level of abstraction for humans.

key_passage.text: Eleanor Rosch and her collaborators proposed that categorization occurred at there different levels of abstraction: superordinate level, basic-level, and subordinate level. Superordinate categories are very general and provide the a high degree of abstraction. Basic level categories correspond to the most common level of abstraction. The subordinate level of categorization is the most specific one.

motivation.text: It is to the organism's advantage not to differentiate one stimulus from others when that differentiation is irrelevant for the purposes at hand. Categorization offers a number of advantages.

concepts.title: Prototypes

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Prototypes are the clearest members of a category, used by humans to recognize categories by measuring similarity.
concepts.content: Natural categories tend to be fuzzy at their boundaries and inconsistent in the status of their constituent members. Rosch suggested that categories can be represented by prototypes, which are the clearest members of a category. Humans recognize categories by measuring the similarity of an object to these prototypes. By using prototypes, it is easier to work with continuous categories, as the categories are defined by "clear cases" rather than by their boundaries.
concepts.motivation_md: Because real-world categories often lack sharp boundaries, prototypes provide a central reference point that makes classification more flexible and robust.
concepts.recap_md: - Categories are defined by clear examples (prototypes) rather than rigid boundaries.

key_passage.text: Prototypes are the clearest members of a category. Rosch hypothesized that humans recognize categories by measuring the similarity to prototypes.

motivation.text: By using prototypes, Rosch suggested that it is easier to work with continuous categories, as the categories are defined by the "clear cases rather than its boundaries."

concepts.title: Standing vs. Occasion Meaning in Affordances

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Objects, like words, have a conventional standing meaning and a context-dependent occasion meaning based on their affordances.
concepts.content:
Object recognition is not always a straightforward categorization task because an object's affordances can change as a function of context. In language, an expression has a standing meaning (its conventional meaning) and an occasion meaning (its particular meaning in a specific context). The same principle applies to visual objects, where the intended use or meaning in a scene may differ from its conventional category.

[FIGURE:cb0694462fa842df | ]

[FIGURE:e401ae49cd70f460 | ]
concepts.motivation_md: This concept addresses the limitations of static categorization by acknowledging that how we perceive and use an object depends heavily on the current situation.
concepts.recap_md: - Standing meaning is the conventional definition, while occasion meaning depends on context.

key_passage.text: An standing meaning corresponds to the conventional meaning of an expression. The occasion meaning is the particular meaning that the same expression might have when used in a specific context.

motivation.text: One example is dealing with the different affordances that an object might have as a function of context. In language, a word or a sentence can have a standing meaning and an occasion meanings.

concepts.title: Image Classification
concepts.one_liner: Image classification is the task of determining if a specific object class is present anywhere within an image.
concepts.content: Image classification is one of the simplest tasks in object recognition. The goal is to determine if object class $c$ is present anywhere in the image ${\bf x}$. While this can be viewed as a machine learning problem focusing on the function $f$, in the context of object understanding, the focus is on the output $\mathbf{y}$. Image classification typically assumes a closed vocabulary of $K$ predefined object classes. The task does not attempt to localize the object or count instances. Mathematically, we build a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$: $$\hat {\bf y} = f({\bf x})$$ The output $\hat {\bf y}$ is a binary response where $1$ indicates the object is present and $0$ indicates it is not.
concepts.motivation_md: Image classification provides a fundamental starting point for computer vision by answering the most basic question of presence or absence before moving to more complex tasks like localization.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to identify if a class is present, not where it is or how many there are.

key_passage.text: Image classification is one of the simplest tasks in object recognition. The goal is to answer the following, seemingly simple, question: Is object class $c$ present anywhere in the image ${\bf x}$?

question.text: Is object class $c$ present anywhere in the image ${\bf x}$?

motivation.text: Image classification typically assumes that there is a closed vocabulary of object classes with a finite number of predefined classes.

concepts.title: Multiclass Classification
concepts.one_liner: Multiclass classification uses an output vector to indicate the presence or absence of multiple object classes simultaneously.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Image classification: Is there a car in this image?)

In general, we want to classify an image according to multiple classes. This is achieved by having an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$ of length $K$, where $K$ is the number of classes. Each component $c$ of the vector $\hat {\bf y}$ indicates whether class $c$ is present or absent in the image. For example, a training set consists of images and their corresponding class indicator vectors.
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world scenes rarely contain only one type of object; multiclass classification allows a system to recognize a variety of different items within a single framework.
concepts.recap_md: - An output vector of length $K$ represents the presence of $K$ different classes.

key_passage.text: In general we want to classify an image according to multiple classes. We can do this by having as output a vector $\hat {\bf y}$ of length $K$, where $K$ is the number of classes. Component $c$ of the vector $\hat {\bf y}$ will indicate whether class $c$ is present or absent in the image.

concepts.title: Uncertainty in Classification
concepts.one_liner: Uncertainty modeling in classification outputs the probability of an object's presence rather than a binary yes/no response.
concepts.content: We want to enrich the output so that it represents the uncertainty in the presence of the object. This uncertainty can stem from a model $f_{\theta}$ that is not perfectly accurate, or from a noisy or blurry input image $\mathbf{x}$ where the object is difficult to see. This is formulated as a function $f_{\theta}$ that takes the image ${\bf x}$ and outputs the probability of the presence of each of the $K$ classes. Letting $Y_c \in \{0,1\}$ be a binary random variable indicating the presence of class $c$, we model uncertainty as: $$\begin{aligned} p(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \hat{y}_c \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: In real-world applications, it is often more useful to know how confident a system is about a detection than to receive a simple binary answer, especially when dealing with low-quality data.
concepts.recap_md: - Uncertainty can arise from model limitations or poor image quality.

key_passage.text: One can formulate this as a function $f_{\theta}$ that takes as input the image ${\bf x}$ and outputs the probability of the presence of each of the $K$ classes. Letting $Y_c \in \{0,1\}$ be a binary random variable indicating the presence of class $c$, we model uncertainty as, $p(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \hat{y}_c$

motivation.text: This uncertainty can be the result of a function $f_{\theta}$ that does not work very well, or from a noisy or blurry input image $\mathbf{x}$ where the object is difficult to see.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Layer-based motion estimation represents the 2D motion field as a collection of superimposed layers, each containing a rigid object with its own motion parameters.
concepts.content: Layer-based motion estimation incorporates knowledge of 3D scene projection by assuming the scene is composed of rigid objects. In this framework, the 2D motion field is represented as a collection of superimposed layers, where each layer contains one object and occludes the layers below. Each layer is described by a different set of motion parameters. This parametric motion field can be integrated into a gradient-based approach, where motion parameters are estimated iteratively using an expectation-maximization (EM) style algorithm. At each step, the algorithm estimates which layer a pixel likely belongs to and then refines the motion parameters for each layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard motion estimation often ignores the 3D structure of a scene. By assuming a scene consists of rigid objects, we can use layers to better model occlusions and the specific parametric forms of motion that occur when rigid bodies move and rotate.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents the motion field as a set of superimposed layers corresponding to rigid objects.

key_passage.text: The 2D motion field can then be represented as a collection of superimposed layers, each layer containing one object and occluding the layers below. Each layer will be described by a different set of motion parameters.

motivation.text: One way of incorporating some of that knowledge is by making some strong assumptions about the moving scene. If the scene is composed of rigid objects, then we can assume that the motion field within each object will have the form described by equation.

concepts.title: Importance of Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Motion estimation is a key attribute in image processing and computer vision for understanding scene dynamics and 3D structure.
concepts.content: Motion estimation is an important task in image processing and computer vision, used in applications such as video denoising and compression. It serves as a key attribute for understanding scene dynamics and 3D structure. Despite extensive study, achieving accurate optical flow remains challenging, even with state-of-the-art deep-learning techniques. Traditional approaches that require no training are particularly useful when exploring unsupervised learning methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion estimation is fundamental for high-level tasks like scene understanding and low-level tasks like video compression, providing the necessary data to interpret how objects and structures move through time.
concepts.recap_md: - Essential for video compression, denoising, and understanding 3D scene dynamics.

key_passage.text: Motion estimation is an important task in image processing and computer vision. It is used in video denoising and compression. In computer vision it is a key attribute to understand scene dynamics and 3D structure.

motivation.text: Motion estimation is an important task in image processing and computer vision. It is used in video denoising and compression. In computer vision it is a key attribute to understand scene dynamics and 3D structure.

concepts.title: Motivation for Learning-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based methods address the failures of traditional motion models by implicitly exploiting semantic properties and complex image cues.
concepts.content: While model-based methods for motion estimation are derived from first principles, they often rely on assumptions that do not hold in real-world scenarios. Modeling errors can occur due to the failure of the brightness constancy assumption, the presence of occlusions, shadows, illumination changes, and deformable surfaces. Additionally, traditional computations often use approximations like finite size discrete convolutions. Learning-based models can implicitly exploit motion-relevant cues that are difficult to model explicitly, such as monocular depth cues and semantic priors (e.g., buildings are stationary, while people are deformable).
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional mathematical models often fail in complex environments with shadows, occlusions, or non-rigid motion. Learning-based approaches allow systems to discover patterns and semantic rules that first-principles equations cannot easily capture.
concepts.recap_md: - Overcomes limitations of the brightness constancy assumption and modeling approximations.

key_passage.text: The reason is that the models make a number of assumptions that are not always true. Also, there are other sources of information that can reveal properties about motion that cannot be modeled but that can be learned.

motivation.text: Causes of modeling errors include failure of the brightness constancy assumption; the presence of occlusions, shadows and changes in illumination; new structures appearing due to changes in the resolution as a result of motion, deformable surfaces; and so on. Those semantic properties can be implicitly exploited by a learning-based model.

concepts.title: Overview of Learning-Based Approaches
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based motion estimation is divided into supervised models using training data and unsupervised models that learn without ground truth.
concepts.content: Learning-based approaches for motion estimation build upon established computer vision concepts and are generally categorized into two families: supervised models and unsupervised models. Supervised models learn to estimate motion by utilizing a database of training examples with known ground truth. In contrast, unsupervised models learn to estimate motion without the need for labeled training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Categorizing learning methods helps distinguish between those that require expensive, labeled ground-truth data and those that can learn directly from raw video sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Supervised models require training databases with ground truth motion.

key_passage.text: Learning-based approaches rely on many of the concepts we introduced in the previous chapters. We will differentiate between two big families of models: supervised models that learn to estimate motion using a database of training examples, and unsupervised models that learn to estimate motion without training data.

concepts.title: Supervised Models for Optical Flow Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Supervised optical flow estimation uses datasets with ground truth motion to train models to predict motion directly from input frames.
concepts.content: The simplest formulation for learning optical flow involves using a dataset of image sequences associated with ground truth optical flow. These datasets are constructed using synthetic data, lidar sensors, or human annotations. While ground truth data was previously used primarily for evaluation, supervised models use it to train the system to predict motion directly from the input frames.
concepts.motivation_md: By providing a model with the 'correct' answer (ground truth), it can learn the complex mapping between pixel intensity changes and actual physical motion through backpropagation.
concepts.recap_md: - Utilizes synthetic, lidar-based, or human-annotated datasets for training.

key_passage.text: The simplest formulation for learning to estimate optical flow is when we have available a dataset of image sequences with associated ground truth optical flow.

motivation.text: Researchers have used synthetic data, using lidar or human annotations to build datasets with ground truth motion. In previous approaches, ground truth data could be used for evaluation; however, we will use it here to train a model to predict motion directly from the input frames.

concepts.title: FlowNet Architecture
concepts.one_liner: FlowNet is an end-to-end neural network architecture that estimates optical flow directly from a pair of image frames.
concepts.content: FlowNet is one of the first neural network approaches to estimate optical flow from two frames using the function: $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$ (see figure: In FlowNet the direct approach estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames.) The architecture is simple and makes no specific assumptions about architectural priors. It is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow to learn the estimation process directly from the input image pair.
concepts.motivation_md: FlowNet demonstrated that a standard convolutional neural network could learn to solve the optical flow problem end-to-end without needing hand-engineered features or traditional optimization steps.
concepts.recap_md: - Estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames using a simple end-to-end architecture.

key_passage.text: One of the first approaches to use this formulation with neural networks was FlowNet. The direct approach learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames. This architecture makes no assumptions about which architectural priors are needed to compute optical flow from images.

motivation.text: The architecture is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow.

concepts.title: Modular Optical Flow Architectures
concepts.one_liner: Modular architectures for optical flow integrate traditional steps like feature extraction and cost volumes into end-to-end trainable networks.
concepts.content:
A common approach in supervised motion estimation is to define an architecture that mirrors traditional procedural steps: 
- Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights, often via a feature pyramid. 
- Form a 3D cost volume indicating local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position. 
- Apply a CNN to aggregate costs over the volume to estimate the best optical flow for each pixel. 
- Use a coarse-to-fine estimation procedure where coarse-scale flow warps features at a finer scale for refined cost volume computation. 
(see figure: Motion estimation. (1) Extract features from each image; (2) compute a 3D cost volume; and (3) aggregate the cost volume in order to estimate the best optical flow for each pixel.) 
Unlike traditional matching or gradient-based methods, these modular architectures are trained end-to-end to minimize optical flow error relative to ground truth.
concepts.motivation_md: By combining the structural insights of traditional computer vision (like cost volumes and pyramids) with the learning power of CNNs, these architectures often achieve higher accuracy and better generalization than simple direct models.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines feature pyramids, 3D cost volumes, and coarse-to-fine refinement.

key_passage.text: Another common approach is to define an architecture that follows the same steps as traditional approaches: Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights. Form a 3D cost volume indicating the local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position. Train and apply a CNN to aggregate (process) the costs over the cost volume in order to estimate a single best optical flow for each pixel position.

motivation.text: Other variations over this architecture incorporate some of the concepts we studied before, such as coarse-to-fine refinement, matching, and smoothing. The main difference between the matching-based and gradient-based methods described earlier is that instead of using predefined functions, the architectures are trained end-to-end to minimize the optical flow error when compared with ground truth data.

concepts.title: Endpoint Error
concepts.one_liner: The endpoint error is the average distance between estimated optical flow vectors and ground-truth vectors across an image.
concepts.content: In supervised optical flow estimation, the most common loss function is the endpoint error. This is defined as the average distance, over the whole image, between the estimated optical flow vector $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and the ground-truth vector $(u,v)$: $$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right) = \sum_{n,m} (\hat{u}[n,m] - u[n,m])^2 + (\hat{v}[n,m] - v[n,m])^2$$ The sum is calculated over all pixels in the image, where each pixel has an associated estimated optical flow $(\hat{u}[n,m],\hat{v}[n,m])$. [FIGURE:94e55f574651d9ae | ]
concepts.motivation_md: To train a neural network for motion, we need a mathematical way to penalize the difference between the predicted motion and the actual motion. Endpoint error provides a simple Euclidean distance metric for this purpose.
concepts.recap_md: - Standard loss function for supervised optical flow training.

key_passage.text: the most common loss is the endpoint error, which is the average, over the whole image, if the distance between the estimated optical flow vector, $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and the ground-truth vector, $(u,v)$

concepts.title: Handling Occlusions in Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Estimating an occlusion map alongside optical flow helps account for pixels that are hidden or revealed as objects move.
concepts.content: One of the challenges for estimating optical flow is that, as objects move, they will occlude some pixels from the background and reveal new ones. Therefore, together with the estimated flow it is also convenient to detect occluded pixels. If we have ground truth data, we can train a function to estimate optical flow and the occlusion map from two frames: $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \hat{\mathbf{o}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: In dynamic scenes, moving objects frequently cover or uncover parts of the background. Standard optical flow assumes every pixel in the first frame has a corresponding pixel in the second; identifying occlusions allows the model to handle areas where this assumption fails.
concepts.recap_md: - Moving objects create occlusions and disocclusions that complicate pixel-wise correspondence.

concepts.title: Datasets for Optical Flow Training
concepts.one_liner: Supervised motion estimation relies on synthetic and specialized real-world datasets to provide the difficult-to-collect ground truth for optical flow.
concepts.content: The biggest challenge of using a supervised model for motion estimation is that ground truth data is very hard to collect. The largest existing datasets are synthetic 3D scenes with moving objects that can be rendered, which provide perfect ground truth data to train the regression function. Examples include the Middlebury dataset, which contains six real and synthetic sequences where real flow was obtained by tracking hidden fluorescent texture. The KITTI dataset contains real motion recorded from a moving car. The MPI Sintel contains synthetic sequences designed to look realistic. Finally, the Flying Chairs dataset is a synthetic dataset consisting of random chairs pasted over background images with affine transformations applied. Because these sequences are easy to generate, they allow for a very large number of training sequences, enabling competitive performance when training neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: Ground truth optical flow cannot be easily recorded in the real world. Researchers use synthetic environments and specialized tracking techniques to create the large-scale data necessary for training supervised deep learning models.
concepts.recap_md: - Ground truth for optical flow is difficult to obtain, leading to a reliance on synthetic data.

key_passage.text: The largest existing datasets are synthetic 3D scenes with moving objects that can be rendered, which will give us perfect ground truth data to train the regression function. There are several examples of existing datasets such as this, like the Middelbury dataset, which contains six real and synthetic sequences with ground truth optical flow.

motivation.text: The biggest challenge of using a supervised model for motion estimation is that ground truth data is very hard to collect. This is probably one of the main limitations of these approaches.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Learning of Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised learning estimates optical flow by assuming brightness constancy, spatial smoothness, and geometric constraints from camera motion.
concepts.content: Collecting ground truth data is the Achilles heel for learning-based approaches, particularly for optical flow which cannot be recorded directly. Real data collection is expensive and nonscalable. Unsupervised methods for training an optical flow model instead make assumptions about dynamic image formation: (1) when motion is due only to camera motion, the optical flow must fit the equations of projected motion; (2) the appearances of objects and surfaces do not change due to motion (brightness constancy assumption); and (3) the optical flow is expected to be smooth over regions, with sharp variations occurring only along occlusion boundaries.
concepts.motivation_md: Because obtaining ground truth optical flow for real-world scenes is often impossible or prohibitively expensive, unsupervised methods allow models to learn motion patterns directly from raw video by enforcing physical and geometric consistency.
concepts.recap_md: - Unsupervised flow estimation avoids the need for ground truth by using physical assumptions.

key_passage.text: Unsupervised methods for training an optical flow model will make some assumptions about dynamic image formation. Those assumptions will be similar to the ones we have presented all along this chapter- (1) when the motion is due only to camera motion, the optical flow will have to fit the equations of the projected motion that provide constraints that can be used to train a model; (2) we can assume that the appearances of objects and surfaces in the scene do not change due to motion (brightness constancy assumption); and (3) we can expect the optical flow to be smooth over regions, although with sharp variations along occlusion boundaries.

question.text: Is it possible to learn to estimate optical flow by just looking at movies without using ground truth data?

motivation.text: Collecting ground truth data is the Achilles heel for learning-based approaches. This is particularly true for optical flow as it can not be recorded directly.

concepts.title: Photometric Loss
concepts.one_liner: Photometric loss measures the reconstruction error between a target frame and a source frame warped by the predicted displacement.
concepts.content: One typical formulation consists in learning to predict the displacement from frame 1 to frame 2, so that if we warp frame 1 we minimize the reconstruction error of frame 2. This is achieved by using the photometric loss: $$L_{photo}(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_2 (x+\hat{u},y+\hat{v}) - \ell_1 (x,y)) \right| ^2$$ where $\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$.
concepts.motivation_md: In the absence of ground truth labels, photometric loss provides a self-supervised signal by checking if the predicted motion can successfully 'undo' the movement between two frames.
concepts.recap_md: - Photometric loss quantifies how well the predicted flow aligns two consecutive video frames.

key_passage.text: This is achieved by using the photometric loss: $$L_{photo}(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_2 (x+\hat{u},y+\hat{v}) - \ell_1 (x,y)) \right| ^2$$

motivation.text: One typical formulation consists in learning to predict the displacement from frame 1 to frame 2, so that if we warp frame 1 we minimize the reconstruction error of frame 2.

concepts.title: Learning with Photometric Loss
concepts.one_liner: Learning involves minimizing photometric loss over large video collections, potentially incorporating robust norms or occlusion weights.
concepts.content: The learning is done by searching over the parameter space for the parameters $\theta$ that minimize the photometric loss over a large collection of videos. The photometric loss can also be replaced by the L1 or other robust norms. If the network also predicts occlusions, the photometric loss can include a weight that cancels the contribution of occluded pixels to the loss. The network can also take as input multiple frames and not just two.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard photometric loss can be sensitive to outliers and occlusions. Refining the loss function with robust norms or occlusion masks makes the training process more stable and accurate in complex scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Parameters are optimized to minimize reconstruction error across video datasets.

key_passage.text: The learning is done by searching over the parameter space for the parameters $\theta$ that minimize the photometric loss over a large collection of videos.

concepts.title: Future Directions in Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Current state-of-the-art motion estimation combines supervised and unsupervised learning, though the search for a perfectly accurate solution continues.
concepts.content: Supervised and unsupervised learning-based methods are now the state-of-the-art in motion estimation. But an accurate solution is still missing. One important question is, do we really need learning in order to solve this problem? Should we abandon the derivation of physically motivated algorithms for motion estimation that require no training? Our answer is that we should pursue both directions of work.
concepts.motivation_md: While deep learning has advanced the field, it is unclear if data-driven methods alone can solve motion estimation or if they should be integrated with classical physical models.
concepts.recap_md: - Learning-based methods currently define the state-of-the-art in motion estimation.

key_passage.text: Our answer is that we should pursue both directions of work.

concepts.title: Complexity of Object Recognition
concepts.one_liner: Object recognition complexity varies based on the level of detail required, occlusion, and the influence of social context.
concepts.content: There are many tasks that researchers use to address the problem of recognition. Although the ultimate goal is to tell what something it is by looking at it, the way that you will answer the question will change the approach that you will use. For instance, you could say, "That is a chair" and just point at it, or we could ask you to indicate all of the visible parts of the chair, which might be a lot harder if the chair is partially occluded by other chairs producing a sea of legs. It can be hard to precisely delineate the chair if we cannot tell which legs belong to it. In other cases, identifying what a chair is might be difficult, requiring understanding of its context and social conventions. (see figure: What is a chair? The definition is based on affordances (i.e., something you can sit on) and on social conventions (i.e., some surfaces you can sit on are meant to be used to support other objects...)
concepts.motivation_md: Recognition is not a single task; it ranges from simple categorization to complex part segmentation, and is often complicated by visual clutter and the functional nature of objects.
concepts.recap_md: - Recognition difficulty depends on the specific question asked and the visual context.

concepts.title: Recognition-by-Components Theory

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: The recognition-by-components theory suggests humans recognize objects by decomposing them into a small set of geometric parts called Geons.
concepts.content: One important theory of how humans represent and recognize objects from images is the recognition-by-components theory proposed by Irving Biederman in 1987. Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing the object into a small set of geometric components (e.g., blocks, cylinders, cones, and so on) that he called **Geons**. He derived 36 different Geons that we can discriminate visually. Geons are defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists in a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations. (see figure: What is this? This drawing from Biederman @Biederman1987, shows a novel object. After looking at this drawing we can conclude the following: (1) we have never seen this object before, (2) it can be...)
concepts.motivation_md: This theory explains how humans can recognize novel objects and handle variations in viewpoint by focusing on fundamental, viewpoint-invariant geometric parts.
concepts.recap_md: - Objects are decomposed into 36 basic geometric shapes called Geons.

concepts.title: Positional Encoding in NeRFs

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: NeRF uses a positional encoding layer to transform raw coordinates into a Fourier representation, enabling the network to model high-frequency variations in radiance fields.
concepts.content:
NeRF includes a positional encoding layer to transform raw coordinates into a Fourier representation. This uses the same positional encoding scheme as is used in transformers. (see figure: The first layer of NeRF applies positional encoding to the input coordinate values. Here we show the resulting positional codes for all possible input coordinate values $(X,Y)$ within some range.)

Fourier positional encodings are very effective for NeRFs because they help the network to model high frequency variations, which are abundant in radiance fields. In regular Cartesian coordinates, the location $(0,0)$ is much closer to $(1,1)$ than it is to $(100,100)$, but this isn't necessarily the case with Fourier positional codes. Because of this, with Cartesian coordinates as inputs, an MLP will be biased to assign similar values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and different values to $(0,0)$ and $(100,100)$. Conversely, with Fourier positional codes as input, this bias is reduced. This makes it so the MLP has an easier time fitting high frequency functions that change in value rapidly, such as assigning very different output values to the locations $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard MLPs struggle to learn high-frequency details when using raw Cartesian coordinates because they are biased toward low-frequency functions. By mapping coordinates to a higher-dimensional Fourier space, positional encoding allows the network to represent sharp edges and fine textures more effectively.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps low-dimensional coordinates to a higher-dimensional Fourier representation.
