concepts.title: Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering computes pixel colors by integrating radiance and density values along camera rays, modeling the scene as a volume of colored particles.
concepts.content:
Volume rendering is the strategy used for rendering images from radiance fields by taking an integral of the radiance values along each camera ray. This process can be conceptualized as looking into a hazy volume of colored dust, where the integral adds up color values along the ray, weighted by the density of the dust.

The volume rendering equation is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \ell(r) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f}\alpha(t) \, \overbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}^{\text{density}} \, \overbrace{L^c(r(t),\mathbf{D})}^{\text{color}} \, dt\\
    \alpha(t) = \exp \Big(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \underbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}_{\text{density}} dt\Big)
\end{aligned}$$
where $r(t)$ gives the coordinates of a point at distance $t$ along the ray, $\mathbf{D}$ is the ray direction, and $t_n$ and $t_f$ are near and far cutoffs. The color is modeled as direction-dependent to capture specularities, while density is direction-independent.

The term $\alpha$ represents the probability that a ray has not hit a particle up to distance $t$. If density is zero, the space is empty; if density is infinite, the object is solid and $\alpha$ immediately goes to zero, terminating the ray. Volume rendering generalizes ray casting by allowing for translucency and media like gases or thin films.
concepts.motivation_md: Volume rendering provides a differentiable way to map a 3D radiance field to 2D images. Unlike traditional surface rendering, it can represent semi-transparent materials and provides smooth gradients that are essential for optimizing radiance fields from photographs.
concepts.recap_md: - Integrates color and density along a ray to determine pixel intensity.

key_passage.text: Volume rendering works by taking an integral of the radiance values along each camera ray. Think of it like we are looking into a hazy volume of colored dust. The integral adds up all the color values along the camera ray, weighted by a value related to the density of the dust.

motivation.text: Volume rendering is a simple generalization of ray casting. One advantage it has is that it can model translucency, and media like gases, fluids, and thin films that let some photons pass through and reflect back others.

concepts.title: Ray Casting
concepts.one_liner: Ray casting is a basic rendering technique that measures the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera.
concepts.content: Ray casting is a fundamental rendering model used in many basic renderers, such as the standard rasterization pipeline. It can be viewed as a special case of volume rendering where particle density is infinite at surfaces and zero elsewhere; in this scenario, the rendering process reduces to measuring the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera.
concepts.motivation_md: Ray casting provides a simple, efficient way to render solid 3D geometry by determining visibility and color at the first point of intersection between a ray and a surface.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies the first intersection point of a ray with scene geometry.

key_passage.text: model, called ray casting, is in fact how many basic renderers work, such as in the standard rasterization pipeline

concepts.title: Quadrature Rule for Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: The quadrature rule approximates the continuous volume rendering integral as a discrete sum of samples along a ray.
concepts.content:
To compute the volume rendering integral, we approximate it as a discrete sum using a quadrature rule:

$$\begin{aligned}    \ell(r) &\approx \sum_{i=1}^T \alpha_i \, (1-e^{-L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_i)\delta_i}) \, L^c(\mathbf{R}_i, \mathbf{D})\\
    &\alpha_i = \exp\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_j)\delta_j\Big)\\
    &\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i
\end{aligned}$$
where the continuous radiance field is replaced by a discrete vector of samples $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$ at world coordinates along the ray $r$.

(see figure: Volume rendering of our Flatland radiance field.)

As visualized in the figure, rays are sent from the camera origin through pixels to query the scene. Each ray is sampled at specific points (drawn as circles). The size of the circle indicates the $\alpha$ value (transmittance), while the color and transparency indicate the density and color of the radiance field. In scenes with solid objects, density is infinite within the object, causing $\alpha$ to go to zero and occluding subsequent points.
concepts.motivation_md: Since the continuous volume rendering integral cannot be solved analytically for complex radiance fields, a discrete approximation is required for numerical computation and implementation in neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Converts the continuous integral into a weighted sum of discrete samples.

key_passage.text: A particularly effective approximation is the following, which is called a quadrature rule: $$\begin{aligned} \ell(r) &\approx \sum_{i=1}^T \alpha_i \, (1-e^{-L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_i)\delta_i}) \, L^c(\mathbf{R}_i, \mathbf{D})\\ &\alpha_i = \exp\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_j)\delta_j\Big)\\ &\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i \end{aligned}$$ where we have now replaced our continuous radiance field from with a discrete vector of samples from the radiance field, $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$, where $\mathbf{R}_t = r(t)$ is the world coordinate of a point distance $t$ along the ray $r$.

motivation.text: One way to do this is to approximate the integral as a discrete sum.

concepts.title: Stratified Sampling along Rays
concepts.one_liner: Stratified sampling divides a ray into intervals and samples one point uniformly from each, ensuring continuous coverage during optimization.
concepts.content:
Instead of taking samples at evenly spaced increments, we can improve the approximation by chopping the ray into $T$ evenly spaced intervals and sampling one point uniformly within each interval. This ensures that all continuous coordinates will be sampled with some probability over multiple iterations, allowing every point in the continuous space to be supervised during the fitting of a radiance field.

For a ray with origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$, the sampled coordinates $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$ are computed as:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{R}_i &= \mathbf{O} + t_i\mathbf{D}\\
    &t_i \sim \mathcal{U}[i-1,i]*\frac{t_f-t_n}{T}+t_n
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathcal{U}[a,b]$ is the uniform distribution over the interval $[a,b]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Regular grid sampling can lead to aliasing and miss details between samples. Stratified sampling introduces stochasticity that ensures the entire volume is explored over the course of training, leading to better reconstruction of continuous scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Divides rays into $T$ bins and samples randomly within each bin.

key_passage.text: we can do better by chopping the ray into T evenly spaced intervals, then sampling one point at uniform within each of these intervals.

motivation.text: The effect of this is that all continuous coordinates will get sampled with some probability, and therefore if we run the approximation over and over again (like we will when using it in an optimization loop) we will eventually take into account every point in the continuous space (they will all be supervised during fitting a radiance field to explain a scene).

concepts.title: Volume Rendering Pipeline
concepts.one_liner: The volume rendering pipeline maps pixel coordinates to RGB colors by tracing rays, sampling coordinates, and applying the volume rendering integral.
concepts.content:
To compute an image $\boldsymbol\ell$ from a camera, we must find the color of each pixel $\boldsymbol\ell[n,m,:]$. The pipeline consists of three main steps:

1. **Pixel to Ray**: Find the ray (origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$) passing through the pixel using the camera origin $\mathbf{O}_{\texttt{cam}}$ and camera matrix $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$.
(see figure: Module for mapping from pixel coordinates to the world coordinates of a ray through that pixel.)

2. **Ray to Coordinates**: Sample world coordinates along the ray, typically using stratified sampling.
(see figure: Module for sampling coordinates along a ray.)

3. **Volume Rendering**: Use the volume rendering integral (via the quadrature rule) to compute the final pixel color.
(see figure: Module for volume rendering of a single ray.)

This pipeline establishes a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values ($n,m \rightarrow r,g,b$), allowing us to infer a radiance field from a set of photos.
concepts.motivation_md: This structured pipeline breaks down the complex task of image synthesis into modular, differentiable steps, enabling the use of gradient-based optimization to solve the inverse problem of vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Converts pixel indices to 3D rays using camera parameters.

key_passage.text: Next we sample world coordinates along the ray, as described previously. Finally, we use the volume rendering integral (using the quadrature rule approximation given previously) to compute the color of the pixel. This pipeline gives a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values: n,m → r,g,b.

motivation.text: Our task is to compute the image ℓ that will be seen by a specified camera viewing the scene. We need to find the color of each pixel in this image.

concepts.title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: Fitting a radiance field involves optimizing parameters to minimize the reconstruction error between rendered images and observed photographs.
concepts.content:
The goal of fitting a radiance field is to find a representation $L_{\theta}$ that explains a set of observed images. While rendering (view synthesis) is a graphics problem, inferring the radiance field from images is the inverse problem of vision. 

The procedure takes a set of images and their corresponding camera parameters $\{\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}, \mathbf{K}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}, \mathbf{O}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}\}_{i=1}^N$ and produces a parameterized radiance field $L_{\theta}$. We optimize the parameters $\theta$ to minimize the reconstruction error between the rendered images and the observed input images.

[FIGURE:ea67f7c877cd7443]

This can be compared to a magic square puzzle, where we find a square (the radiance field) that integrates to observed row and column sums (the images). Radiance fields like NeRF serve as a constrained hypothesis space; while less general than an unconstrained transformer, they are much more sample efficient and require less data to find a good solution.
concepts.motivation_md: By treating 3D reconstruction as an optimization problem over a differentiable rendering pipeline, we can recover high-quality 3D scene representations from 2D images without requiring explicit 3D supervision.
concepts.recap_md: - Minimizes the difference between rendered and real pixel colors.

key_passage.text: Fitting a $L_{\theta}$ to explain the images just involves optimizing the parameters $\theta$ to minimize the reconstruction error between the images of the radiance field rendered through $\texttt{render}_{\theta}$ and the observed input images.

motivation.text: In this section our goal is to find a radiance field that can explain a set of observed images. Rendering radiance fields into images (view synthesis) is a graphics problem. We are now moving on to the vision problem, which the inverse problem and is where we really wanted to get: inferring the radiance field that renders to an observed set of images.

concepts.title: Computation Graph for Rendering

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: The NeRF computation graph connects camera parameters, ray sampling, and volume rendering into a fully differentiable pipeline for image synthesis.
concepts.content:
Given a radiance field $L_{\theta}$, an image is rendered using the volume rendering process. The entire computation graph is designed to be fully differentiable, which is critical for fitting parameters to data. 

(see figure: Full NeRF pipeline for rendering an image.)

In this graph, camera parameters are input into the $\texttt{pixel2ray}$ module. The resulting direction $\mathbf{D}$ and the sampling points $\mathbf{t}$ computed by $\texttt{ray2coords}$ are then passed to the $\texttt{vrender}$ module to produce the final output.
concepts.motivation_md: A fully differentiable computation graph allows for the use of backpropagation to update the weights of the neural radiance field, enabling the system to learn 3D geometry and appearance directly from 2D image loss.
concepts.recap_md: - Links camera geometry, coordinate sampling, and volumetric integration.

concepts.title: In-context learning

position.section_title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

concepts.one_liner: In-context learning is a kind of learning, emergent in a sequence modeling problem, where a model performs supervised learning by processing a sequence of examples.
concepts.content: In-context learning is a phenomenon emergent in sequence modeling. In this framework, supervised learning is treated as the problem of taking a sequence of examples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \mathbf{y}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}, \mathbf{y}^{(n)}\}$ as input to produce a function $f$ as output. For example, after an RNN processes this training sequence, it arrives at a specific hidden state. When the RNN is then fed a new query $\mathbf{x}^{(n+1)}$, the mapping it applies to produce an output $\mathbf{y}^{(n+1)}$ represents the learned function $f$. This function is defined by the parameters of the RNN along with the hidden state derived from the training sequence. Consequently, the RNN operates as a learning algorithm that can apply the inferred function to any arbitrary query.
concepts.motivation_md: In-context learning allows models to adapt to new tasks during inference without updating their internal weights, enabling flexible problem-solving based purely on the provided input sequence.
concepts.recap_md: - It treats a sequence of input-output pairs as training data to infer a specific function $f$.

key_passage.text: Another name for this kind of learning, which is emergent in a sequence modeling problem, is in-context learning.

motivation.text: The goal of supervised learning is that after training on the training data, we should do well on any random test query. After processing the training sequence, an RNN will have arrived at some setting of its hidden state. Now if we feed the RNN a new query, the mapping it applies, which produces an output, can be considered the learned function.

concepts.title: Image Representations
concepts.one_liner: Images can be represented as ordered arrays, sets of pixels, or continuous functions, each offering distinct advantages for signal processing, geometry, or modeling priors.
concepts.content: Images can be represented in several ways, each making different aspects of information explicit. The most common representation is the **ordered array**, where images are ordered arrays of pixel values sampled on a regular spatial grid: $$\boldsymbol\ell=\left[ \begin{matrix} \ell[1,1] & \dots & \\ \vdots & \ell[n,m] & \vdots \\ & \dots & \ell[N,M] \\ \end{matrix} \right]$$ This representation simplifies signal processing operations like convolution. Alternatively, an image can be represented as a **set of pixels**: $$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$ where $\ell_i$ is the intensity at location $(x_i,y_i)$. This makes geometry explicit and simplifies geometric transformations. A third option is the **continuous function** representation, $\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$, which is useful for making image priors explicit and handling continuous spatial variables. These representations are not mutually exclusive and can be used simultaneously depending on whether the goal is 3D geometry, visualization, or image modeling.
concepts.motivation_md: Different computer vision tasks require different data structures; while arrays are optimized for convolution, sets are better for geometric transformations, and functions allow for resolution-independent modeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Ordered arrays represent pixels on a regular grid, which is ideal for signal processing and standard computer input.

key_passage.text: an image can be represented in different ways, making explicit certain aspects of the information present on the input. What else could we do to represent an image? Another very different, but equivalent, representation is to encode an image as a collection of points, indicating its color and location explicitly. In this case, an image is represented as a set of pixels: where ℓᵢ is the pixel intensity (or color) recorded at location (xᵢ,yᵢ).

question.text: What else could we do to represent an image?

motivation.text: These three representations induce different ways of thinking about architectures to process the visual input. These representations are not opposed and can be used simultaneously.

concepts.title: Ordered array representation
concepts.one_liner: The ordered array representation treats an image as a regular spatial grid of pixel intensity values, facilitating operations like convolution.
concepts.content: The ordered array is the standard representation for images in most contexts, where an image is treated as an ordered array of pixel values. Each value represents a sample on a regular spatial grid, with $s$ representing the pixel intensity at a specific location: $$\boldsymbol\ell=\left[ \begin{matrix} \ell[1,1] & \dots & \\ \vdots & \ell[n,m] & \vdots \\ & \dots & \ell[N,M] \\ \end{matrix} \right]$$ For color images, this may consist of three such arrays. This representation is typical for signal processing perspectives and makes it simpler to describe operations such as convolution.
concepts.motivation_md: This format aligns with how digital sensors capture data and provides a structured matrix that is computationally efficient for neighborhood-based operations like filtering.
concepts.recap_md: - It organizes pixel intensities into a matrix corresponding to a regular spatial grid.

key_passage.text: In most of the chapters, we have represented images as ordered arrays of pixel values, each pixel described by its grayscale value (or three arrays for color images). We will call this representation the ordered array. Each value is a sample on a regular spatial grid.

motivation.text: This is the representation we are most used to and the typical representation used when taking a signal processing perspective. It makes it simpler to describe operations such as convolution.

concepts.title: Set of pixels representation
concepts.one_liner: The set of pixels representation encodes an image as a collection of points with explicit color and location, simplifying geometric transformations.
concepts.content: The set of pixels representation encodes an image as a collection of points, explicitly indicating color and location: $$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$ where $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity or color recorded at location $(x_i,y_i)$. This representation makes the geometry of the image explicit. It simplifies certain operations, such as geometric transformations, by allowing direct manipulation of spatial coordinates. For instance, translating an image to the right by one pixel is achieved by creating a new set of translated pixels: $\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i+1,y_i] : i \right\}$. This format is common in geometry-based computer vision and is useful for handling image geometries where points are not on a regular array.
concepts.motivation_md: By making coordinates explicit, this representation allows for easier manipulation of image geometry and supports non-grid-based spatial data essential for 3D vision.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents an image as a collection of points with explicit $(x, y)$ coordinates and intensity values.

key_passage.text: an image is represented as a set of pixels: where ℓᵢ is the pixel intensity (or color) recorded at location (xᵢ,yᵢ). This representation makes the geometry explicit.

motivation.text: This representation makes the geometry explicit. It might seem like a trivial representation but it makes some operations easy (and others complex).

concepts.title: Continuous function representation
concepts.one_liner: The continuous function representation models an image as a parameterized function mapping spatial locations to intensity or color values.
concepts.content: An image can be represented as a continuous function where the input is a location $(x, y)$ and the output is an intensity or color $\ell$: $$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$ This function $f_{\theta}$ is parameterized by coefficients $\theta$, which are estimated from the original image. This representation is commonly used to make image priors more explicit. Once learned, the function $f$ can take continuous spatial variables as input, allowing the image to be evaluated at any coordinate rather than just on a fixed pixel grid.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach enables resolution-independent image representation and allows for the application of continuous mathematical tools and explicit priors in image analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - It defines an image as a function $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ mapping coordinates to colors.

key_passage.text: Another option is to represent an image as a continuous function whose input is a location (x, y) and it output is an intensity, or a color, ℓ: ℓ(x,y) = f_θ(x,y)

motivation.text: This image representation is commonly used when we want to make image priors more explicit. But once learned, the function f should be able to take as input continuous spatial variables.

concepts.title: Homogeneous coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates represent $N$-dimensional vectors in $N+1$ dimensions, enabling scale-invariant point descriptions and simplifying geometric transformations.
concepts.content: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$. To transform from heterogeneous (Cartesian) to homogeneous coordinates, an additional coordinate, 1, is added: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Similarly for 3D: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ In this system, all non-zero scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar $\lambda$. To return to the heterogeneous representation, all entries of the homogeneous vector are divided by their last dimension: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ w \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} x/w \\ y/w \end{pmatrix}$$ Geometrically, a point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant, which is closely related to perspective projection. (see figure: Transformation rule between heterogeneous and homogeneous coordinates in 2D. All the points along the dotted line correspond to the same point in heterogeneous coordinates. Note that the points...)
concepts.motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates simplify complex geometric operations like translation and perspective projection by allowing them to be expressed as linear matrix multiplications.
concepts.recap_md: - They add an extra dimension to standard coordinates to enable scale-invariant representation.

key_passage.text: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$. The homogeneous coordinates have the additional rule that all (non-zero) scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent.

motivation.text: We can already see that this is closely related to the operation performed by perspective projection.

concepts.title: Heterogeneous coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Heterogeneous coordinates are conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of points in 2D or 3D space, typically denoted with rounded brackets.
concepts.content: Heterogeneous coordinates refer to conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of a point in 2D, such as $(x,y)$, or 3D, such as $(x,y,z)$. In geometric contexts, these are typically written with rounded brackets to distinguish them from square-bracketed homogeneous coordinate representations.
concepts.motivation_md: They provide the standard, intuitive way to describe locations in Euclidean space before applying projective transformations or homogeneous scaling.
concepts.recap_md: - They are standard Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$ or $(x, y, z)$. - They are typically represented with rounded brackets in geometric contexts.

key_passage.text: We will refer to conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of a point in 2D, such as $(x,y)$, or 3D, such as $(x,y,z)$, as **heterogeneous coordinates** and write with rounded brackets in this

concepts.title: 2D Image Transformations
concepts.one_liner: Geometric transformations like translation, rotation, and scaling can be efficiently represented as affine transformations using homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content: Geometric transformations of shapes, such as translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing, are essential operations in computer vision and graphics. These can be written as affine transformations of the coordinate system. The mathematical description of these transformations is simplified when using homogeneous coordinates, providing the basis for more complex operations like 3D perspective projection and camera calibration. (see figure: 2D geometric transformations. The final transformation is an arbitrary warping with a more complex deformation field.)
concepts.motivation_md: To provide a unified mathematical framework for manipulating the position, orientation, and size of objects within an image using linear algebra.
concepts.recap_md: - Common transformations include translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing.

key_passage.text: These transformations can be written as affine transformations of the coordinate system. The mathematical description of these transformations becomes surprisingly simple when using homogeneous coordinates, and they will become the basis for more complex operations such as 3D perspective projection and camera calibration as we will see in later sections.

motivation.text: One important operation in computer vision (and in computer graphics) is geometric transformations of shapes. Some of the common transformations we'll want to represent include translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing.

concepts.title: Motion Field from Camera Translation
concepts.one_liner: The 2D motion field for a translating camera relates image velocity to camera velocity and scene depth.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how camera translation generates image motion is fundamental for computer vision tasks like structure from motion. It allows us to relate the physical movement of a camera to the perceived velocity of pixels in the image plane.
concepts.recap_md: - Camera translation creates a motion field where image velocity is inversely proportional to depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: The 2D motion field by using equation is: $$\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\\dot{y}\end{bmatrix}= \frac{1}{Z}\begin{bmatrix}-f & 0 & x \\0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}V_X\\V_Y \\V_Z \end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: Let's now assume that the scene is static and that only the camera is moving. In this case, all the observed motion in the image will be due to the motion of the camera.

concepts.title: Lateral Camera Motion and Parallax
concepts.one_liner: Lateral camera motion occurs when the camera moves parallel to the image plane, creating a parallax effect where closer objects appear to move faster.
concepts.motivation_md: Lateral motion isolates the effect of depth on image velocity. By observing how fast objects move relative to one another during lateral translation, a system can infer their relative distances (parallax).
concepts.recap_md: - Lateral motion occurs when $V_Z = 0$, resulting in image velocity inversely proportional to depth.

key_passage.text: Objects close to the camera will appear moving faster than objects farther away. Objects that are very far will appear as not moving. This parallax effect is the same one used in stereo vision to recover depth.

motivation.text: This parallax effect is the same one used in stereo vision to recover depth.

concepts.title: Focus of Expansion
concepts.one_liner: The focus of expansion is the point in the image where the observed motion is zero during camera translation.
concepts.motivation_md: The focus of expansion identifies the camera's heading. It is a critical cue for navigation and obstacle avoidance, as it indicates the point toward which the camera is moving.
concepts.recap_md: - The focus of expansion is the stationary point $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$ in the motion field.

key_passage.text: The observed motion is zero at the focus of expansion, (x_∞, y_∞).

motivation.text: Second, the observed motion only depends on the ratio V_Z/Z, which is the inverse of the time to contact.

concepts.title: Time to Contact
concepts.one_liner: Time to contact is the time required for a moving camera to reach an object at a specific distance.
concepts.content: The observed motion in a forward-moving camera depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact. The time to contact, $Z/V_Z$, is the time it will take the camera to reach an object located at a distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$. Notably, the rate of expansion in the image plane does not depend on the focal length $f$, only on this ratio.
concepts.motivation_md: Time to contact is a vital metric for autonomous systems to avoid collisions, as it provides a temporal measure of proximity that is independent of absolute distance or camera focal length.
concepts.recap_md: - Time to contact is defined as the ratio $Z/V_Z$.

key_passage.text: The time to contact, $V_Z/Z$, is the time it will take the camera to reach the object located a distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$.

motivation.text: Second, the observed motion only depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact.

concepts.title: Motion Field from Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The motion field for a camera undergoing both translation and rotation relates 2D image velocity to 3D linear and angular velocities.
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world camera motion is rarely purely translational. Modeling the combined effects of translation and rotation is necessary to accurately interpret optical flow in complex scenarios like handheld filming or vehicle navigation.
concepts.recap_md: - The motion field is the sum of a translational component (dependent on depth $Z$) and a rotational component (independent of $Z$).

key_passage.text: This is the expression we were looking for. It relates the 2D motion field with the camera velocity and rotation. The matrices are only a function of the intrinsic camera parameters (focal length, f) and the camera coordinates.

motivation.text: To compute the motion field with a compact expression, we will do a number of simplifications assuming a small motion between consecutive frames. Now we are ready to compute the 2D motion field by using equation.

concepts.title: Motion Field under Pure Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: Under pure camera rotation, the 2D motion field is independent of the 3D scene structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between rotational and translational motion is crucial because only translation provides depth cues. Understanding pure rotation helps in calibrating camera parameters and stabilizing images.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure rotation fields are independent of scene depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: The first thing to notice is that the 2D motion field does not depend on the 3D scene structure, Z, and it is only a function of the rotational velocity and the camera parameters. Therefore, under camera rotation we can not learn anything about the scene by observing the motion field. The only thing we can learn from the 2D motion field is about the motion of the camera.

motivation.text: In the previous section we saw what happens when there is no rotation; now we can focus on the case when there is only camera rotation, that is V_X=V_Y=V_Z=0.

concepts.title: Motion under Varying Focal Length
concepts.one_liner: Changing the focal length of a static camera produces a motion field that scales the image without providing depth information.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights that not all image motion is caused by physical movement. It warns that 'zooming' can mimic the expansion of forward motion but lacks the parallax necessary for depth perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Changing focal length results in a radial scaling of the image plane.

key_passage.text: changing the focal length only results in a scaling of the projected image on the image plane. It does not create any parallax.

question.text: What will the motion field be?

motivation.text: Before moving into motion estimation, let's consider one final scenario: a static camera observing a static scene, but the focal length changes over time.

concepts.title: Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow is an approximation of the 2D motion field calculated by measuring the displacement of image brightness between frames.
concepts.content:
Optical flow approximates the 2D motion field by measuring the displacement of image brightness. Given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, the optical flow $[\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}]$ indicates the relative position of each pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ to its corresponding pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. This definition assumes a one-to-one mapping between frames and that a single motion explains all brightness changes. These assumptions may fail during occlusions, when objects appear/disappear, or when illumination changes.

(see figure: Two frames of a sequence, ground-truth optical flow (color coded), and the color code to read the vector at each pixel.)
concepts.motivation_md: While the motion field is a purely geometric concept, optical flow is the practical method used to estimate that motion from actual pixel data in video sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow measures the apparent motion of brightness patterns between consecutive frames.

key_passage.text: Optical flow is an approximation to the 2D motion field computed by measuring displacement of image brightness. The ideal optical flow is defined as follows: given two images ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ ∈ ℝ^(N × M × 3), the optical flow [u, v] ∈ ℝ^(N × M × 2) indicates the relative position of each pixel in ℓ₁ and the corresponding pixel in ℓ₂.

motivation.text: Optical flow is an approximation to the 2D motion field computed by measuring displacement of image brightness.

concepts.title: Object Localization
concepts.one_liner: Object localization consists of localizing where an object is in an image, typically by finding the image-coordinates of a tight bounding box around each instance.
concepts.content:
For many applications, saying that an object is present in the image is not enough. If a visual system for an autonomous vehicle only tells the navigation system that there is a person in the image, it will be insufficient for deciding what to do. Object localization consists of localizing where the object is in the image. There are many ways one can specify where the object is. The most traditional way of representing the object location is using a **bounding box** (@fig-object_detection_bb), that is, finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each of the instances of class $c$ in the image $\bf x$.

(see figure: Car localization using bounding boxes. Each instance is shown with a different color.)
concepts.motivation_md: In tasks like autonomous driving, simply knowing an object exists is insufficient; the system must know exactly where the object is located to make navigation decisions.
concepts.recap_md: - Object localization identifies the specific spatial location of an object within an image.

key_passage.text: Object localization consists of localizing where the object is in the image. The most traditional way of representing the object location is using a bounding box, that is, finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each of the instances of class c in the image.

motivation.text: For many applications, saying that an object is present in the image is not enough. Suppose that you are building a visual system for an autonomous vehicle. If the visual system only tells the navigation system that there is a person in the image it will be insufficient for deciding what to do.

concepts.title: Bounding Box
concepts.one_liner: A bounding box is a tight box around an object instance defined by specific image coordinates.
concepts.content:
The most traditional way of representing the object location is using a **bounding box** (@fig-object_detection_bb), which involves finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each of the instances of class $c$ in the image $\bf x$.

(see figure: Car localization using bounding boxes. Each instance is shown with a different color.)
concepts.motivation_md: Bounding boxes provide a standardized, low-dimensional way to represent the spatial extent and location of objects for computer vision algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - A bounding box is the standard representation for object location in images.

key_passage.text: The most traditional way of representing the object location is using a bounding box, that is, finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each of the instances of class c in the image.

concepts.title: Mathematical Formulation of Object Detection
concepts.one_liner: Object detection is formulated as a function mapping an image to a list of bounding boxes and their associated class vectors.
concepts.content:
We will formulate object detection as a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into a list of bounding boxes $\hat {\bf b}_i$ and the associated classes to each bounding box encoded by a vector $\hat {\bf y}_i$, as illustrated in @fig-object_detection_bb.

(see figure: Car localization using bounding boxes. Each instance is shown with a different color.)

The class vector, $\hat {\bf y}_i$, has the same structure as in the image classification task but now it is applied to describe each bounding box. Bounding boxes are usually represented as a vector of length 4 using the coordinates of the two corners, ${\bf b} = \left[ x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2 \right]$, or with the center coordinates, width, and height, ${\bf b} = \left[ x_c, y_c, w, h \right]$. Our goal is a function $f$ that outputs a set of bounding boxes, $\mathbf{b}$, and their classes $\mathbf{y}$: $$\hat {\bf y}_i, \hat {\bf b}_i = f({\bf x})$$
concepts.motivation_md: Defining object detection mathematically allows researchers to apply optimization and machine learning techniques to solve the problem of identifying and locating multiple objects.
concepts.recap_md: - Detection maps an image to a set of pairs containing a class vector and a bounding box.

key_passage.text: We will formulate object detection as a function that maps the input image into a list of bounding boxes and the associated classes to each bounding box encoded by a vector, as illustrated in fig-object_detection_bb. Our goal is a function f that outputs a set of bounding boxes, and their classes: {ŷᵢ, b̂ᵢ} = f(x)

concepts.title: General Steps for Object Detection
concepts.one_liner: Object detection typically involves proposing candidate boxes, classifying the image patches within them, and postprocessing to remove redundancies.
concepts.content: Most approaches for object detection have three main steps. In the first step, a set of candidate bounding boxes are proposed. In the second step, we loop over all proposed bounding boxes, and for each one, we apply a classifier to the image patch inside the bounding box. In the third and final step, the selected bounding boxes are postprocessed to remove any redundant detections.
concepts.motivation_md: Breaking detection into proposal, classification, and refinement stages makes the complex task of finding objects of any size at any location computationally manageable.
concepts.recap_md: - Step 1: Propose a set of candidate bounding boxes.

key_passage.text: Most approaches for object detection have three main steps. In the first step, a set of candidate bounding boxes are proposed. In the second step, we loop over all proposed bounding boxes, and for each one, we apply an classifier the image patch inside the bounding box. In the third and final step, the selected bounding boxes are postprocessed to remove any redundant detections.

concepts.title: Window Scanning Approach
concepts.one_liner: The window scanning approach turns a binary classifier into a detector by sliding it across the image or image pyramid.
concepts.content:
In its simplest form, the problem of object localization is posed as a binary classification task, namely distinguishing between a single object class and background class. Such a classification task can be turned into a detector by sliding it across the image (or image pyramid), and classifying each local window as shown in @alg-scanningWindow2.

(see figure: Window scanning approach using a multiscale image pyramid.)

The window scanning algorithm is the following:

(see figure: Window scanning algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: This approach allows a simple image classifier to be repurposed for object detection by exhaustively checking every possible location and scale.
concepts.recap_md: - Slides a local window across an image pyramid to detect objects at different scales.

key_passage.text: Such a classification task can be turned into a detector by sliding it across the image (or image pyramid), and classifying each local window as shown in

motivation.text: In its simplest form, the problem of object localization is posed as a binary classification task, namely distinguishing between a single object class and background class.

concepts.title: Selective Search
concepts.one_liner: Selective search efficiently proposes candidate bounding boxes using a fast mechanism before applying a more expensive classifier to the selected regions.
concepts.content:
The window scanning approach can be slow as the same classifier needs to be applied to tens of thousands of image patches. Selective search makes the process more efficient by proposing an initial set of bounding boxes that are good candidates to contain an object (@fig-selective_search_pipeline). This proposal mechanism is performed by a selection mechanism simpler than the object classifier. This approach was motivated by the strategy used by the visual system in which attention is first directed toward image regions likely to contain the target. This first attentional mechanism is very fast but might be wrong. Therefore, a second, more accurate but also more expensive, processing stage is required in order to take a reliable decision. The advantage of this **cascade** of decisions is that the most expensive classifier is only applied to a sparse set of locations dramatically reducing the overall computational cost.

The algorithm for selective search only differs from the window scanning approach on how the list of candidate bounding boxes is generated. Some approaches also add a bounding box refinement step. The overall approach is described in algorithm @fig-selective_search.

(see figure: Selective search algorithm.)

This algorithm has four main steps. In the first step, the algorithm uses an efficient window scanning approach to produce a set of candidate bounding boxes. In the second step, we loop over all the candidate bounding boxes, we crop out the box and resize it to a canonical size, and then we apply an object classifier to classify the cropped image as containing the object we are looking for or not. In the third step, we refine the bounding box for the crops that are classified as containing the object. And finally, in the fourth step, we remove low-scoring boxes and we use **nonmaximum suppression** (NMS) to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object, so as to output only one bounding box for each instance present in the image.

@fig-selective_search_pipeline.

(see figure: A first classifier selects candidate bounding boxes. A second, stronger, classifier makes the final detections (e.g., cars). Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) removes overlapping detections.)

(see figure: Sketch of the selective search architecture. The image is first broken into candidate regions. Then each region is processed individually using a classifier and a regression.)
concepts.motivation_md: Exhaustive window scanning is computationally expensive; selective search reduces the search space by identifying likely regions of interest first.

concepts.title: Cascade of Decisions
concepts.one_liner: A cascade of decisions applies expensive classifiers only to a sparse set of locations selected by a cheaper mechanism to reduce computational cost.

concepts.title: Nonmaximum Suppression (NMS)
concepts.one_liner: Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is an iterative algorithm used to discard overlapping bounding boxes by keeping only the highest confidence detections.
concepts.content:
Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is used to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object. The nonmaximum suppression algorithm takes as input a set of object bounding boxes and confidences, $S=\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$, and outputs a smaller set removing overlapping bounding boxes. It is an iterative algorithm as follows:
(1) Take the highest confidence bounding box from the set $S$ and add it to the final set $S^*$.
(2) Remove from $S$ the selected bounding box and all the bounding boxes with an IoU larger than a threshold.
(3) Go to step 1 until $S$ is empty.
concepts.motivation_md: Detectors often produce multiple overlapping boxes for the same object; NMS ensures that each physical object is represented by only one bounding box.
concepts.recap_md: - Iteratively selects the highest confidence box and removes others with high IoU overlap.

key_passage.text: The nonmaximum suppression algorithm takes as input a set of object bounding boxes and confidences, and outputs a smaller set removing overlapping bounding boxes. It is an iterative algorithm as follows: (1) Take the highest confidence bounding box from the set and add it to the final set. (2) Remove from the set the selected bounding box and all the bounding boxes with an IoU larger than a threshold. (3) Go to step 1 until the set is empty.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation Loss
concepts.one_liner: The instance segmentation loss is a weighted sum of classification, localization, and segmentation losses.
concepts.content:
The loss can be written as a combination of the classification, localization, and segmentation losses:
$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \left( 
     \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
     +
     \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i)
     \right)
$$ 

The first classification loss corresponds to the classification of the crop as containing the object or not. If the object is present, the second term measures the accuracy of the bounding box, and the third term measures whether the segmentation, $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i$, inside each bounding box matches the ground truth instance segmentation, $\mathbf{s}_i$. The parameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ control how much weight each loss has on the final loss.
concepts.motivation_md: To train an instance segmentation model, we need a single scalar loss that penalizes errors in identifying the object class, locating its bounding box, and delineating its specific pixel-level mask simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md:
- The total loss combines classification, localization (bounding box), and segmentation (mask) components.
- A mask loss is only calculated for regions where an object is actually present.
- Hyperparameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ balance the relative importance of box accuracy and mask precision.

key_passage.text: The loss can be written as a combination of the classification, localization, and segmentation losses that we discussed before: $$\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) + \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) \left( \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i) + \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i) \right)$$

motivation.text: The first classification loss corresponds to the classification of the crop as containing the object or not; if the object is present, the second term measures the accuracy of the bounding box, and the third term measures whether the segmentation, $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i$, inside each bounding box matches the ground truth instance segmentation, $\mathbf{s}_i$.

concepts.title: Limitations of Current Object Representations
concepts.one_liner: Current object representations like bounding boxes and masks are often insufficient for complex tasks like robotics and 3D interaction.
concepts.content:
(see figure: A family of object recognition definitions.)

The representations we have described—image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression—feel very incomplete. For applications like robotics or autonomous vehicles, these representations are hard to act on. A robot planning to grasp an object needs accurate 3D modeling and an understanding of physical properties to plan grasping points. Similarly, an autonomous vehicle requires a 3D description of object locations and their dynamics. Object segmentation and classification provide only part of the necessary information.

Furthermore, these techniques rely heavily on language to define objects. An advanced computer vision system should behave like a scientist, asking deeper questions about its visual stimuli: Is this piece of matter a distinct object? What is its 3D shape? How is it supported? What are its mechanical properties (e.g., rigid or deformable)? How will it react to external actions? Is it stable, or what will it do next? A system should formulate hypotheses about visual input and perform interventions to answer them, rather than relying solely on language as an internal representation.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard recognition tasks like classification and segmentation are useful, they lack the physical and 3D depth required for real-world interaction and scientific reasoning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Standard representations (boxes, masks) lack the 3D and physical data needed for robotics.
- Current systems rely too much on linguistic labels rather than physical or functional understanding.
- Future systems should act as scientists, hypothesizing about object dynamics, stability, and utility.

key_passage.text: However, the representations we have described in this chapter feel very incomplete. If you are building a robot or an autonomous vehicle, such object representations are very hard to act on. A robot planning to grasp an object will need an accurate three-dimensional (3D) modeling of the object as well as an understanding of some of its physical properties in order to plan for the best grasping points. An autonomous vehicle will also need an accurate 3D description of the locations of objects in the world, together with a characterization of their dynamics. Therefore, object segmentation and classification only provide one part of the information needed.
