A robot planning to grasp an object will need an accurate three-dimensional (3D) modeling of the object as well as an understanding of some of its physical properties in order to plan for the best grasping points.

concepts.title: The Relationship Between Vision and Language
concepts.one_liner: Vision and language are both mental models used to represent the world for higher-level cognition and decision making.
concepts.content: While vision and language might initially seem unrelated if language is viewed only as communication, another perspective suggests that language is a representation of the world used by the brain for higher-level cognition. Visual perception is similarly about representing the world and forming mental models that serve as a substrate for reasoning and decision making. From this perspective, both language and vision are solving essentially the same problem. This view is powerful, as language and vision can support each other in numerous ways within artificial intelligence systems.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the deep connection between vision and language allows for the development of multimodal models that leverage the strengths of both to better represent the world.
concepts.recap_md:
- Language and vision are both internal representations of the world for reasoning.
- Both fields aim to form mental models that support decision making.
- Integrating the two allows vision systems to improve through language and vice versa.

key_passage.text: Visual perception is also about representing the world around us and forming mental models that act as a substrate for reasoning and decision making. From this perspective, both language and vision are trying to solve more or less the same problem.

motivation.text: The last few decades have seen enormous improvements in both computer vision and natural language processing. Naturally, there has been great interest in putting these two branches of artificial intelligence (AI) together.

concepts.title: Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
concepts.one_liner: Vision-language models (VLMs) are AI models that integrate visual and linguistic information.
concepts.content: In order to understand vision-language models (VLMs), we first need to understand a bit about language models.
concepts.motivation_md: VLMs are designed to bridge the gap between visual perception and linguistic description, enabling tasks like image captioning and visual question answering.
concepts.recap_md:
- VLMs combine computer vision and natural language processing.
- Understanding VLMs requires a foundational knowledge of how language models function.

key_passage.text: In order to understand vision-language models (VLMs) we first need to understand a bit about language models.

concepts.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
concepts.one_liner: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field of AI focused on the interaction between computers and human language.
concepts.content: This field is called natural language processing (NLP).
concepts.motivation_md: NLP provides the tools and models necessary for computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
concepts.recap_md:
- NLP is the standard term for computational language modeling.
- It forms a core component of vision-language integration.

key_passage.text: called natural language processing (NLP).

concepts.title: Word-Level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Word-level encoding maps each unique word in a vocabulary to a unique one-hot code.
concepts.content: One option for representing text as numbers is to use a word-level encoding scheme, mapping each word in our vocabulary to a unique one-hot code. This requires $K$-dimensional one-hot codes for a vocabulary of $K$ different words.
concepts.motivation_md: To process text with neural networks, words must be converted into a numerical format that the model can interpret.
concepts.recap_md:
- Each word is represented by a unique one-hot vector.
- The vector dimension is equal to the size of the vocabulary ($K$).

key_passage.text: One option, which we have already seen, is to use a word-level encoding scheme, mapping each word in our vocabulary to a unique one-hot code.

question.text: So our first question is, how can we represent text as numbers?

motivation.text: This requires K-dimensional one-hot codes for a vocabulary of K different words.

concepts.title: Character-Level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Character-level encoding assigns a one-hot code to each individual character rather than to whole words.
concepts.content: Instead of words, we could use a strategy where we assign a one-hot code to each character in our vocabulary. If we represent all alphanumeric characters and common punctuation marks, this might only require a few dozen codes. The disadvantage is that representing a single word now requires a sequence of one-hots rather than a single code, which the model must then account for.
concepts.motivation_md: Character-level encoding significantly reduces the vocabulary size and avoids the problem of out-of-vocabulary words, though it increases sequence length.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a small vocabulary of characters and punctuation.
- Words are treated as sequences of character codes.
- Reduces dimensionality but increases the complexity of modeling sequences.

key_passage.text: we assign a one-hot code to each *character* in our vocabulary, rather than to each unique word. If we represent all alphanumeric characters and common punctuation marks in this way, this might only require a few dozen codes.

motivation.text: Instead, we could use a different strategy, where we assign a one-hot code to each *character* in our vocabulary, rather than to each unique word.

concepts.title: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
concepts.one_liner: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is a subword encoding strategy that assigns codes to common substrings found in text.
concepts.content: A happy middle ground can be achieved using byte-pair encodings (BPE). In this approach, we assign a one-hot code to each small chunk of text. The chunks are common substrings found in text, like "th" or "ing." This strategy is popular in language models like the generative pretrained transformer (GPT) series and the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) model.
concepts.motivation_md: BPE balances the efficiency of word-level encoding with the flexibility of character-level encoding, effectively handling rare words by breaking them into common sub-components.
concepts.recap_md:
- Encodes text using common substrings (subwords) rather than full words or single characters.
- Used in major models like GPT and CLIP.
- Provides a balance between vocabulary size and sequence length.

key_passage.text: In this approach, we assign a one-hot code to each small chunk of text. The chunks are common substrings found in text, like "th" or "ing."

motivation.text: A happy middle ground can be achieved using byte-pair encodings.

concepts.title: Text Tokenization
concepts.one_liner: Text tokenization converts one-hot encoded text sequences into dense token vectors via a projection matrix from the vocabulary dimensionality to a target dimensionality.
concepts.content: Once we have converted text into a sequence of one-hot codes, the next step is to convert these into tokens via a projection, $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$, from the one-hot dimensionality ($K$) to a target dimensionality for token code vectors ($d$). (see figure: Tokenizing text. Note that these steps can be implemented with a lookup table that simply stores the token code vector for each unique item in our vocabulary.) These steps convert an input string to tokens. For simplicity, word-level one-hot encoding is often shown rather than byte-pair encoding.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw text cannot be processed directly by neural networks. Tokenization maps discrete vocabulary items into a continuous vector space, allowing transformers and other architectures to perform mathematical operations on linguistic data.
concepts.recap_md: [FIGURE:fig-VLMs-tokenizing_text | Tokenizing text. Note that these steps can be implemented with a lookup table that simply stores the token code vector for each unique item in our vocabulary.]

key_passage.text: Once we have converted text into a sequence of one-hot codes, the next step is to convert these into tokens via a projection, from the one-hot dimensionality (K) to a target dimensionality for token code vectors (d).

concepts.title: Autoregressive Language Models

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive language models generate text by predicting each next vocabulary item based on the sequence of tokens generated so far.
concepts.content: To handle the output side, where we produce text as an output, we need to convert tokens back to text. The most common way to do this is to use an autoregressive model that predicts each next item in our vocabulary (word/character/byte-pair) given the sequence generated so far. Each prediction step can be modeled as a softmax over all $K$ possible items in our vocabulary.
concepts.motivation_md: While encoders map text to tokens, generative tasks require a mechanism to produce coherent sequences. Autoregressive modeling breaks down the complex task of sequence generation into a series of conditional probability predictions.
concepts.recap_md: - Predicts the next vocabulary item based on the preceding sequence.

key_passage.text: The most common way to do this is to use an autoregressive model that predicts each next item in our vocabulary (word/character/byte-pair) given the sequence generated so far.

motivation.text: To handle the output side, where we produce text as an output, we need to convert tokens back to text.

concepts.title: Visual Representation Learning from Language Supervision

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Language supervision uses free-form natural language as a pretext task to learn rich visual representations of scenes.
concepts.content: One approach of learning visual representations is to set up a pretext task that requires arriving at a good representation of the scene, using language association as the pretext task. Historically, image classification (associating an image with one of $K$ nouns) was a form of language supervision. However, human languages contain much richer linguistic structures than simple noun sets, including adjectives, verbs, and relational words. The most effective approach at scale is to train a vision system that associates images with free-form natural language, utilizing all the structure present in language.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional supervised learning is limited by fixed label sets. Using natural language as supervision allows models to learn from the vast, diverse descriptions available on the internet, capturing more nuanced visual concepts than simple categories.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses language association as a pretext task for visual representation learning.

key_passage.text: train a vision system that associates images with free-form natural language

question.text: could we use richer linguistic structure to supervise vision?

motivation.text: Researchers have tried using all kinds of language structures to supervise vision systems, including adjectives and verbs, words indicating relationships between objects, and question-answer pairs. What seems to work best, once you reach a certain scale of data and compute, is to just use all the structure in language, and the simplest way to do this is to train a vision system that associates images with free-form natural language.

concepts.title: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP)

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP is a contrastive learning method that aligns co-occurring visual and linguistic views by maximizing the similarity between image and caption embeddings.
concepts.content:
Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) is a contrastive method in which one data view is the image and the other is a caption describing the image. Specifically, CLIP is a form of contrastive learning from co-occurring visual and linguistic views formulated as follows:

[FIGURE:7d5ab02809b91736]

where $\boldsymbol\ell$ represents an image, $\mathbf{t}$ represents text, $\mathbb{S}^{d_z}$ represents the space of unit vectors of dimensionality $d_z$, $f_{\ell}$ is the image encoder, and $f_t$ is the text encoder. Image inputs are represented as $[3 \times N \times M]$ pixel arrays, while text inputs are represented as $d_t$ dimensional tokens. The objective is a symmetric version of the InfoNCE loss. Both $f_\ell$ and $f_t$ output unit vectors via $L_2$-normalization, ensuring the denominator cannot dominate by pushing negative pairs infinitely far apart.
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP was designed to create a robust visual representation that understands natural language descriptions, enabling models to generalize to new visual tasks without needing task-specific labeled data.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a symmetric InfoNCE loss to align image and text encoders.

key_passage.text: CLIP is a contrastive method in which one data view is the image and the other is a caption describing the image. Specifically, CLIP is a form of contrastive learning from co-occurring visual and linguistic views

concepts.title: CLIP Training Procedure

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP training involves maximizing the dot product between matched image-text pairs while minimizing it for all other pairings in a batch.
concepts.content:
To train CLIP, we first sample a batch of $N$ language-image pairs, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Next, we measure the dot product between all these text strings and images using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$, producing text embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_t\}_{i=1}^N$ and image embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\}_{i=1}^N$. To compute the loss, we take the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$. Terms where $i = j$ are positive pairs, and we seek to maximize these dot products. Terms where $i \neq j$ are negative pairs, and we seek to minimize these dot products.

(see figure: CLIP training for one batch of six language-image training examples. Green boxes are positive pairings (we seek to increase their value); these are the six training pairs. Red boxes are negative...)
concepts.motivation_md: By training on large batches of image-text pairs, the model learns to identify the specific features that link a description to its corresponding image, creating a shared semantic space.
concepts.recap_md: - Maximizes dot products for positive (matched) pairs and minimizes them for negative pairs.

key_passage.text: Next we embed measure the dot product between all these text strings and images using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$, respectively. To compute the loss, we take the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,6\}$. Terms for which $i \neq j$ are the negative pairs and we seek to minimize these dot products (denominator of the loss); terms for which $i == j$ are the positive pairs and we seek to maximize these dot product (they appear in both the numerator and denominator of the loss).

concepts.title: CLIP Embedding Space and Visualization

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: The CLIP embedding space maps images and text to a shared hypersphere where small angles indicate high semantic similarity.
concepts.content:
After training, the text encoder $f_t$ and image encoder $f_\ell$ map to the same embedding space. In this space, the angle between a text embedding and an image embedding will be small if the text matches the image. The dot product between unit vectors is proportional to the angle between the vectors.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning mapping diagram, using the same technique as described in @sec-neural_nets_as_distribution_transformers. To reduce dimensionality we apply t-SNE @tsne separately for the...)

In the image encoder, early layers may group images by color while later layers group by shape; in the text encoder, color and shape words are equally accessible. The final stage normalizes outputs so embeddings lie on the surface of a hypersphere. Text descriptions are embedded near matching image embeddings, though visualization in 2D (using kernel PCA or t-SNE) may have limitations.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning joint embedding)
concepts.motivation_md: A shared embedding space allows the model to compare different modalities (vision and language) using simple geometric operations like dot products or cosine similarity.
concepts.recap_md: - Embeddings are $L_2$-normalized to lie on a hypersphere.

key_passage.text: After training, we have a text encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$ that map to the same embedding space. In this space, the angle between a text embedding and an image embedding will be small if the text matches the matches.

question.text: Why do you think this is?

motivation.text: After passing the data through these two encoders, the final stage is to normalize the outputs and compute the alignment between the image and text embeddings.

concepts.title: Zero-Shot Image Classification with CLIP

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP enables zero-shot image classification by comparing a query image embedding to embeddings of arbitrary text descriptions of classes.
concepts.content:
CLIP connects images to language, allowing the construction of novel image classifiers on the fly using natural language descriptions. To classify an image among a set of classes $a, b, \ldots$:

1. Embed each class description sentence into a vector: $\mathbf{z}_t^{a} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{a}), \mathbf{z}_t^{b} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{b}), \ldots$
2. Embed the query image into a vector: $\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{q} = f_{\ell}(\boldsymbol\ell^{q})$.
3. Predict the class whose sentence embedding is closest (in angular distance) to the image embedding.

(see figure: Making a ``striped red circles'' (class $a$) versus ``polka dotted green square'' (class $b$) classifier using a trained CLIP. The CLIP model parameters are frozen and not updated. Instead the...)

This approach leverages the compositional power of language to distinguish complex concepts like "striped red circles" without further training.

[FIGURE:bbc557ba56150a05]
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional classifiers require retraining to learn new categories. Zero-shot classification allows a model to recognize concepts it has never seen as explicit labels by leveraging its general understanding of language.
concepts.recap_md: - Classifies images by finding the closest text embedding among candidate class descriptions.

key_passage.text: Given a set of sentences that describe images of classes a, b, and so on, Embed each sentence into a z-vector, Embed your query image into a z-vector, See which sentence embedding is closest to your image embedding; that's the predicted class.

motivation.text: CLIP connects the domain of images to the domain of language. This means that many of the powerful abilities of language become applicable to imagery as well. One ability that the CLIP paper showcased is making a novel image classifier on the fly.

concepts.title: Translating between Images and Text
concepts.one_liner: Modality translation involves using deep networks to forge links between disparate data types, such as images and text or sounds and lyrics.
concepts.content: It is possible to translate between entirely different data modalities (X2Y and Y2X). For any type of data X and any other type Y—such as images and sounds, music and lyrics, or amino acid sequences and protein geometry—deep networks can be used to forge links between these disparate domains of knowledge. These systems allow tools and discoveries from one domain to become applicable to other linked domains.
concepts.motivation_md: Translating between modalities allows models to transfer knowledge across different forms of data, enabling applications like text-to-image generation or automated music transcription.
concepts.recap_md: - Forges links between disparate domains of knowledge (e.g., images and sounds).

key_passage.text: For any type of data X, and any other type Y, there is, increasingly, a method X2Y (and Y2X) that translates between these two data types.

motivation.text: X2Y systems are powerful because they forge links between disparate domains of knowledge, allowing tools and discoveries from one domain to become applicable to other linked domains.

concepts.title: Conveying the main idea with a simple example
concepts.one_liner: A paper should include a simple example that captures its main idea and highlights the specific problem or drawback being addressed.
concepts.content: A paper should include an example that captures its main idea. For instance, a figure can convey a core concept very simply, such as demonstrating how a specific representation lacks desirable features. (see figure: Effect of translation on the wavelet representation of a signal (caption and figure after @Simoncelli92. (a) An input signal. (b-d) The high-, mid-, and low-frequency coefficients within a wavelet...) In the case of wavelet representations, a figure can show the failure to form a translation-invariant representation. By showing two versions of the same signal differing only by a one-sample translation, the figure points out the drawback of aliased subbands: as the signal translates, the representation energy moves to different frequency bands and changes form.
concepts.motivation_md: Complex technical arguments can be difficult to grasp quickly. A simple, well-chosen example or figure allows the reader to immediately understand the core problem and the paper's primary contribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Use a simple example to capture the paper's main idea and core contribution.

key_passage.text: Here is a figure from a different paper that conveys the main idea very simply.

motivation.text: The figure points out in a simple way the drawback of a wavelet representation with aliased subbands that was the focus of the paper: as the signal translates, the signal representation energy moves to different frequency bands and changes form within the mid-frequency band.

concepts.title: Standards for experimental results
concepts.one_liner: Modern research standards require that all assertions in a paper be backed up with quantitative experimental evidence and comparisons to the state-of-the-art.
concepts.content: Modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence. Readers will expect a table quantitatively comparing the performance of your algorithm with that of the previous state-of-the-art. If you are proposing a new task for which there aren't previous benchmarks, you should still compare with an algorithm that solves a related task, noting that the algorithm was designed for a different task. (see figure: prototypical table of results, from \cite{Owens2016} Rows are different algorithms, or ablations of a favored algorithm. Columns are datasets or tasks, and the numbers indicate performance, with the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Plausibility arguments are no longer sufficient in computer vision; quantitative evidence is necessary to prove that a new method actually improves upon existing work.
concepts.recap_md: - Back up all claims with quantitative experimental evidence.

key_passage.text: modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence. Readers will be expecting a table quantitatively comparing the performance of your algorithm with that of the previous state-of-the-art.

motivation.text: In earlier days of computer vision research, good ideas could be presented with only plausibility arguments to support them. However, modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence.

concepts.title: How to (and how not to) end a paper
concepts.one_liner: A paper should conclude by reviewing contributions and new research directions rather than listing unfinished work.
concepts.content: You should resist the temptation to describe items that were left unfinished in a section on "Future Work." It is a weak way to end a paper by enumerating all the things the paper doesn't accomplish or providing a summary of where it falls short. Instead, the paper can finish with a review of what has been presented, emphasizing the contributions. Address how the world has changed now that the reader has read the paper, what new research directions have been opened up, and what can be done now that couldn't be done before.
concepts.motivation_md: Ending on unfinished work highlights weaknesses. Ending on contributions reinforces the value of the research and its impact on the field.
concepts.recap_md: - Avoid ending with a list of unfinished "Future Work."

key_passage.text: Instead, the paper can finish with a review what has been presented, emphasizing the contributions. How has the world changed, now that the reader has read this paper? What new research directions have been opened up; what can we do now that we couldn't do before?

motivation.text: It is hard to imagine a weaker way to end the paper than to enumerate all the things the paper doesn't accomplish, providing a summary of where it falls short.

concepts.title: Keep the reader uppermost in mind
concepts.one_liner: The most important principle of good writing is to anticipate the reader's knowledge and expectations at every step.
concepts.content: Perhaps the most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why? The ideal writer acts like a great host who anticipates every need of their guest, knowing at every moment what the reader might be wanting and how to help them find it.
concepts.motivation_md: Writing is an act of communication; if the author does not account for the reader's perspective, the technical content may become inaccessible or confusing.
concepts.recap_md: - Constantly ask what the reader knows and what they expect next.

key_passage.text: Perhaps the most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why?

question.text: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why?

motivation.text: Our mental image is that of a great host, who anticipates every need of their house guest: after you arrive, they say, "Can I take your coat? Would you like something to drink?" At every moment, they know what you might be wanting and how to help you find it.

concepts.title: The importance of concise writing
concepts.one_liner: Vigorous writing is concise, containing no unnecessary words or sentences to ensure clarity and fit within page limits.
concepts.content: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words and a paragraph no unnecessary sentences. Writing more concisely helps a paper in two ways. First, researchers often face strict page limits, particularly in conference submissions; tighter text allows the author to say more or include additional figures. Second, concise text is usually clearer and easier for the reader to understand. For example, a technical paragraph can often be reduced significantly in length (e.g., from 149 words to 88 words) without changing its meaning, simply by removing roundabout descriptions.
concepts.motivation_md: Conciseness respects the reader's time and maximizes the information density allowed by strict publication constraints.
concepts.recap_md: - Remove unnecessary words and sentences to improve clarity.

key_passage.text: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.

motivation.text: Note that writing more concise text helps your paper in two ways. First, researchers are typically fighting against a page limit, particularly in conference submissions, so tighter text lets the author say more or add another figure. Second, concise text is usually clearer and easier to understand.

concepts.title: Engagement levels of paper readers
concepts.one_liner: Since many readers only skim papers, the title, abstract, and figures should independently convey the paper's core message.
concepts.content: Most readers will probably only skim your paper rather than reading every word. Because of this, you should write your paper so that readers will learn from it even at reduced levels of engagement. The title should convey the top-level message of the paper. The abstract should provide a good summary, and the figures and their captions should be self-contained to tell the story of the paper. (see figure: The conjectured readership of a computer science paper (conjectured relative amounts). Many people will read the title, but far fewer will read the abstract or look at the figures. Fewer still will...)
concepts.motivation_md: In an era of high publication volume, authors must ensure their main contributions are accessible to skimmers who may never read the full text.
concepts.recap_md: - Ensure the title, abstract, and figures convey the main message independently.

key_passage.text: We suspect that the engagement of readers with your paper will look something as shown in Many people will read the title, but far fewer will read the abstract or look at the figures. Fewer still will read the entire paper.

motivation.text: in our current era of many published papers, most of your readers will probably only skim your paper. If only because that is where most of your readership lies, you should write your paper so that readers will learn from it, even at those reduced levels of engagement.

concepts.title: Catchy titles and top-level messages
concepts.one_liner: A good title generates attention and interest by clearly stating the paper's main point or asking a compelling question.
concepts.content: A good title can generate attention and interest for a paper. Effective titles often let the reader see the delight or the main point of the work immediately, such as "What makes Paris look like Paris." While a technical title like "Shiftable Multi-scale Transforms" may be appropriate, adding a catchy subtitle or phrase that tells the main point—such as "What's wrong with wavelets?"—can make the paper much more engaging.
concepts.motivation_md: The title is the first thing a potential reader sees; a catchy title increases the likelihood that the paper will be noticed and read.
concepts.recap_md: - Use titles that generate interest and convey the main point immediately.

key_passage.text: A good title can generate attention and interest for the paper.

motivation.text: A good title can generate attention and interest for the paper. "What makes Paris look like Paris" is a delightful paper, and the title lets the reader see that right away. In contrast, one of us coauthored a paper called "Shiftable Multi-scale Transforms." While that title is appropriate, it's not catchy. After the paper was in print, we realized that we should have added the subtitle, "What's wrong with wavelets?" --- a catchy phrase that tells the main point of the paper.

concepts.title: Writing self-contained figure captions
concepts.one_liner: Figure captions should be self-contained and explicitly state what the reader is supposed to notice.
concepts.content: Because many readers of figure captions will not be reading the full paper, the captions should be self-contained. They should point out what readers are supposed to notice about the figure, helping both the full-paper reader and the figures-only reader understand the takeaway. (see figure: Figure and caption from \cite{FreemanShapetime}. The caption should be understandable by itself, and should point to what the reader should take away from the figure.)
concepts.motivation_md: Self-contained captions ensure that the visual evidence of a paper remains informative even when viewed in isolation from the main text.
concepts.recap_md: - Write captions that are understandable without reading the main text.

key_passage.text: the captions should be self-contained. They should point out what readers are supposed to notice about the figure, to help both the full-paper reader and the figures-only reader.

motivation.text: Because you can assume that many of the readers of your figure captions will not be reading the full paper, the captions should be self-contained.

concepts.title: Robustness and Generalization in Vision Systems
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision systems gain robustness and generalization by training on diverse data, allowing them to handle conditions that break fragile, hand-crafted models.
concepts.content:
Transitioning from hand-crafted systems to neural networks allows for 3D interpretation without manually detecting edges or features. The neural network learns to compute the features it deems necessary to solve the task. While a learned-based model might lose some local accuracy—such as recovering a ground plane as concave rather than flat or producing twisted cube faces—it gains significantly in robustness and generalization.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using a pretrained model. The images show multiple view points of the reconstructed 3D scene from @fig-simplesystem_revisited_img1)

Hand-crafted approaches can produce precise results when images fit their specific world assumptions, but they are fragile. Poor illumination or a simple change in the scene, like changing the ground color, can break edge detectors and cause a cascade of errors. Conversely, learning-based approaches like MiDaS produce results of consistent quality regardless of conditions. 

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

(see figure: Out of domain generalization. For the pretrained model, these images might still be within the domain of the training, as it contained a very diverse set of natural images. The simple system model...)

While hand-crafted models offer a comprehensive understanding of their own mechanisms and require no training data, they do not generalize outside the space defined by their assumptions. Pretrained systems are able to deal with configurations that were not part of the original modeling assumptions and are robust to changes in illumination. Even though these networks do not rely on explicit hand-coded heuristics, they may still be performing equivalent operations internally, as 3D information is fundamentally contained in edges and junctions.
concepts.motivation_md: Hand-crafted vision systems are often brittle, failing when lighting changes or assumptions are slightly violated. This concept explores how deep learning models trade perfect geometric precision for the ability to function reliably across diverse, unpredictable real-world environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Hand-crafted models are precise under strict assumptions but fragile to environmental changes like lighting or color.

key_passage.text: However, while the learned-based model may have lost accuracy in this example that fits our simple world assumptions, it has gained in robustness and generalization.

question.text: How does the pretrained model work exactly?

motivation.text: When the images fit the assumptions of the world model, the hand-crafted approach can produce beautiful results. However, it is very fragile, and poor illumination can break the output of the edge detectors, which results in a cascade of errors that propagate to the output.

concepts.title: LLM-based Scene Understanding
concepts.one_liner: Large Language Models like GPT-4v can interpret and reason about the 3D geometry of scenes by leveraging massive training data and transformer architectures.
concepts.content:
Large Language Models, such as GPT-4v, provide an alternative for interpreting visual scenes by allowing users to ask questions about images. This method is remarkably accurate because the underlying transformer, trained on massive data, may have learned rules equivalent to detecting edges, using wavelet-like filters, and reasoning about perspective geometry to estimate shape.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

However, scene understanding is not yet fully solved. While GPT-4v can recognize geometric figures and their spatial configurations, the integration with rendering engines remains fragile. For example, attempting to reconstruct or re-render an image from the model's text description often results in errors or inconsistencies.

(see figure: Output by ChatGPT when asked to render a new image with the same elements as in @fig-chatgpt_blockworld This conversation is a continuation of the same chat from @fig-chatgpt_blockworld)

[FIGURE:2d5b0345de81fa09]

These failures provide clues to the next fundamental questions in computer vision, such as how to better integrate high-level recognition with precise geometric rendering.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional vision systems often struggle with semantic context. LLMs offer a way to combine visual recognition with high-level reasoning, though they still face challenges in perfectly translating that understanding back into precise 3D reconstructions.
concepts.recap_md: - GPT-4v uses transformer architectures to reason about perspective, vanishing points, and spatial configurations.

key_passage.text: Another option is to use GPT4-v to interpret the scene. GPT4-v can take as inputs images, and it allows asking questions about images.

question.text: What is missing? How would you improve it.

motivation.text: This method is remarkably accurate, and now you know how it works.

concepts.title: Unsolved Solved Computer Vision Problems
concepts.one_liner: In computer vision, many seemingly 'solved' problems are actually illusions that mask deeper, underlying challenges requiring creative new directions.
concepts.content:
Computer vision is making amazing progress, but it is important to be wary of "unsolved solved computer vision problems." For certain tasks, it may appear as if a single method has perfectly resolved the issue or that foundational problems are fully addressed. However, this is often an illusion; the problem may not be truly solved, and many unsolved problems typically lurk in the background of every perceived success.

Advances in the field are the result of exploring new directions with an open mind and using creativity as a tool. The precise answers to current questions are less important than the ability to challenge existing approaches and identify relevant questions for new systems. With the rise of learning-based systems, researchers find themselves performing experiments similar to psychophysics to understand the internal mechanisms of these artificial visual systems.

[FIGURE:a9cf6077c82fad75]
concepts.motivation_md: This concept encourages a critical mindset, reminding students that 'state-of-the-art' solutions often have hidden limitations and that the field advances by questioning what is currently accepted as solved.
concepts.recap_md: - Many foundational problems in computer vision are only partially solved despite appearing finished.

key_passage.text: For some vision task, it might appear as if there is one method that perfectly resolves the task. It might appear as if some foundational problems in computer vision are solved. It might often seem as if it is not possible to make progress regarding certain questions. But more often than not, it is just an illusion, and the solved problem was not really solved at all.

motivation.text: Computer vision is making amazing progress, but beware of the unsolved solved computer vision problems. And even when a problem was genuinely solved (and probably is not), it's important to remember that for every solved problem, there are many unsolved problems lurking in the background.

concepts.title: Precision-Recall Curve
concepts.one_liner: The precision-recall curve measures the performance of a detection algorithm as a function of the decision threshold.
concepts.content:
The precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold. As each bounding box comes with a confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$, we use a threshold, $\beta$, to decide if an object is present at the bounding box location $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ or not. Given a threshold $\beta$, the number of detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)$ and the number of correct detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i$.

From these two quantities we compute the precision as the percentage of correct detections:

$$
Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}
$$

The precision only gives a partial view on the detector performance as it does not account for the number of ground truth instances that are not detected (misdetections). The recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$

Both precision and recall are quantities between 0 and 1, where high values correspond to high performance. The graph below shows the precision-recall curve as a function of $\beta$.

(see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)
concepts.motivation_md: A single accuracy metric often fails to capture the trade-off between finding all objects (recall) and ensuring detections are correct (precision). The precision-recall curve allows practitioners to visualize this trade-off across all possible decision thresholds, helping to select the optimal operating point for a specific application.
concepts.recap_md: - Precision measures the percentage of detections that are correct for a given threshold $\beta$.

key_passage.text: Precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold. As each bounding box comes with a confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$, we need to use a threshold, $\beta$, to decide if an object is present at the bounding box location $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ or not.

motivation.text: The precision only gives a partial view on the detector performance as it does not account for the number of ground truth instances that are not detected (misdetections). The recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$.

concepts.title: Precision
concepts.one_liner: Precision is the percentage of correct detections among all detections made by a model at a specific threshold.
concepts.content:
Precision is computed as the percentage of correct detections for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$
Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Precision is essential for understanding how much we can trust a model's positive predictions. In many applications, such as medical diagnosis or autonomous driving, the cost of a false positive is high, making precision a critical metric.
concepts.recap_md: - Precision represents the ratio of true positives to the total number of predicted positives.

key_passage.text: From these two quantities we compute the precision as the percentage of correct detections: Precision(β) = Σᵢ 𝟙(ŷᵢ > β) × yᵢ / Σᵢ 𝟙(ŷᵢ > β)

concepts.title: Recall
concepts.one_liner: Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are correctly detected for a given decision threshold.
concepts.content:
Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Recall is used to evaluate a model's ability to find all relevant objects in a dataset. It is particularly important in scenarios where missing a target (a false negative) is more costly than a false alarm.
concepts.recap_md: - Recall represents the ratio of true positives to the total number of actual ground truth instances.
