concepts.title: Average Precision (AP)
concepts.one_liner: Average Precision (AP) is the area under the precision-recall curve, summarizing detector performance with a single number between 0 and 1.
concepts.content: The precision-recall curve is non-monotonic. The average precision (AP) summarizes the entire curve with one number. The AP is the area under the precision-recall curve, and it is a number between 0 and 1.
concepts.motivation_md: While a precision-recall curve provides a detailed view of performance, it is difficult to use for comparing multiple models directly. AP provides a single, standardized scalar value that represents the overall quality of the detector across all thresholds.
concepts.recap_md: - AP is the area under the precision-recall curve.

key_passage.text: The average precision (AP) summarizes the entire curve with one number. The AP is the area under the precision-recall curve, and it is a number between 0 and 1.

motivation.text: The precision-recall curve is non-monotonic. The average precision (AP) summarizes the entire curve with one number.

concepts.title: Stuff vs. Objects
concepts.one_liner: The distinction between 'objects' with well-defined boundaries and 'stuff' like grass or sky determines whether bounding boxes are an appropriate representation.
concepts.content:
Using bounding boxes to represent the location of objects is not always appropriate, particularly for objects with long, thin structures or regions without well-defined boundaries. It is useful to differentiate between **stuff** and **objects**. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky. 

However, the distinction is not always sharp. In some images, object instances might be easy to separate, while in others they become a texture where instances cannot be detected individually. In cases with many instances, it may be better to represent the region as a category (e.g., "trees") rather than detecting each instance.

(see figure: Bounding boxes are not an appropriate representation of the location of trees. This is true for many object classes with extended shapes that are hard to approximate with a box.)

Even with few instances, bounding boxes can provide ambiguous localization when objects overlap, making it unclear which pixels belong to which object. Furthermore, bounding boxes are insufficient for tasks like robot manipulation, which require detailed descriptions of pose and shape.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard object detection relies on bounding boxes, but this geometric primitive fails for amorphous regions or complex shapes. Recognizing the difference between 'stuff' and 'objects' helps researchers choose between detection, semantic segmentation, or instance segmentation approaches.
concepts.recap_md: - Objects have well-defined boundaries, while 'stuff' refers to amorphous regions like sky or water.

key_passage.text: It is useful to differentiate between stuff and objects. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky.

motivation.text: Using bounding boxes to represent the location objects will not be appropriate for objects with long and thin structures or for regions that do not have well-defined boundaries.

concepts.title: Semantic Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation is the process of classifying each pixel in an image with an object class label.
concepts.content:
Semantic segmentation is the per-pixel classification of object labels. Instead of using bounding boxes, which may not well-describe 'stuff' or wiry objects, this approach attempts to classify every pixel in an image.

(see figure: Semantic segmentation. Every pixel is annotated with a semantic tag (red = car, blue = building, green = road, yellow = sidewalk, and cyan = sign).)

In its generic formulation, semantic segmentation takes an image $\mathbf{x}(n,m)$ and outputs a classification vector at each location:
$$\hat{\mathbf{y}} \left[n,m \right] = f(\mathbf{x} \left[n,m \right])$$

This function $f$ is generally implemented as a neural network with an encoder-decoder structure. Alternatively, a window-scanning approach can be used where $f$ outputs the class of the central pixel of an image patch. Training requires a dataset of segmented images with ground truth $y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right]$. The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel:
$$\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} \sum_{n,m}  y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right] \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right])$$

To avoid focusing too much on large objects, classes can be weighted by their average area. Quality is often measured by the average Intersection over Union (IoU) across classes, which is more informative than simple pixel accuracy.

### Shortcomings
This representation cannot count instances; two instances of the same class in contact will appear as a single segment. It also typically labels each pixel with a single class, failing to handle transparencies or depth ordering.
concepts.motivation_md: Bounding boxes are often too coarse for complex shapes or amorphous regions. Semantic segmentation provides a dense, pixel-level understanding of the scene, which is necessary for tasks like autonomous driving where identifying the exact boundaries of the road, sidewalks, and obstacles is vital.
concepts.recap_md: - Semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every individual pixel in an image.

key_passage.text: Per-pixel classification of object labels, illustrated in is referred to as semantic segmentation.

motivation.text: Not everything is well-described by a bounding box (stuff, wiry objects, etc.). Instead we can try to classify each pixel in an image with an object class.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder for Semantic Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation functions are commonly implemented using a neural network with an encoder-decoder architecture.
concepts.content:
Generally, the function $f$ used for semantic segmentation is a neural network with an encoder-decoder structure, first introduced by Badrinarayanan et al. (2015).

(see figure: Sketch of the encoder-decoder architecture for semantic segmentation.)
concepts.motivation_md: To perform pixel-level classification, a model needs to capture both high-level global context (via the encoder) and low-level spatial detail (via the decoder). The encoder-decoder architecture efficiently compresses information and then maps it back to the original image resolution.
concepts.recap_md: - The encoder-decoder structure is a standard architecture for dense prediction tasks like segmentation.

key_passage.text: the function f is a neural network with an encoder-decoder structure, first introduced in Badrinarayanan2015.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation to output pixel-level masks for every individual object instance.
concepts.content:
Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation to output a set of localized objects represented as pixel-level masks. Unlike semantic segmentation, which provides an aggregate region for a class, instance segmentation can distinguish between $K$ different objects of the same type and delineate overlapping instances.

(see figure: Instance segmentation. Each instance of the class car is assigned to a different color.)

One approach is to use an object localization pipeline to propose bounding boxes, then feed the cropped image within each box to a binary semantic segmentation function. This function predicts whether each pixel in the box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ belongs to the object.

(see figure: Architecture for instance segmentation. This architecture combines several of the components we have seen previously. The image is first broken into overlapping regions, and then class segmentation...)

The model uses a detector $f_0$ to propose regions and a function $f_1$ to perform classification and segmentation:
$$\left[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i,   \hat{\mathbf{s}}_i \right]= f_j(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)$$
where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$ is the confidence and $\hat{s}_i$ is the mask. The total loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation components:
$$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}} + \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) (\lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} + \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}})$$

### Shortcomings
While this is a complete representation that can classify, localize, and count, it can be extremely challenging to implement precisely. It also remains limited by its reliance on language to define classes.
concepts.motivation_md: Semantic segmentation fails to distinguish between individual objects of the same class (e.g., a crowd of people), while object detection only provides coarse boxes. Instance segmentation solves both problems by providing precise boundaries for every unique object instance.
concepts.recap_md: - Instance segmentation identifies and masks every individual object separately, even if they belong to the same class.

key_passage.text: We can combine the ideas of object detection and semantic segmentation into the problem of instance segmentation. Here the idea is to output a set of localized objects, but rather than representing them as bounding boxes we represent them as pixel-level masks.

motivation.text: The difference from semantic segmentation is that if there are K objects of the same type, we will output K masks; conversely, semantic segmentation has no way to telling us how many objects of the same type there are, nor can it delineate between two objects of the same type that overlap.

concepts.title: Cascade of Classifiers
concepts.one_liner: A cascade of classifiers divides object search into a sequence of classifiers with increasing computational complexity and accuracy to efficiently localize objects in images.
concepts.content:
Trying to localize an object in an image is like finding a needle in a haystack: the object is usually small and might be surrounded by a complex background. Selective search reduced the complexity of the search by dividing the search into two steps: a first, fast, and cheap classification function that detects good candidate locations; and a second, slow, and expensive classification function capable of accurately classifying the object that only needs to be applied in a subset of all possible locations and scales. Cascade of classifiers pushes this idea to the limit by dividing the search into a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

The algorithm for the cascade of classifiers is:

(see figure: Cascade of classifiers algorithm.)

Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced it in 2001 with a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers. In parallel, Fleuret and Geman also proposed a system that performs a sequence of binary tests at each location. Each binary test checks for the presence of a particular image feature. Early versions of this strategy were also inspired by the game "Twenty Questions".

In a cascade, computational power is allocated into the image regions that are more likely to contain the target object while regions that are flat or contain few features are rejected quickly and almost no computations are allocated in them. The following figure shows a beautiful illustration of how a cascaded classifier allocates computing power in the image when trained to detect faces. The intensity shown in the heat map is proportional to the number of levels in the cascade applied to each location.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

It is interesting to point out that the scanning window approach ($Levels = 1$) and the selective search procedure ($Levels = 2$) are special cases of this algorithm. The cascade of classifiers usually does not have a bounding box refinement stage as it already started with a full list of all bounding boxes, but it could be added if we wanted to add new transformations not available in the initial set (e.g., rotations).
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection is computationally expensive because most image regions do not contain the target. Cascades solve this by using cheap, fast classifiers to quickly reject empty regions, reserving expensive, accurate computations only for high-probability candidate areas.
concepts.recap_md: - A cascade uses a sequence of classifiers where each subsequent stage is more complex and accurate than the last.

key_passage.text: Cascade of classifiers pushes this idea to the limit by dividing the search in a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

motivation.text: Trying to localize an object in an image is like finding a needle in a haystack: the object is usually small and might be surrounded by a complex background. Selective search reduced the complexity of the search by dividing the search in two steps: a first, fast, and cheap classification function that detects good candidate locations; and a second, slow, and expensive classification function capable of accurately classifying the object and that only needs to be applied in a subset of all possible locations and scales.

concepts.title: Object Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: The object localization loss combines classification and localization tasks into a single objective function to train object detectors end-to-end.
concepts.content:
The object localization loss has to take into account two complementary tasks: classification and localization.

- Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$): For each detected bounding box, does the predicted label match the ground truth at that location?
- Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$): How close is the detected location to the ground truth object location?

For each image, the output of our object detector is a set of bounding boxes $\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. The first step in the evaluation is to associate each detection with a ground truth label so that we have a set $\{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. For each of the predicted bounding boxes that overlaps with the ground truth instances, we optimize parameters to improve predicted locations and labels. Predicted bounding boxes that do not overlap with ground truth instances are assigned to the background class, $\mathbf{y}_i=0$, and we optimize the model to reduce their predicted class score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$.

(see figure: (left) Detector output (using a low threshold to generate many detections). (middle) Ground truth bounding boxes (one color per instance). (right) Detector outputs that overlap with ground truth...)

For the classification loss, we can use the cross-entropy loss:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$
where $K$ is the number of classes.

For the localization loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$, a typical measure is the Intersection over Union (IoU):
[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]
The loss is defined as $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})$. Alternatively, the L2 regression loss can be used:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

The overall loss is computed as:
$$\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) + \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$$
where the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$ sets the location loss to zero for bounding boxes that do not overlap with ground truth. The parameter $\lambda$ balances the relative strength of both losses.
concepts.motivation_md: Training an object detector requires optimizing both what an object is and where it is located. A combined loss function allows these two distinct tasks to be optimized simultaneously through backpropagation.
concepts.recap_md: - The total loss is the sum of a classification loss (typically cross-entropy) and a weighted localization loss (typically IoU or L2).

key_passage.text: The object localization loss has to take into account two complementary tasks: classification and localization. Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$): For each detected bounding box, does the predicted label matches the ground truth at that location? Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$): How close is the detected location to the ground truth object location?

motivation.text: For each of the predicted bounding boxes that overlaps with the ground truth instances, we want to optimize the system parameters to improve the predicted locations and labels. The remaining predicted bounding boxes that do not overlap with ground truth instances are assigned to the background class, $\mathbf{y}_i=0$. For those bounding boxes, we want to optimize the model parameters in order to reduce their predicted class score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$.

concepts.title: Classification Loss
concepts.one_liner: Classification loss measures whether the predicted label for a detected bounding box matches the ground truth label at that location.
concepts.content:
Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$) evaluates if the predicted label matches the ground truth at a specific location for each detected bounding box. Since each bounding box can only have one class, the cross-entropy loss is typically used:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

where $K$ is the number of classes.
concepts.motivation_md: In object detection, it is not enough to find a box; the system must also correctly identify the category of the object within that box. This loss provides the gradient needed to improve category predictions.
concepts.recap_md: - Classification loss determines if the predicted object label matches the ground truth.

key_passage.text: For each detected bounding box, does the predicted label matches the ground truth at that location? For the classification loss, as each bounding box can only have one class, we can use the cross-entropy loss: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$ where $K$ is the number of classes.

question.text: For each detected bounding box, does the predicted label matches the ground truth at that location?

concepts.title: Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: Localization loss measures how close a detected bounding box is to the ground truth object location.
concepts.content:
Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$) measures the distance between a detected location and the ground truth object location. One typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes is the Intersection over Union (IoU).

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]

The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, where 0 means no overlap and 1 means the bounding boxes are identical. The loss can be defined as:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$

IoU is translation and scale invariant. A simpler alternative is the L2 regression loss:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

The L2 regression loss is translation invariant but not scale invariant, meaning the loss is larger for bigger bounding boxes.
concepts.motivation_md: Localization loss is necessary to refine the coordinates of predicted bounding boxes, ensuring they tightly enclose the target objects rather than just roughly overlapping them.
concepts.recap_md: - Localization loss quantifies the spatial error between predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.

key_passage.text: The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, with 0 meaning no overlap and 1 meaning that both bounding boxes are identical. As the IoU is a similarity measure, the loss is defined as: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$

motivation.text: How close is the detected location to the ground truth object location?

concepts.title: Intersection over Union (IoU)
concepts.one_liner: Intersection over Union (IoU) is a scale-invariant similarity measure between 0 and 1 that quantifies the overlap between two bounding boxes.
concepts.content:
Intersection over Union (IoU) is a typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes. 

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]

The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, with 0 meaning no overlap and 1 meaning that both bounding boxes are identical. As the IoU is a similarity measure, the localization loss can be defined as:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$

The IoU is translation and scale invariant, and it is frequently used to evaluate object detectors.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard distance metrics like L2 are sensitive to the size of the object. IoU provides a normalized metric that treats small and large objects equally by focusing on the ratio of their overlap to their total area.
concepts.recap_md: - IoU ranges from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect match).

key_passage.text: One typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes is the Intersection over Union (IoU) as shown in the following drawing: The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, with 0 meaning no overlap and 1 meaning that both bounding boxes are identical.

motivation.text: The IoU is translation and scale invariant, and it is frequently used to evaluate object detectors.

concepts.title: L2 Regression Loss
concepts.one_liner: L2 regression loss is a translation-invariant but scale-sensitive metric used to optimize the coordinates of predicted bounding boxes.
concepts.content:
The L2 regression loss is a simple loss function used to optimize bounding box coordinates:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

While this loss is translation invariant, it is not scale invariant. Consequently, the L2 loss is larger for big bounding boxes. This can be compared to the IoU loss as a function of relative displacement.
concepts.motivation_md: L2 loss is often easier to optimize than IoU because it has a simple derivative. However, its lack of scale invariance means it may over-prioritize large objects during training.
concepts.recap_md: - L2 loss calculates the sum of squared differences between predicted and ground truth coordinates.

key_passage.text: A simpler loss to optimize is the L2 regression loss: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$ The L2 regression loss is translation invariant, but it is not scale invariant.

motivation.text: The L2 loss is larger for big bounding boxes.

concepts.title: Average Precision-Recall Evaluation
concepts.one_liner: Average Precision (AP) summarizes the precision-recall curve into a single value representing the area under the curve to evaluate object detector performance.
concepts.content:
The most common approach for evaluating object localization is measuring the average precision-recall. This requires assigning detection outputs to ground truth labels, often using the methodology from the PASCAL challenge.

Precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold $\beta$. Given a threshold $\beta$, we compute the precision as the percentage of correct detections:

$$Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}$$

The recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$

Both precision and recall are quantities between 0 and 1, where high values correspond to high performance. 

(see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)

The precision-recall curve is non-monotonic. The average precision (AP) summarizes the entire curve with one number, representing the area under the precision-recall curve.
concepts.motivation_md: Detectors produce many candidate boxes with different confidence scores. A single accuracy number isn't enough; we need to understand the trade-off between finding all objects (recall) and ensuring detections are correct (precision) across all possible confidence thresholds.
concepts.recap_md: - Precision is the fraction of detections that are correct, while recall is the fraction of ground truth objects successfully detected.

key_passage.text: The AP is the area under the precision-recall curve, and it is a number between 0 and 1.

motivation.text: The average precision (AP) summarizes the entire curve with one number.

concepts.title: Assigning Detections to Ground Truth Labels
concepts.one_liner: This procedure matches predicted bounding boxes to ground truth labels by sorting detections by confidence and selecting the highest IoU overlap.
concepts.content:
To assign detections to ground truth labels, follow this procedure for each image:
1. Sort all detections by their confidence score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$.
2. Loop over the sorted list in decreasing order.
3. For each bounding box, compute the IoU with all ground truth bounding boxes.
4. Select the ground truth bounding box with the highest IoU.
5. If the IoU is larger than a predefined threshold (typically 0.5), mark the detection as correct and remove that ground truth bounding box from the list to avoid double counting.
6. If the IoU is below the threshold, mark the detection as incorrect and do not remove the ground truth label.
7. Repeat until no more detections remain. Mark any remaining ground-truth bounding boxes as missed detections.
concepts.motivation_md: In evaluation, we must decide which predicted box corresponds to which real object. This greedy matching process ensures that each ground truth object is only 'found' once and that high-confidence predictions are prioritized.
concepts.recap_md: - Detections are matched to ground truth based on the highest IoU above a specific threshold.

key_passage.text: For each image, sort all the detections by their score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$. Then, loop over the sorted list in decreasing order. For each bounding box, compute the IoU with all the ground truth bounding boxes. Select the ground truth bounding box with the highest IoU. If the IoU is larger than a predefined threshold, (a typical value is 0.5) mark the detection as correct and remove the ground truth bounding box from the list to avoid double counting the same object.

concepts.title: Modular Encoder-Decoder Translation
concepts.one_liner: One approach to solving translation problems is to hook up an encoder for the source domain to a decoder for the target domain.
concepts.content: One approach to solving X-to-Y translation problems is to do it in a modular fashion by hooking up an *encoder* for domain X to a decoder for domain Y. This approach is popular because powerful encoder and decoder architectures, and pretrained models, exist for many domains. If we have an encoder $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ and a decoder $g: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, then we can create a translator simply by function composition, $g \circ f$.
concepts.motivation_md: This modular approach allows researchers to leverage existing, high-performance pretrained models for specific domains (like vision or language) and combine them to solve complex cross-domain translation tasks without building a monolithic system from scratch.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation can be achieved by composing an encoder $f$ and a decoder $g$ into a single function $g \circ f$.

key_passage.text: If we have an encoder $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ and a decoder $g: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, then we can create a translator simply by function composition, $g \circ f$.

motivation.text: This approach is popular because powerful encoder and decoder architectures, and pretrained models, exist for many domains.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Alignment Strategies
concepts.one_liner: Encoder-decoder alignment can be achieved by finetuning the full composition or by training a latent-space mapping between frozen components.
concepts.content: To *align* the encoder and decoder we can follow several strategies. One is to simply finetune $g \circ f$ on paired examples of the target translation problem, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Another option is to freeze $f$ and $g$ and instead train a translation function in latent space, $h: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, so that $g \circ h \circ f$ correctly maps each training point $\mathbf{t}^{(i)}$ to the target output $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Simply connecting a pretrained encoder and decoder is often insufficient because their latent spaces may not be naturally aligned; these strategies provide ways to bridge that gap using available paired data.
concepts.recap_md: - Alignment can be done by finetuning the entire end-to-end composition on paired data.

key_passage.text: One is to simply finetune g ∘ f on paired examples of the target translation problem, {t^(i), ℓ^(i)}_{i=1}^N. Another option is to freeze f and g and instead train a translation function in latent space, h: Z → Z, so that g ∘ h ∘ f correctly maps each training point t^(i) to the target output ℓ^(i).

concepts.title: Text-to-Image
concepts.one_liner: Text-to-image is the problem of synthesizing an image from a text description using generative models.
concepts.content: One amazing ability of modern generative models is to synthesize an image just from a text description, a problem called **text-to-image**. This can be achieved using any of the conditional generative models. We simply have to find an effective way to use text as the conditioning information to these models. (see figure: Text-to-image.) shows how this problem looks as a mapping from the space of text to the space of images. On the right is an example of such a system translating input text $\mathbf{t}$ to an output image $\hat{\boldsymbol\ell}$ that matches what the text describes. This new problem is not so different from representation learning and generative modeling diagrams seen previously.
concepts.motivation_md: Text-to-image synthesis allows humans to generate complex visual content using natural language, bridging the gap between symbolic communication and visual creation.
concepts.recap_md: - Text-to-image maps a text description $\mathbf{t}$ to a synthesized image $\hat{\boldsymbol\ell}$.

key_passage.text: One amazing ability of modern generative models is to synthesize an image just from a text description, a problem called text-to-image. This can be achieved using any of the conditional generative models we saw in chapter. We simply have to find an effective way to use text as the conditioning information to these models.

motivation.text: One amazing ability of modern generative models is to synthesize an image just from a text description, a problem called text-to-image.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with cVAE
concepts.one_liner: A conditional VAE for text-to-image uses a text encoder to provide the conditioning vector for an image decoder.
concepts.content: A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) can be used for text-to-image synthesis, as seen in the DALL-E 1 model. A cVAE for text-to-image can be trained just like a regular cVAE; the special thing is just that the encoder is a text encoder—a neural net that maps from text to a vector embedding. (see figure: Training a cVAE to perform text-to-image. The dotted lines indicate that the image encoder is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path. In this cartoon we draw the output...) After training this model, we can sample from it by simply discarding the image encoder and instead inputting a random Gaussian vector to the decoder, in addition to providing the decoder with the text embedding. (see figure: Sampling from a trained cVAE.)
concepts.motivation_md: The cVAE framework provides a probabilistic way to map text to images, allowing for diverse outputs from the same text prompt by sampling from a latent distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Training involves a text encoder and an image encoder to form the latent space.

key_passage.text: A cVAE for text-to-image can be trained just like a regular cVAE; the special thing is just that the encoder is a text encoder, that is, a neural net that maps from text to a vector embedding.

motivation.text: This was the architecture used by the DALL-E 1 model, which was one of the first text-to-image models that caught the public's imagination.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models generate images from text by inserting text embeddings into the layers of a denoising U-Net.
concepts.content: Text-to-image generation can be performed with a conditional diffusion model, an approach used by DALL-E 2 and other popular systems. A key challenge is effectively inserting text embeddings into the decoder. One way to do this is to insert text embedding vectors into each denoising U-Net, and even into multiple layers of each U-Net. This makes it very easy for the diffusion model to condition all of its decisions on the text information. (see figure: A text-to-image diffusion model.) A conditional diffusion model is very similar to a cVAE: at sampling time, both take text and Gaussian noise as input. However, while the VAE maps these to an image in a single forward pass, the diffusion model maps to an image via a chain of denoising steps.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models often produce higher-quality and more detailed images than VAEs by iteratively refining noise into a coherent image guided by text conditioning.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models condition on text by injecting embeddings into multiple layers of a denoising U-Net.

key_passage.text: we insert text embedding vectors into each denoising U-Net, and even into multiple layers of each U-Net. This makes it very easy for the diffusion model to condition all of its decisions on the text information.

question.text: how do you most effectively insert the text embeddings into the the decoder, so that it can make best use of this information?

motivation.text: The difficulty we will focus on here is as follows: how do you most effectively insert the text embeddings into the the decoder, so that it can make best use of this information?

concepts.title: Image-to-Text (Image Captioning)
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-text, or image captioning, translates visual information into natural language descriptions using an image encoder and a text decoder.
concepts.content: Naturally, we can also translate in the opposite direction. We just need to use an *image encoder* (rather than a text encoder) and a *text decoder* (rather than a text encoder). In this direction, the problem can be called **image-to-text** or **image captioning**. This kind of translation is very useful because text is a ubiquitous and general-purpose interface between almost all domains of human knowledge. As an example of an image-to-text system, we will use a transformer to map the input image to a set of tokens, and we will then feed these tokens as input to an autoregressive text decoder, which is also implemented with a transformer. (see figure: Image-to-text using a small transformer with cross-attention. The edges in gray are cross-attention edges. Many variations of this architecture are possible. For example, each layer of the text...)
concepts.motivation_md: Translating images to text allows visual data to be processed by language models, enabling automated reasoning, accessibility through descriptions, and integration with vast textual knowledge bases.
concepts.recap_md: - Image-to-text (image captioning) uses an image encoder and a text decoder.

key_passage.text: We just need to use an image encoder (rather than a text encoder) and a text decoder (rather than a text encoder). In this direction, the problem can be called image-to-text or image captioning.

motivation.text: This kind of translation is very useful because text is a ubiquitous and general-purpose interface between almost all domains of human knowledge (we use language to describe pretty everything we do and everything we know). So, if we can translate images to text then we link imagery to many other domains of knowledge.

concepts.title: Cross-Attention
concepts.one_liner: Cross-attention is a mechanism that allows text tokens to attend to image tokens, effectively integrating visual information into a text decoder.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-attention provides a mathematically principled way for a model to 'look' at relevant parts of an image while generating each word of a text description.
concepts.recap_md: - Cross-attention allows text queries $\mathbf{Q}_t$ to interact with image keys $\mathbf{K}_\ell$ and values $\mathbf{V}_\ell$.

key_passage.text: This layer addresses the question of how to insert image tokens into a text model. The answer is quite simple: just let the text tokens attend to the image tokens.

motivation.text: The image tokens will emit their value vectors which will be mixed with the text token value vectors according to the attention weights to produce the next layer of tokens in the text decoder.

concepts.title: Text as a Visual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Text can be viewed as a high-level visual representation that captures the semantics of an image and interfaces directly with language models.
concepts.content: One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation. Just like we can represent an image in terms of its frequencies, its semantics and geometry, or its feature embeddings, we can also represent it in terms of a textual description of its content. (see figure: Four representations computed from the input on the left. The input image itself (its pixel values) is in fact a fifth representation of the scene.) Text is a powerful visual representation because it interfaces with language models. This means that after translating an image into text we can use language models to reason about the image contents.
concepts.motivation_md: Treating text as a representation allows us to apply the reasoning and logic capabilities of Large Language Models to visual data, which is otherwise difficult to 'reason' about in raw pixel form.
concepts.recap_md: - Text serves as a semantic visual representation alongside Fourier transforms or depth maps.

key_passage.text: One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation. Just like we can represent an image in terms of its frequencies (Fourier transform), its semantics and geometry (scene understanding), or its feature embeddings (DINO, CLIP, and others), we can also represent it in terms of a textual description of its content.

question.text: Think about the relative merits of each of these representations, and what advantages or disadvantages text might have over these other kinds of visual representation.

motivation.text: Text is a powerful visual representation because it interfaces with language models. This means that after translating an image into text we can use language models to reason about the image contents.

concepts.title: Camera-Intrinsic Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Camera-intrinsic parameters capture the internal image formation process, translating 3D scene coordinates into 2D pixels while accounting for units and geometric distortions.
concepts.content: Camera-intrinsic parameters model the image formation process by capturing how a camera translates the 3D world into 2D pixels. While 3D to 2D projection can be modeled using homogeneous coordinates and vector computations, the relationship is not always straightforward. The model must account for the fact that the world is measured in meters while image points are measured in pixels, and it must incorporate factors such as geometric distortions that influence this relationship.
concepts.motivation_md: These parameters are necessary because raw 3D coordinates do not directly correspond to pixel indices. We need a way to bridge the gap between physical measurements (meters) and digital representations (pixels) while accounting for the camera's internal geometry.
concepts.recap_md: - Intrinsic parameters model the internal camera properties that transform 3D coordinates into 2D pixels. - They account for the conversion from physical units like meters to digital units like pixels.

key_passage.text: We want to construct a camera model that captures the image formation process. Cameras translate the world into pixels, but the relationship between the 3D scene and the 2D image captured by the camera is not always straightforward.

motivation.text: To start with, the world is measured in units of meters while points in images are measured in pixels. Factors such as geometric distortions can influence this relationship, and we need to account for these elements in our camera model.

concepts.title: Mapping from Meters to Pixels
concepts.one_liner: This mapping transforms 3D camera coordinates into 2D pixel coordinates by accounting for focal length scaling, sensor resolution, and principal point offsets.
concepts.content: Mapping from 3D camera coordinates to pixels requires accounting for perspective projection and sensor sampling. (see figure: An image is projected into the sensor. World coordinates are transformed into pixels at the sensor. The focal length is $f$, and the physical width of the sensor is $w$. The sensor has $N \times M$...) The focal length $f$ is scaled to $a = f \, N / w$, where $N$ is the image width in pixels and $w$ is the sensor width in meters. The intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ also accounts for the image center $[c_x, c_y]^\mathsf{T}$. If pixels are not square, different scaling factors $a$ and $b$ are used for each axis: $$\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 & c_x & 0 \\ 0 & b & c_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ The transformation from 3D coordinates $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$ to pixels $[n,m]^\mathsf{T}$ is: $$\begin{bmatrix} a & 0 & c_x & 0 \\ 0 & b & c_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} a X/Z+c_x \\ b Y/Z+c_y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} n \\ m \end{pmatrix}$$ In conventions used by Python and OpenCV, where the camera looks toward positive $Z$ and the origin is top-left, the signs of $a$ and $b$ are negative. ![(a) 3D representation of the image plane. (b and c) Two different conventions for the image coordinate systems. In this book we have been using (b).](figures/imaging_geometry/conventions_coordinates.png)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard projection equations yield coordinates in the same units as the 3D world. This mapping is required to convert those physical units into the discrete pixel grid used by digital sensors and software.
concepts.recap_md: - The intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ scales focal length by the pixel density of the sensor. - It shifts the projected coordinates so that the optical axis aligns with the image's principal point. - Different scaling factors $a$ and $b$ can be applied if the sensor pixels are non-square.

key_passage.text: a = f N / w where f is the focal length (in meters), w is the width of the sensor in meters, and N is the image width in pixels. The ratio N/w is the number of pixels per meter in the sensor.

motivation.text: We need to account for the perspective projection of the point, P, described in camera coordinates, to pixel coordinates in the sensor plane of the camera.

concepts.title: From Pixels to Rays
concepts.one_liner: A calibrated camera allows deriving the 3D ray associated with a specific pixel, enabling the recovery of 3D coordinates if the depth is known.
concepts.content: For a calibrated camera, the equation of the ray leaving the image at a specific point can be derived. By expressing a 2D image point $\mathbf{p}$ in 3D coordinates as $(x, y, f)$, where $f$ is the focal length, we define the ray connecting the camera center and $\mathbf{p}$ as $\lambda (x, y, f)$ for $\lambda > 0$. (see figure: The 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ is obtained by scaling the point $\mathbf{p}=(x,y,f)$ with a scaling factor $Z/f$. The ray that passes by the point $\mathbf{p}$ is the line defined by $\lambda (x,y,f)$...) Any 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ along this line projects to the same image point. The 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ is obtained by scaling the ray by $\lambda = Z/f$: $$\frac{Z}{f} \begin{pmatrix} x\\ y\\ f \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{pmatrix}$$ If coordinates are in pixels, the parameter $a$ is used instead of $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: While projection maps 3D to 2D, computer vision often requires the inverse: determining where in the 3D world a pixel might have originated. This concept establishes the line of sight for every pixel.
concepts.recap_md: - Every pixel corresponds to a 3D ray originating from the camera center and passing through the image plane. - If the depth $Z$ is known, the full 3D coordinates $(X, Y, Z)$ can be recovered from the pixel position.

key_passage.text: The ray that connects the camera center and the point p is λ (x,y,f), with λ being a positive real number. Any 3D point along this line will project into the same image point p under perspective projection.

question.text: If we know Z for an image pixel with camera-coordinates x,y, can get the point world-coordinates X and Y?

concepts.title: Extrinsic Camera Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Extrinsic camera parameters, consisting of rotation and translation, define the camera's position and orientation relative to the world coordinate system.
concepts.content: Extrinsic camera parameters, $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$, relate the camera's coordinate system to the world coordinate system. These parameters describe the camera's external pose—its rotation and translation—relative to the world origin and axes, which is necessary when the camera is not positioned at the world origin or aligned with the world $Z$-axis.
concepts.motivation_md: To project real-world points into an image, we must first transform those points from a global coordinate system into the camera's local coordinate system. Extrinsic parameters provide this necessary spatial transformation.
concepts.recap_md: - Extrinsic parameters consist of a rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$ and a translation vector $\mathbf{T}$. - They describe the camera's pose (position and orientation) relative to the world.

key_passage.text: The camera parameters, R and T, that relate the camera to the world are called the extrinsic camera parameters. These parameters are external to the camera.

concepts.title: Full Camera Model
concepts.one_liner: The full camera model concatenates extrinsic and intrinsic matrices into a single projection matrix that transforms 3D world coordinates directly into 2D pixel coordinates.
concepts.content: The full camera model concatenates extrinsic and intrinsic transformation matrices to map world coordinates to rendered pixel coordinates. The transformation from a 3D point $[X, Y, Z]^\mathsf{T}$ to pixel indices $[x, y]^\mathsf{T}$ is given by: $$\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} ~ \mid ~ -\mathbf{R} \mathbf{T} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}_W$$ where $\mathbf{K}$ represents the intrinsic parameters and perspective projection, while $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$ represent the camera's extrinsic parameters (rotation and translation). (see figure: Projection of a point into the image plane. This summary puts together @fig-pinholeGeometry2bis and @fig-camera_calibration. First, we change the world-coordinates system, in which the point is...) The combined camera projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is typically written as: $$\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & -\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ By substituting different intrinsic parameters into $\mathbf{K}$, this model can represent various camera types, including orthographic, weak-perspective, and affine cameras.
concepts.motivation_md: This unified model allows for a single mathematical operation to represent the entire image formation process, from the object's position in the world to its final location on a digital sensor.
concepts.recap_md: - The projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ combines the camera's pose (extrinsic) and internal geometry (intrinsic). - It transforms 3D world points in homogeneous coordinates to 2D image points.

key_passage.text: The concatenation of the extrinsic and intrinsic transformation matrices yields the desired transformation matrix, which will transform world coordinates to rendered pixel coordinates.

motivation.text: By replacing K with different intrinsic parameters we can build models for different camera types such as orthographic cameras, weak-perspective model, affine cameras, and so on.

concepts.title: calibrated camera
concepts.one_liner: A camera is calibrated when the transformations relating 3D world coordinates to 2D pixel coordinates, including both intrinsic and extrinsic parameters, are known.
concepts.content: A camera is said to be calibrated if we know the transformations relating 3D world coordinates to pixel coordinates within the camera. Those transformations involve two types of parameters: (1) parameters that depend on where the camera is physically located in the world, and (2) parameters that are a function of the camera itself. These two types of parameters are called extrinsic and intrinsic parameters, respectively.
concepts.motivation_md: Calibration is the prerequisite for most quantitative computer vision tasks, such as measuring distances, reconstructing 3D scenes, or overlaying virtual objects accurately onto real-world images.
concepts.recap_md: - Calibration requires knowing both where the camera is (extrinsic) and how it forms images (intrinsic). - It enables the precise mapping between the 3D world and 2D image pixels.

key_passage.text: A camera is said to be calibrated if we know the transformations relating 3D world coordinates to pixel coordinates within the camera.

motivation.text: Those transformations involve two types of parameters: (1) parameters that depend on where the camera is physically located in the world, and (2) parameters that are a function of the camera itself. These two types of parameters are called extrinsic and intrinsic parameters, respectively.

concepts.title: extrinsic and intrinsic parameters
concepts.one_liner: Camera transformations involve extrinsic parameters, which depend on the camera's physical location, and intrinsic parameters, which are functions of the camera's internal properties.
concepts.content: Transformations from 3D world coordinates to pixel coordinates involve two types of parameters. Extrinsic parameters depend on where the camera is physically located in the world. Intrinsic parameters are a function of the camera itself, capturing its internal image formation characteristics.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between these two sets of parameters allows us to separate the camera's identity (what kind of lens/sensor it has) from its state (where it is currently placed).
concepts.recap_md: - Extrinsic parameters describe the camera's external pose in the world. - Intrinsic parameters describe the camera's internal optical and sensor properties.

key_passage.text: parameters that depend on where the camera is physically located in the world, and (2) parameters that are a function of the camera itself. These two types of parameters are called extrinsic and intrinsic parameters, respectively.

concepts.title: direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm
concepts.one_liner: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) algorithm recovers a camera's projection matrix by solving a linear system of equations derived from known 3D-to-2D point correspondences.
concepts.content: The direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm recovers the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ from known 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and their corresponding image pixels $\mathbf{p}_i$. For each pair, the relationship $\mathbf{p}_i = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{P}_i$ provides two linear equations: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_0 - x_i \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_2 &= 0\\ \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_1 - y_i \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_2 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$ By stacking equations from $N$ correspondences, we form a system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{m}$ is a vector of the 12 elements of $\mathbf{M}$. Since the result is invariant to global scaling, $\mathbf{m}$ has 11 degrees of freedom. The solution is the smallest eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$, which minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{m} \|^2$. This method requires at least six correspondences and that the points are not all coplanar. Note that rearranging the vector $\mathbf{m}$ back into the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is a potential source of bugs; it is recommended to verify the implementation with simulated points.
concepts.motivation_md: DLT provides a straightforward way to estimate a camera's parameters from image data. It is a fundamental technique for camera calibration and pose estimation when the internal and external parameters are unknown.
concepts.recap_md: - DLT solves for the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ using at least six 3D-to-2D point correspondences. - The algorithm minimizes a linear residual using the smallest eigenvector of the system matrix. - It requires that the reference points are not coplanar to avoid degenerate solutions.

key_passage.text: The solution is the vector that minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{m} \|^2$, which can be obtained as the smallest eigenvector of the matrix $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$. Once we estimate $\mathbf{m}$ we can rearrange the terms into the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$. This method to obtain the projection matrix is called the direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm.

motivation.text: If we have six correspondences, then, under certain conditions, we can recover the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ by solving a linear system of equations. As the measurements of the points in correspondence will be noisy, it is generally useful to use more than six correspondences.

concepts.title: Independence vs. knowing the literature
concepts.one_liner: Balance the creative freedom of independent thinking with a thorough understanding of existing research literature.
concepts.content: Sometimes it is useful to think that everyone else is completely off-track, as this mindset allows you to explore directions no one else is pursuing. When doing so, it is often best to remain humble and simply state that you are trying out a new direction. However, it is equally important to remember that many smart people have worked on related problems and documented their results. You should avoid being caught unfamiliar with the large body of literature closely related to your work.
concepts.motivation_md: Researchers must navigate the tension between following established paths and forging new ones. This concept helps researchers maintain original thought without wasting time reinventing the wheel or ignoring critical context.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use independent thinking to explore novel directions others might overlook.
 - Stay familiar with the existing literature to avoid repeating known mistakes or missing context.
 - Maintain a balance between creative isolation and scholarly awareness.

key_passage.text: It's also sometimes useful to remember that many smart people have worked on this and related problems and written their thoughts and results down in papers.

motivation.text: Don't be caught flat-footed with a large body of closely related literature that you aren't familiar with.

concepts.title: Building your personal brand
concepts.one_liner: Build a professional reputation by consistently delivering high-quality work, ideas, presentations, and software.
concepts.content: In a professional context, you have a personal brand. There are many impressions you want to build regarding this brand: that you always do great work, possess good ideas, deliver excellent talks, and write high-quality software. You should promote your brand and build a strong reputation by consistently behaving in the way you wish to be perceived.
concepts.motivation_md: Success in academia and industry depends not just on technical skill, but on how others perceive your reliability and expertise. Building a brand ensures your contributions are recognized and valued.
concepts.recap_md:
- Your personal brand is the sum of others' impressions of your work and conduct.
 - Consistently deliver high-quality outputs to establish a reputation for excellence.
 - Actively manage how you are perceived by the community through your professional behavior.

key_passage.text: You have a brand: you. There are many impressions you want to build up about your brand: that person always does great work, they have good ideas, they give great talks, they write wonderful software. Promote your brand. Build up a great reputation for yourself by consistently behaving in the way you'd like to be thought of.

concepts.title: Cultivate and play to your strengths
concepts.one_liner: Identify and cultivate your specific strengths, such as creativity, implementation, or theory, to maximize your impact.
concepts.content: Cultivate your strengths and play to those strengths. Some possible strengths include being broad in your knowledge, being creative, being a great implementer, or being highly skilled at theoretical work.
concepts.motivation_md: Research is diverse; no one is perfect at everything. Identifying where you naturally excel allows you to contribute more effectively to teams and projects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Identify whether your strengths lie in theory, implementation, creativity, or breadth.
 - Focus your efforts on tasks where your specific skills provide the most value.
 - Actively develop these strengths to distinguish yourself in your field.

key_passage.text: Cultivate your strengths and play to those strengths. Some possible strengths include being broad, being creative, being a great implementer, or being great at doing theory.

concepts.title: Progress and specific reporting of failures
concepts.one_liner: Define progress broadly to include understanding failures, simplifying tasks, and dedicated learning.
concepts.content: When reporting issues, avoid simply stating that something doesn't work. Instead, analyze why it failed, whether it should have worked, if there is a simpler case that does work, and if the issue is general to the category. Try to identify the specific failure point or create an example that does work; at minimum, make it fail more clearly to help understand the system. Progress should be viewed broadly. It includes showing why a method fails, simplifying a task to get it started, or spending time reading to gain the necessary understanding for future advancement.
concepts.motivation_md: Effective communication between students and advisors requires moving beyond binary 'success/failure' reporting. Understanding why something failed is often as valuable as a success.
concepts.recap_md:
- Report failures with specific analysis of why they occurred and how they might be simplified.
 - Recognize that proving why something doesn't work is a valid form of progress.
 - Include learning and background research in your definition of productive work.

key_passage.text: Progress can include things like "I've shown why this doesn't work," "I've simplified the task to get it to start working," or "I spent the whole time reading because I know I have to understand this before I can make any progress."

question.text: Why doesn't it work? Why should it work? Is there a simpler case we can make work? Do you think it's a general issue that affects all problems of this category? Can you think of what's not working? Can you contort things to make an example that does work? At the very least, can you make it fail worse, so we understand some aspects of the system?

motivation.text: I love to hear about progress when I meet with students, but note that I have a very general notion of progress.

concepts.title: Collaboration and authorship in science
concepts.one_liner: Prioritize impactful team-based science and ensure authorship reflects all meaningful contributions to the research.
concepts.content: Science is generally a team sport where the insight, foundation, and impact of the work matter more than the number of people involved. It is better to be one of many contributors to a great paper than the sole author of an unimportant one. These collaborations often lead to lifelong professional friendships. Regarding authorship, everyone who contributed to the paper should be included. Contributions can take the form of experimentation, providing a seminal idea, assisting with writing, or even exploring a research direction that ultimately did not work. If authorship is unclear, it is best to ask the individual and respect their preference.
concepts.motivation_md: Modern research is complex and collaborative. Clear guidelines on communication and authorship help maintain healthy professional relationships and ensure fair credit.
concepts.recap_md:
- Value being part of a high-impact team over individual authorship on minor works.
 - Include as authors everyone who contributed through ideas, experiments, writing, or failed explorations.
 - Maintain open communication with collaborators and advisors to foster long-term professional bonds.

key_passage.text: Science is generally a team sport. What matters in a collaboration is whether the work is insightful, foundational, or impactful. Everyone who contributed to the paper should have their name on it.

motivation.text: The relationships formed through collaborations can become friendships that last over your career. It is much better to be one of 10 contributors to a great paper than to be the sole author on an unimportant paper.

concepts.title: Only the good papers count
concepts.one_liner: Focus on producing high-quality research, as only the truly good papers significantly impact a career.
concepts.content: While the number of papers is a rough measure of productivity, experienced mentors and hiring committees find that only the good papers count. You should strive to make all your papers high-quality, as only the really good papers matter for your career. This relationship between quality and career impact is summarized in (see figure: Plot of conjectured data showing the impact of a paper on one's career, as a function of paper quality.). Consequently, it is essential to learn how to write the best possible paper from any given piece of research work.
concepts.motivation_md: Students often feel pressured to publish frequently, but long-term career success is driven by the depth and quality of contributions rather than sheer volume.
concepts.recap_md:
- Prioritize paper quality over quantity to maximize long-term career impact.
 - Recognize that influential research managers and faculty search committees value 'good' papers almost exclusively.
 - Invest time in learning how to communicate research effectively to ensure its quality is recognized.

key_passage.text: only the good papers count.

motivation.text: While the number of papers a student has can be a rough measure of research productivity, it is our experience as mentors, faculty search committee members, and industrial research managers that only the good papers count. Only the really good papers matter for your career.

concepts.title: Adelson's advice on paper organization
concepts.one_liner: Organize research papers by stating the problem, critiquing existing solutions, explaining your solution, and discussing related work.
concepts.content: Prof. Edward Adelson suggests a specific structure for writing a good paper: 1. Start by stating the problem and explaining why the audience should care about it. 2. Briefly state existing solutions and explain why they are unsatisfactory. 3. Explain your own solution, compare it with others, and demonstrate why it is better. 4. Conclude by discussing related work where similar techniques were applied to different problems. This structure aligns with typical conference paper headings, such as: Introduction, Related Work, Main Idea, Algorithm (including specific sub-steps like estimation or reconstruction), Experiments (covering various cases), and Discussion.
concepts.motivation_md: A clear, logical structure helps readers quickly grasp the value of a research contribution and follow the author's reasoning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Begin by defining the problem and establishing its importance to the reader.
 - Contrast your approach with existing solutions to justify the need for your work.
 - Use a standard progression of headings from introduction through experiments to discussion.

key_passage.text: Start by stating which problem you are addressing, keeping the audience in mind. Then state briefly what the other solutions are to the problem, and why they aren't satisfactory. Then explain your own solution, compare it with other solutions, and say why it's better. At the end, talk about related work where similar techniques and experiments have been used, but applied to a different problem.

concepts.title: Writing a dynamite introduction
concepts.one_liner: Write a 'dynamite' introduction that immediately clarifies the problem, the solution, the novelty, and the importance of the work.
concepts.content: Regarding paper introductions, Kajiya emphasizes the necessity of making a paper easy to read from the very beginning. You must write a 'dynamite introduction' that allows anyone to immediately understand what the paper is about, what problem it solves, why that problem is interesting, what is genuinely new versus what is not, and why the contribution is significant. All of this must be done up front.
concepts.motivation_md: The introduction is often the only part of a paper a reviewer or researcher reads thoroughly. It must successfully 'sell' the paper's value immediately.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ensure the introduction clearly states the problem, its interest, and your specific solution.
 - Explicitly distinguish what is new in your work from what is existing literature.
 - Make the paper's value proposition obvious 'up front' to engage the reader immediately.

key_passage.text: You must write a dynamite introduction.

motivation.text: You must make your paper easy to read. You've got to make it easy for anyone to tell what your paper is about, what problem it solves, why the problem is interesting, what is really new in your paper (and what isn't), why it's so neat.

concepts.title: Best practices for writing with equations
concepts.one_liner: Sentences should flow smoothly even when formulas are replaced by simple placeholder sounds, and equations should be identified by both phrase and number.
concepts.content: Equations interposed with text can pose a challenge to the reader, who must decide whether to stop to work through each equation or continue reading as if the equation were words. Knuth advises that because many readers skim formulas on a first reading, your sentences should flow smoothly when all but the simplest formulas are replaced by "blah" or some other grunting noise. Mermin adds that when referring to an equation, you should identify it by a phrase as well as a number. For example, instead of saying "inserting (2.47) and (3.51) into (5.13)," it is more helpful to say "inserting the form (2.47) of the electric field $E$ and the Lindhard form (3.51) of the dielectric function $\epsilon$ into the constitutive equation (5.13)."
concepts.motivation_md: Mathematical writing is often difficult to parse. These practices ensure that the narrative flow of a paper remains intact for skimmers while providing clear context for readers who are deeply analyzing the derivations.

concepts.title: Maintaining a generous and reliable tone
concepts.one_liner: Maintaining a generous, clear, and reliable tone wins over readers and builds a reputation for integrity in the research community.
concepts.content: The tone of your writing is important. While you may feel pressure to oversell your work, hide drawbacks, or disparage others, it is in your long-term interest to resist this. If your work has a shortcoming, it is better to point it out yourself than to have someone else do so later. Papers written from the perspective that researchers are all doing their best are much more pleasant to read than those that treat others as incompetent. A generous tone, such as acknowledging related independent work and urging readers to review it for a complete picture, wins over readers and promotes professional friendships. Furthermore, you should develop a reputation for being clear and reliable by conveying an accurate impression of an algorithm's performance. If a method fails in important cases, let the readers know; describing counterintuitive results or failures can prove valuable to the field later on.
concepts.motivation_md: Scientific progress relies on trust and collaboration. A generous and honest tone prevents future embarrassment, builds professional relationships, and ensures that the research community can accurately build upon your findings.

key_passage.text: Papers written from the point of view that "we're all good researchers, doing our best" are much more pleasant to read than papers written from the standpoint that everyone else is an idiot. This generous tone wins over the reader and promotes long-lasting friendships with people who study the same problems you do.

motivation.text: You should develop a reputation for being clear and reliable. Always convey an accurate impression of the performance of an algorithm.

concepts.title: Author List Best Practices
concepts.one_liner: The quality of a paper is more important than your specific position on the author list.
concepts.content: The quality of the papers you write matters much more than your positions within the author lists. If adding more authors will make a paper better, you should add them. If a collaborator feels they should be an author, but you are unsure, it is generally a good idea to trust the collaborator and add them as a coauthor. It is much better to be one of many authors on a great paper than to be one of just a few authors on a mediocre paper.
concepts.motivation_md: Collaboration often improves the depth and quality of research. Prioritizing the final output over individual ego or ranking fosters better science and healthier professional relationships.

motivation.text: The quality of the papers you write matters so much more than your positions within the author lists of the papers. It's much better to be one of many authors on a great paper than to be one of just a few authors on a mediocre paper.

concepts.title: Avoiding Paper Rejection
concepts.one_liner: To avoid paper rejection, ensure you deliver on promises, cite relevant work, provide believable results, and maintain high writing quality.
concepts.content: Conference area chairs often look for reasons to reject papers to manage high submission volumes. To avoid giving them easy reasons for rejection, ensure your paper addresses the following: Do the authors deliver what they promise? Are important references included to show the authors are current on the state of the art? Are the results more than just incremental? Are the results believable with sufficient tests to support claims? Is the paper well-written and free of mistakes or incorrect statements? Most decision-making effort goes into borderline papers, which can be categorized as either "cockroaches" or "puppies with six toes."
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the criteria and pressures faced by reviewers helps authors proactively address weaknesses that lead to quick rejections.

Here's a summary of reasons that are commonly used, and it is best not to provide the area chair with any of these easy reasons to reject your paper

concepts.title: Cockroach Papers
concepts.one_liner: Cockroach papers are mundane submissions with incremental improvements and no exciting contributions that are difficult for reviewers to reject.
concepts.content:
"Cockroaches" have no exciting contributions, but the reviews are okay and the results show incremental improvement to the state of the art. They are hard to kill (hence the nickname); typically, two-thirds are accepted as posters and one-third are rejected. As an author, it is best to work harder for fresh results to move a paper out of this category.

concepts.title: Puppy with Six Toes Papers
concepts.one_liner: Puppy with six toes papers are delightful and fresh works that are easily rejected due to a single, minor, but obvious flaw.
concepts.content:
"Puppies with six toes" are delightful papers that possess an easy-to-see flaw. The flaw may not truly matter—much like six toes on a puppy—but it makes the paper easy to reject even if the work is fresh and wonderful. Approximately two-thirds of these papers are rejected, while one-third may be accepted as posters. As an author, it may be better to wait for another submission cycle to remove the obvious flaw, which could lead to an oral presentation in the future.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks on Writing
concepts.one_liner: Good writing requires significant time for rewriting, often making structural and clarity improvements more valuable than last-minute result tweaks.
concepts.content: The approaches to writing and editing described previously all take time, as good writing involves significant rewriting. The final days before a paper submission deadline are often better spent improving the structure, presentation, and clarity of the paper rather than attempting to obtain last-minute improvements to the results.
concepts.motivation_md: Authors often over-prioritize data over presentation. This concept emphasizes that a well-communicated result is more likely to be accepted and understood than a slightly better result that is poorly explained.
