concepts.title: The Importance of Giving Good Talks
concepts.one_liner: The ability to give a good talk is a critical skill that helps researchers and engineers successfully communicate their work.
concepts.content: Giving good talks is important for students, researchers, and engineers. While one might think the work itself is all that counts, the ability to give a good talk is like having a big serve in tennis; it doesn't win the game alone, but it is a hallmark of the best players. This chapter provides heuristics for giving effective talks, though readers are encouraged to access other sources to find the tips that work best for them.
concepts.motivation_md: Technical work has little impact if it cannot be communicated effectively. Mastering public speaking ensures that your ideas reach and influence your audience.
concepts.recap_md: [object Object]

key_passage.text: Giving good talks is important for people who use the material of this book--for students, researchers, and engineers.

motivation.text: One might think, "It is the work itself that really counts. Giving a talk about it is secondary." But the ability to give a good talk is like having a big serve in tennis---by itself, it doesn't win the game for you, but it sure helps.

concepts.title: Connecting with the audience
concepts.one_liner: Connecting with the audience by sharing excitement and showing genuine interest in the topic is essential for a successful technical presentation.
concepts.content: Connecting with the audience is a vital component of scientific presentations. Actor Alan Alda has noted that scientific speaking improves significantly when presenters engage in improvisational theater exercises, which prime them to connect with others and make their talks sparkle. An audience generally wants three things from a technical talk: (a) for the presentation to follow a logical sequence that makes sense, (b) to learn a few new things, and (c) to connect with the speaker and share their excitement for the topic. Ultimately, the audience wants to watch you love something.
concepts.motivation_md: Technical talks often fail not because of poor data, but because the speaker fails to engage the audience. Establishing a human connection ensures the audience remains attentive and receptive to the information being shared.
concepts.recap_md: - Audiences value logical flow and the opportunity to learn new things.

key_passage.text: To connect with the speaker, to share their excitement for the topic. They want to watch you love something!

motivation.text: Alda noted the improvement in scientific speaking of volunteers after they engaged in improvisational theater exercises. After the exercises, the volunteers were primed to engage and connect with others, and their scientific talks sparkled.

concepts.title: Ending a presentation
concepts.one_liner: Ending a presentation with a clear "Thank you" signals the audience to applaud and provides a professional transition to the Q&A session.
concepts.content: How you end a talk significantly impacts the audience's response. A common but awkward method is to end by asking, "Are there any questions?" This often leaves the audience confused about whether to applaud or ask a question, resulting in scattered applause. A better approach is to close with "Thank you," which clearly signals the time for applause; you can then ask for questions afterward. However, some experts, like Patrick Winston, disagree with ending with "thank you," arguing it implies the audience did the speaker a favor. Winston preferred to conclude by reminding the audience how he fulfilled his initial promise regarding what they would learn.
concepts.motivation_md: A clear ending prevents the awkward silence or confusion that occurs when an audience isn't sure if a presentation has concluded, ensuring the talk ends on a high note.
concepts.recap_md: - Closing with "Thank you" provides a clear cue for audience applause.

key_passage.text: Better is to close with "Thank you." The audience then knows it's their time to applaud, and they will.

question.text: How should you end your talk?

motivation.text: A common, but awkward, way is to end by asking, "Are there any questions?" The audience wants to clap at the end of a talk, but with that ending, they don't know whether to applaud or to ask a question, and they're likely to give only scattered applause.

concepts.title: Pretrained end-to-end vision systems
concepts.one_liner: Large-scale pretrained vision systems can solve complex tasks out-of-the-box, though bridging the gap to truly robust systems remains a challenge.
concepts.content: Modern computer vision embraces the use of large-scale pretrained models that can solve diverse tasks such as natural language processing, image generation, and object classification. These models, including DALL-E, GPT, and AutoPilot, are trained on massive datasets across diverse domains to improve generalization. They can be used as standalone systems with little fine-tuning or as building blocks within more complex architectures. While these systems produce astonishing results, a close analysis suggests there is still a gap to bridge to build truly reliable and robust systems. This approach revisits simple-world problems by applying high-performing, out-of-the-box pretrained models rather than relying solely on hand-crafted algorithms.
concepts.motivation_md: Pretrained models leverage massive computation and data to solve problems that were previously handled by fragile, hand-coded algorithms, offering a more generalizable approach to vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Pretrained models like DALL-E and GPT can be used with little to no fine-tuning.

concepts.title: Revisiting the simple world
concepts.one_liner: Revisiting the simple world involves recovering 3D scene structure from a single image using both first principles and modern pretrained models.
concepts.content: The goal of analyzing the simple world is to recover the three-dimensional (3D) structure of a scene from a single image (see figure: Image from the simple world.). This process involves deriving an algorithm from first principles: studying image formation, identifying where information is preserved, building a representation to make that information explicit, and integrating evidence to recover the 3D data lost during the image formation process.
concepts.motivation_md: By returning to a simplified environment, we can compare traditional algorithmic approaches based on physics and geometry with modern deep learning methods.
concepts.recap_md: - The primary goal is recovering 3D structure from a 2D image.

key_passage.text: We derived an algorithm to recover the 3D scene structure from the first principles: we started studying the image formation process, we then reasoned where the information might be preserved, how to build a representation that makes the information explicit, and finally how to integrate all the evidence left in the image in order to recover the 3D information that was lost during the image formation process.

concepts.title: MiDaS
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS is a state-of-the-art neural network trained end-to-end to solve 3D perception and depth estimation from single images.
concepts.content: MiDaS is a state-of-the-art pretrained model designed to solve the 3D perception problem from single images. It is a neural network trained end-to-end using a diverse set of real images containing ground truth depth information, as well as stereo images. From a user's perspective, the system functions as a simple function call, though effectively using it out-of-the-box requires understanding its training, its output format, and how it can be adapted to specific tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: MiDaS provides a high-performance, ready-to-use solution for depth estimation, sparing developers from building complex geometric reconstruction pipelines from scratch.
concepts.recap_md: - MiDaS is an end-to-end neural network for single-image depth estimation.

key_passage.text: The current state of the art is MiDaS. The system is a neural network trained end-to-end using a diverse set of real images that had ground truth depth information and also using stereo images.

concepts.title: MiDaS training and invariant loss
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS uses an invariant loss during training to handle ambiguities in scale and camera parameters across diverse datasets.
concepts.content:
### How Was It Trained?

This model has been trained using a mix of four datasets with real images. (see figure: Images and depth maps from the training set. *Source*: Image from @Ranftl2022) As the model is trained with a diverse collection of data sources, there is an ambiguity on the overall scale, camera parameters, and stereo baselines. Therefore, the loss is defined in a way that it can be invariant to all those ambiguities. The invariant loss makes the training more robust, but it also makes the output less convenient to use. To deal with these ambiguities, the model is trained to predict disparity (inverse depth up to scale and shift). This means that we cannot directly use the output; we need to convert it first into world coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Using diverse datasets improves generalization but introduces inconsistencies in scale; an invariant loss allows the model to learn from these varied sources without being confused by different camera setups.
concepts.recap_md: - MiDaS predicts disparity, which is inverse depth up to an unknown scale and shift.

key_passage.text: As the model is trained with a diverse collections of data sources, there is an ambiguity on the overall scale, camera parameters, and stereo baselines. Therefore, the loss is defined in a way that it can be invariant to all those ambiguities. To deal with the ambiguities mentioned before, the model is trained to predict disparity (inverse depth up to scale and shift).

motivation.text: The invariant loss makes the training more robust, but it also makes the output less convenient to use.

concepts.title: Converting disparity to world coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Converting disparity to world coordinates requires inverting the disparity value and applying intrinsic and extrinsic camera matrices.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw disparity maps from neural networks lack physical scale and orientation; this technique maps those relative values into a meaningful 3D coordinate system for spatial reasoning.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth $z$ is calculated as the inverse of disparity plus a constant $d_0$.

key_passage.text: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity after adding the constant: $z \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{ d \left[n,m \right] + d_0}$. Now we need to recover the world coordinates for every pixel. Assuming a pinhole camera and using the depth $z \left[n,m \right]$ and the camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$, we obtain the 3D coordinates for a pixel with image coordinates $(n,m)$ in the camera reference frame as, $\begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = z\left[n,m \right] \times \mathbf{K}^{-1} \times \begin{bmatrix} n \\ m \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

motivation.text: MiDaS returns disparity values, up to an unknown constant ($d_0$), but what we need are world coordinates ($X,Y,Z$) for each pixel.

concepts.title: Camera Tilt Angle (theta)
concepts.one_liner: The camera tilt angle $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane.
concepts.content: The parameter $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane. While it is possible to estimate this angle accurately by determining the surface normal of pixels on the ground and measuring the angle relative to the vertical axis, a simpler approach for many applications is to set it to a heuristic value. For instance, setting $\theta = \pi / 4$ is often sufficient as it approximately matches the angle at which many handheld or tripod-mounted pictures are taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the tilt of the camera is essential for correctly orienting the reconstructed 3D scene relative to the ground.
concepts.recap_md: - $\theta$ is the angle between the camera's optical axis and the ground.

key_passage.text: θ: Represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane.

motivation.text: It would be possible to estimate this angle accurately by determining the direction of the surface normal in pixels corresponding to the ground and measuring the angle with respect to the vertical axis.

concepts.one_liner: Motion estimation consists of finding, for each pixel in one frame, the location of the corresponding pixel in the next frame.

concepts.recap_md: - Motion estimation involves finding corresponding pixel locations between two frames.

concepts.title: Human Motion Perception and the Fluted Square-Wave Illusion

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: The fluted square-wave illusion distinguishes between pattern matching and spatiotemporal filtering, supporting the theory that the human visual system uses spatiotemporal energy models.
concepts.content: While researchers aren't sure of the precise computations involved in human motion processing, experiments can distinguish between classes of algorithms the visual system may use. Pattern matching methods are often based on image correlations, while spatiotemporal filtering uses the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate motion. Adelson and Bergen proposed the fluted square-wave illusion to distinguish between these classes. The illusion involves temporal filtering, motion processing, and aliasing. A stationary sinusoid $f(x,y,t) = \cos(\pi \omega x)$ has a spatiotemporal Fourier transform $(\delta(w_x + \omega) + \delta(w_x - \omega)) \delta(w_y) \delta(w_t)$, with energy along the $w_t = 0$ line. A moving sinusoid shears this energy according to speed. A square wave moving in 1/4 period jumps creates a spectrum replicated over temporal frequencies. (see figure: Derivation of the fluted square-wave motion illusion, continued from @fig-motionIllusion1 . Top row shows that the square wave moves in 1/4 wavelength jumps, instead of continuously. This staggered...) Because orientation in space-time tells motion direction, the space-time plot of @fig-motionIllusion2 [b] shows motion to the left. However, if the lowest spatial frequency sinusoid is removed, the lowest spatiotemporal frequency component is oriented in the other direction. While pattern matching would still suggest leftward motion, the human visual system perceives rightward motion, supporting spatiotemporal energy models.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between matching and filtering models helps researchers understand the underlying computations of human motion perception and design more effective computer vision systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Pattern matching and spatiotemporal filtering are two primary theories for human motion perception.

key_passage.text: Adelson and Bergen proposed a beautiful motion illusion that distinguishes between two classes of motion algorithms that might be used by the visual system. The illusion involves temporal filtering, motion processing, and aliasing and thus provides a good review of the material in this chapter and also chapters on sampling and temporal filters.

concepts.title: Introduction to 3D Motion Projection
concepts.one_liner: Understanding how 3D motion projects into the 2D camera plane is necessary to distinguish between moving cameras and moving objects.
concepts.content: As objects or the camera move, the projection of the dynamic scene into the two-dimensional (2D) camera plane produces a sequence of temporally varying pixel brightness. Studying how three-dimensional (3D) motion projects into the camera allows us to understand the difference between a moving camera and a moving object, and what types of constraints can be used to estimate motion.
concepts.motivation_md: Establishing how physical movement translates to image changes is a prerequisite for developing algorithms that can accurately estimate motion from video data.
concepts.recap_md: - 2D motion in images is a projection of 3D motion in the world.

key_passage.text: Studying how three-dimensional (3D) motion projects into the camera will allow us to understand what the difference is between a moving camera or a moving object and what types of constraints one might be able to use to estimate motion.

motivation.text: Before diving into how to estimate motion from pixels, it is useful to understand the image formation process.

concepts.title: 3D Motion Projection
concepts.one_liner: 3D motion projection defines the relationship between the instantaneous 3D velocity of a point and its corresponding 2D velocity in the image plane.
concepts.content: A 3D point follows a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$ with an instantaneous 3D velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. Its projection into the image plane location is $\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and moves with the 2D instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$. (see figure: A 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, moving in the world projects a 2D moving point, $\mathbf{p}$, into the camera plane.) Using perspective projection equations $x=f X/Z$ and $y=f Y/Z$, the relationship between instantaneous velocity in the camera plane and 3D world coordinates is: $$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\ \dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} \end{aligned}$$ This can be written in matrix form as: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} f & 0 & -x \\ 0 & f & -y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{X} \\ \dot{Y} \\ \dot{Z} \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$${#eq-motionprojection}
concepts.motivation_md: This mathematical model is fundamental for computer vision tasks that require recovering 3D information or predicting image changes from known physical motion.
concepts.recap_md: - The 2D velocity of a projected point depends on its 3D velocity and its depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: Using the equations of perspective projection x=f X/Z and y=f Y/Z (assuming that the camera is at the origin of the world-coordinate system), we can derive the equations of how the instantaneous velocity in the camera plane relates to the point motion in 3D world coordinates: $$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\ \dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} \end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: As the point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The projection of this point into the image plane location is $\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$.

concepts.title: Properties of Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow properties describe how 3D motion, such as lateral or longitudinal movement, projects into specific velocity patterns on the image plane.
concepts.content: The motion projection equations reveal interesting properties of optical flow. Points moving parallel to the camera plane ($\dot{Z} = 0$) project to a motion parallel to the 3D motion with a magnitude inversely proportional to the distance $Z$: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{X} \\ \dot{Y} \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$${#eq-parallelmotion} For points moving parallel to the $Z$ axis ($\dot{X} = \dot{Y} = 0$), the projection is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{\dot{Z}}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$${#eq-forward_objects} Points at the same distance $Z$ moving toward or away from the camera with the same velocity will project into points moving at different velocities on the image plane depending on their $(x, y)$ location. (see figure: (left) Geometry of the projection of 3D motion into the camera for points moving parallel to the camera plane, and (right) parallel to the optical axis of the camera.)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these properties allows us to infer depth information and movement direction from the patterns of motion observed in a 2D image sequence.
concepts.recap_md: - For lateral motion, image velocity is inversely proportional to depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: This expression reveals a number of interesting properties of the optical flow and how it relates to motion in the world. For instance, points that move parallel to the camera plane ($\dot{Z} = 0$) will project to a motion parallel to the motion in 3D but with a magnitude that will be inversely proportional to the distance $Z$

motivation.text: This expression reveals a number of interesting properties of the optical flow and how it relates to motion in the world.

concepts.title: Vanishing Point in Motion
concepts.one_liner: A vanishing point in motion is the image location where a point moving in a straight 3D line with constant velocity converges as time approaches infinity.
concepts.content: For a point moving in a straight line in 3D with constant velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (V_X, V_Y, V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$, its location at time $t$ is $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X+V_Xt, Y+V_Yt, Z+V_Zt)^\mathsf{T}$. If $\dot{Z} \neq 0$, then as time goes to infinity, the projected point converges to a vanishing point: $$\begin{aligned} \lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) &= f \frac{V_X}{V_Z} = x_{\infty}\\ \lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) &= f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z} = y_{\infty} \end{aligned}$${#eq-motionvanishingpoint} (see figure: Projection onto the camera plane of the sequence produced by a bird flying away. The bird will vanish at the **vanishing point**) The location of the vanishing point $\mathbf{p}_{\infty}=(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})^\mathsf{T}$ is independent of the initial point location and depends only on the 3D velocity vector $\mathbf{V}$. Multiple points moving with the same velocity will converge to the same vanishing point.
concepts.motivation_md: Vanishing points provide a stable reference for determining an observer's heading or identifying groups of objects moving in the same direction in a 3D scene.
concepts.recap_md: - The vanishing point is the limit of a projected trajectory as time goes to infinity.

key_passage.text: The vanishing point is the location $\mathbf{p}_{\infty}=(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})^\mathsf{T}$ where the moving point slowly converges to. The location of the vanishing point is independent of the point location at time $t=0$, and it only depends on the 3D velocity vector, $\mathbf{V}$.

motivation.text: In the camera the bird gets smaller as it flies away until it disappears at the vanishing point. Therefore, if the scene contains multiple points at different locations moving with the same velocity, they will converge to the same vanishing point.

concepts.title: Brightness Constancy Assumption
concepts.one_liner: The brightness constancy assumption states that the brightness of a scene element captured by a camera does not change over time as it moves.
concepts.content: The **brightness constancy assumption** says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time. Mathematically, this assumption translates into the following relationship, given a sequence $\ell(x,y,t)$: $$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  = \ell(x,y,t)$$ where $u$ and $v$ are the element displacement over one unit of time and are also a function of pixel location, $u(x,y)$ and $v(x,y)$. The previous relationship is equivalent to saying that $\ell(x, y, t + 1) = \ell(x-u,y-v,t)$. (see figure: Translation to the right of a simple $6 \times 6$ size image.)
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption provides a fundamental physical constraint that links pixel intensity changes to underlying motion, forming the basis for most optical flow estimation algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes the brightness of a scene element remains constant as it moves between frames. - Expressed mathematically as $\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1) = \ell(x,y,t)$.

key_passage.text: The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time.

concepts.title: Gradient-Based Optical Flow Estimation (Lucas-Kanade)
concepts.one_liner: The Lucas-Kanade method estimates optical flow by solving a system of linear equations derived from the gradient constraint and local spatial consistency.
concepts.content: The Lucas-Kanade method approximates the change between consecutive frames using a first-order Taylor expansion. Combined with the brightness constancy assumption, this yields the **gradient constraint equation**: $u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$. This equation alone is insufficient to determine motion (the aperture problem), so the method assumes motion is constant over a local image patch. By minimizing a weighted sum of squared constraints over a neighborhood using a Gaussian window $g(x,y)$, we solve for $(u,v)$: $$\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum g \left| u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t \right| ^2$$ Setting derivatives with respect to $u$ and $v$ to zero leads to a $2 \times 2$ system at each location: $$\begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x ^ 2  & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\ \sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\ \sum g \ell_y \ell_t \end{bmatrix}$$ The matrix $\mathbf{A}$ must be invertible for a unique solution, which fails in regions with 1D structure. (see figure: Gradient-based optical flow estimation using two input frames.) (see figure: Toy sequence with two moving squares. The red arrows indicate the direction of motion of each square.) (see figure: Spatial and temporal derivatives for the sequence from @fig-square_grandient_based_1) (see figure: Computation of all the products between derivatives from @fig-square_grandient_based_2) (see figure: Estimated optical flow for the sequence in @fig-square_grandient_based_2) To identify reliable regions, one can use the Harris corner measure $R = \det (\mathbf{A}) - \lambda \mathrm{Tr}\hspace{1pt} (\mathbf{A})^2$. (see figure: Estimated optical flow in the regions with $R > 2$ (around *good features to track* @shi1994goodfeatures)
concepts.motivation_md: It offers a computationally efficient way to estimate dense motion by leveraging local image gradients, though it requires additional constraints to solve the aperture problem.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a first-order Taylor expansion to relate image gradients to pixel motion $(u, v)$. - Solves a system of linear equations over a local neighborhood to overcome the aperture problem. - Works best for small displacements where the linear approximation holds.

key_passage.text: We can write the previous two equations in matrix form at each location (x',y') as: $$\begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x ^ 2 & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\ \sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\ \sum g \ell_y \ell_t \end{bmatrix}$$ We will have an equivalent set of equations for each image location. The solution at each location can be computed analytically as $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \textbf{b}$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is the $2 \times 2$ matrix.

motivation.text: This is not enough to estimate motion and we will need to add additional constraints. The second assumption that we will add is that the motion field is constant (or smoothly varying) over an extended image region.

concepts.title: Gradient Constraint Equation
concepts.one_liner: The gradient constraint equation relates image motion to spatial and temporal derivatives, defining a line of possible motion vectors perpendicular to the image gradient.
concepts.content: The **gradient constraint equation** is defined as: $$u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$$ This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ in location $(x,y)$ to be along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell= \left( \ell_x, \ell_y \right)$ at that location. This is the same relationship that appears when describing the aperture problem, where local motion cannot be uniquely determined from a single point.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a fundamental mathematical link between observable intensity changes and the underlying velocity field, though it only constrains motion in one dimension locally.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates spatial and temporal image derivatives to the velocity components $u$ and $v$. - Constrains motion to a line perpendicular to the local image gradient, leading to the aperture problem.

key_passage.text: This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ in location $(x,y)$ to be along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell= \left( \ell_x, \ell_y \right)$ at that location.

motivation.text: This is not enough to estimate motion and we will need

concepts.title: Iterative Refinement for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Iterative refinement improves optical flow accuracy by minimizing photometric reconstruction error through successive warping and multiscale Gaussian pyramids.
concepts.content: Iterative refinement improves motion estimation by directly minimizing the **photometric reconstruction** error: $$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$ Unlike the single-step gradient method, this approach uses gradient descent to iteratively update the flow $(u, v)$. At each iteration $n$, the current estimate is used to compute a warped frame $\ell_1 (x+u_n,y+v_n,t+1)$, and an update $(\Delta u_n, \Delta v_n)$ is computed. To handle large displacements, this is performed across a Gaussian pyramid, starting from the lowest resolution and upsampling the result to initialize the next level. (see figure: Multiscale iterative refinement for optical flow. Optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid.) (see figure: Comparison between the optical flow estimated using the gradient-based algorithm and the multiscale iterative refinement approach.) Regularization terms can be added to the objective, such as the Horn-Schunck formulation: $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + \lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard gradient methods fail when motion is large; iterative refinement and pyramids allow for accurate estimation of significant displacements by linearizing the problem at multiple scales.
concepts.recap_md: - Minimizes photometric reconstruction error directly using gradient descent and iterative warping. - Employs a Gaussian pyramid to estimate large motions at coarse scales before refining at finer scales. - Can incorporate regularization terms like the Horn-Schunck objective to enforce smoothness.

key_passage.text: At each iteration n, the estimated optical flow will be used to compute the warped frame ℓ1(x+un,y+vn,t+1) and we will compute an update, Δun and Δvn, of the optical flow: un+1 = un+Δun and vn+1= vn + Δvn. To improve the results, the optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid.

motivation.text: The gradient-based approach is efficient but it only provides an approximation to the motion field because it ignores higher order terms in the Taylor expansion. However, adding iterations will provide a more accurate estimate of optical flow.

concepts.title: Photometric Reconstruction Error
concepts.one_liner: Photometric reconstruction error measures the squared difference between a reference frame and a warped subsequent frame to evaluate motion estimation.
concepts.content: The **photometric reconstruction** error is a loss function that measures the difference between a reference frame and a warped version of the subsequent frame: $$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: It serves as a direct measure of how well a motion field aligns two images, acting as the primary objective for optimization and unsupervised learning in optical flow.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the squared difference between a reference frame and a warped subsequent frame. - Acts as a data-fidelity term in optical flow optimization and unsupervised learning.

key_passage.text: approach consists of directly minimizing the photometric reconstruction error: L(ℓ₁,ℓ₂,u,v)= Σₓ,ᵧ |ℓ₁(x+u,y+v,t+1) - ℓ₂(x,y,t))|²

concepts.title: Horn-Schunck Objective
concepts.one_liner: The Horn-Schunck objective combines photometric reconstruction error with a regularization term to estimate a smooth and consistent optical flow field.
concepts.content: The Horn-Schunck objective incorporates a regularization term penalizing fast variations on the estimated optical flow: $$ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + \lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) $$ This problem formulation was introduced by Horn and Schunck in 1981.
concepts.motivation_md: It addresses the ill-posed nature of the optical flow problem by introducing global constraints, ensuring the resulting motion field is physically plausible and smooth.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines photometric reconstruction error with a regularization term $R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$. - Uses a parameter $\lambda$ to balance matching accuracy with the smoothness of the flow field.

key_passage.text: The photometric reconstruction can incorporate a regularization term penalizing fast variations on the estimated optical flow: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + \lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$$

motivation.text: The photometric reconstruction can incorporate a regularization term penalizing fast variations on the estimated optical flow

concepts.title: Slow Prior
concepts.one_liner: The slow prior is a regularization term that penalizes large velocity magnitudes to favor smaller motion estimates.
concepts.content: The **slow prior** is a regularization term that penalizes large velocities in the estimated optical flow field: $$ R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( u(x,y) \right)^2 + \left( v(x,y)  \right)^2 $$
concepts.motivation_md: It helps resolve ambiguities in motion estimation by assuming that, in the absence of strong evidence, scene elements are likely to be stationary or moving slowly.
concepts.recap_md: - Penalizes the magnitude of velocity vectors to favor smaller motion estimates. - Helps resolve ambiguities by assuming scene elements are likely to move slowly.

key_passage.text: R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( u(x,y) \right)^2 + \left( v(x,y) \right)^2

concepts.title: Smooth Prior
concepts.one_liner: The smooth prior is a regularization term that penalizes spatial variations in the optical flow field to encourage neighboring pixels to move similarly.
concepts.content: The **smooth prior** is a regularization term that penalizes spatial variations in the optical flow field, encouraging neighboring pixels to have similar motion: $$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}  \right)^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: It enforces the physical intuition that objects are generally coherent, meaning adjacent pixels on the same object should have nearly identical motion vectors.
concepts.recap_md: - Penalizes spatial derivatives of the optical flow to encourage neighboring pixels to move similarly. - Models the physical coherence of objects to produce a less noisy motion field.
